item.title: Sami Abusamra’s Soviet-Era Short ‘Tank’ Fires a Dry Comic Warning Shot About Weak Men Masquerading as Strong Ones
item.dc:creator: Mark Brennan
item.description: Shot in rural Bulgaria on black and white SD with a real tank, Sami Abusamra’s satirical adaptation asks what happens when power lands in the wrong lap.
item.content:encoded:
It’s no easy thing feeling like a passenger in your own life. When one day blurs into the next, people see through you, and it feels like nothing will ever change – that this is simply your lot in life. Now imagine being able to change all that in an instant. Sami Abusamra’s comedy, Tank takes this notion to an absurd level, as one put-upon sad sack is gifted a piece of military hardware that will change his life explosively. It’s also an exploration of how power is perceived and treated by those who don’t have it, whatever form that power may take, and how it changes the people within its orbit. As part of Tank’s premiere on Directors Notes, Abusamra talks to us about his experience filming with a working tank, collaborating with the author of the original short story to adapt it into short film form, shooting in Bulgaria to recreate a Soviet-era setting for this period comedy, and using outdated camera equipment to creative and practical effect.

Tank is actually based on a short story. Can you tell us about that and how it came to your attention?

The story itself was literally a gift. I’m British-Sudanese and a few Christmases ago I was given a book of Sudanese short stories called The Book of Khartoum. The first story in that anthology is called The Tank by Ahmad al-Malik. It’s only a few pages long but it really resonated with me and its potential for adaptation to screen was very apparent. First and foremost, as a comedy director, I found The Tank really funny. It’s very visual and I loved its absurdity. But the most powerful thing about reading it was how portentous Ahmad’s writing had proven to be. The Tank was written almost 30 years ago as Omar al-Bashir’s authoritarian regime was taking hold of Sudan. Anyone reading this already knows that the al-Bashir regime did not end well for the people there. Coups and civil war have followed.

Weak men masquerading as strong men, misplaced power and misused power – these things are now everyone’s problem.

Almost all of my aunts, uncles, cousins and their families are now displaced from their homes and scattered across the region. By writing against authoritarianism three decades ago, I felt Ahmad had written the perfect warning for today. You only need to glance at the UK, at Europe and the wider Western World to see similar stories repeating. Weak men masquerading as strong men, misplaced power and misused power – these things are now everyone’s problem. So the story’s relevance seemed very apparent. I was very motivated by how personal it was to me. I knew it contained lots of opportunities for potent, absurd imagery and, on a creative level, I had a strong, clear sense of how to adapt Ahmad’s story into a script.

Ahmad is now based in Amsterdam so I met him there in 2023. We discussed adapting his short story and he was generous enough to allow me a free run at making changes for reasons of structure and cost, etc. From there it was a question of working out how to put the pieces of the production together. The challenge of doing so was part of the appeal, to be honest. I knew it wouldn’t be easy but I knew I wanted to try.

Our tank couldn’t travel on concrete streets because the metal tracks would chew up the tarmac and when it’s loaded on to its massive transport lorry the vehicle is so long, wide and heavy that it can’t get down certain roads or over certain bridges.

The film was shot in Bulgaria with a real, working tank. How did all of that come about?

I’ve shot commercials in Bulgaria before so was friends with a few production people there. I knew that relocating the story would be more cost-effective but I also had a sense that the post-Soviet setting would give the film teeth in a way that shooting in, say, an English village, just never would. I met with a few potential producing partners and ultimately linked up with Bazuka Productions because they asked all the right questions. The way “The Eddies” (producers Eddy Schwartz and Edward Michongwe) engaged with the project in our first conversations convinced me that they genuinely wanted to do it and that they also believed we could pull it off.

Sourcing the tank itself was obviously the biggest piece of the production puzzle so we started with that. After running down many dead ends, we found some great people at Bulgarian Civil Defence (kind of like an arm of the Fire Department) in a town called Veliko Turnovo who were open to helping us out. Peter Yamakov, the guy with a moustache who plays the Tank Dealer in our film, is actually just one of the blokes who works at the Civil Defence base. We simply had to put his big moustache on camera.

Shooting with a tank, you won’t be surprised to hear, is complicated. It’s expensive and dangerous to move a tank around. Our tank couldn’t travel on concrete streets because the metal tracks would chew up the tarmac and when it’s loaded onto its massive transport lorry, the vehicle is so long, wide and heavy that it can’t get down certain roads or over certain bridges. So we had to recce locations with tank access very firmly in mind. Once we’d agreed on what worked for the story, budget, schedule, etc., then the Civil Defence guys had to approve our locations for tank-access purposes.

Ultimately, we shot the film in two days. On day one we shot in and around the Tank’s actual base in Gorna Oryahovitsa. On day two the Tank came out to a nearby village called Hotnitsa. The fact that the Tank was a rescue service vehicle did present some issues. In reality it’s bright orange and it doesn’t have a gun. So we made a big plastic gun and turret to place on top of the tank and we decided to make the film black and white so that the tank would appear more like a piece of authentic military kit.

What was your experience in shooting in another country?

I really like Bulgaria. Between Tank and some commercial jobs, I’ve probably been there 15 or more times over the years. As someone more familiar with trying to get stuff made in the UK, I find Bulgaria’s tight-knit filmmaking community, general atmosphere of creative ambition, and its ‘can do’ energy genuinely refreshing. I did make some accommodations in the writing to ensure things were as manageable as possible for myself on location. The script itself was deliberately very light on dialogue, which helped with directing because I don’t speak Bulgarian.

There’s actually only one scene, the ladder scene, which is driven by Bulgarian dialogue so I just made sure I had good translators around me through the shooting and cutting of that one. Which wasn’t hard because the crews there speak English to a standard that truly exposes how appalling my “Hi, thanks, bye” Bulgarian is.

Most Popular

We obviously have to ask, did you get to drive the tank?

I did not. Devastatingly, one of the main rules of hiring a tank is that it’s not a toy. Not even our actor Yuriy Rahnev drove the tank actually. He’s basically straddling the real driver, who is sitting down in the cockpit bit. I presume it’s called the cockpit bit.

Yuriy Rahnev is wonderful as the put-upon man reborn after the tank changes his life. How did you cast his role and what was the collaboration like?

Yuriy’s performance is so good. He genuinely feels like he transforms across 16 minutes of screen time. The most amazing thing is that he doesn’t even consider himself an actor. In Bulgaria he’s better known as a writer. Collaborating with Yuri was a pleasure. As a writer he had lots of smart questions and brought a few notes on the script too. For example, there was no sex scene until Yuriy made the suggestion that it might help add some colour to his character’s journey.

The way he got involved was the same way everyone else did: our casting director Ana-Maria Lakova got him in. I’ve worked with Ana multiple times over the years and she was the first person I called when thinking about trying to make this film in Bulgaria. We share very similar taste when it comes to film generally and to acting performances especially. For us the humour has to be dry. Very, very, ‘very’ dry. Ana was a huge part of this project because she introduced me to The Eddies at Bazuka in the first place and was closely involved throughout the production process. It’s no exaggeration to say that Tank wouldn’t have happened without her. She made sure I met with Yuriy on one of my early location scouting trips because she knew that he would want to know me before agreeing to audition. Thankfully, he was up for it. So, on a later trip to Bulgaria, Yuriy came in and read some sides along with other actors as normal.

Ana arranged auditions with three actors per role. I honestly wasn’t expecting the number to be that low but it indicates how confident she was in her vision for the ensemble. And I think she absolutely nailed it. The whole cast is brilliant, best I’ve ever worked with. The only change I made was to swap Evgeny Budinov (who plays the police officer – hilariously) with Bogdan Kazandzhiev (who plays the neighbour returning a ladder – hilariously) because initially Ana had them the other way around. Ultimately, all five actors were our first choices, which almost never happens, so we were very lucky.

Violina Dotseva played the Butcher and brought an amazing amount of texture and depth to her scenes. Her career is really taking off in Bulgaria at the moment. The only other actor we cast was Gergana Galabova, who played Yuriy’s wife, and again, she brought great detail and commitment to her work on the film.

Everyone else you see onscreen is either a crew member or someone from the nearby towns – it was that sort of job. Eddy Schwartz, one of the producers, is the guy ordering sausages in the first scene. Edward Michongwe, also a producer, got his Mum to play the bar lady. Casting director Ana is even an extra herself in the first scene.

There’s a mysteriously British voice at the end of the phone who first offers up the tank, and then expects some help in return by the end. Who is the voice at the end of the phone to you and what is it they want?

If anyone has 500,000 spare Euros we can shoot the feature version of Tank. Based on my current plan for that story, you would definitely see more of the Caller character and that would answer your question. So check down the back of the sofa for loose change and then let’s chat again.

Tank has an unmistakable early 2000s look to it with the cinematography and camera used. What was the creative choice behind this aesthetic for the film and the equipment used?

The director of photography, Daniel Purse, looked absolutely nuts shooting this to be honest. Despite having a regular-sized shoulder mount, the camera itself is a palm-sized handicam from the mid-noughts called a Canon FS2000. The choice was both creative and practical. We didn’t have much money so we didn’t have much time and I knew we’d move faster with a camera team of one person than a camera team of lots of people. By choosing to lean into that limitation, it was important to find a camera format that fed the story as well as speeding up the shoot.

The way Ahmad’s writing from the 1990s spoke with such clarity to the 2020s made me want to build that sense of ‘history repeating’ into our aesthetic choice. The imperfections and limited resolution of the old, SD, digital format felt right because we wanted the film to feel like we’d observed genuine events on available equipment some decades ago. We wanted to suggest that all this actually happened and therefore imply it can all happen again.

The imperfections and limited resolution of the old, SD, digital format felt right because we wanted the film to feel like we’d observed genuine events on available equipment some decades ago.

We also knew we’d be shooting in a reasonably remote part of Bulgaria. Veliko Turnovo is a decent sized town but we were out in the villages which orbit it. That meant we were almost four hours from the capital, Sofia, which was where we’d need to source any technical support if it was required. So we didn’t want to shoot on tape and tie ourselves in knots with the process of digitising analogue rushes, etc. Our team just wasn’t big enough for that to be a sensible choice. Which meant we could only really go as far back in the camera catalogue as the beginning of SD cards.

I think Dan bagged a couple of Canon FS2000s off eBay and tested them at home in the UK. We both felt it really hit the mark. It was quick and easy to shoot with, small and light to travel with, it evoked a previous era but was also fairly straightforward in terms of post-production workflow. Again, there were limitations to accommodate. We couldn’t control the focus at all and the speed of the zoom was a bit hit-and-miss. But we leaned into all that with the way we chose to stage and shoot the film.

The production design really sells the period of the film, particularly in the butchers. With that period setting in mind, how did you go about showing that on screen?

Yes, it was always going to be a period setting. That was one of the reasons to travel so far from Sofia when scouting. The towns and villages closer to the capital basically looked too new. The further we went, the older it felt and ultimately a lot of the locations we shot in haven’t changed much over the last few decades. A benefit of shooting close to Veliko Turnovo is that it’s where producer Edward Michongwe grew up. In the end his Mum, Iskra Petrova (who played the bar lady), was a really useful fixer for us because not only is she an ex-commercials producer herself but she knows absolutely ‘everyone’ for miles around. She helped us open doors we never could have managed without her.

The staff knew nothing about what we’d agreed with their landlord who, and I swear this is 100% true, turned out to be an actual, bonafide Nazi.

Ivelina Mineva, the production designer, did an incredible job on the whole film – which isn’t surprising because she’s one of the best there is in Bulgaria. But I agree, the butcher shop looks especially good. And that’s doubly amazing because our preferred location for those scenes actually fell through two days before the shoot. We’d agreed to use a long-disused shop but when we turned up with our crew to do a final tech recce, the place had been rented out and was a fully stocked and operational newsagent instead. The staff knew nothing about what we’d agreed with their landlord who, and I swear this is 100% true, turned out to be an actual, bona fide Nazi. Seems you can still find them. So, I’m very glad we didn’t use his place in the end. ANYWAY, what you see in the film is a very quickly cobbled together Plan B in a contingency location that we’d initially scouted only because it shares an entrance hall with the bar location.

So, I’m really glad you’ve singled out Ivelina’s work in that space because it was so impressive what she managed to do in there. All of the extras who came in for those butcher shop scenes were blown away by Ivelina’s work and I think over the afternoon’s shooting every single one of them commented (according to what the A.D. told me) something along the lines of “this is exactly how it used to be in Soviet times.” So yeah, Ivelina absolutely smashed it. And she was also doing wardrobe, which is another element that I think turned out brilliantly.

There is a wonderful metallic quality to the music which chimes perfectly with the mechanical centrepiece of the film. Can you tell us how the score came together?

I love the music too. While we were on location I started chatting with Petar Parmakov who was recording location sound. The producers had already mentioned that he made music but, to be honest, I was sceptical about bringing it up with him because I knew the requirements on this film were very particular. Firstly, I wanted the score to sound like it was literally played on the metal surfaces of a tank. Secondly, we also needed to make the disco tunes in Yuriy’s car from scratch. We didn’t have money for two composers so I was bravely hoping to find one person who could do both. In the end, I did loosely describe what I thought was needed to Petar and it transpired that he and his partner Yoanna Robova release experimental music under the moniker Trohi – I’d loosely describe their work as sitting somewhere between electronic and noise art. Also, it turned out, they sometimes make retro-sounding pastiche disco tunes for fun. The fact that their skills and interests mapped so perfectly onto what the film needed was simply too improbable to say no to. Full credit to the producers for their creative matchmaking.

The scoring process itself was a long one, which I think involved Petar and Yoanna dismantling and playing various parts of their own oven over many weeks and months. They’d send tunes, phrases and stems to me, which I’d chop and change and muck around with in the edit. Everything they delivered sounded so interesting and their capacity for creativity and iteration was genuinely overwhelming. So, at least from my side, it was much more a whittling process than a ‘note-making’ process per se. It was about paring down their ideas and suggestions into something that felt like a cogent and considered element in the storytelling. Eventually, I think it took us 6-8 months, we got to what you hear in the film.

What’s next for you?

For me, making Tank was a response to being a director in commercials where I typically use 5% of my brain 5% of the time. I wanted to do something difficult, do something unique, do something that I’d actually watch. On balance I think I succeeded to be fair. But in doing something so singular and operating entirely on my own terms, I’ve created a bit of a monster of myself. Everything I’ve been sent since Tank has seemed massively underwhelming by comparison. So, even though our industry has slowed down enormously over the last year, I’ve found myself turning work down too. I haven’t read a good commercial script for almost a year (big up yourself ITVX) and, in addition, budgets in my portion of the commercials sector are trending towards laughably small. It makes me think of that old “the food in this place is terrible and such small portions” joke.

The decision to try and make the short version of Tank in the first place was honestly driven by the sense that this might be the last thing I ever make.

In that context, I do wonder where the next step might take me. A Tank feature would be a dream but I won’t be cashing that cheque any decade soon, I don’t think. The decision to try and make the short version of Tank in the first place was honestly driven by the sense that this might be the last thing I ever make. I couldn’t bring myself to leave directing behind without doing one thing that feels 100% like my voice. So to that end, I’m happy.

Looking ahead is difficult though. A.I. is chewing up the commercials industry, especially the mid-range projects which I used to pick up regularly. Moreover, A.I. prompting is something I have no interest in learning. Can you imagine what this interview would contain if the film was made by button pushing? Zero stories. In addition, UK scripted TV comedy is in the bin creatively speaking. So, I can’t really see where the exciting projects are. Which is a shame, because through the 90s and 00s the UK was the world’s superpower at making comedy. If any other world-leading British industry had been blandified and diminished as much as UK scripted comedy has over recent decades, it would be a national scandal. Heads would roll. But instead things just seem to slip deeper and deeper into the bin. I’ll get off my soapbox now. Available for hire.

And finally, what short film by another filmmaker would you recommend to the Directors Notes community and why?

I’ve run a comedy short film night via my company Mister Tibbs for ten years now so I could give you a list as long as your arm. But I reckon if you watch one short film and one short film only, make it The Procedure by Calvin Lee Reeder. And put that bagel down before you do.

item.title: We’re All Clowns Dancing Through Capitalism in Zen Pace’s Gig Economy Horror Comedy ‘Are You Fucking Kidding Me?!’
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: A clown’s latest kids' party gig takes a sinister turn in Zen Pace’s queer horror comedy, where camp and social critique collide.
item.content:encoded:
What happens when a clown becomes terrifying? We’ve seen this trope explored in cinema before, but rarely with the same sharp social commentary on display in Are You Fucking Kidding Me?!, particularly when it comes to the crisis facing the entertainment industry, especially live entertainment. On a broader scale, this horror comedy narrative also reflects a more general crisis within the entertainment world, which includes short films as a medium, too. DN alum Zen Pace—who was last on our pages with poetic experimental short Little Mirror—cleverly uses comedy in the opening scenes to introduce us to Jordyn, a young man who works as a children’s party clown and tries his best to enjoy his demeaning job while struggling to make ends meet. Unfortunately, as professional boundaries dissolve under intense pressure, things don’t go as planned and the situation takes a volatile turn. For today’s premiere of Are You Fucking Kidding Me, Pace returns to DN to take us inside the project and shares how his understanding of camp evolved throughout the production of the short, the wonderful films that served as inspiration, and the importance of ensuring that the film maintained a distinctly queer perspective.

The script arrived to you from writer/actor Zachary Solomon with a wig mannequin, razor-sharp teeth, and a switchblade in its head. The film clearly announced itself as completely unhinged. What was the first thing you saw underneath all that which made you think, “There’s actually a movie here I want to make”?

Zach poured a lot of trust in me, which I’m really grateful for. I suggested things like a script doctor and script ideas to help ground the piece. So I think it was a combination of trust, but also I related to Zach. When we got on a call I saw a part of myself in him, someone who came from nothing, who’s dealt with their own fair share of shit in life, and who’s had to define themselves in a society that is so eager to define you. There was this unnerved nature to him that felt very honest when you got to it. It was very camp, but it came from a genuinely truthful place, and that’s what pulled me in.

Camp is something you don’t naturally gravitate toward. Did making this project change your perspective on it? Was there anything about the form that you unexpectedly found yourself enjoying?

It expanded my idea of camp. And now, I see camp in so many things. Primetime for example is riddled with it, both in tone and performance. But this film was always going to be camp because it’s in the DNA. To omit it wouldn’t be truthful to Zach or what the writing called for. I think if you are directing something someone else wrote, you need to meet them where the soul of the piece is. So the more I worked on it, the more I started to see how camp is in so much horror today, especially with so many films toying with the line between ‘serious psychological drama’ and comedy. Even in films like Hereditary, you can sense what Susan Sontag called failed seriousness, this elevated, high camp in some of the performances, to the point where it teeters on the ridiculous. Like Toni Collette sawing her head off with piano wire. (Please, someone make a techno remix of that image.)

What I unexpectedly enjoyed was the permission it gives you. Camp lets you be loud and strange and sincere all at once, and once I stopped fighting it, I felt free to fully realize what this film could be. There was this moment where Zach, in character, is watching a vision of his mother vomiting blood. It was ridiculous, but we paired it with this really earnest performance Zach tapped into. I think you really need dichotomy in film to create a synthesis you didn’t expect.

The more I worked on it, the more I started to see how camp is in so much horror today, especially with so many films toying with the line between ‘serious psychological drama’ and comedy.

You use the phrase “grounded camp”, which sounds almost contradictory. What does “grounded camp” mean to you? If you were to describe Are You Fucking Kidding Me to someone who doesn’t know anything about it, what other words would you use?

I love a good contradiction. It’s the Libra in me. I use that phrase now after having sat with the piece and asking myself what I wanted to achieve with it, in the performances, music, color. So much of this film is loud so the grounded nature of it was finding ways to bring everything down a bit, to make things a bit more approachable. There’s this really lovely moment after our hero in the bathroom realizes they’ve been screwed over, and we just sit on their face as it all washes over them. In something strictly camp that type of scene wouldn’t exist. It’s quiet. And because it’s quiet, it’s sad, and deeply relatable. If everything in your film is at a 10, it doesn’t allow a journey for the audience. Even in films I work on now, with actors of all calibers, there is a time and place for the full emotional outpouring of a scene. Often it’s not needed. Often it’s more interesting to struggle through feelings, because repression is more psychologically honest than simply feeling, or worse… playing a mood.

If I had to describe it to someone who knows nothing about it: it’s a horror comedy about the absurdity of the gig economy, of hustling just to survive. In a few words: unhinged, loud, sad, and deeply relatable. Or I’d say “saddest blow job ever.”

Most Popular

You cite The Following and American Psycho as tonal reference points. Both balance humour with menace and psychological unease. I think this shows in the early scenes when it’s already obvious there’s something weird going on. What did that tonal tension give you that a more straightforward comedy couldn’t? Was there ever a moment where you worried the comedy might let the audience off the hook, or the darker elements might overwhelm the humour?

No, I wasn’t worried about that. I spent a lot of time with Zach working on tone. I drafted out the emotional architecture of the film: what do I want the audience to feel here, here, and here. Of course your film can shift during each phase of production, but if your North Star is clear, it helps frame up the tone of the film for yourself, your DP, your PD, the actors. Having a playlist of music really helps me, and a deck where I break down every scene and talk through it.

Horror that laces in comedy allows for humor that irks you, that gets under your skin. It’s the uncanny, the familiar made strange. It’s some of my favorite uses of humor because it catches you off guard, like a jump scare but with levity instead. Having levity in the piece allows for a bigger roller coaster ride, almost a catharsis, when some of the more dramatic scenes happen. I love watching this film with an audience cause they are VERY active. People never know what to expect, but they love it. It’s been a joy to witness the spectacle of horror and comedy with an audience.

Horror that laces in comedy allows for humor that irks you, that gets under your skin. It’s the uncanny, the familiar made strange.

You’ve said the biggest thing you walked away with was that no detail is too small. Looking back, what do you think you nailed, what would you do differently, and did that experience change the way you think about prep and the things that need to be protected before you ever get to set?

What I’m most proud of is that the film feels cohesive. We enter a world and it feels uniquely like its own film. Of course I wish we did 100 things differently, but that’s anything I do. It was my first time working with VFX makeup at this level, and I wanted the Mom scenes and blood to feel more realistic. The campiest thing in the film is probably her makeup. It did change how I think about prep. No detail is too small. I’m grateful for our DP Peter Pasucci, a collaborator whose curiosity and dedication to the craft is inspiring. Our lens test at Old Fast Glass was essential. Testing vintage glass let us find the texture of the film before we shot a frame: how the lenses rendered skin, blood, and that muted palette. We work in a medium of mediums, and every department head is their own artist. When budgets are tight, things fall through the cracks. Like our stunt knife arrived the day of the shoot looking laughably fake. Fixing it in post cost us time and money we didn’t have to spare. Big learning lesson on prop testing.

On the day, there’s only so much experimentation you can allow for as a director, something ECHO taught me too. I’m very collaborative. I started in comedy in New York, working for Stephen Colbert and doing improv at Upright Citizens Brigade, where so much good comedy comes from 1000 shit ideas. It makes me less emotional about my ideas because I know there’s something better around the corner. But that can bite you in the ass. Spend too much time trying things out and you aren’t getting the film. A great filter for any idea: does this serve the central dramatic argument of the film? No? Cut it.

The film was made predominantly by queer artists. How did that collective queer perspective influence the story, characters, or humour, particularly in a film that also speaks to the much broader anxieties of economic survival?

I think that perspective is in the film’s bones. A lot of us know what it’s like to hustle, to perform a version of yourself just to get by, to put on the makeup even when you’re falling apart. That’s the heart of this film. We’re all clowns dancing through capitalism trying to keep the party going. The humor comes from that place too. It’s survival humor. Camp has always been a queer survival language. It shaped the set too. I remember one moment when an actor was really trying to nail a line and it just wasn’t landing. The inherent comedy in the line wasn’t there. And the team around me, all queer, knew it wasn’t the actor, it was the line (I believe one that I pitched earlier). CUT IT. On the opposite end of that, when we all laugh, I know it’s actually working. Having this community there not only helps ensure a sense of safety on set but is also a great barometer.

Camp has always been a queer survival language.

You used slow push-ins, zooms and Steadicam to gradually tighten the pressure, letting the dread sit just beneath the humour. How do you technically know when a scene needs to stay funny and when to let the discomfort take over? What was the approach like with your cinematographer Peter Pascucci?

A big part of it is already planned. But we were always balancing something sad with something funny. Like when we see the Porky Wiggles mask go on Jordyn. I knew from the start that technically the best way to feel his own sense of claustrophobia would be a subjective POV, being in there with him. So the moment from Being John Malkovich came to mind, when John Cusack is seeing out of Malkovich’s eyes, shot by Lance Acord. Technically, this was quite complex to get right, ESPECIALLY when we needed to have him look in the mirror. There was a very fine line for us before you see the camera and reveal our world. We fought hard in prep for the right equipment to rig the pig outfit. With that emphasis on humanity, Peter and I built a look with a distressed, lived in quality. Muted, almost harsh, mirroring the characters’ interiority rather than where the comedy might suggest. We leaned on slow push-ins, zooms, and Steadicam to build tension the way films like Parasite and Shiva Baby do, with dread sitting right underneath the humor. The comedy lives in the script and the performances, so the camera doesn’t have to chase the joke. The camera stays with the dread.

I think it’s all in the script, and when something in the script is funny but, when read aloud, it’s not, we adjust and find something new. I’ve worked with Peter more than any other DP. I trust him, and we have a working relationship where we are both very honest. He’s not a typical DP who is only focused on his department; he really wants to understand the world we are designing. And it starts with the script for him, which I really appreciate. Our approach for this film was ambitious. We planned for a lot of shots, and while we got most of them, we probably didn’t need all of them.

The edit taught you not to settle, even when a simpler choice might make the process easier. What was the process like technically and how do you know when you’re just being a perfectionist and when you’re fighting for something the film genuinely needs? When is a sacrifice worth making?

It’s very very very very hard. We took our time with this edit and I’m very thankful for Will Mayo getting us there. He is always down to clown and try things. We completely changed the beginning to set the tone of the movie immediately and hook our audience. Starting on his face was never intended, but it helped draw us in. That helped a lot, but it really wasn’t till the last 3 edits that it started to feel like the film. I got the first cut and was sweating. I think a big part of every process in filmmaking is listening to that little part of you that says “this can be better.” But on the opposite end of that, there’s also a part that just wants to be done with the project and move on to the next thing. I avoid that part because it’s lazy.

As a director you have to fight quite a bit, because everyone else is going to suggest ideas that might be simpler, easier, or make for a smoother process. And you have to decide when and if it’s worth it.

What I’ve learned is that sometimes you have a project and it feels like there’s no way to make it better, but then you take a week, or say fuck it and shift something massive, and then you realize, oh wait, if that works and we cut it, what else can work? I haven’t had a project where my gut needs to keep pushing to make something better has become a negative. And it’s all a sacrifice, because it’s your time. As a director you have to fight quite a bit, because everyone else is going to suggest ideas that might be simpler, easier, or make for a smoother process. And you have to decide when and if it’s worth it.

What upcoming projects do you have that we can look forward to?

I have ECHO, a new short I’m submitting to festivals, and I’m writing my feature Gutter Kidz, which I had at the Cine Qua Non Lab recently.

And finally, which is your favourite short of all time and why?

Andrea Arnold’s Milk. It’s such a beautifully raw and gritty film. For so long our society has made women feel that losing a pregnancy is somehow their fault. After a stillbirth, the protagonist skips the funeral and there is this feeling of her saying “fuck it” and choosing healing in her own way. I love that kind of autonomy and I found the end so heartbreakingly beautiful. Grief has become so sterilized in America and here we see a character mourn in a way that feels natural to her.

item.title: “No script. No money. No locations” – How Industry Frustrations Shaped Jared Hogan’s Latest Short ‘Dogbite’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Shot over 4 days with no script, director Jared Hogan joins us to discuss the instinctual process behind creating short film, 'Dogbite'.
item.content:encoded:
One of the things that has consistently motivated my involvement with Directors Notes is the DIY ethos that underpins almost everything we do. As a small team, we’re often required to wear many different hats and while the lack of funding or opportunities could easily have brought our work to a halt at various points over the past 20 years, we’ve continued through a shared passion for independent filmmaking and the people who make it possible. These are qualities I recognise in many of the filmmakers featured on our site, perhaps none more so than today’s returning director, Jared Hogan.

A writer-director whose work I’ve followed closely since discovering it in 2019, Hogan’s filmmaking offered an immediate reminder of what first drew me to short films. Bold, unapologetic and distinctive, his work has consistently embraced risk, but always with a clear creative purpose. When Hogan last joined us on Directors Notes, in 2019, it was with his unsettling short Pray for the Children. So, when his latest film, Dogbite, recently landed in our submissions queue, it was encouraging to see those defining qualities still present, now accompanied by a greater sense of maturity. With his feature Jackrabbit currently on the festival circuit, Hogan joins us to discuss where Dogbite sits within his evolving body of work and how the short’s stripped-back production proved formative in the development of his feature.

Hi Jared, welcome back to Directors Notes. I know you’re currently in the midst of releasing your debut feature, Jackrabbit, so I was a little surprised when you reached out with this new short for us to check out. How does Dogbite fit into the timeline of making Jackrabbit and are the two films connected in any way?

Hey Rob. First, it’s always a pleasure to catch up with you. You’ve been such a support for me and my films throughout the years. Trying to tell stories at any level is really hard, so having support of any kind goes such a long way. So, thank you to Directors Notes for always being a place that champions independent voices and filmmakers.

As for Dogbite, yeah. It was a film that was born out of an abundance of frustration. Leading up to it, I’d finished a script that I’d been grinding on for nearly three years. By the way, I’d wager to say a script that is taking you three years to write is perhaps beyond fixing, but that’s another conversation for another time. Whatever the case, I had also recently signed with a Film & TV manager and gone on the ‘water bottle tour’ as they call it. I’d met with a lot of great people. I had a handful I was really excited to send the script to when it was finished.

I came to that moment when I felt it was finally time to send it out. I clicked send and anxiously waited for my life to change. It did not. To be fair, I’m not sure the script was really ready to share. But I just wanted to go make my first feature-length film so badly. And I thought I’d finally gone about it the ‘right’ way. This was my third or fourth feature script I’d written. I’m living in LA. I have representation. I had all the meetings and still, no one was like – “Yes, Jared, Go make your movie now”. It felt horrible. Our lives as filmmakers are almost entirely rejection, so that wasn’t new. But I thought I was about to cross over, and I didn’t. And that hurt.

No script. No money. No locations. I just wanted to go make something. With no expectation of what it would be or how it would serve my career.

After feeling bad for myself for a few weeks, I decided I wanted to try and funnel the frustrated energy into making something, instead of just being mad. But I wanted to lay down some ground rules. I wanted to remove parts of the equation that always seemed to get in the way. No script. No money. No locations. I just wanted to go make something. With no expectation of what it would be or how it would serve my career or anything like that. Just creating with my friends as some sort of salve for the frustration I was feeling.

So I called up my friend Corey Waters and asked him if he wanted to go do whatever this was with me. He said yes and also brought out his amazing wife, Ines, to join the very small team. Then I called my friend and actor/filmmaker Frank Mosley (The Event). Frank had reached out a year or so before after seeing a short film I’d written and directed called How To Make A Ghost. We went for coffee and immediately knew we were cut from the same cloth. We circled some dates on the calendar and headed out together.

When we last spoke on DN, about your short Pray for the Children, we discussed your interest in exploring the idea of our “darkest thoughts transcending into the physical world” and those themes seem to be present here again. What is it about exploring the darker sides of the human mind that continues to draw you in as a filmmaker?

I’ve been in therapy most of this year and this is one of the questions I’ve actively been exploring. I grew up as a pastor’s kid in the South. Fear was so central to my experience growing up – fear of death, the apocalypse, hell – and I think the experience of growing into an adult and being able to engage with that fear and the darker sides of our existence through film has been incredibly healing for me.

Most Popular

Coming from a world where everything was presented to me as certain and binary, being able to explore the vastness in between has brought me so much relief. Seeing how the complexities of our lives expose the arrogant certainty at the center of the world I was raised in – it’s uninstalled so much fear that I’d been handed. And part of that is seeing how much more complex and fluid the transition from right and wrong, good and evil really is. It’s a long crossfade and trying to define or articulate where each begins and ends is never the goal, but a constant fascination for me to explore.

There’s a real looseness to the storytelling in Dogbite, with this feeling of unpredictability flowing through it that really keeps you gripped. With that in mind, I wanted to ask about the writing process. How much of the story was already in place when you started shooting and how much emerged through improvisation and collaboration on set?

Like I explained earlier, by design there was little to no forethought. Definitely not a script or anything really written at all. But there was one idea I did have going in that served as some sort of starting point. At the time, I’d been getting these spam calls. Incessantly. Every time, they’d leave these bizarre voicemails. No voices. Just clicks and hums. I got them every day for almost a month. For whatever reason, I couldn’t help but imagine there was some message hidden within it. Someone trying to tell me something through some kind of code or hypnosis tactic. One of those voicemails is actually the sounds in the teaser. So, that’s where we began: What if there was a character getting these cryptic phone calls telling him what to do? Beyond that, we were making it up entirely as we went.

Talking of the shoot and looking at the credits, it seems like Dogbite was a real bare-bones production – you’re directing and producing, Corey C. Waters is producing and shooting and Matt Yocum is handling sound. What was the appeal of working with such a small crew and how did that setup shape your approach to the visual language of the film?

An obsession of mine, regardless of the size of the team or resources, is how much can we say with the absolute least. I’m speaking more to visual economy here. But of course in a situation like this, we’re talking about money too, or lack thereof. This has been the beat I’ve marched to forever. It’s how I came up – mostly from limitation. I remember shooting with the Canon 5D early on and realizing – if you run around with this thing, it looks like shit. But if you let this camera sit on a tripod… it can do anything. So, that plus not really knowing how to write early on and working with primarily non-actors or bad actors growing up, I found I liked communicating a lot more with the camera than with badly written and/or performed dialogue.

It was as stripped down as physically possible, and I think their talent is so evident.

It was one of those things you fall into and serves as this formative limitation. But then you read something like Bresson’s Notes on the Cinematographer and his actors-as-models approach and all of a sudden you have vocabulary from a master that you can use to validate your shortcomings as a director. That’s the visual language I feel most drawn to and excited by.

But here I’m surrounded by some of the most talented people in the world, so this approach takes on a whole new life. Corey finding the right light. Composing the frame together. Setting the camera down and letting something unfold when Frank is in the frame all of a sudden becomes much more compelling. Then handing these moments over to someone like Matt Yocum (The Last of Us, Widow’s Bay), who can truly transport the film into another realm. Same for Jacob McKee, my long-time colorist. It really allowed these master craftspeople to shine in a way that wasn’t gummed up by an overly complex process. It was as stripped down as physically possible, and I think their talent is so evident.

Frank Mosley also seems to have been particularly important to the project, both as an actor and as someone willing to embrace your approach to filmmaking. What was it about Frank that made you feel he was the right person to bring into the production and how did you work together to develop his character in Dogbite?

Frank’s a filmmaker himself, in addition to being an incredibly gifted actor. We just understood each other almost immediately when we first met over coffee. Like so much of my work – and this film – it was just instinct. Frank has also become this compass for me. When other people might tell me to take it easy or soften an edge, he’s a consistent voice encouraging me to be me and to follow my instincts. And I love Frank. He’s one of my closest friends. So we were just excited to go shoot something with zero expectations of where it might lead.

Returning to the aesthetic for a minute, there’s a sense of restraint running through into the visual language of the film. You rely heavily on locked-off shots and long takes, which I felt were crucial not only in conveying the isolation of your central character, but in placing us inside his headspace. Can you talk us through your decision-making in terms of the visual language of Dogbite and what you wanted that stillness to achieve?

I like framing things and seeing what happens. Creating this space for actors to play and the environment around them to unfold. We didn’t pay for a trained dog to wander into the shot while Frank was eating his ice cream cone. That was a wild street dog. It just happened. It was magical. That’s the stuff that makes experiences like this so beautiful. Being open and receptive to what comes.

So much of what we are asked to do in this line of work is to imagine and pre-visualize every moment, every frame. Some people work like that, and I respect it and applaud that approach. But so much of the magic for me lies in aggressively defending patience throughout the process. Time seems to play a big part in my films. Curiosity as a virtue. Allowing myself to be surprised – anticipating it. Whether that’s a dog walking into frame or watching Frank do his karaoke rendition of Steal My Sunshine for the first time.

Could you also tell us a little about the camera and lenses you used to shoot the film, and why you settled on that particular setup? What attracted you to the aspect ratio you chose for Dogbite?

The goal was to get out there and shoot. So we used whatever Corey had access to. At the end of the day, it was his Alexa, a set of primes and sound equipment I borrowed from my friend and sound designer Christian Stropko.

At 25 minutes, Dogbite is on the long side for a narrative short. I know you’ve already mentioned that you weren’t making this short with thoughts of furthering your career and it was more of an instinctual creative process. However, I’m wondering if there were any discussions around the length of the film and how that would impact it getting seen?

There was zero expectation of what would come out of this experience. For us, it was much more about making something together that was ours. We got into this rhythm of shooting later in the day and deep into the night. We were all staying in a small hotel. So I’d wake up the next morning and work through the footage in my room. Corey, Ines and Frank would come over to my room around noon and I’d show them what I’d put together.

It was never really a consideration to make it anything other than what it became. I’m fully aware this film is the prototype of what to make if you don’t want to get programmed at a festival.

It was so exciting to see this weird story begin to emerge. And then we’d sit there together and talk about what we should shoot next. It’s hard not to be outcome-oriented in what we do, but I think with this being on the tail of so much frustration, we just wanted this to be something we loved making together. We want people to see it and enjoy it. Of course. But it was never really a consideration to make it anything other than what it became. I’m fully aware this film is the prototype of what to make if you don’t want to get programmed at a festival. But we love this bizarre little film that was birthed out of this beautiful experience.

Can you talk us through that editing process? How did you approach the cut to maintain the audience’s engagement across that runtime? And do you tend to seek external perspectives during the editing process to help you judge whether the film is working?

Whether I’m writing or directing or editing – there’s really one thing I’m after. One thing I am acutely attuned to: does this excite me? I am helplessly, irreversibly a slave to it. Sometimes that voice weaves and overlaps with what an audience wants or expects, but often it does not. Regardless, that really does serve as my true north. I’m of course aware of how someone might feel or react to a scene or a sound or a transition. But those considerations are all subject to the same filter: is it exciting to me?

We mentioned your feature, Jackrabbit, at the start of this interview and I want to return to it as we wrap up. Did the experience of making Dogbite change your understanding of what was required to make a feature? And did making this short influence your approach to making the feature?

I remember sitting at Starbucks the morning of our last shoot day on Dogbite. In addition to Frank, I’d invited some other really talented actor/filmmaker friends to come out for a day to play some small part in the film. Sophia Dunn-Walker and Hannah Alline both agreed, knowing full well no one knew what in the world their part was going to be. So on the last day, it was me, Frank, Corey and Hannah sitting over coffee, about to go shoot, and I had this realization. We’d come out here together for 4 days or so to shoot this film for absolutely nothing. Why couldn’t we come out for 8 days or 12 days and make a feature? In that moment, there was genuinely this sort of agreement that we would. And 10 months later that same team had wrapped production on my first feature film called Jackrabbit. Hannah as producer, Corey behind the camera and Frank in front of it.

I feel so lucky to have found people who are as equally delusional and driven as I am.

Somehow, being able to channel our collective frustration and turn it into this experience is ironically what led to getting my first feature film made. I think it’s bullshit when people with profoundly successful careers tell young filmmakers to grab their phone and go make a movie. Like it’s so easy. But I do feel there is maybe something within that sentiment that is more helpful. It’s not the oversimplifying or flattening of the difficulty we all face in trying to go tell our stories. That helps no one. But I do think something lies within that inherent fork in the road we face when we are brutally presented with rejection and the ensuing frustration: action or inaction. I’m not trying to be rah-rah. To me, it’s the truth. And so much of that decision is contingent on the community of artists you find yourself in. I feel so lucky to have found people who are as equally delusional and driven as I am. And Dogbite only exists because of my friends. Corey, Ines, Frank, Sophia and Hannah.

Jared, thanks so much for joining us to talk about Dogbite. It’s always a pleasure to discuss your filmmaking. Before we wrap up, is there anything else you’d like to share about Jackrabbit, or any other projects you have coming up?

Jackrabbit premiered at the truly incredible Oldenburg International Film Festival in Germany in September. It’s also just been programmed to play at the prestigious Thessaloniki International Film Festival in Greece in November. It’s continuing to spread and find its audience and people who truly connect with it.

We’re excited to see where it premieres as it heads to the States soon. You can follow its festival journey and beyond HERE. And much of the same team is also in development on a new film we are gearing up for and looking to shoot fall of 2027. We’re hoping to keep the momentum rolling and continue to make films together.

And finally, a question we ask all our interviewees – and one I’m particularly interested to hear your answer to: what’s one short film by another filmmaker that you’d recommend to the Directors Notes audience and what is it about that film that makes it worth watching?

It’s so easy to want to cram a feature film’s worth of ideas into a short film. But I always love when I come across a short that does so much with so little and keeps its aims focused on what can make the format so special. I think Caleb Wild is one of the most exciting young directors working right now and his short film When I Wake isn’t screaming at you to pay attention. Instead, it simply exists as a moment in time that holds so much humanity within it. A rich subtext where both the frame and the phone serve to limit our view of the larger life of this unnamed character as he balances the immediacy of both life and work. I find it profound in its simplicity and how it alludes to a larger world we can’t help but project onto our own experiences and the balance we all try to strike.

item.title: 11 Gems From Conero Film + ADV 2026 to Look Out For
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: Conero Film + ADV’s Pianeta Fresco is full of short films that surprise. DN picks 11 must-watch titles from the 4th edition of this mighty event in Ancona.
item.content:encoded:
Our friends at Conero Film +ADV have invited Directors Notes once again to serve as Media Partner for the festival and creative retreat, this year entitled Pianeta Fresco, taking place at the Ridotto del Teatro Le Muse, in Ancona on October 30th. As part of the event, I’ll also have the pleasure of sitting down for a Q&A with some of the directors behind the selected short films, while our very own MarBelle returns as part of the CFA jury. Our fascination with this small but mighty event is nothing new, but I have to say that the selection I was presented with really blew me away. It was genuinely difficult to choose which shorts to include in this Best of Fest collection. Ultimately, the fact that the festival takes place so close to my hometown of Fano certainly plays a part in the affection I feel for it.

Here are 11 short films — 10 + 1 — from across the festival’s various sections, both branded and unbranded, that are absolutely worth checking out. We encourage you to follow @conerofilmadv over on Instagram and take a closer look at its full official selections list. There’s so much worth discovering!

Just Evolve – Martin Holzman

It is rare to come across a short film that is so immediate: brief but powerful, and straight to the point. Just Evolve starts from the observation that Italian frequently uses a derogatory and offensive word to refer to people with Down syndrome, a term that associates them with the inhabitants of Mongolia because of the shape of their eyes. Martin Holzman’s work perfectly illustrates how human beings have abandoned practices that have become obsolete over time, even though they were once considered perfectly normal. It lists examples such as selling one’s wife at a market, using urine to wash clothes, and using mouse skin to make one’s eyebrows more attractive. Humanity has, of course, abandoned all these practices. The film then asks whether we can do the same with words that perpetuate prejudice, as part of CoorDown’s 2026 campaign video for World Down Syndrome Day. Absolutely adorable.

FEUERWERK – Timothy George Kelly

Five years in the making, 20 minute documentary FEUERWERK is a visually memorable investigation of the usage of fireworks in Germany, presenting an explosive “portrait of Berlin as it explodes itself into the new year.” What are the laws behind it and what are people’s feelings towards this annual onslaught of pyrotechnics on the city streets? Reflecting on the social and cultural relevance of a long standing tradition, this beautifully photographed work—all the more impressive given the choice of a grainy black-and-white palette for this most colourful of subject matters—by Timothy George Kelly is true fire!

The Nymph – Vanessa Stachel

Queer fairy tale The Nymph reminds me of another great queer story from this year, No Rest for the Wicked, a feature film that takes a much darker and more gruesome approach to its themes. Both stories capture that same sense of twisted enchantment, blending queer storytelling with unsettling undertones and a world where beauty and horror seem to go hand in hand. Vanessa Stachel’s short is an extremely mature and accomplished work that weaves together elements of German folk fairy tales with a harsh critique of the ever-worsening effects of climate change, while also incorporating a queer context, as mentioned. There is a lot going on here, but it is all skilfully brought together in just a few minutes.

Most Popular

Clothes Hanging Out To Dry In Daily Faith – Alberto Valletta

Even though Clothes Hanging Out To Dry In Daily Faith is not particularly original from a structural and stylistic standpoint, being mostly composed of talking heads, it has an incredible power due to its topic. As an Italian, it touches me even more deeply, given the complications that queerness has always caused in the country due to its strong religious foundations. Also, Alberto Valletta wins the award for having the best film title of the festival.

The Tanks are Coming Out – Emma Chitty

This music video, shot for London-based Nrvs, is a clear example of how sometimes a song seems to have been made for its accompanying video, and vice versa. In this case, it almost feels as though the song was written to fit perfectly into the folds of Emma Chitty’s short film, which conveys a powerful social message touching on both mental isolation and the context of protests and social movement, communicated through a metaphor of going up in flames, literally.

Ana’s Dream – NONO

Brief yet extremely clear in its message, DN alum director NONO’s Ana’s Dream focuses on the years of struggle, hard work, and perseverance that some people go through in order to pursue their dreams. Through Ana’s story, the film speaks to the experiences of many, particularly Mexican people, highlighting the sacrifices people make, often in countries other than their own, to achieve the life they dream of. It is a tribute to those who leave their homes and navigate the challenges of migration in the hope of building a better future. At the same time, the film expresses gratitude towards the generations who made these sacrifices to give their children more favourable conditions in which to grow and thrive. In this sense, Ana’s Dream also becomes a reflection on legacy, exploring what we inherit from those who came before us and how their struggles help shape the opportunities available to future generations. The best thing about all this? It’s a beer ad.

Stop Being So Dramatic – Lorenzo Follari

In a highly surreal atmosphere, we encounter unforgettable female protagonists, both in their appearance and in the way the camera interacts with them, bringing out the more eccentric aspects of their femininity. Cryptic yet simultaneously easy to watch and fall in love with, Stop Being So Dramatic is clearly inspired by the cinema of the immortal David Lynch. However, it is not a mere imitation. In fact, Lorenzo Follari reinterprets his style through a feminist lens. The snowy, slightly muffled landscape gives the film a distinctive, self-contained quality, and it shows promise for possible future expansions.

Five More Minutes – GUTTO & Diego Santana Claudino

Five More Minutes explores the final wishes of people who would have wanted just five more minutes with a loved one before their death. Blending documentary elements with an artistic, kinetic representation through dance, the film portrays a final dance between the person who must let go and the person who is leaving their life forever. Beautifully crafted and exceptionally well choreographed, the film opens with real people sharing what their final moments together might have looked like had they been given the choice. Moving and far from clichéd, Diego Santana Claudino and GUTTO’s heartfelt project avoids easy emotional tropes and instead reflects on an experience that most people will eventually face in their lifetime, albeit at different ages.

My Name is Oil – Igor Smola

As the title (inspired by the book My Name is Red by a Turkish writer Orhan Pamuk) already suggests, Igor Smola’s My Name is Oil explores the importance of oil in our lives. However, rather than examining it through the end product and its consumerist role in global manufacturing, it focuses on the actual process of extraction. Through a highly cinematic style, the oil itself almost seems to speak and take centre stage, speaking to us with quotes and ideas inspired by Iranian philosopher Reza Negarestani. This approach makes the subject accessible even to viewers who have no idea what goes on behind the scenes in the processes that ultimately allow us to use “black gold” in our daily life. Mesmerising.

Songs of Salt – Isabella Bazoni

Set along the Romagna coast, Songs of Salt explores the ownership of beach resorts and bathing establishments, which are passed down from generation to generation. These places represent family traditions and livelihoods, but also deep emotional attachments. This tradition has recently come under threat as a result of new legislation. The editing, along with the film’s distinctly pop-inspired yet deeply nostalgic style, ensured that Isabella Bazoni’s short struck a chord with me. It feels close to home geographically, since it talks about the area near where I was born and raised, but I strongly believe that it can also resonate with an international audience thanks to its themes, which transcend geographical boundaries.

Faceless – Carlos Santana

We simply couldn’t leave this one out, even though I usually prefer to stick to a top ten for these pieces. The atmosphere of this Spanish short, which draws heavily on the palettes and geometric shapes associated with Pedro Almodóvar, makes us fall in love with its protagonist, Valeria Palmeiro, better known as Coco Dávez. Totally loved the contrast that Carlos Santana’s Faceless creates between the black-and-white world and the colourful one that art makes possible.

You can find more unmissable films like these in our Best of Fest collections.

item.title: Émile Lavoie Delivers an Unabashedly Grizzly, Expectation Defying Horror Comedy With ‘Mean Ends’
item.dc:creator: Mark Brennan
item.description: Émile Lavoie twists horror expectations to bloody ends in his darkly humorous short film that shows what happens when you dare judge a book by its cover.
item.content:encoded:
There’s an old saying that goes something along the lines of, “If it walks like a duck, swims like a duck, and quacks like a duck, then it’s probably a duck.” Émile Lavoie combines that notion with a splash of grisly violence and dark humour in his horror comedy Mean Ends (Mourir en silence). It takes every expectation you have of a horror film and turns it against you with devilish delight – and even has something to say about the heartache that comes when your craft isn’t working out the way you’d hoped. Joining us for the Mean Ends online premiere, Lavoie talks to Directors Notes about the filmmaking misfortune that led to this brilliant short, collaborating with his other half, both on and off screen, the hole the lead actor dug for himself during filming, making Québec look like a sinister backwater town straight out of a Hollywood horror film, and the real-life characters they encountered during location scouting who could have stepped straight off the screen.

Mean Ends is as smart and atmospheric as it is entertaining and beautifully captured. How did this story come about?

Much like the story of the film itself, the journey of Mean Ends begins with a failure. In November 2021, I head to Beauce, a rural region of Quebec, with my film crew to shoot my first independent, self-financed short film, set entirely in a ploughed field alongside a railroad track. The first day of shooting goes off without any major hiccups. That evening, we go to bed feeling satisfied and excited about what lies ahead. However, overnight, an unprecedented and completely unexpected snowstorm hits the region, burying the field under a foot of snow. It’s a disaster. There’s no way our shots will ever match. I’m forced to cancel the shoot and return to Montreal, with my dreams and tens of thousands of dollars down the drain.

The only remnant of this abandoned project is a fake decapitated corpse that my partner and co-writer Camille Mongeau and I are forced to live with. An entire year goes by in the company of this corpse. Whenever we want to watch a movie, we move it onto the bed. When it’s time to go to sleep, we put it back on the couch. Not only does this body take up most of the space in our tiny Montreal apartment, but more importantly, it serves as a constant reminder of my failure, literally lying dead on my couch, just like my directing career.

Then, one day, I hear the mailman climbing the stairs of my building. My eyes drift toward the corpse, still lying on my couch, right next to the front window. I wonder: “What would happen if he happened to glance inside my apartment?” An idea begins to take shape, and I mention it to Camille. It’s May 2022. Just a few weeks later, she comes back to me with a story: Éric, a horror filmmaker (like me), a somewhat pathetic, washed-up loser (like me), whose dreams have all but collapsed (like mine), decides to bury every last remnant of his failed career, including a decapitated corpse. There’s just one problem: his neighbour, a young woman to whom he’s always been something of a surrogate father, has gone missing. The rest is history.

The opening scene sees Eric standing in a grave dug for a headless corpse, so this question has two parts – how did you dig that hole and how did you make that corpse?

As for the massive hole in the ground, the hardest part, which we had actually underestimated quite a bit, was finding a property owner with a suitably run-down house who would agree to let us completely tear up a good portion of their yard. Luckily, we stumbled upon the owner of this sad-looking little house, with an RV parked right in the middle of the property, who couldn’t have cared less what we did to his landscaping. Strangely enough, though, he told us that a new tenant was moving in the day after our shoot. I can only imagine the shock when they arrived!

As for the actual digging, Hugo Giroux, our lead actor, going full method acting, asked if he could dig the hole himself to really get into Éric’s headspace. After three or four shovelfuls of dirt, he admitted that maybe he’d been a little too ambitious, so we ended up renting a small excavator from a place right across the street to get the job done. Once the hole was dug, we had to go back in and rough up the edges, since the excavator had left these very straight, obvious marks in the dirt. Quite the undertaking!

After three or four shovelfuls of dirt, he admitted that maybe he’d been a little too ambitious, so we ended up renting a small excavator from a place right across the street to get the job done.

For the body, we worked with our longtime collaborator, Rémy Couture, who has been taking care of my bloody prosthetics for nearly ten years now! We made a full-body cast of our actress Léa Girard-Nadeau (the actress from Living Grounds), including her head. If you’ve seen MaXXXine, you’ll have a pretty good idea of how the process works! Things got a little scary, though, when a slight miscalculation in the proportions of the materials caused the latex to harden much faster than expected and stick to Léa’s skin, making it almost impossible to remove. So, Léa ended up trapped inside a mold of her own body for several hours!

Another fun anecdote: just a few days before the casting session, Léa told us she had just found out she was pregnant! Of course, we made absolutely sure that none of the materials we were using posed any risk to her pregnancy.

I asked Camille to push her portrayal of Marika a little further, to make the character slightly more exaggerated.

You wrote and produced the film with your partner, Camile Mongeau, who also stars. What is the collaboration like between you both pre-production and then on the shoot when the relationship becomes director to actor?

Our working relationship is pretty much like any romantic relationship: there are highs and, occasionally, there are lows! Luckily, whenever one of us is dealing with disappointment or stress, the other is usually able to step in, take over, and keep the ship on course. On a typical project, Camille will write the first draft of the screenplay, laying all the groundwork, establishing the tone of the story and its characters, finding their voices, and making sure the whole thing makes sense. I’ll usually come in for a second pass, adding certain ideas for staging and visual storytelling directly into the script, and sometimes finding more unusual ways to approach specific scenes or plot developments.

During pre-production, Camille handles locations, actors and their agents, and the overall logistics of the shoot (production coordination, craft services, accommodations, etc.), before handing things over to the production manager. I generally take care of the crew and equipment, along with the usual directing responsibilities: shot lists, rehearsals, and creative discussions with the production designer, costume designer, and cinematographer.

Most Popular

On set, even when she’s acting, Camille has a very hard time keeping herself from getting involved in the minute-by-minute details of the production, which, ultimately, is a very good thing! As for our director-actor relationship, I think we have an enormous amount of trust in each other. For example, on Mean Ends, I asked Camille to push her portrayal of Marika a little further, to make the character slightly more exaggerated. It wasn’t necessarily something she was used to doing, since most of her previous work had been in more restrained, naturalistic dramatic features. She was skeptical at first, but ultimately decided to trust me!

Likewise, once we get to post-production, I’ll usually work on the first cut with our editor, but Camille gets the final say, especially when it comes to the actors’ performances and the emotional impact of a scene. She has an incredible sensitivity and instinct for those things. I’m also a colorist by trade, so I’m usually the one handling the color grading on our projects. But once again, Camille is the final stamp of approval when it comes to the overall look and feel of our films. Because, as any good colorist knows, it’s very easy to get a little carried away!

Hugo Giroux is pitch-perfect as the suspicious friend of the family. How did you go about casting and collaborating with him?

Camille’s sister is a talent agent, and one of the actors she represents is Hugo Giroux! So we had been following his work for quite some time and had been wanting to collaborate with him. We actually wrote the role specifically for him, which really helped us find the right voice for his character, especially when it came to the dialogue. I think Hugo was really happy about it, because he’s often cast as the villain. But this time around, even though Éric might initially come across as a big, intimidating bad guy, he gradually reveals himself to be a much more sensitive and tormented character as the story unfolds. This gave Hugo the opportunity to explore a different emotional range and bring a lot more depth and nuance to his portrayal of Éric.

The locations are straight out of a horror film and really add to the belief that what we see playing out is real. Where did you shoot the film and how did you find those locations?

Finding locations is often the worst part of pre-production for us. Our budgets are usually pretty tight, our ambitions are ridiculously high, and we’re very aware of just how much of a film’s credibility comes from the environments in which it’s shot. So, location scouting often becomes the biggest challenge of our entire pre-production process. We basically need to find locations that are almost perfect as is, at least structurally, because we rarely have the budget to build sets. We can dress them up, but that’s about it.

On top of that, the spaces need to be relatively large to allow us to execute our shots as intended. In Hollywood, when they build a rundown house, they’ll often double or even triple the size of each room to accommodate the camera and crew. But in real life, a rundown house is usually just a tiny, cramped little place. Ahah! To find unusual, relatively untouched locations that haven’t already appeared in a dozen other productions, we usually browse real estate listings. The problem is, when a house is literally a ‘teardown’, real estate agents don’t exactly advertise that as a selling point. Over time, though, we’ve discovered a pretty reliable trick: when a listing doesn’t include any pictures of the interior, that’s usually a very good sign.

We also do most of our own location scouting, and let me tell you, more than once, we’ve literally found ourselves inside a horror movie, meeting some truly bizarre characters straight out of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre. I remember this one elderly woman, a hoarder who was almost completely deaf, sitting in the dark eating a rotisserie chicken, illuminated only by the flickering light of her old CRT television. It was like walking straight into a movie scene. For Mean Ends, we wanted to create this sort of ‘Québec redneck’ atmosphere, as if the film were taking place somewhere deep in the Louisiana bayou or rural Texas, except transplanted to Québec. Something sweaty, humid, grimy, and slightly rotten. Which isn’t particularly realistic, considering Québec isn’t exactly known for its hot weather, but I think we managed to sell the illusion!

For Éric’s house, we shot in the Rawdon area, roughly half an hour northeast of Montréal. For Marika and her mother’s house, we went to Saint-André-d’Argenteuil, about half an hour west of Montréal. And yes, despite appearing to be right next to each other in the film, the two locations are actually an hour and a half apart!

We wanted to create this sort of ‘Québec redneck’ atmosphere, as if the film were taking place somewhere deep in the Louisiana bayou or rural Texas, except transplanted to Québec.

What did you shoot and then later edit Mean Ends on, and was there a particular reason for your choice of gear?

We shot on an Arri Alexa Mini because we were shooting in pretty cramped spaces so we needed as much space as possible/distance from the subjects without using ultra-wide lenses. We also liked the great natural grain, even at higher ISO in low light, of the Arri sensor. We used Cooke S4 lenses because of their relative small size, and because they could open at T2 throughout the whole set/range of optics. They also have a nice cinematographic bokeh.

We edited in Premiere Pro. There’s not really a reason other than that’s the software our editor was using!

The production design also adds a lot of authenticity for a horror film, including some great effects with the worms in the dinner and the bubbling drink. What was the process to achieve the look of the homes and the dinner table effects?

Mathilde Donnard and Philippe Gauvin are extraordinary production designers: dedicated, resourceful, and incredibly quick to understand exactly the kind of film we’re trying to make. We’ve worked with them on every single one of our projects ever since! One slightly heartbreaking thing is that we barely get to see Éric’s house in the finished film. We wanted to preserve a certain mystery around his character and keep up his facade, but in reality, Mathilde and Phil had completely redecorated the entire house, and it looked absolutely incredible. Sorry, guys!

As for Marika’s house, they covered the walls in wallpaper and replaced most of the furniture, using a combination of items already on location and pieces from prop rental houses. The earthworms, meanwhile, came from a little fishing shack nearby.

For the special effects, we worked with the Blood Brothers, a Québec-based practical effects company. The trick behind the glass filling up with blood was actually pretty simple: we drilled a hole in the back of the glass and connected it to a pressurized tube that allowed us to pump fake blood directly into it! As for the fake shovel, that was Rémy Couture’s work. I won’t lie, it was incredibly floppy, almost like a giant buckwheat pancake, so we ended up having to rebuild it in post!

With regard to the soundtrack, you had one song in mind to use but had to pivot to your composer. Can you tell us about that and your creative choices for the score?

Théo Porcet, our composer, is what you might call a Swiss Army knife: he does absolutely everything. Multi-instrumentalist, experimental musician, DJ, electronic music producer, frontman of a punk band, and sound designer. The guy is unstoppable. He’s also a huge horror movie fan, so he had all the right references to build the soundtrack for Mean Ends. Since he was also handling the sound design, he was able to compose the music in a way that seamlessly blended with the sonic environments he was creating.

It’s actually Theo who saw Beau is Afraid first and told us that our main theme was in that movie. When we had to rethink the film’s main theme because the original piece also appeared in Beau Is Afraid, Théo immediately got to work. And I’d be lying if I told you that the piece you hear in the finished film isn’t the very first version he sent us. Flawless victory.

I guess I feel a little bad for her every time, knowing how disturbing the whole experience might be for some viewers.

The film had its world premiere at Fantasia International Film Festival, where it won Best Director and Audience Choice awards. What has the festival run been like for you and what has been your experience sharing the film with audiences?

The festival run for Mean Ends has been incredible! The film screened at around thirty festivals, including the very exciting Palm Springs ShortFest, which we were lucky enough to attend, and won about ten awards along the way!
