We noticed that the film was particularly popular in the United States, even getting selected for more general-interest festivals, which still surprises me considering how gory the film actually is!

That being said, I have to say that horror fans are simply the best moviegoing crowd ever. Their reactions are so lively, genuine, and enthusiastic. There’s always such a great atmosphere during screenings, followed by tons of conversations afterward. It’s a wonderful, tight-knit community of passionate film lovers who really support one another.

I have to admit, whenever I’m attending a screening, I always find myself eagerly waiting for the film’s final twist, when the audience realizes that Sophie isn’t actually dead. I guess I feel a little bad for her every time, knowing how disturbing the whole experience might be for some viewers. And I’m also always looking forward to the moment people realize that Éric isn’t actually such a bad guy after all!

What’s next for you?

We’re currently in the middle of the festival run for our second short film, Living Grounds (the one we actually started shooting before Mean Ends, ahah!). The film won Best Short Film at Fantasia this year and was also selected for the Tampere Film Festival, the Busan International Short Film Festival, and the Vancouver International Film Festival, among others! We’re really proud of it!

We’re also wrapping up post-production on an anthology project called Six Tiny Broken Hearts, which consists of six short stories about broken hearts that, well, generally don’t end particularly well! The project will be released as a feature film starting in 2027, so keep an eye out! We’ve also secured funding for two more short films, Denise and All Cats Have Nine Lives, which we’ll be shooting in 2027. And finally, we’ve received development funding to write our first traditional feature film, Peachskin, a horror comedy/body horror film produced by 12PM and Maria Gracia Turgeon (Fauve, Brotherhood, Who Do I Belong To). Looks like we’ve got a pretty busy year ahead of us!

And finally, what short film by another filmmaker would you recommend to the Directors Notes community and why?

I just watched Skinny Boots (Skinny Bottines) by Romain F. Dubois, and I genuinely think it’s one of the best short films to come out of Québec (and anywhere in the world, really) that I’ve ever had the pleasure of seeing. The film won the Sony Discovery Award for Best Short Film at Cannes’ Critics’ Week, and it’s absolutely well deserved. It’s an incredibly dynamic film, simple in its story yet wonderfully complex in the way it tells it. It captures Montréal’s grey, slushy winter in a way that feels completely magical and exhilarating. It’s as if the Safdie brothers had directed Home Alone 2. An absolute must-watch.

item.title: Life Reflects Art in Émile V. Schlesser’s ‘Backstage’ Blending On-Stage Power Play With Real-Life Abuse
item.dc:creator: Mark Brennan
item.description: Émile V. Schlesser draws on personal experience for his absorbing drama about abuse and power dynamics between directors and actors in the theatre world.
item.content:encoded:
In the theatre, every performance is an illusion. But what happens when the most dangerous drama unfolds beyond the audience’s view? In Backstage, director Émile V. Schlesser draws on personal experience to take us into the unsettling world behind the curtain, where artistic ambition, attraction and authority become entangled in a perilous psychological game. When a young actor finds his future resting in the hands of a demanding director, the boundaries between mentorship and manipulation begin to dissolve. The result is a gripping exploration of the abuse of power, vulnerability and the invisible forces that can make saying no feel impossible. Returning to Directors Notes for his third appearance on our pages, Schlesser talks to us about the tight shooting schedule in one of Luxembourg’s prestigious theatres, the crew’s belief in the project and generosity in making the most of the location, and the trust he built with his actors to capture scenes of both intimacy and abuse. He also reflects on the catharsis of co-writing and sharing his story, and offers advice to anyone facing a similar situation.

Welcome back to Directors Notes! Your latest film, Backstage, is a sobering depiction of power play that is based on your real-life experience. How did you work with your co-writer to adapt that story for the screen?

We’ve all heard, witnessed, or experienced stories of powerful people taking advantage of their authority to manipulate people in vulnerable positions into emotional, psychological, or even sexual abuse. Unfortunately, abuse of power continues to be a problem, particularly in the entertainment industry. I myself experienced an unpleasant episode of that nature in my past. It took me a very long time to unpack what had really happened and how things had evolved, one subtle step at a time, into something that was almost impossible to escape. It’s not easy to come forward and talk about these things – perhaps even more so for men, I suspect, as they may be more prone to feeling shame and fear of being seen as ‘a victim’ – but making this film has been quite therapeutic for me. I owe it all to my co-writer, Jonas Brand, who encouraged me to finally tackle this topic and dare to turn a trauma into an entertaining piece of film.

For me personally, the most interesting and eye-opening part was trying to understand both perspectives – that of the victim as well as that of the predator.

Working on the screenplay with Jonas was a cleansing experience. It came together quicker than any of our other projects. It just flowed. We came up with the whole story and the first draft in only a few days. For me personally, the most interesting and eye-opening part was trying to understand both perspectives – that of the victim as well as that of the predator. Putting myself in Cosima’s shoes helped me process some things from my own past. Adding a pinch of humor here and there also helped approach this topic without making the film too dark or heavy-handed.

The film relies heavily on the chemistry between all the cast, but especially that between Lukas and Cosima. How did you go about casting these roles and what was it like for you directing them given your own experience?

From the very start, I knew I wanted Sascha Ley to take on the role of the seductive, manipulative director, Cosima. We wrote the part specifically for Sascha. I’ve known her for quite a long time and knew she had everything such a complex character required: demanding, seductive, fearless, yet vulnerable – all of these contradictory attributes that make up Cosima’s personality. I admire Sascha’s courage and willingness to unflinchingly dive into the shady areas that, to a certain extent, exist within us all. She loved the challenge and took the part head-on.

We all had wonderful chemistry, made each other feel safe and protected, and we encouraged each other to openly discuss the film’s subject matter, including our own experiences with abuse.

I’d seen Jonathan Joèl Albrecht in another short film (see my recommendation below) and was amazed by his raw, honest, and vulnerable aura. He’s an incredibly authentic actor with an amazing sense of truthfulness and an astonishing ability to dig deep into his own emotional self. I can’t see anyone else pulling off what he did in the role of Lukas. He totally made it his own.

It was pure bliss working with these two actors. There was a lot of trust between us. We all had wonderful chemistry, made each other feel safe and protected, and we encouraged each other to openly discuss the film’s subject matter, including our own experiences with abuse.

Most Popular

Intimacy coordinators now play a huge role when capturing intimate scenes. Did you work with an intimacy coordinator on Backstage or rehearse directly with the actors for those scenes?

The single most important thing on this production was trust. We did not have an intimacy coordinator on set – which, I know, might seem strange on a project with a topic like this. I talked a lot with my cast members, and together we realized that we had built so much trust between us that the actors didn’t feel the need for an intimacy coordinator. They actually felt more comfortable without an outside third party intervening. For me, it’s all about what my actors want and need to feel safe, so I respected their wishes. In any case, as a director, I believe it is vital to create a positive and creative working environment in which everyone feels safe, respected, and supported.

There are interesting parallels between the play being rehearsed on stage and the story being played off it. How did you use those in your story and what was it like directing someone directing?

What makes the theater the perfect setting for a story about power abuse is multifaceted. On one hand, it’s a world that’s defined by a very clear-cut hierarchical structure, confined to a closed, intimate environment where tapping into your emotions and vulnerabilities is part of the job. On the other hand, it offers the possibility of exploring the grey zones where fiction and reality blur into one another. Over the course of the film, it becomes increasingly difficult to discern where unorthodox professional methods end and actual abuse, fueled by personal desire, begins. Narratively, it all serves to further complicate Lukas’ assessment of the situation, making it difficult for him to see clearly what’s happening to him.

Having actors play actors who are themselves acting on stage proved to be quite a mind-bending meta-experience. Python, the play the actors are performing on stage, already portrays an abusive relationship between a man and a woman. So, things quickly become disorienting, as it gets harder to differentiate between play and real life.

Directing someone who is directing others also proved interesting, to say the least. I encouraged Sascha to direct the play herself, but in character, as Cosima. I think she really enjoyed that. At times, while shooting the rehearsal scene, for instance, I myself felt like I was losing sight of who was directing whom – so it was all a big, weird meta-experience. Fun, but somewhat mind-boggling.

The scale of the production, including the impressive theatre location, belies the small budget you had to work with. How were you able to achieve the scope of this production with the resources you had?

Trying to finance a rather ambitious project like this – especially one that required shooting in an actual working theater of renown – proved to be extremely challenging. We did not receive any funding from official film institutions. The daunting topic probably scared a few people off. However, we were tied to a specific window of a week and a half during which we were allowed to shoot in one of Luxembourg’s main theaters – a small miracle in itself! I therefore had to find alternative ways to raise the minimum amount we needed, and I had to act quickly, as we had only about a month before the theater’s proposed shooting dates.

We shot the film on a very tight budget, but were adamant about not compromising on production value. I reached out to a lot of people, asking for support of any kind, and I even went as far as selling paintings I had left from my time as an artist (I studied fine arts at the academy in Düsseldorf, Germany). What ultimately made the film possible was the persistence, dedication, and belief in its themes shared by the entire crew. Instead of renting expensive camera equipment, we shot the film on our DP Thorsten Harms’s own Blackmagic 6K. Our gaffer, Stepan Novotny, brought all the lighting equipment he owned himself. As for me, I tried to wear as many hats as I could.

How did you work with your cinematographer to make the most of the locations in the short shooting schedule you had and decide on the visual language you wanted to capture this story?

I had a wonderful collaboration with my amazing DP, Thorsten Harms, who intuitively understood what the story needed in terms of visual language. Thankfully, the locations themselves – especially the theatre and its backstage area – were so visually appealing that it naturally gave the film extra production value oomph. We pretty quickly came up with a palette and structure to not only make the various sets have their own distinctive look, but to also reflect the power balance and inner workings of their complex relationship.

For instance, we chose three colors – red, blue, and gold – and gave each a specific meaning, using them very consciously throughout the film. Red symbolizes abuse and gradually appears more and more as the story unfolds. Blue, by contrast, represents liberation. The two colors are in constant dialogue with one another throughout the entire film. Lighting was another important part of our visual grammar. Whenever Lukas is being seduced, for example, we used a cozy, golden light to make the atmosphere feel warm and inviting.

The two colors are in constant dialogue with one another throughout the entire film.

There is a stillness to the soundscape at times, allowing the tension of the scenes to play out with sparse musical inference. What was the intention behind this creative choice?

I realized early on that there was no need for score or any extra non-diegetic sound. In fact, the soundscape’s subliminal power lies in the moments of awkward silence, when you get a real sense of unwanted intimacy. When you strip away unnecessary music and sounds, the characters become alone, vulnerable, and helpless, and all these small yet transgressive subtleties start to feel uncomfortably close. You can sense the other person’s presence closing in, invading your space, as the sound of their breath, their whispers, and the rustling of their clothes almost turn into something threatening. A tiny, intimate gesture suddenly becomes intrusive and unsettling.

What advice would you have for anyone who might find themselves in a similar situation to Lukas, and indeed the one you experienced?

If you haven’t lived through a similar situation, it’s easy to look at it from the outside and judge the victims, thinking, “That would never happen to me.” But it really isn’t that simple. So many factors can make it difficult to even recognize that you’re being manipulated or taken advantage of. And once you do realize what’s going on, it can feel like it’s already too late to speak up. On one hand, what’s paralyzing you is fear – the fear of losing career opportunities, being punished, or provoking the abuser’s temper. On the other hand, it can also be love, admiration, or friendship. You may feel close to the person, or believe you’ve had a good collaboration, and simply don‘t want to hurt their feelings. And the longer you avoid taking action, seeking help, or clearly communicating how you feel, the messier it gets.

It’s important to understand that anyone can be abused – and anyone can be an abuser. Men and women alike. If you’re living through a situation like the one portrayed in this film, chances are you’re probably not even fully aware that it’s actually happening to you. It’s important to confide in people you trust and feel safe around, who might be able to help you work out whether there are misunderstandings or misinterpretations, or whether there’s real abuse gradually developing. Sometimes it’s hard to notice the tricks and mechanisms clearly, despite the fact that something feels very wrong. Don’t be afraid to share your experiences, feelings, thoughts, and doubts with people you trust. An outside perspective can open your eyes and give you the strength to stand up for yourself.

It’s important to confide in people you trust and feel safe around, who might be able to help you work out whether there are misunderstandings or misinterpretations, or whether there’s real abuse gradually developing.

Now that Backstage has been completed and released, what has it been like for you to screen such a personal story?

Contrary to what I initially expected, the experience of making Backstage was a true blessing and an overwhelmingly warm and positive one. I’m really proud we pushed through and made this film against all odds. Not only was the making of it therapeutic for me personally, giving me some sort of closure, but I’m particularly happy to see the film connecting with audience members – especially female audience members, unsurprisingly – who might have lived through something similar. Seeing your situation fictionalized and portrayed on the screen can make you feel understood and not alone, and that in itself can already be very helpful.

What’s next for you?

I’m currently in post-production of my first feature film that we just shot during summer in Luxembourg and Belgium. I’ve been working on it for five years – writing, directing, and right now, I’m deep into editing. It’s called Mortal Beings. It’s a dark comedy anthology of five stories that each explore different crises around growing older and having to deal with unavoidable life changes. It’s a film about us Millennials in today’s angst-ridden world. As you might guess – it’s absolutely nothing personal this time. Not in the least. Nope.

What short film would you recommend to the Directors Notes community and why?

I’d like to give some love to the German short that made me want to cast Jonathan Joèl Albrecht as my lead in Backstage. It’s a funny, sexy little film called Cowboy by Munich-based director Artur Althen. Funnily enough, it also shows a young man in a sexual relationship with a mature woman. You can find it online in the ARD Mediathek. It’s 14 minutes well spent. And Jonathan, of course, is superb in it.

item.title: 10 Short Films Capturing the Essence of Riga International Film Festival 2026
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: From experimental documentaries to unconventional animation, DN picks out ten standout shorts from the 2026 Riga International Film Festival.
item.content:encoded:
Every October, the Riga International Film Festival welcomes audiences into a diverse programme of films that span a wide range of styles and perspectives while placing a particular focus on the Baltic region. This is especially important, as film festivals can sometimes lose sight of the need to tell the stories of the places in which they are based, becoming overly internationalised in the process and allowing local gems to slip through the cracks. In this respect, the RIGA IFF stands out as an example of best practice.

Alongside its international selection of 24 short films, the festival presents seven Latvian shorts as part of its National Short Film Competition. Both sections feature a diverse range of works, although the overall direction of the 2026 edition seems to lean toward experimentation and animation. The programme includes numerous experimental films with documentary elements, as well as several distinctive animated works that push beyond more conventional, mainstream approaches. With that spirit of adventure in mind, here are ten shorts from this year’s line-up, each reflecting the festival’s appetite for taking creative risks.

Patronymic – Mariia Ponomarova

Mariia Ponomarova, director and protagonist of Patronymic, delves into and explores a fundamental element of Slavic tradition: the patronymic, a part of someone’s name derived from their father’s name. She reflects on its significance in Ukraine, particularly in the aftermath of the outbreak of war, and on how the disappearance of her own documents has made this aspect of her identity feel more important than ever. The film thus explores questions of identity and the importance of passing traditions down through generations, even when those traditions may seem somewhat outdated. Ponomarova, for instance, wonders why the equivalent of a matronymic, a middle name derived from one’s mother’s name rather than one’s father’s, is not used instead. More broadly, the short reflects on the need to reconsider and adapt traditions as society evolves. A witty chorus, reminiscent of those found in ancient Greek tragedy, challenges the young woman, asking why she is preoccupied with such questions when war is raging and there are far more pressing issues to consider. Yet this is precisely what makes Patronymic’s perspective so compelling: it gives space to a subject that might otherwise be overlooked, reminding us of the importance of questioning and preserving cultural identity even in the midst of greater crises.

Soulmate – Jens-Julius Gunderlund Dall

Soulmate dials into the importance of the divide between what is tangible, and therefore belongs to the conscious world, and what belongs to the virtual world, represented here by a VR headset. The film’s protagonist attempts to establish a relationship with a girl who does not exist, whom he creates according to his own desires. While doing so, Jens-Julius Gunderlund Dall’s work moves across different narrative styles, as it alternates between conventional live action footage and virtual reality sequences that allow viewers to fully immerse themselves in what they are watching, almost as if they were inside a virtual reality themselves. It thus explores the evolution of technology in the context of romantic relationships, taking Her by Spike Jonze as its starting point. Although the concept is not particularly original, as several short and feature length films have attempted—and continue to attempt—to do the same thing, what stands out as this particular project’s main strength is the remarkable believability of the whole experience. This is largely due to its documentary-like touch, which adds to the interest in the story.

Pacific Islands – Adas Burksaitis

Pacific Islands is a cryptic short that is difficult to decipher, yet strangely familiar. We have all experienced an ambiguous situation with someone at some point in our lives, a situation that might have seemed strange or inexplicable to an outside observer. This is the premise at the heart of Adas Burksaitis’s film. A man and a woman meet each other in a hotel. Here, everything seems so familiar, yet strange, and past events seem to resurface. What is bound to happen?

Most Popular

2:Love – Ronni Shalev

As the RIGA IFF description of this short reads, if Italian director Luca Guadagnino had created his Challengers using the language of animation and had paid more attention to the more marginal characters of his love triangle, it would, most likely, look just like this short film by Ronni Shalev. 2:Love is indeed a love letter to tennis, but also to love itself. It’s a colourful and lovable call to let attraction run free and to make sure that no net gets in the way!

Whispers of a Burning Scent – Mo Harawe

The working day of a quiet wedding musician is over before it has even begun. Instead of playing music, he finds himself in a courtroom, where his terminally ill wife’s adult children accuse him of acting in bad faith, claiming that he may be exploiting her dementia to gain control of her property. They eventually agree to drop their accusations on one condition: he must divorce his wife. A gripping story that makes us wonder where the lines are drawn when it comes to personal relationships. Directed by Mo Harawe as part of the Displacement Film Fund, which we also discussed in our London Film Festival Best of Fest selection.

Uka-Uka – Henri Veermäe

In adorable stop-motion short Uka-Uka, my unconditional love for the technique is once again richly rewarded. A little boy plays a rather unusual game of hide and seek, frightening his grandparents in the process, with some rather predictable, occasionally gory, consequences. Henri Veermäe’s animation is delightful, the story is tender and sweet, and the young protagonist’s cheeks are unforgettable. A nostalgic tribute to childhood and to the playful spirit we all shared when we were young, even when the adults around us were not exactly on board with our games.

The Truth Rejects You, Cornelius – Khris Cembe & Marc Torices

A psychedelic journey that feels almost like being in the middle of a drug-induced trip, this animated short blends different styles, from stop-motion to a cartoon aesthetic reminiscent of early Walt Disney. Marc Torices and Khris Cembe’s brainchild, The Truth Rejects You, Cornelius is an emotional roller coaster in which our protagonist, an adorable dog named Cornelius, attends therapy sessions with a psychologist who turns out to be a cigarette-smoking shrimp, immediately setting the tone for what follows. Alongside his friend Avalutsa the frog, he embarks on a series of incredible adventures, but they don’t necessarily make sense in his (and our) head. A journey through different animation styles, but also a surprisingly profound psychological exploration that leaves you wondering, in the best possible way, what on earth you are watching.

Portrait of Granny – Ieva Ozoliņa

This very short film created by Ieva Ozoliņa, running at just six minutes, immerses viewers in the world of Baltic grandmothers, particularly those of Latvia, as befits a film which is part of the national competition. Drawing on the visual language of archival footage, Portrait of Granny makes us fall in love with its protagonist. Regardless of where we were born or raised, it is difficult not to feel the warmth and comfort associated with being cared for by our grandmothers, whether they are still with us or have passed away.

Lines of Riga – Andrejs Brīvulis

Through skilful animation, Lines of Riga captures the rhythm of urban life, following a food delivery worker, a tram driver, and a young girl as they make their way through the city on a summer day. Their journeys unfold through a series of small animated tableaux that piece together the many details of Riga, from gulls circling above the Central Market and sushi deliveries to the No. 7 tram, discarded cigarette butts and Soviet housing blocks, among other things. Together, these fragments form an affectionate portrait of a city shaped as much by its everyday rhythms as by the people who inhabit it. A love letter to Riga and its residents, to those who bring it to life, those who visit and fall in love with it, and those who leave or arrive in search of something new. Andrejs Brīvulis delivers an enchanting city symphony that finds poetry in the ordinary.

Tuesday or Thursday – Dušan Kasalica

A delicate tribute to Olivier Assayas’ cult film Irma Vep, Tuesday or Thursday explores the themes of mirroring and illusion through a self-reflexive examination of filmmaking itself. Montenegrin director Dušan Kasalica offers a subtly critical portrait of the creative process, mixing elements of comedy, suspense, and absurdity. By letting us peer into the creative process behind a film, Kasalica demonstrates that the process of creation is a confused one. As we follow the director’s struggles, we cannot help but wonder whether the filmmaker himself experienced similar anxieties in bringing this very work to life.

You can find more unmissable films like these in our Best of Fest collections.

item.title: From “Back Alley Head Job” to SXSW Award-Winner: Lee Lawson on the Evolution of ‘Man Eating Pussy’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Lee Lawson discusses the practical effects and unexpected tenderness behind the provocative premise of her SXSW award-winning short, 'Man Eating Pussy'.
item.content:encoded:
Winner of the Midnight Short Special Jury Award at SXSW and recently screened as part of the BFI London Film Festival, Lee Lawson’s unforgettable short film Man Eating Pussy has made quite an impression on the festival circuit in 2026. With its provocative premise, striking practical effects and what Lawson describes as a “birth in reverse”, the film is certainly difficult to forget. However, beneath the body-horror lies something unexpectedly tender: a story about acceptance, vulnerability and the need for connection.

It’s to Lawson’s credit that instead of simply becoming an exercise in the grotesque, Man Eating Pussy evolves into something much more complex. With the short continuing to provoke discussion wherever it plays, we invited Lawson to join us on Directors Notes to not only discuss the origins behind the unique premise of her film, but also to dive into the practical effects needed to bring the film’s central character to life and the “spiritual valence” in exploring the connection between birth and death.

Welcome to Directors Notes, Lee. We’re so excited to dive into your truly unique short film today. I’m always reluctant to begin an interview by talking about inspiration, but with Man Eating Pussy, the premise is so unusual that it feels impossible to avoid. How would you describe the film to someone who hasn’t seen it and what was it about this story that made you want to bring it to the screen?

Hi! Thanks for having me! Yeah, I mean the logline for Man Eating Pussy is: a dying man meets with a sex worker seeking the ultimate release: a birth in reverse. And that hints at the act the film centres on, but doesn’t really capture the heart of it. I’ve often described the film as a mixture of Lost in Translation and Alien. Which is a brain tickle and gets a laugh, but I really do mean it.

I call ideas for films “divine inspiration bubbles” and I think they are a gift.

For me, Lost in Translation captures this brief moment of mutual recognition between two unlikely companions, both feeling estranged from their own lives. Their connection gives them room to consider who they are, to see themselves through someone else’s eyes. I fundamentally see MEP as a film about two people taking care of each other in highly specific ways. Two people taking care of each other in ways that only work if you really see the person you’re with. Alien (in addition to many essays’ worth of capitalism-critique) fuses sex and death and motherhood in a way that feels simultaneously like a violation of the body and also a visceral, almost logical extension of its capacities – I think because it makes explicit the violence of birth. So those are definitely touchstones.

I wanted to bring it to the screen because I couldn’t stop thinking about it. I call ideas for films “divine inspiration bubbles” and I think they are a gift. Once you have an idea that persists so much it becomes a place you can go to in your head it’s your responsibility to make it.

With such a visually memorable premise, I’m interested in how the story developed. Did the film begin with the image of Kitty and this unusual world, with the narrative growing from there, or did the story come first? And where did the idea of a “birth in reverse” originate?

The earliest germ of this story was a silly little piece of background action in a script about a space brothel. I was feeling very creatively stuck and I was listening to a lot of nightcore remixes while running. I just wanted to give myself permission to dream and think and be a little trashy and obvious. Sometimes I get bogged down with the desire to make films that feel important. Like real art. And wanting to do that is rarely the path to it.

On the way into this space brothel, one of the characters glimpses what I initially described as a “back alley head job” in their peripheral vision. Just this seedy act that happens before the main action of the story to set the tone. But the more I thought about it, the more I realized how potent the imagery was. That’s the thing about the body and what can be thought of as ‘body horror’. Yes, bodies are messy and base but anytime you invoke the architecture of birth and death and pleasure and connection, it’s hard for those images not to take on a spiritual valence, not to be interpreted in a million different ways. It’s just such rich terrain. The idea of a “birth in reverse” simply came from the struggle to find a more elegant way to describe this “back alley head job”. Because what is it if not a return to the womb?

Grace Glowicki gives a remarkable performance as Kitty, particularly given how much of her face is concealed throughout the film. How did Grace become involved and what was it about her that made you feel she was right for the role?

Grace is a fixture of the Toronto independent scene. She is such a force. I think I first saw her in Her Friend Adam and Tito and I was just in awe. I thought, “There’s an artist who can be so many things. She’s chameleonic and yet somehow, always fully herself.” She’s also an incredible physical performer. Capable of going to some truly strange places and creating gestural cinema that feels like a cartoon come to life but not silly; it’s hard to describe.

I had no track record, no funding at the time and no concept art but she was brave and signed on.

I got to meet her when I briefly worked as a 2nd AC on the set of The Heirloom. I’m talking 2 days. I had been developing the script for MEP and by this point Julian Richings and Black Spot FX were already attached. I guess I was confident enough to take a chance and send the script to her. At the time, it had a much more dommy/subby feel to it but the bones were there. And to my amazement, she said yes. I will always be eternally grateful for that. I had no track record, no funding at the time and no concept art but she was brave and signed on, which gave me one of the key tools I needed to make the film happen.

Most Popular

So much of Grace’s performance has to be communicated through physicality and voice rather than facial expression. How did you work with her to build Kitty’s character while working within those restrictions?

I didn’t have to work too much with Grace on the physicality. I think she just instinctively knew that what she was doing was mask work. That Kitty HAD to be alive in her body, especially her hands. We don’t think of prosthetics that way, but from a performance standpoint there is very little difference between classical Greek chorus masks and encasing your entire head in silicone.

We were also very lucky to have a CCA-funded research portion that allowed Grace and me to work with Monica Pavez of Black Spot FX. Simply getting to put on those earlier iterations of the prosthetic allowed us to put it through its paces. This allowed us to experiment with more threatening physicalities, for Grace to see what happened if she moved her jaw laterally, etc. It helped Monica figure out how to streamline the design and it helped me understand that with this piece we didn’t have to perform monstrosity. The image was already monstrous, so Kitty could be softer and still hold complexity and latent danger.

The practical makeup is such a defining element of the film. How did you approach creating Kitty’s appearance and what was the process of developing the final design?

There was a very early armature that I made from a life cast of a vulva. I won’t say whose but it was a really neat experiment. Pouring a material called Monster Clay into the mould created a malleable piece that I could then shape over an armature. It was really fascinating watching this sculptural version of a body part that is seen as inherently vulnerable being stretched over a head and fashioned into a face that could be read as monstrous and threatening.

Vulvas aren’t that ‘femme’. They’re messy and wiggly and uneven so the prettiness came from carving out a very delicate neck and the painting choices.

Then Monica ran with it and I simply gave notes. It should be said, Black Spot FX, which is run by Monica Pavez and Alexandra Anger, did the bodily prosthetics work for Crimes of the Future and The Shrouds. They are able to create the most unbelievable, visceral and yet beautiful pieces. I think we explored some versions that were a little more floral. Ultimately, it was about finding the balance between the fleshy, foldy-ness of the design and the delicateness, the high femininity of Kitty as a character. In a strange way, vulvas aren’t that ‘femme’. They’re messy and wiggly and uneven so the prettiness came from carving out a very delicate neck and the painting choices.

I also think a really interesting effect occurs where your brain just wants to map a face onto Kitty, so you use her ‘clit’ as an eye landmark. But the image vacillates back and forth between being a thing and being a person. I find that object/subject dialectic, or switcheroo, conceptually in harmony with the piece.

The film could very easily have treated its central premise as a visual spectacle, but instead there’s a surprising tenderness to the relationship between Kitty and Freddie. What did you want the audience to feel towards these two characters and how important was it to you that their interaction retained a sense of humanity?

This dovetails beautifully with the whole object/subject piece from the previous question. MEP’s characters, Kitty and Freddie, are people that the world tends to misunderstand and dehumanize: as a sex worker, hell, as a woman, Kitty is interpreted as an object of pleasure to be used/transacted with. Whereas Freddie, as an elderly man at the end of his life, is likely to be ignored and no longer be seen as a full human being with sexual or romantic needs. Or worse, to be seen as a ‘creepy old man’ by default. I hoped the audience would feel tenderness towards both of them. I hoped the audience would see the person inside whatever assumptions they might bring. I think sex work describes a complicated spectrum of interactions, but I do believe there is dignity in taking care of another person. I also believe that taking care of people so often means taking care of their bodies.

It was so important to me that Kitty subverted the idea of being a ‘man eating pussy’. The title invokes this monstrous literal personification of pussy (or a man engaged in cunnilingus) and it is the starting point for how we see her. Getting to know her takes us somewhere more human and not just in a pretentious, “I want the audience to see her as a subject rather than an object” way. But also in a deglamourizing sense, an anti-fantasy sense? There’s a line where Kitty talks about how when she gets her nails done she always goes to the same girl, and that it’s nice to have someone take care of you. I intended for that to be something Kitty says to Freddie to let him know that she doesn’t judge him, that she’s giving him permission to ask for what he wants/needs.

The idea of her as “the literal personification of pussy” starts to break down the moment you imagine her doing normal human things.

But I also kind of love the idea of Kitty just sitting in a nail salon, soaking her fingertips and pouring her heart out to her manicurist. The mundanity of that is funny, but it also lets us imagine her outside of the artifice she adopts to be her clients’ fantasies. She has her own life, her own needs, someone she goes to for care. The idea of her as “the literal personification of pussy” starts to break down the moment you imagine her doing normal human things. I could describe her as the fusion of the virgin and the madonna and the whore. That’s the fancy way of putting it, but she’s also just a girl who gets acrylics that make her happy.

As for Freddie, I hope the audience feels for him, loves him even. The way I love him. I hope they can see the superimposition of the older dying man and the little boy who yearns for his mother and the sexually viable man who longs for pleasure too. I hope they see him not as a creepy old man, but as someone whose desire holds a need for comfort, for safety, for someone to take care of him. I don’t think you get to have that without treating both characters gently and letting them be vulnerable.

Although much of the film takes place inside this one room, you create a strong sense that there’s a much larger world beyond the window. How much thought went into developing the universe in which Man Eating Pussy takes place and how did you and your production team establish that world without taking attention away from the central relationship?

This is a tricky one, because I know the backstory of the type of being Kitty is, including that she has many sisters and how they move through the world, how they’re thought of. However, I don’t know that any of that is relevant to the story and the character interactions. So if anything, I didn’t try to nod to it beyond letting it inform Kitty’s characterization. Instead, I worked with Ashley Frederick, the film’s production designer, to create a ‘cocoon’ of sorts.

It was important to me that the hallway felt like a passage/portal away from the world. That’s also why the diegetic sound of the music pumping through the walls fades away. It’s a very romantic notion: the idea that once Kitty and Freddie are in the room together, they’re the only people that exist. Another very Lost in Translation element, I suppose.

The cinematography has a wonderfully unobtrusive quality. Rather than turning the unusual premise into something that feels voyeuristic or grotesque, the camera allows us to become invested in Kitty and Freddie. How did you work with your cinematographer to establish that visual approach? And what camera/lenses did you use to achieve the look?

Gabriela Osio Vanden shot MEP. In addition to being an incredible DOP, she’s an incredibly accomplished documentarian (everyone has to go watch Nuisance Bear). I think there were the obvious technical choices, like, higher-contrast lenses for the low-light portions, trying to sculpt Kitty’s face using the specular highlights that let you map its contours. Those were Panavision Panaspeeds. And then Gabi’s choice to use really beautiful low-contrast glass with these incredible chromatic flares for the moment when the sun is coming up behind the two characters (Panavision Ultraspeeds).

There are those technical elements but then there’s that ineffable thing of Gabi’s ability to ‘breathe with her subjects’. She knows when to follow and when to give space. The film was really precisely storyboarded because I needed to limit the amount of time that we saw Kitty’s face head-on because of the cost of animating her speech, but within that structure, Gabi found so much life. We also used an Alexa 35, which was wonderful because we could really just have the lower-light environments/moments be that way. There was no need to expose brighter and then bring it down in the grade. I think this makes a huge difference, tonally, to the actors.

The film was really precisely storyboarded because I needed to limit the amount of time that we saw Kitty’s face head-on because of the cost of animating her speech.

The editing has a similarly restrained quality. We get a real sense of time passing within the room, but the film never feels hurried. What were you looking for when it came to the rhythm of the edit and again, can you provide a little technical insight into the post-production – how long did it take, what software did you cut on?

The edit was largely defined by two factors: First, the cost associated with showing Kitty’s face, because the articulation of her lips had to be painstakingly animated by the incredible Geoff Sayer of Sayer VFX. He and Scott Riopelle did such beautiful work, but because of the VFX, every time we show her speaking with her face straight on, it’s a very intentional choice. Second, my desire to, as much as possible, hold Kitty and Freddie in 2-shots where we feel both of them. This keeps the energy flowing back and forth between Julian and Grace alive and intact.

So much of Kitty is synthetic; it felt necessary to privilege shots where they read as just two people sitting on a bed, letting their guards down in real time. This helps temper the fantasy with real human interaction and I think the majority of the rhythm emerged naturally from that. That was also shaped by my desire for Kitty and Freddie to be able to watch one last sunrise together. To facilitate that, we had to calibrate the rising light levels throughout the film. That was something that Sam Holling, the film’s gaffer, and Clinton Homuth, the film’s colourist, worked on in tandem, but at different stages. It’s funny, actually, that the gaffer and the colourist are a team that never meet.

Dan Haack, who edited MEP, also shaped the pacing through the way he built the temp sound. Dan has the most incredible facility with temp music, and he always has a hand in shaping the sonic worlds of my films. I actively have to battle temp lock, because he so often understands the space between what the image gives us and the emotional work the music will eventually have to do. We edited for two months I think? Dan uses Premiere.

One screening can have people laughing hysterically while another can be pin-drop silent.

Man Eating Pussy has enjoyed an impressive festival run. Given how unusual the film is, I’m curious about the response you’ve had from audiences. Have there been particular reactions, questions or interpretations that have surprised you?

I think its festival run is largely attributable to the fact that it can be read in a few different ways. Obviously it’s been embraced by the genre community, which I am so deeply grateful for. The fantastic film community is the nicest film community. Really and truly, if you’re ever feeling out of place at a film festival, head to the genre events/centre and they’ll always make sure everyone is included. But overall, genre audiences tend to laugh and enjoy MEP’s more bodily pleasures, though I think it doesn’t go quite as hard as many dyed-in-the-wool horror fans would like to see a creature feature go. They often wish it was scarier. That said, they still meet it where it’s at and are so welcoming.

When it’s featured in an experimental program, the room is very quiet and it’s neat to experience those audiences navigating it from a more perhaps spiritual or conceptual vantage point. I think it’s that range, really, that’s so interesting. One screening can have people laughing hysterically while another can be pin-drop silent, but then elicit Instagram message novels about the image schema of the piece. I love both!

Thanks so much for taking the time to talk to us, Lee. Before we wrap up, do you have any upcoming projects you’re excited to tell us about?

Thank you for chatting with me! It’s so lovely to get to go in depth into the process and construction. I actually just wrapped my latest short, Polycepolis, and we’re now in post on it. It’s an exploration of coupledom through a neurodivergent lens, putting pairs of performers into a single, tandem suit. It’s my attempt to figure out what it means to navigate your life through the needs of another person, and it’s going to be a fun one to put together! I’m also developing my debut feature, which is going to be a big step forward.

And finally, this is a question we ask all our featured filmmakers: what’s one short film by another filmmaker that you’d recommend to the Directors Notes audience and why?

Ohhh, I saw a stop-motion animation called The End by Niki Lindroth von Bahr recently that blew me away. It features poetic, existential musings from animals at an airport. Just brilliant.

item.title: Max Clendaniel Wields a Cheesy Horror Prop as an Ego-Shattering Weapon in Improvised Comedy ‘Dummy’
item.dc:creator: Mark Brennan
item.description: Max Clendaniel's improv comedy magnifies the fine line between an actor's vanity & their justifiable concerns about how a director depicts them onscreen.
item.content:encoded:
It’s a well-known fact that actors’ egos can be very fragile. This is hardly surprising, considering how exposing their work can be: performing in front of fellow cast members and crew, pouring their own emotions and experiences into their portrayals, and having those performances captured on film forever, then screened for audiences everywhere. They have to trust their director and surrender themselves to a storytelling vision in which they hope to play an integral part, without being made to look foolish in the process. Max Clendaniel’s Dummy takes this notion and cranks it up to eleven. In this short comedy, an earnest performer comes face to face with a laughably grotesque fake body double, sending him into an existential and career-ending crisis when he cannot accept that anyone might believe the dummy looks like him. Clendaniel talks to Directors Notes about creating his largely improvised story, working with the three principal cast members who bring it to life, building the world of the film on a shoestring budget, and designing and constructing the inanimate lead character who serves as the catalyst for the ensuing chaos.

Congratulations on Dummy, it’s a brilliantly entertaining short. Where did the idea come from to have an actor so appalled by his prop-double that he’s willing to take its place?

Phew! I’m so pleased to hear you enjoyed it! I’ve always been a fan of Christopher Guest films and really wanted to make something that was heavily improvised. For my other projects, I usually have every shot and line planned out in my head, so the idea of keeping things loose and unexpected was both freeing and terrifying. As this was a little different to how I’d usually structure my comedies, it’s a relief to hear at least one person found it funny.

Seeing bad dummies in movies can immediately turn the darkest film into a comedy.

When I want junk food for the brain I’ll put on a cheesy horror film because sometimes they are unintentionally my favourite comedies. And that was definitely the case with Lucio Fulci’s Don’t Torture a Duckling. For every dead body they used the same terrible ventriloquist puppet, even though it didn’t look anything like the actors – or even remotely human. Seeing bad dummies in movies can immediately turn the darkest film into a comedy. You’re not expecting it to be so poorly made so instead of a jump scare, it’s like a jump joke.

Off the back of this, I started thinking about how much I would have loved to have been a fly on the wall when they brought that dummy to set and what the cast’s reaction to it would have been. Then I tried to picture it from the actor’s POV and how offended I’d be if someone thought I looked anything like the stunt dummy. So, this short came from watching a bad movie really. Since then I’ve definitely lied to myself that watching something terrible is considered research because who knows what will come from it?

Jordan Brookes is pitch-perfect as the actor whose good nature, insecurity and vanity collide to grizzly effect. What brought him to the project and what was the collaboration before and during the shoot?

I first worked with Jordan on a music video where he had to dress as a mermaid. He didn’t know me at all but without any questions he put on a tail and swam on a bed. His dedication to every role is why I always have him top of mind for projects because I know I can throw anything at him and he’ll nail it. Leading up to production of Dummy, I shot Jordan’s show, Fontanelle and it was honestly the funniest gig I’d ever seen. A surreal, dark theme hidden behind the jolly veneer of a musical. Seeing that show made me realise Jordan is brilliant at finding the balance between comedy and pain that I think works well in something as twisted as Dummy.

The only thing I wanted Jordan to follow script-wise was the beginning and end as I liked the idea of him saying the same lines but with different context.

For this shoot I wanted him be unleashed to his full potential so when I wrote the script I said he could improvise the middle section as long as he hit the story beats to keep the plot moving along. The only thing I wanted Jordan to follow script-wise was the beginning and end, as I liked the idea of him saying the same lines but with different context.

Most Popular

Brookes is supported by Poppy Hillstead and Nim Odedra. Due to the improvisational nature of the film, what was the collaboration like between all three of them?

Since I’ve never directed something with so much improv I wanted to make sure I could rely on a cast with strong improvisational skills. Jordan and Poppy work together a lot and their chemistry is just glorious. The stuff they can say to each other without cracking a smile blows my mind. Then I always bring Nim on board to make things funnier. She can take a nothing role and give it so much life. And she has some of my favourite moments in the short and it was all down to her strange noggin.

So, the middle section of the short is just them playing around, adapting the script I had in place and then making sure I could capture every decision they made across four cameras at once. The benefit of having it take place on a film set is that cameras can be in the shot and filming another angle at the same time. Every photo of me from that shoot, I’m smiling because I got to enjoy their process of making jokes up on the spot and I never knew where they’d take it next.

The benefit of having it take place on a film set is that cameras can be in the shot and filming another angle at the same time.

The titular Dummy is an obvious scene-stealer. Can you tell us about how the final design for it came about and how the physical prop was made?

The dummy went through so many phases before settling on the right level of weird. I had a side story that hinted the dummy might actually be alive, but it’s never addressed, so every so often it’d gurgle and leak. Originally, I thought making it look creepily realistic in an ‘uncanny valley’ sort of way might be funniest but then I realised it had to be so ridiculous the audience was always on the side of the actor from the beginning. Plus, having it too realistic was just SO creepy and it diluted the comedy.

With this new direction in mind, I redesigned the dummy to look more innocent and cute. So I started with baby features like the completely round head, little curl in the front and the tiny milk tooth. Then I gave it the eyes of a possum and the nose from the creatures in The Brood. Last minute I added ear penises as an extreme feature which Jordan could focus on in his improv if he wanted to. Turns out he did! Even on the day we kept changing elements of the dummy. The penises looked way too real and I was worried it would get banned online so we just kept adding an insane amount of pubes to hide it. Seeing the wisps of hair that close to Jordan’s mouth really sends a shiver down my spine whenever I see it.

The production design ensures the singular space is immersive to both the world of the story and that story being told within the film. Was the newspaper-lined ‘murder room’ something you always had in mind?

I wanted the film to have two very defined spaces to contrast the surreal ‘film world’ vs the unglamorous reality on the other side. I feel like when you see BTS on film sets they always romanticise the day (this film is definitely guilty of that as well), of crew members caught mid-action doing something cool or collaborating with a happy cast member. They rarely show the sweaty director stress-eating fried chicken in a dark corner of the room looking at the rushes while the producer chimney vapes trying to keep everything from catching fire. So, having the heightened, movie world contrasted against the underwhelming, stress-filled set world added to the comedy for me.

For the murder room, I set the movie scene in an environment I thought I could make interesting for very little money. In the past I’ve used cheap materials like crate paper, bottles or balloons and by just layering them hundreds of times over it suddenly looks visually striking. So, by glueing hundreds of sheets of newspaper onto the set walls I can effectively make that whole space look distinct for about £30.

There’s a music cue that comes in when Jason decides he’s going to replace the Dummy. Can you tell us about the creative choice behind both the cue and the piece of music that you went for?

Jordan and I worked on his character to show a (somewhat) plausible reason to sacrifice himself. The plot is already so ridiculous but we tried to show his character’s ego clash with his need for people to like him. After being unable to hide his disdain for the dummy, he has a moment of realisation that he’s slowing down production and everyone is annoyed with him. So he comes to terms with the fact there’s only one option where he can get the film back on track and also not use the dummy. I felt that moment needed a minute to breathe to give Jordan a chance to convey this, so the music highlights his reflection and acceptance of his fate. If we sped through that section it might have felt too random for an already nonsensical story.

As Dummy was improvisational in execution, how did this experience compare to your work on other projects which were far more prescriptive?

It was a huge challenge! I was definitely nervous because a lot of my work is a balancing act of being funny and fucked up, so I have to control so much of my comedy to get the right tone. Also, I like to have a lot of technical shots in my films as there’s something funny to me about putting so much care into something so dumb. But with this, the DOP had to keep on his toes and find moments as the cast moved around a lot, so it had more of a documentary feel to it. Thankfully, we filmed on four cameras at once, which managed to cover us but definitely made it trickier.

I think if I did it again I’d have it lit more evenly to make sure we were covered safely from all angles, no matter where they moved to. There were a few hot spots that work if they stayed in one place but not as well when they moved around. But that’s what I love about trying new things and being more ambitious with each project. Even if you make mistakes you become a better filmmaker.

To be honest, this was a really hard movie to cut down because it was a balance of knowing when you needed a joke or when you had to move on.

What was your personal favourite piece of improv in the film and why?

Everyone had a shining moment for sure. Nim’s line, “So if we can clear the dummy please, the really ugly one… it’s the one sat down”, followed by Jordan reacting to that last minute insult is why I wanted this to be improvised. I couldn’t have written such a wonderfully mean comment like that. Then Jordan finally snapping at Nim saying, “Yeah, but fuck off, because it doesn’t,” gets the biggest laugh every time. Then Poppy’s line, “That’s just lobe and cartilage” when defending the penis ears is said so seriously, it kills me. To be honest, this was a really hard movie to cut down because it was a balance of knowing when you needed a joke or when you had to move on. I couldn’t kill my darlings so I’m glad I got Casey Boyle to be the bad cop and edit it down to a pace that was to the benefit of the film.

What’s next for you?

I’m just wrapping up post on my new short, Scrape, which will be done by the end of this month. It’s definitely more of a drama but because a lot of my work has elements of pathos and horror it was an easy transition to make. Thanks to Julie Bower’s incredible script it feels like a massive step up. We had stunts, special effects and a lot of access to locations, so I’ve felt like a kid in a toy store with all the new, fun things to play with. I can’t thank her enough for getting me on board to bring her twisted idea to life.

Other than that, I’m pushing a pilot I co-wrote with Sam Bailey (not the X-Factor winner) to any companies that’ll listen and prepping a very personal, very strange documentary that I was able to shape through NFTS earlier this year. Finally, I just finished a 1st draft of a feature I’d really love to make, which is a heightened version of the intensely stressful three weeks I had getting power of attorney over my mother earlier this year. It’s a comedy, I swear.

And finally, what short film by another filmmaker would you recommend to the Directors Notes community and why?

It has to be [WeAreDN Awards winner] Tell Me Where I’m Going Wrong by Kyle Jon Shepherd. I’ve had the pleasure of having numerous pints with Kyle and the pleasure of seeing this film at various screenings and it just gets better each time (as does Kyle after a few pints). I went to one screening with my cousin where it was playing alongside a sketch I made and she sooooo clearly preferred Kyle’s short to mine. I couldn’t help but laugh.

item.title: Who Gets Believed? Susan Wokoma Confronts the Adultification of Black Children in ‘Dark Skin Bruises Differently’
item.dc:creator: Mark Brennan
item.description: Drawing on her childhood, Susan Wokoma writes, directs and stars as a teacher torn between instinct and complicity in a staffroom deciding a girl’s fate.
item.content:encoded:
Who’d be a teacher? It’s a famously underpaid, undervalued and overworked profession, wherever you are in the world. It’s also one rife with emotional and ethical minefields, particularly when dealing with children who may be in your classroom but are not in your care or custody. Actor, writer and comedian Susan Wokoma adds another string to her bow as director for Dark Skin Bruises Differently. The emotive short explores the blurring of boundaries between well-meaning teachers and struggling students, alongside the racial stereotyping and predetermined expectations faced by people of colour in the education system. Drawing on her own childhood experiences and inspired in part by a tragic, high-profile child murder case, Wokoma joins us for Dark Skin Bruises Differently’s premiere today and talks to Directors Notes about producing and directing her short drama while also taking the lead acting role. We also discuss how she assembled her antagonistic ensemble, finding her own shining child star to play the role at the heart of the story, the London exhibition that informed the film’s visual language, and the risks she was willing to take to bring it all to the screen.

Dark Skin Bruises Differently is an amalgam of your own childhood experiences and being incredibly mindful of the Victoria Climbié abuse and murder case here in the UK. What drew you to tell this story and how did you approach writing it?

The Victoria Climbé murder, it’s haunted me since I was a little girl and I wanted to explore some of the reasons why a young girl in danger might not get saved. Or be believed. During her life in Britain, Victoria was known to four local authorities (four social services departments and three housing departments), two child protection police teams, two hospitals, an NSPCC centre, and a few local churches and yet not one of those authorities saved her life.

The case has always haunted me but it wasn’t until I became an adult and started discussing instances that occurred in my childhood with other black women that I realised why it especially resonated – there was a commonality of a particular experience between us all and that experience was the ‘adultification’ of black children. Be it at home, at school, in a newsagents or Woolworths at the weekend, presumed misbehaviour was something we constantly faced, innocence was rarely assumed and protection (at worst) was never offered. The ‘Strong Black Woman’ trope starts in childhood it seemed. I have wanted to explore the very notion of belief for a long time now – who do we believe and why? Can advantages be found in who we easily believe and who we don’t? What happens when this knowledge of ‘adultification’ is weaponised by people who really should know better?

I have wanted to explore the very notion of belief for a long time now – who do we believe and why?

I have wanted to write about the ‘adultafication’ of black children for a very long time but I just wasn’t sure how much of my own ‘adultification’ I wanted to really explore. You see it all the time – the young black girl in a London secondary school that was strip searched a couple of years ago and even the way Nolan Wells’ mother had to correct a reporter from describing her 18 year old son as a man. Coming of Age movies have always been my favourite kind, but now I’m 38, I am realising that my attraction to them was because I had to grow up very, very fast. It’s almost like science fiction to me. This film was always going to be a personal pivot and so I was determined to avoid melodrama and cliché. It says a hell of a lot without saying too much and that’s always how I was going to approach this story.

As a producer on the film, alongside Maëva Demurger, what was the process needed to bring that script to the screen, challenges faced, and how long did that process take?

Well, I wrote it in a couple of days. I’d just had my directorial debut feature completely fall apart and I needed to make something, fast. The main hurdle to making anything is funding so I knew from the jump that I would finance it myself. Maëva I’ve known for over a decade and knew she was a tremendous producer who just gets shit done. I presented her with how much I had, which was £10k and the script. She obviously didn’t love the budget (lol) but she truly fell in love with the script and so we set about contacting everyone we knew and trusted and loved. From me first approaching Maëva with the script to the 2 day shoot was all in all 5 months. Completely and utterly incredible.

Most Popular

My dear friend Deborah Frances-White came on as an EP with an extra £2k and we were away. Post took longer, another 6 months, but everything was more or less favours and people working around their actual paid jobs. 13 months after sending Maëva the script, we were submitting to festivals. It was an electric feeling and I loved every single minute of it. The hardest challenge was not having an edit budget but again, we kept meeting people who believed in the story and were willing to go old school and just HELP. I’m sure Maëva could tick off a litany of challenges but honestly, it was the smoothest creative process I’ve had as a writer and producer and director – all thanks to Maëva.

As well as writing and directing, you also star in the film. Was that always your intention and what was it like juggling all those roles?

In the unwritten version in my head, Ms Lawson was white because the real ‘Ms Lawson’ was white. It wasn’t until I sat down to write it that I thought actually it could be interesting if there was an element of self-betrayal in how Ms Lawson saw a bit of herself in young Maria – and the story opened up in a big way. So much more layered and interesting. I found juggling all the roles quite easy.

Doing so much comedy makes you very bloody skilled at making decisions and improvising – especially as a woman where you’ll often get sidelined in comedies in favour of the boys’ club. You end up self-directing, self-noting and being a bit of a Swiss Army knife of a performer. But kudos to Maëva, who is a very direct and transparent producer, which I LOVE. It’s super rare. If there was something I didn’t understand when it came to the producing, she’d break it down. She also knew EXACTLY when to take me off the email thread!

It wasn’t until I sat down to write it that I thought actually it could be interesting if there was an element of self-betrayal in how Ms Lawson saw a bit of herself in young Maria.

You have a brilliantly antagonistic ensemble cast of teachers. How did you go about casting them and working with them in rehearsals/on set?

All the adults I knew – Zainab Hasan, I met 10 years ago on a play in New York and think she’s one of the most beautiful understated screen actors. Charlotte Randle is a close friend who again I’m a big fan of and just knew she’d body the role. Leo Bill is one of our finest actors who also happens to be married to Maëva, which was very kind of them to come as a pair! Nah, honestly, he got the heart and politics of the film straight away and just leaned in in such a profound way. Stephanie Cole, our main antagonist, is a childhood friend of mine who I did youth theatre with in Deptford. However, as a result of a litany of serious chronic illnesses, didn’t become an actor. I’ve always loved her as an actor and I thought now is my moment – the lovely thing about producing your own film is money people can’t tell you shit.

The way I’ve heard producers talk about so-called bankable actors – even crew – would make you vomit. I had a female producer once say I should choose a particular male DOP cos he was sexy. What does sexiness have to do with how you fucking shoot something? Honestly, if shorts aren’t the space to take risks, then when can you? So, Steph was in. The final ingredient was finding our child actor to play Maria. This is where the fantastic Tamsyn Manson, our casting director came in and found a corker!

The lovely thing about producing your own film is money people can’t tell you shit.

Of course, Moizelle Olaleye is quietly heartbreaking as Maria. How did you cast her and what was it like directing a child actor?

We sent out a call for self-tapes which I just bloody hate because it’s not the same as being in a room. However, with school and whatnot, it made sense to let these young performers record in their own time. Tamsyn, Maëva and I then whittled this number down to, I think, 4 actresses to meet and Moizelle just… had it. Being a child on TV and a child actor, the key is there’s just a magic to it. There’s an instinct to how a fantastic child actor actualises story and you’ve got to step out of the way of it.

As for directing a child, first and foremost they must feel safe and free. I remember telling the crew before she arrived that we have to treat this like a day at Disneyland for her. I don’t want her to even smell a drop of stress and Moizelle just glided. We are very, very lucky. She makes the film. Thank you Tamsyn!

The film was visually inspired by the Lagos, Peckham, Repeat: Pilgrimage to the Lakes exhibition at the South London Gallery. What about that aesthetic inspired you and how did you go about creating that with your cinematographer?

Goodness, it was such a gorgeous exhibition – there was such a sense of archived familiarity to it. Extremely personal and grainy, with so much care given to how dark skin was captured. This was a 2 day shoot, shot with an Alexa 35 on digital by Ben Cotgrove, our DOP, who was positively fizzing with excitement when I shared the images with him and it’s definitely what I want to push when we make the feature.

A sparsity in the soundscape lets the words of the teachers and the sound of the school fill the void, with only a touch of score at the end of the film. What was the creative choice to keep music to a minimum throughout?

Music is so powerful in film – all you’ve got to do is compare the film Drive with its original soundtrack vs the Zane Lowe reworking. It’s not the same film. So, in lieu of a massive budget, I didn’t want to crowbar in music that I couldn’t agonise over for months and months. That was my original thinking. Then I thought about the purposeful economical use of Maria – the fact we hear so much about her but only hear her actual voice right at the end. Then I thought, “Aha! We hear children at the end!” That’s where Abide With Me over the end credits happened. We actually used the choir of the school we shot in to sing the hymn so big thank you to Emmanuel Church of England Primary School!

I hope this film challenges people and also encourages audiences to examine their own biases and the ripples they might cause.

What has the response to the film been like, particularly from those who have had similar childhood experiences to yours and/or those working in the education system currently?

It’s been overwhelming – particularly during our festival run. To have something live in your mind and body and then for it to be received by people who get it and believe it is a sensation I will never ever get used to. A lot of people also found it frustrating, which is chef’s kiss – I wanted people to leave frustrated, confronted and uncomfortable. A job well done. I hope this film challenges people and also encourages audiences to examine their own biases and the ripples they might cause.

What’s next for you?

I continue the balance of writing and acting because let’s face it, very few people can afford to live in London with one job! But now our festival run is finished, it’s time to lock in and make the feature of Dark Skin – very exciting!

What other short film would you recommend to the Directors Notes community and why?

Shagbands by Luna Carmoon because I am a huge over 90s/2000s coming of age films.

item.title: Robert Piel’s ‘The Lap’ Harvests the Unspoken Fears and Desires Behind a Teenage Struggle for Power
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: With only 4 days, expired 35mm stock and an apple harvest dictated schedule, Robert Piel learned to trust instinct over coverage for his coming of age drama.
item.content:encoded:
Certain feelings, those disruptive, explosive and inexplicable ones we feel in our early teens, are not always easy to capture on camera – nonetheless, their universality means they can fit any location or time period. Autumn 1913, and the cold is settling over the Lithuanian countryside as the harvest draws to a close. For the young farmhand at the centre of Robert Piel’s graduate short, The Lap (Der Schoß), the end of the season means another departure. He has always moved from family to family, surrounded by people yet never belonging anywhere, but for the first time that inevitable leaving is something he can’t quite make peace with. What follows is a coming-of-age drama in which a fragile friendship is slowly misread as a power struggle, threatening to destroy the human connection between two teenagers on the edge of adulthood. Neither is cast as hero or villain. Both are victims of their circumstances, grappling with an internal transformation they lack the words to express.

Piel, who began his film studies at Fachhochschule Dortmund intending to become a cinematographer, shot The Lap with DOP Kaspar Hornikel over just four days in the Žemaitija region on expired 35mm Fujifilm stock with vintage lenses, giving the film the tactile feel of a 1960s or 70s historical drama. Ahead of today’s premiere, we spoke to Piel about using the period setting as a filter for emotions that might feel too personal in a contemporary story, why the ending emerged naturally from his characters rather than being imposed on them, and working with sound designer and composer Ole Brandt to blur the line between reality and a subconscious fear of exile.

You describe wanting the film to have an “archaic rawness” while still showing very vulnerable moments between the characters. I think that is particularly true towards the ending scene. So let’s start from the end! When did you know that your film would develop towards that direction?

It was clear to me from the beginning that I wanted to tell a coming-of-age story. For me, growing up is connected to a real tumult of feelings. Characters who are going through that transition into adulthood have a very vulnerable side, which they often try to hide. And quite often, that tension eventually results in an emotional outburst. As I developed the characters, I wanted to give both of them a certain duality. Neither should be a clear hero or antagonist. They are both victims of their circumstances, while at the same time struggling with an internal transformation. Once I understood who these characters were, the ending felt like a natural consequence of that development rather than a direction I had imposed on the story from the outside.

It was clear to me from the beginning that I wanted to tell a coming-of-age story. For me, growing up is connected to a real tumult of feelings.

The Lap is set in the past, but you describe historical drama as a way of exploring emotions while still drawing parallels with the present. What kind of possibilities do you think this strategy allows? What are the contemporary elements that you wanted to include in this film?

I believe this strategy creates a certain form of abstraction. It’s almost like a filter that allows me to approach topics or emotions that might feel too personal if they were told in a contemporary setting. I also find it fascinating that we can still relate to so many ancient stories and myths. Existential struggles have always been there, and probably always will be. In a way, making a period piece is an attempt to create something timeless — to free the story, at least to some degree, from the specific circumstances of contemporary society. At the same time, I feel that conflicts over power and influence are becoming increasingly present in our world. That is something that has occupied me for a long time. With The Lap, I wanted to explore these larger dynamics on a very intimate scale, by depicting a struggle for power between two teenagers.

You’ve mentioned wanting to make a film that conveys “a somewhat elusive sense of impending change and a longing for security,” and that it quickly became clear you wanted to explore “the power dynamics between two characters in an age of transformation.” How did these ideas come together for you and in what way do you think the final version of The Lap fulfils them?

Once I realised that the protagonist was a farmhand — someone who moves from family to family and is constantly surrounded by people, but never really has a home of his own — it became clear to me that he would have a deep, perhaps even unconscious desire for security and a sense of belonging. When I was that age, I found it difficult to express my feelings. If you struggle with that, it often reveals itself indirectly, particularly in the way you interact with other people. Sometimes it can result in an outburst of emotions.

While developing the characters, these two ideas — the longing for security and the difficulty of expressing what you feel — naturally began to inform each other. With The Lap, I wanted the audience to experience the protagonist’s state of mind rather than have the thematic ideas explained to them verbally. For me, the final version of the film carries a feeling of unease and a tumult of suppressed feelings, fears, and desires. I hope the audience can connect with that on their own terms.

Most Popular

Your collaboration with your Lithuanian wife Inga Aleknaviciute-Piel seems to have been fundamental to the project, from the screenplay all the way through production design and location choices, with Lithuania becoming more than simply a location for the film. Did you ever consider how different the short would have been if you shot it somewhere else?

I haven’t really thought about it in those terms. In a way, I see the story as existential and universal, so it could probably take place in many different parts of the world. Every country has its own beautiful corners and a rich folklore, and I think the film would inevitably be shaped by whichever culture it was made in. In this case, though, I knew quite early on what kind of aesthetic I was looking for and where I could find it. Lithuania became an important part of the film not simply because we happened to shoot there, but because its landscapes, architecture, and cultural history naturally became intertwined with the story.

You had only four days to shoot the film, and even the apple harvest helped determine the schedule. How does working under that kind of extreme limitation affect your directing? Does having very little time force you to become more instinctive, or does it make the preparation beforehand even more important? Have you run across any significant cuts that have affected the editing?
