The limited shooting time required an enormous amount of concentration from everyone involved. From the very beginning of the shoot, it became clear how valuable it had been to photograph all the shots during our location recces. We already had a very clear idea of what we needed, which allowed us to move through the days quite efficiently. But having limited time definitely forces me to be more instinctive as well. Unexpected problems always occur, and with such a tight schedule you have to find solutions quickly. I actually quite like that aspect of filmmaking — when there isn’t enough time to overthink everything.

We didn’t have to make any significant cuts. At the beginning, I was a little worried that we would run out of film stock, but in the end it worked out well. We shot very little coverage, so the final edit is quite close to the script. Of course, I think there can be real value in discovering an unexpected shot during filming. It can give the editor an interesting new possibility. But we simply didn’t have the time for that kind of experimentation on this shoot. I don’t think the film necessarily would have benefited from more coverage, but something I would really like to try one day is having the time and budget for an extensive rehearsal period before principal photography. I’d love to explore scenes and ideas together with the actors without constantly looking at the clock. Maybe it’s a slightly romanticised idea, but the thought of having enough space for experimentation, mistakes, and a real deep dive into the characters together with the actors is very appealing to me.

We chose the 1.66:1 aspect ratio for several reasons. I like the way it resembles the proportions of historical paintings. At the same time, it is wide enough to place the characters within the landscape, but narrow enough to isolate them visually and give the individual shots a certain intimacy.

You usually use 16mm and prefer film over digital, and here you chose to shoot on expired 35mm stock, vintage lenses and a 1.66:1 aspect ratio. What was your specific camera setup and why was it the right choice for this particular story?

For this particular film, I wanted to portray the rural environment as naturally as possible. I love the aesthetic of films like Come and See by Elem Klimov or Days of Heaven by Terrence Malick, where the exteriors are largely shaped by available light. I especially love the way celluloid captures the earthy tones and textures of nature. And, to be completely honest, I sometimes find the very clean look of contemporary period films difficult to believe. The films I grew up watching were shot on film, and they inevitably shaped the way I see cinema. The period pieces I admire tend to go hand in hand with a certain grittiness, rich textures, and small imperfections. That felt much closer to the world I wanted to create with The Lap. The film was shot on an Arri Arricam Studio (3-perf), Bausch & Lomb Super Baltar Lenses and Zeiss Master Prime Lenses (for night scenes). We chose the 1.66:1 aspect ratio for several reasons. I like the way it resembles the proportions of historical paintings. At the same time, it is wide enough to place the characters within the landscape, but narrow enough to isolate them visually and give the individual shots a certain intimacy.

Your background in cinematography means you naturally approach filmmaking through images and visual language. How does that visual instinct shape the way you develop a character or build a story? Do you sometimes find yourself discovering narrative through images rather than the other way around?

Yes, definitely. A story idea often starts for me with a single image, a visual idea, or a location. But once that initial idea for the story or characters has taken shape, I try to take a step back and temporarily forget about the visuals. Sometimes that is difficult for me, but I believe that focusing on the narrative is at the core of making a good film. Once there is a strong story as a foundation, the plot and the film’s form become equally important to me. I think the interesting part is finding a balance between what the story needs and how the film can express it visually. My background in cinematography naturally makes me think in images, but I don’t want the visual language to dictate the story. Ideally, the two should develop together.

You talk about exploring the boundary between reality and the subconscious fear of exile. That’s a deeply psychological idea to bring into a historical drama. How did you work with your sound designer Ole Brandt to convey that uncertainty?

From the beginning, we knew that off-screen sound would play an important role in creating a sense of uncertainty and expanding the world beyond what we actually see on screen. One of the more exciting challenges was finding the transition from a seemingly naturalistic scene into something more dreamlike and subjectively surreal. We wanted the sound to subtly change the audience’s perception of what was happening without making the shift too explicit. It was particularly helpful that Ole also composed the music for the film, which was intended to reflect the protagonist’s inner life. We wanted the sound design and the music to interact and gradually convey his emotional state. But our aim was to do this in a minimal and almost unconscious way, rather than using sound to tell the audience exactly what to feel.

You’re currently developing a social-realist short as well as two features, including another period piece. Could you tell us more about that?

I like films of all kinds, so it feels very liberating to me to be working on projects in different genres at the same time. In a strange way, I think the projects benefit from each other. If I reach a point where I feel stuck on one project, I can move on to another one. Most of the time, that helps me to approach the original problem from a different perspective. I hope to shoot my social-realist short film SWARM (working title) in the spring or early summer of next year. I’m planning to shoot it in my home region, the Ruhr district.

I often feel that aspiring filmmakers see short films primarily as a first step towards making features, or almost as a kind of demo reel. To me, they are much more than that. Short film is an independent art form, and I think it is an amazing way to develop your skills, your style, and your perspective. It requires a real economy of storytelling and offers a great space for experimentation. Developing a feature and getting it financed can take a long time, and I think short films are a wonderful way to keep telling stories in the meantime. My wife Inga and I have also recently founded our own production company, Good Bones, so making a short film is a great opportunity for us to develop and prove our production skills as well.

I often feel that aspiring filmmakers see short films primarily as a first step towards making features, or almost as a kind of demo reel. To me, they are much more than that.

Finally, what is a short film that has stayed with you for a long time? What did it teach you about filmmaking, or what did it make you want to do yourself?

A short film I came across a long time ago is Kitchen Sink by Alison Maclean. It has stayed with me ever since I first saw it. I found it incredibly inspiring how the film takes you on a kind of rollercoaster ride through so many different emotions. I was also fascinated by how much it manages to communicate with almost no dialogue. To me, it’s a great piece of cinematic art: from the precise camerawork to the beautiful black-and-white photography. I also love the way it seems to pay homage to British horror cinema while constantly playing with the audience’s expectations. It reminded me how much can be expressed through images, sound, rhythm, and performance without having to explain everything. That’s something I always want to keep exploring in my own work.

item.title: Exclusive First Look at the BIFA 2026 Best British Short Film Longlist
item.dc:creator: MarBelle
item.description: Fearless, inventive and wonderfully varied - Directors Notes is proud to announce the 29th BIFA Best British Short Film longlist.
item.content:encoded:
Announcing the BIFA 2026 Longlist for Best British Short Film

Directors Notes’ heart and soul has always been short film, so partnering with the British Independent Film Awards to announce the 15 longlisted films vying for the Best British Short Film award at the 29th edition of the BIFAs is a true honour. As we’ve consistently seen over our 20 years, the short form has long been a space where filmmakers take risks, find their voice and announce themselves to the world. This longlist is proof of how fearless, inventive and wonderfully varied that work continues to be. Discover the 15 longlisted films and their directors below, and keep an eye on DN as we’ll be continuing our BIFA interview series as the awards journey unfolds.

Mark your calendars: This year’s BIFA nominees will be revealed on Tuesday, 3rd November, with the 2026 awards ceremony returning to Camden’s Roundhouse on Sunday, 6th December.

Allies in Exile
Hasan Kattan

For fourteen years, Syrian filmmakers Hasan Kattan and Fadi Al-Halabi have documented war, revolution and each other. Now, confined to a UK asylum hotel, they turn their cameras inward.

The Animals
Calvin Demba

After another man is hailed as a hero, an insecure boyfriend becomes determined to prove that he, too, can protect the woman he loves.

Coyotes
Said Zagha

A Palestinian surgeon drives home after a long night shift, but little does she know that a commute through a desolate West Bank road will change her forever.

Every Time I See A Yellow Car
Matt Chandler

After a violent act shatters the lives of two brothers, Olly attempts to articulate a fractured and repressed truth, whilst his older brother Liam spirals between guilt and revenge. Every Time I See A Yellow Car is a haunting meditation on sexual assault, silence, and the cyclical nature of memory.

Forgotten Spaceman
Elham Ehsas

In 1988, Afghanistan sent its only astronaut into space, a journey that proved home can be farther than the stars.

Free Lyric
Cherish “Chez” Oteka

Set against the rise of social media, Free Lyric revisits one of rap culture’s earliest viral moments: the public shaming of a 17-year-old female rapper after a sexual confession spreads online. Through Niki’s story, the film explores gender, consent, and the early roots of online call-out culture.

Hag
Anna Ginsburg

One woman’s quest for love and meaning in a hellscape of waning fertility, dating apps and the rotten stench of the patriarchy. In a world where being yourself makes you monstrous, what is the cost of compromise and repressing your authentic self?

i have a
Rory Waudby-Tolley

A man lists the things he has.

Maybe Tomorrow
Waad al-Kateab
& Wafa Mustafa

Activist Wafa Mustafa searches for the truth about her father’s disappearance under Assad’s regime in Syria, in this story of hope, memory and resilience.

A Pint of Bitter
Conor Kehelly

You are trying to enjoy a quiet pint in the pub, but a patron and his son seemingly have a problem with your demeanour…

Unauthorised Absence
Georgia Parris

A single mother fighting for support for her autistic daughter is fined, threatened and pushed to breaking point by an education system that wasn’t built for them.

Untitled Woman
Camille Summers-Valli

Dawn is invisible to those around her in a world that favours youth. She fights back to be seen in the most unexpected of ways.

Vote Gavin Lyle
Aneil Karia

Gavin Lyle, a proud flag-waving and full English breakfast-eating Brit, seeks to help his country overcome its deep-rooted problems, problems he blames squarely on immigration.

Wonderwall
Róisín Burns

Liverpool, 1995, the dockers are on strike. Nine-year-old Siobhan has only one thing on her mind: to see if Oasis will win the pop duel against Blur. But an argument breaks out with her older brother Rory, leading the little girl to run away at nightfall. As she wanders, the decaying city takes on an unreal allure.

Yellow Bucket
Simon Brooke

When gay teenager Connor and his family realise they are able to decide his younger brother’s sexuality at his upcoming birthday party, it causes a breakdown in communication.

item.title: Sam Baron Unearths an Elegiac Reckoning Within a Decade of Doomsday Predictions in ‘Everything Will Be Totally Fine’
item.dc:creator: Sarah Smith
item.description: Ten years ago, Sam Baron asked loved ones to predict 2026. Now he confronts the messy, unscripted grief for his late mum hidden in the footage all along.
item.content:encoded:
My mum died unexpectedly in August, and I’m learning that grief isn’t a single wave so much as an all-engulfing and unpredictable tide that keeps devastating the shoreline. I mention it because it’s the lens through which I watched Everything Will Be Totally Fine. In 2016, bereaved and dejected, filmmaker Sam Baron did what felt natural, picked up a camera and asked the people around him to predict the world of 2026, hunting for a hope he couldn’t generate himself. A decade on, with plenty of those forecasts excruciatingly accurate, the footage turned out to be about something else entirely: not the farcical dystopian future we seem to be sleepwalking into, but the loss quietly steering the project all along.

Regular DN readers will know Baron for his tragicomedy trilogy—The Orgy, Big Ears and Tall Dark and Handsome—and the deadpan carnage of Office Royale, comedies powered by Jungian shadow work: the parts of ourselves we splinter off because facing them is frightening. With Everything Will Be Totally Fine, there’s no fictional veil to hide behind. Friends and family are asked about the future 10 years hence, revisited as lockdown reshapes the decade, then once more in 2026 as it arrives on its own terms. The rehearsed composure of those early interviews gives way to the unguarded, and predictions about nations and technology become portraits of the people making them. The loose-grip improvisation of his fiction guides an edit, built with collaborator Ian Robertson, from untreated archive, with Baron splitting himself into different eras to wrestle the footage. As the film premieres today on DN, I speak to Baron about building a structure around something as formless as grief, how he judges what’s too much when the pain is his own, and whether filming is a way of being present or a way of not losing things.

You planned to revisit this footage in 2026 as a film about the world that future had become. What was the original idea, and when did you realise it couldn’t be that film?

Back in 2016, I was freaking out about the state of the world. Between Brexit, Trump, climate change, the war in Syria and so on, I was struggling to imagine a future that I could believe in. So I picked up my camera and started interviewing people around me, asking them to predict what life would be like in 2026, ten years away. When I started, I thought I was making a state-of-the-world exploration of what life felt like on the precipice of the apocalypse. I thought it might be about how accurate our predictions are about the future. Maybe about the human urge to know where we’re heading, even though we never really have a clue. I had just seen the Adam Curtis documentary HyperNormalisation and I wanted to capture the mood of the moment, to see whether the pessimistic trajectory presented in that film would turn out to be true, or whether the pendulum would swing back.

Like all of my films, it was clearly about a man (me) having an existential crisis.

When the pandemic struck in 2020, I watched the Michael Apted series 7 UP, and realised I could film lockdown updates with my contributors to see how they were doing, nearly halfway through the decade. Those interviews were still focused on trying to predict the future on a global scale. It was only when I brought the project to my brilliant editor Ian Robertson in late 2025 and we looked through all the footage, that we began to see the real story. Like all of my films, it was clearly about a man (me) having an existential crisis.

Because in 2016, my Mum had just died. I was spinning out, clinging to a future that no longer existed, struggling to accept that she was gone, unable to see a way to carry on. That was clearly the emotional heart of the film, and we realised that the unscripted, accidental moments in the footage were more interesting than the predictions themselves. We spent a month editing a version of the film which wove that grief story into the original premise, but when we showed it to the incredible documentarian Duncan Cowles, he pushed us to go further – to find a way to bring my Mum properly on-screen. We went back to the hard drive and were stunned to discover 18 hours of home video footage that my Dad had filmed in the early 1990s. Not only did it capture the relationship I had with my Mum when I was young, it was also narrated by my Dad, who had been fascinated by the same questions about the future, and the strange intersection between global politics and ordinary domestic life. When we put those clips into the timeline at resonant moments, something clicked.

In 2016 you feared a future of nuclear weapons, Trump and a world on the edge. What were you chasing in those early interviews, and what was it like to watch that fear again in 2026, when so much of it has come true?

I was definitely doomscrolling a lot in 2016, and it felt overwhelming – like my internal landscape of grief-fuelled hopelessness was being reflected in every news story I read. I couldn’t imagine a version of the future that wasn’t apocalyptic. I think I was asking other people to predict the future because I was searching for glimmers of hope that I couldn’t generate myself. They didn’t know that was my motivation – I didn’t really even know it myself. But when people occasionally offered me smart perspectives about why everything was going to be fine, it felt like the oxygen that I desperately needed.

You’re right that a lot of the fears I had in 2016 have subsequently come true, so you’d think it would destabilise me to revisit the footage in 2026 – and I’d be lying if I said it wasn’t unsettling at times – but I think the main thing I see in the 2016 footage is how narrow my viewpoint was back then. I was obsessing over the bleakness of the future in a way that was missing the rest of the picture. It’s not that I think everything will be totally fine now – it’s clearly still an absolute mess. But I have more capacity to hold space for contradiction now, to accept that light and darkness are always dancing together.

You’ve described writing The Orgy by improvising without knowing where it was going. Was finding the form for this film the same instinct, and how did it differ now that the material you were working with was real?

As an anxious person, I’ve always sought to control everything, but I’ve had to learn that gripping the wheel too tightly can keep you in a safe zone that misses the richness of life. The loose grip approach often brings amazing surprises and discoveries – that’s why I love improvisation, and why I try to keep an open mind at every stage of the creative process.

Obviously, this material being real meant I was bound to tell the truth of what happened, but there are infinite ways to tell a story, so I tried to remain open in the process as we figured out how to tell it. I did have to split myself into ‘filmmaker Sam’ and ‘character Sam’ at times, and would often talk to Ian about Sam in the third person – we even split him into 2016 Sam, 2020 Sam and 2026 Sam as if they were different people. Each era’s Sam had captured footage in a different way, so we were in conversation with many viewpoints.

Ultimately, I kept trying to make the film that I would have needed to watch on my worst days in 2016, a film that could have given 2016 Sam some kind of hope (without being fluffy bullshit). I had to trust that by following that thread, in my stumbling search for meaning, the right form would reveal itself. In the process of making it, I definitely healed something, so perhaps that’s the feeling I want to share with the world: that you don’t always need to know where things will go to be able to move forward. In fact, sometimes it’s better not to know.

I did have to split myself into ‘filmmaker Sam’ and ‘character Sam’ at times, and would often talk to Ian about Sam in the third person.

You’ve talked about comedy that invites us to face our shadow sides. Here you’re facing yours on camera. What did you find yourself avoiding?

In the 2016 footage, there was a lot of material in which I was trying to present the documentary with a kind of professional brave face, so the big edit choice was to gravitate towards footage that felt exposing and raw – exactly the opposite of the more curated mask that I’d been attempting to construct in 2016. But I’ll admit, even as we were editing, I still felt resistant to making myself the protagonist of the film.

I tried to put the contributors and the predictions more in the spotlight. Yet when we shared early edits with trusted filmmaker friends like Duncan, the feedback was very clear: it had to be about me. That did require some shadow work. I’ve become comfortable playing characters called ‘Sam’ in films like Fragile Package and Tippy Toes, but those guys aren’t me. This project meant going beyond ‘playing Sam’ into ‘being Sam’, without the veil of fiction to hide behind.

Most Popular

I have always been impressed by the bare honesty I’ve seen you draw out of performers, particularly your frequent collaborator Amit Shah. What changed when you were the one being honest on camera, and what did documentary ask of you that fiction never has?

Well, there’s plenty of footage in this film that was never intended to be seen publicly, especially the clip of me in 2016, six weeks after my Mum died, which I filmed whilst I was genuinely experiencing suicidal thoughts, in an attempt to keep them at bay. That rawness was captured precisely because I thought it would never be seen, and we nearly didn’t include it. But I didn’t want this documentary to be hamstrung by the fact that the director was also the subject, so when we found powerful pieces of footage like that, we had to use them. In the ten years since 2016, I have learned so much about the power of honesty on camera, from working with Amit and also from starring as ‘blurred line’ toxic versions of myself in films like Fragile Package, so I think this kind of material was probably the natural next step. I hate to think where I’ll have to go next in my stupid pursuit of ‘truth in art’ – perhaps by 2036, I’ll be releasing footage of my colonoscopy.

Where do you see Everything Will Be Totally Fine in the lineage of filmmakers turning their cameras on grief and family, and did any film give you permission or warn you off?

I remember seeing Toby Bull’s short film Some Kind of Intimacy at This Is England [now SHORT UP Rouen]: in 2018 and feeling that he’d captured something very true about grief, while also leaving enough space for the vastness that can’t be nailed down. I thought about what Toby did a lot while we were editing this film – the way he balanced the mundanity of ordinary life and relationships with the poetry of nature, and the emotions that swirl and broil just below the surface after a giant loss.

The other major touchstone was the Sarah Polley film Stories We Tell, which is so clever and creative in its use of interviews and old home movie footage, and in the way it uses humour to weave the most affecting and nuanced tone. Louder Than Bombs by Joachim Trier also resonated powerfully when I was in my grief hole – another quiet, tender little film that went largely unnoticed, but which found me right when I needed it in 2016. And Sarah, I know we both share a deep love of Six Feet Under, which has always been the GOAT when it comes to capturing the complex strangeness of grief on-screen.

He brought what he always does: a razor-sharp attunement for humanity. What is emotional? What makes us feel something?

Ian Robertson is a frequent collaborator of yours. How did your relationship change when the footage was a decade of your own life, and what did he bring to the shape and sound of this film that you couldn’t have found alone?

I’m so glad you asked this question, because Ian is an absolute genius and I cannot give him enough credit. We’ve edited a bunch of films together and have developed such deep trust in our collaborative process. Ian is amazing at scouring through footage and music to find the perfect choices for any given moment, and in this case that involved him sitting through – my god, maybe 30 hours of footage? Maybe 50? I hate to imagine how much rubbish he had to wade through to find the golden nuggets that ended up becoming the major building blocks of our editing timeline.

Ian’s trusted outside eye was particularly essential in this case, as I was undeniably too close to the material to judge it myself at times. More than anything, he brought what he always does: a razor-sharp attunement for humanity. What is emotional? What makes us feel something? Who do we care about, at each moment? How could we care even more, without tipping into crass sentimentality? And what else can we shave away, so we keep tightly to the core spine of the story whilst still allowing the film to breathe?

The old family footage is the film’s most powerful material, and for you the most painful. How did you decide what to use, how did you cut it, and did you treat sound and music differently with the archive?

We had 18 hours of home videos to draw from, and after Ian had sat through all the interview material, I couldn’t ask him to do the same again, so I did the first watch-through, grabbing anything that made me feel something, trying not to judge whether it might fit the edit (although there were some clips, like the rocking horse moment, which made my jaw hit the floor when I found them). We already had a pretty clear shape to the film before we found these clips, so it was really a case of putting the most powerful clips into the existing structure. As always, Ian had fantastic instincts for where things might work. There were great clips that we couldn’t fit in, but through trial and error we found the ones that resonated loudest, which of course were the ones that connected most strongly to the core themes.

We experimented with sound and music variations for the archival material, but in the end we found that the raw footage was affecting enough on its own. It feels different to the rest of the film precisely because it’s largely untreated (aside from a few clean-ups of particularly damaged old tape).

You knew going in that grief isn’t linear. Did that shape the structure from the start, and how do you build a film around something you know has no shape without structure implying that it does?

This is a really important question, and my biggest fear is that we failed at this task. It was extremely difficult to find a structure that could make the film accessible and digestible for an audience coming to it fresh, while simultaneously capturing the messy, mushy, formless vortex of grief. I included a line of voice over towards the end of the film that I hope keeps it anchored in that place of irresolution, despite the emotional evolution that’s on-screen. But honestly, this challenge still haunts me. I have experienced new waves of grief since finishing the edit, both around my Mum and in the sudden unexpected loss of a close friend – feelings that aren’t captured in the edit, and that might even contradict the implications of the structure. I hope that what comes through, more than anything, is that everything keeps evolving: life, death, grief, love, all of it. We never know what’s coming next.

It was extremely difficult to find a structure that could make the film accessible and digestible for an audience coming to it fresh, while simultaneously capturing the messy, mushy, formless vortex of grief.

The lockdown footage returns to the family and friends grieving around you. What does a camera do to grief, and how did you handle the consent of the people on screen, both when you shot it and when you came to cut it?

Most of these people are close friends and family, who have known me for a long time and know the kind of filmmaker I am. I did have some interesting chats with a few contributors when it came time to film updates – a few people wanted to know what exactly I was trying to show, what I was getting at with this film, etc. But in opening up about my own grief, and showing them some of the footage we were intending to use, they seemed to get that this film wasn’t out to make them look bad. Quite the opposite, I think what comes through is how amazing the community around me has been. You’re right that we do often use ‘found moments’ which they may not have intended to be seen – that is a risk, and perhaps it’s a moral grey area. I hope we’ve made choices with integrity and from a place of love for everyone. The most affecting clip for me is the 2026 interview with my Dad, about his grief, and I did ask him if there was anything he didn’t want me to include. He said, “I trust you”.

Do you wonder whether the film is an overshare? As writer, director and subject at once, which role decides what stays, and how do you judge what’s too much when the material is your own pain?

This was another huge challenge and one I took very seriously. It’s where having amazing collaborators like Ian, and my trusted community of filmmaker friends around me, has been essential. I still don’t know if we got the balance right on this one. Even up to the final edit, there were clips that people I trust were urging me to cut. I always make sure to listen to everyone, and if everyone is giving me the same note, then I have to take it seriously. But part of being an artist is also following your own intuition and taste. If I’ve got it right, great. And even if I’ve missed the mark, I think it’ll still be interesting for strangers to watch.

What became of your Nicholl-winning script about cancer, and how has grief been present across your career, even when you weren’t naming it?

I tried for 10 years to get that film made, but sadly I was unable to raise the money. I would still love to make it one day. My focus ended up shifting into other projects, including a script called Blue that I wrote with James Appleby in 2018, that was about AI and grief (that one very nearly got made many times, and still might), and a TV series based on The Orgy (which added a grief layer into the main character’s life, as part of his motivation for stepping out of his ordinary existence and expanding his horizons). In 2020, when I was filming the updates for this documentary, I was also making Fragile Package (which was about a man going through a similar existential crisis, feeling like the world was going to hell as he faced stepping into potential new fatherhood). Grief has infused itself into every day of my life since 2016, into every choice and every idea. It’s certainly emboldened me as a filmmaker – I’m willing to take risks and get out of my comfort zone because I know how short life can be.

You talk about becoming a father in the film. Did fatherhood play a part in why you wanted to make it, and how did it affect what you chose to share?

Without getting into spoilers, let’s just say that when we started editing this film in late 2025, I was not a father and I had no idea how the film would end. I jokingly said to Ian, “Maybe by the time we’ve finished, I’ll be able to hold up an ultrasound picture in the final shot”. In the end, something even more magical happened. I did think twice about whether to include this stuff in the film – whether that choice was even mine to make. And like with many things in this film, I still don’t know if I made the right decision. In the end, I simply had to trust my instincts.

Grief has infused itself into every day of my life since 2016, into every choice and every idea.

With your debut feature Circles in post, why release the most personal thing you’ve made now, and do the two films ask related questions in different registers?

In many ways they do, yet they’re also very different. In Circles, I play a character called ‘Sam’ (just as I did in Fragile Package, Tippy Toes and Useless). But although he shares superficial characteristics with me, he’s not me – he’s a siphon for the collective unconscious, a totem of modern masculinity in crisis. It’s a performance, even when the lines separating him and me are deliberately unclear. This documentary really is me, and although it’s a quirk of timing that they’re both coming out within a year of each other, perhaps there is also something nice about being able to distinguish myself from the characters I play on-screen.

“Bad things happen and they are going to keep happening.” What does a camera understand about time and love that living through it doesn’t, and is making films a way of being present or a way of not losing things?

This is such a profound question. I don’t know how I can do it justice. I’ve always loved the films of Richard Linklater, especially the Before trilogy and Boyhood, both of which use film to evoke the emotion and meaning inherent in the passage of time so effectively. God, I wish I had the words to properly answer your question. All I can say is that I’ve been obsessed with filming things my whole life. And when my Mum died, I combed through old footage as a way to keep her alive. I did the same thing when I lost my close friend recently. I have sometimes worried that filming things stops me from being present in the moment, but I think at this point it has become such second nature to me that I do it almost without thinking. And god, I’m glad that I have the wealth of footage that I do.

What’s your favourite short film? Only one!

I’m sure I change my answer every time. Today I’m going to say 22. Anna Matthews by Ben Hector because I can watch it a million times and it gets me every time.

What’s next for you, and how do you take the idea of “looking at an unknown stretch of time but interested to see what happens” into whatever comes after this?

I wish I knew! I’m extremely committed to the idea of flow state right now. I genuinely have no idea what’s coming next. I’m finishing Circles with that amazing team of collaborators. I’m starting to dream up new projects I could make next. But mostly, I’m enjoying being a dad.

item.title: Craig Bingham Demonstrates How “Restraint Breeds Creativity” with His Mythic Fantasy Sci-Fi Short ‘FARANOOKA’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Real sparks from an angle grinder, weeks of unnerving sonic experiments and a lead laid bare; Craig Bingham on forging a raw, rusty-bladed mythology.
item.content:encoded:
When we think about low-budget independent filmmaking, our first instinct might be to imagine grounded, realistic narratives set within recognisable worlds. However, after years of speaking to the filmmakers who make these films, we’ve learnt that it’s often those working with the greatest restrictions who have the biggest imaginations, finding ways to create worlds that far exceed the resources available to them. Craig Bingham’s FARANOOKA is a perfect example. Set in a world where darkness reigns, until a child’s introduction brings with it the first light this universe has known, it’s an ambitious piece of world-building that feels considerably larger than the production behind it. With Bingham using these limitations as a creative opportunity rather than a constraint, the result is a short that feels less like a complete world than an intriguing glimpse into a much larger one.

With that in mind, we invited DN alum Bingham to join us to discuss his plans for expanding the world of FARANOOKA, the importance of light within its visual and narrative universe and why he believes “restraint breeds creativity”.

Hi Craig – we’re excited to talk to you today about your truly striking short film, FARANOOKA and I wanted to start right at the beginning. The film opens on a black screen with eight simple lines of text introducing us to the universe of the short. Given how visually explosive the film becomes, what made you choose such a restrained form of exposition to introduce this world?

Initially, I wanted to throw the audience straight into a story that felt charged with emotion, without giving them any context. I liked the idea that you had to find your feet in this world and work out what was happening for yourself. But after finishing the film, my producer, James Baines, and I felt the story needed a little more context to bring the audience into the space. There’s a history to FARANOOKA and I wanted to give the audience just enough of that history to understand that what they’re watching is part of something much bigger. For me, the opening text is a way of doing that without slowing the film down. It gives you the mythology, but then we can let the visuals and the performance take over.

It’s clear from this opening that sound plays an important role in the world-building of FARANOOKA. We hear our hero before we see him, while the film’s evil presence is often communicated through sound rather than image. How early in the film’s conception did you decide to put such a strong emphasis on sound and how did you work with Hugo Ellingham to develop its sound design?

I always knew that sound would play an important part in the film, especially given that you never actually see the creature Angbor is hunting. Looking back, I never expected the project to become quite as experimental as it did, but as soon as I got into the edit, it was clear that the sound, the silence and the otherworldly chants were essential to bringing the audience into the space. So we decided to really lean in and create a bed that felt jarring and unpredictable.

It gives you the mythology, but then we can let the visuals and the performance take over.

It took weeks and countless days of Hugo and me experimenting and playing with different sounds to find something that felt raw and immersive. It was not easy. We wanted the sound to throw you into this world without forcing a particular emotion. It needed to create a sense of unease. This for me, was the hardest thing to execute. Hugo went above and beyond, completely leaning into the madness of the world we were creating to bring it to life. There was a lot of experimentation, a lot of things that didn’t work, but that process was really important to find something that felt unsettling and immersive.

As we’re immersed in your universe, one of the first things we see is a blinding white light and throughout the film light plays an important role in establishing its world. What drew you to light as such a central element of the film’s visual language and mythology?

The story of FARANOOKA is set in a shrouded land – a land covered in darkness. Only now, with the arrival of FARANOOKA, is the land beginning to experience the true beauty of light. It’s a story inspired by Dante’s Inferno, travelling into the deepest depths of hell before emerging on the other side, into the light. Our lead must descend into darkness in order to find the light – something I think we can all relate to in some way. So light became more than just a visual element; it became part of the mythology of the world and a symbol of hope and love.

As a filmmaker, I’m drawn to simplicity. I’m also a realist and I was very aware of what we wanted to create and how we could achieve it. I try to only imagine things that I genuinely feel are achievable for me as a filmmaker. Light felt like a simple but powerful cinematic device.

Most Popular

After we’re almost assaulted by that bright light, we’re confronted with a shot of your hunter hero, Angbor, screaming directly at the camera with his shield and spear raised. Bringing him to life is a captivating, physical performance from Connor Newall (28 Days Later). How did you work with him to get into the headspace of Angbor and make this complex universe feel tangible through his performance?

Conor Newall is a vulnerable actor. On his audition tape I saw a deep-rooted rage in his performance, it gave me goosebumps and I really wanted to explore that. It sounds strange, but at times being on set felt like a bit of an acid trip. I was shouting in the woods just as much as he was, trying to make him feel the space and react to the world we were creating. I think we all became completely immersed in the story.

The light you see passing over his shield in the final scene is actually hot shards of metal from an angle grinder. It was real, and it felt dangerous and you can see that on his face. There was a real sense of danger in that moment, and I think that helped make the performance feel as raw as it does. With every take, I asked more of Conor, and every time he gave it to me. He completely laid himself bare and I’m all about that – don’t hold back.

Light felt like a simple but powerful cinematic device.

Another thing that immediately strikes you in these opening shots is the stark black and white photography. Rather than feeling like a stylistic gimmick, it gives the film a sense of timelessness and adds to the feeling that we’re witnessing a fragment of a much larger mythology. How did you work with DoPs Joey Knox and Adric Watson to establish the film’s visual language and what ultimately led you to black and white?

From the get-go, we always imagined FARANOOKA having a metallic edge. We didn’t want the film to feel overly stylised or polished; it needed to feel real, with a raw, gritty quality. Joey and Adric are both incredible DoPs. They both have a raw style and approach to photography, and they can tap into the most intimate scenes just as easily as the most explosive. Our visual approach to storytelling is very much in sync. The references we drew from were films such as The Seventh Seal (1957), Stalker (1979) and The Silver Globe (1988). They all explore a supernatural presence, but they also have this gritty, real kind of DNA embedded within them. That was something I really wanted to bring into FARANOOKA.

Adric shot the intimate, dark studio scenes with actor Robert Goodman, while Joey shot all of the outdoor sequences – both using the ARRI Alexa 35 in Super 16 mode with Zeiss MK3 Super Speeds. We kept the lighting to a minimum. All the outdoor scenes were shot using natural daylight, alongside the light and sparks from the angle grinder on set. We talked about the film feeling like a rusty blade – rough, raw and worn. And I think Joey and Adric really captured that.

Then, in the grade, Toby Tomkins really brought that chrome-like quality to life, leaning into our references. For me, it was about finding that balance between something feeling metallic but also something that felt dirty. I always like to keep things stripped back and let the cast and performances do the heavy lifting. With FARANOOKA, we doubled down on that.

One of the things I particularly admired when discussing FARANOOKA with the Directors Notes team was how effectively the film builds such an impressive universe without showing us everything. We’re often given close-ups of characters’ faces, while the larger battles and threats happen just beyond the frame. How much of that restraint was an aesthetic decision and how much was shaped by the practical realities of making the film? Did you ever consider showing more or was withholding that information always part of your vision?

I’m a big believer that restraint breeds creativity. All of my favourite films show less and I’ve always been drawn to that. Yes, from a practical point of view, we had a very limited budget, but that was never the reason I was forcing myself to work this way. It was a creative choice. My previous film, IRONSTONE, is about two men entering a pit, knowing that only one of them is going to get out. It taps into violence and what I learned from making that film is that you don’t necessarily have to see the violence to feel it. Sometimes the emotion on someone’s face can tell the story with so much more depth.

I think it’s important to make the audience work. I’ve always tried to lean into that. I want the audience to fill in the gaps themselves, to imagine what they’re not being shown. For me, that’s when cinema gets exciting.

That sense of withholding also makes the world feel considerably larger than what we see on screen. From your director’s statement, I know the short is “part of a much bigger story”. How much of FARANOOKA represents a glimpse into a larger mythology that you’ve already developed and where would you like to take that story next?

I want to take the story into a much larger world. The short is really just a glimpse into a much bigger mythology. I want to explore the birth of this dark land, its people, where this darkness came from and what happened after Angbor lifted his shield into the blaze. There’s a much bigger world sitting behind what we see in these few minutes.

I want the audience to fill in the gaps themselves, to imagine what they’re not being shown. For me, that’s when cinema gets exciting.

The feature would allow me to explore that world and the relationship between Angbor and Faranooka in much more depth. This isn’t a classic hero’s journey. It isn’t even clear whether Faranooka is Angbor’s to save. As an audience member, you naturally root for our protagonist, but as this story unfolds, it becomes clear that saving Faranooka might not necessarily be the right decision – it might actually be a selfish one. That’s something I want the feature to explore in a much deeper way, tapping into themes that feel very relevant to the world we live in today. At what cost do we keep pushing until we lose the thing we love the most?

Given the scale of the world you’ve created, what would expanding FARANOOKA look like for you? Are there particular characters, locations or elements of this mythology that you’re especially keen to explore in future?

There are characters and stories within this world that we’ve only hinted at. The larger story would explore the history of the land, what it looked like before Faranooka arrived, and how her arrival changed the community that lived there. Angbor’s relationship with Faranooka is also at the heart of the larger story. I can already see how I’d like to approach that.

I want every new location and character to tell us something about the mythology and push the story forward.

Visually, I’d love to take the world beyond the woods and into the wider landscape. I want to see the places that have been shaped by this darkness. But I’d still want to retain the grounded, tactile, raw quality of the short. I don’t want to make the world bigger simply for the sake of scale. I want every new location and character to tell us something about the mythology and push the story forward. For me, the exciting thing is that the short only opens the door. There’s a much bigger world on the other side of it and I’d love the opportunity to step through.

Before we wrap up, are there any other projects on the horizon you’re excited about that you can share with us?

I’ve just wrapped a small film with Tetsuro Shimaguchi, the samurai artist who choreographed the fight sequences in Quentin Tarantino’s Kill Bill films. It’s called Practicing How to Die, and it reflects on Tetsuro’s relationship with his cultural heritage of the samurai. Revisiting his childhood, he confronts the idea of the glorious death he once imagined but will never receive. Instead, he transforms that longing into performance, repeatedly enacting death on stages around the world. The film pays tribute to Tetsuro’s work as a choreographer on Kill Bill, drawing heavily on the visual language and legacy of Japanese cinema, but with my own fingerprint on it. It’s been a really special project to make and an opportunity for me to explore the space between documentary, narrative and performance.

Finally, this is a question we ask all our featured filmmakers: what’s one short film by another filmmaker that you’d recommend to our audience, and why?

I’d recommend watching Other Life by Tom and Theo Tennant. It’s a documentary that follows two best friends investigating UFO sightings across South Wales. It’s a really beautiful film with a genuine human touch, whilst still tapping into the supernatural. I absolutely loved it. Watched it several times now.

item.title: 10 Exciting Shorts to Keep an Eye on from the 70th BFI London Film Festival
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: LFF’s shorts this year look squarely at the world we live in and invite us to reflect. These 10 titles are thoughtful, gripping and hard to forget.
item.content:encoded:
The 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival brings, as it does every year, a rich selection that showcases the best of contemporary filmmaking through twelve shorts programmes, spanning comedy, horror, drama and political themes. In addition to those sections, there’s also the inaugural Displacement Film Fund collection of films, which grew out of Cate Blanchett’s support. You may recognise some of the shorts presented at LFF 2026 from their screenings at other festivals earlier in the year, with some also having featured in previous DN Best of Fest selections such as Anna Mantzaris’ Please, which was part of our Encounters Best of Fest last month. There are also films like Remi R.M. Moses’ Hindsight that will be getting the full Directors Notes interview treatment in the near future and so aren’t included here. As always, we have consciously picked shorts from across the festival’s sections to give you an idea of the breadth of this year’s programme, but, needless to say, a lot of great films we loved have been left out of the following list. That caveat out of the way, dive into DN’s favourite short film picks of London Film Festival 2026 with us.

Super Afghan Gym – Shahrbanoo Sadat

Featured in the Displacement Film Fund section, this short helmed by Shahrbanoo Sadat brings together a group of women in a gym in Kabul and puts before the viewer the condition of women in the country. The concerns about appearance, and the expectations that come with them, are explored through a community of women of different ages, all of them adorable. The strength of Super Afghan Gym lies in the universality of its theme, despite its political implications. Its tone, which is almost entirely that of a comedy, makes this slice of humanity even more enjoyable.

The Clouds of Odessa – Luca Arcangeli

Luca Arcangeli’s deeply moving mix of animation and documentary screens as part of LFF’s Life / Drawing strand. The Clouds of Odessa takes us inside one of the most intense conflicts of our time, the war in Ukraine, through a love story and aesthetics that make us forget, for a moment, the brutality of war. There are many ways to tell the story of a conflict: in this instance, it’s what we could almost call a childlike approach, in the best way possible, drawing on the instinctive way children express themselves to convey the film’s drama.

Into the Forest (Vers la forêt) – Antonin Niclass

My passion for stop motion shows in the fact that shorts like this appear in almost all of my Best of Fest collections, and Into the Forest—which, after touring several festivals, has now reached the competition here at the London Film Festival—is a striking example of how the cuteness of stop motion can also serve as social critique. Here, it shows how monkeys have to rethink the concept of nature once they live alongside humans. It’s impossible not to fall in love with their big eyes and their movements, which Antonin Niclass orchestrates adorably.

Most Popular

How to Hide it – Ramla Ali & Richard A.Moore

Ramla Ali and Richard A.Moore’s short, presented within the Call Your Bluff programme, is a very intelligent comedy, where the comic elements still prompt reflection on broader themes and give the story a breadth that goes beyond funny situations. The young protagonist (played by Ali herself) finds herself in limbo: she wins the lottery, but gambling is forbidden for her as a respectful Muslim, and the fear of someone finding out (especially her family) about her good fortune terrifies her. At the same time, that win would change her life for the better and save her from a supermarket job that doesn’t seem to contain her explosive character. Set in an ultra-pop world and boosted by a great soundtrack and editing, this is a short you shouldn’t miss. Don’t hide from How to Hide It!

A Twist of Hate – Maddy Shenai

One of the most remarkable aspects of Maddy Shenai’s A Twist of Hate is the quality of the acting from all three of its performers, and Sally Phillips in particular. The story and setting are very simple: a room where a lawyer gets a young couple, expecting a child, to think about how to divide their assets, and how catastrophic events that can happen in life could completely change the outlook of their relationship. Cynical, irreverent, simple but very effective, A Twist of Hate is here to stay.

Sphinx Alberta’s Smile (Sfinksas Albertas Smaids) – Dace Rīdūze

In all this adult madness, it felt right to include a short from the Animated Shorts for Younger Audiences programme, too. Sphinx Alberta’s Smile’s surreal, incredible story weaves together the cold Baltic landscapes of Latvia with the exoticism of Egypt, and with it the visual warmth of Africa, making this children’s short unmissable for adults as well. Indeed, its meticulous aesthetic, which feels almost lifted from a wild piece of contemporary art, lets Dace Rīdūze’s crazy story win over the hearts of young and old alike.

The Sorrows of Young Charlotte – Shir Ariya

Land Of Hope and Gory, a collection for bold voices who are not worried about shocking their audiences, which very much speaks to us here at DN. The Sorrows of Young Charlotte is the perfect representative: it sits halfway between comedy and horror, telling a story about how hard it is to get back into the dating game after an important relationship has ended. All done in an absolutely irreverent, hyperbolic and distinguished grotesque style. What happens when you decide to take a sexual performance pill which belonged to the ex of the girl you’ve always liked? We’re not going to tell you. You’ll have to buckle up and experience Shir Ariya’s short for yourself.

To The North – Amer Nasser

Sadly, in these fraught times it seems hard not to talk about politics and the current state of the world, and that is true of Amer Nasser’s Altered States programmed film To The North. Shorts of just a few minutes often risk not being able to hold everything they could say because the story can end up too compressed, making it hard to enter its world. Yet, as is the case with Nasser’s short, the best ones can get deeply under your skin, especially with this film when years of viewing the rubble of Gaza on our screens brings instant knowledge of the depth of suffering and loss endured there. An extremely effective use of black and white cinematography coupled with the charisma of a great up-and-coming actor Feras Almasri—recently seen in the masterpiece feature Thirteen in Gaza—makes To The North particularly memorable.

Untitled Woman – Camille Summers-Valli

Camille Summers-Valli’s Untitled Woman is one of the best examples of LFF’s As the Years Roll By—a programme that celebrates adulthood and old age—looking as it does at what it means to grow older in a society where the tendency is to swim against nature’s current and try to look as young as possible. Here, Julianne Nicholson’s extraordinary performance allows a story with a relatively straightforward core to express itself with a rare delicacy and beauty. Indeed, the strength of this short lies precisely in its ability to be deeply human and reflect a pressure shared by all women, across generations too, since women go through many different feelings over the course of their lives in relation to their bodies, but in an original context. In fact, the art gallery setting allows for a very distinct aesthetic and Krzysztof Trojnar’s impressive cinematography reflects that accordingly.

Aman – Rahul Roye

Part of the most intimate programme of all, I See Myself, Aman shares its premise with a feature recently presented in Toronto, Soy Mario, and deals with the delicate concept of a trans man falling pregnant. Rahul Roye’s concept is wrapped in a well-told, powerful story that hits you straight in the gut. In this sense, the short uses very dense, very dark cinematography to convey, flawlessly, all the emotions present in the narrative.

You can find more unmissable DN film festival favourites in our Best of Fest collections.

item.title: Sam Tricomo Asks Audiences to Find Empathy Without Forgiveness in His Darkly Transgressive Pilot ‘Puke Bitch’
item.dc:creator: Sarah Smith
item.description: How do you make audiences care about people who do terrible things? Sam Tricomo's dark pilot strips away backstory, letting silence and loneliness do the work.
item.content:encoded:
How do you make an audience empathise with people who do bad shit? That’s the uncomfortable question at the heart of Puke Bitch, a darkly comic pilot that refuses to neatly explain the behaviour of its characters. Instead, it drops us into a murky world of loneliness, repression, desire and violence, asking us to spend time with people whose actions are difficult to swallow, yet who also feel disturbingly relatable.

For filmmaker Sam Tricomo, that tension is not only the point; it’s one of the main talking points of this interview. Puke Bitch is a multi-layered watch, with a visceral score sitting alongside naturalistic performances to create a world that feels both heightened and recognisably human. Tricomo isn’t interested in justifying his characters – or asking us to forgive them. Instead, he wants us to consider what it means to build empathy without absolution and how we might find humanity in even the most monstrous of characters.

You talk about empathy for these characters and refusing to write them as villains, but empathy and endorsement aren’t the same thing, and yours do repellent things. So here’s the harder version: how do you build empathy for someone without quietly asking the audience to forgive them?

I don’t think forgiveness is necessary for empathy. Because understanding someone’s cruelty does not equal endorsing it. I see the acts committed here as desperate and deeply tragic, and I can empathize with someone suffering on the inside, while choosing not to glorify their abuse of others because of it.

In order to swallow characters like this, you need to understand that what we may read as depravity on screen is actually desperation to them.

That said, I understand that most people don’t feel the same way I do, and I want to make it clear that you are welcome to feel whatever you want about these people. But if you’re like me and desire putting yourself through the kind of mental circus it takes to empathize with these people, here’s what I have to say: Choices, agreeable or disagreeable, are all born from the same core desire, shame, loneliness, and fear we all share. Everything can be broken down to the basics. In order to swallow characters like this, you need to understand that what we may read as depravity on screen is actually desperation to them.

Is there a difference, for you, between understanding a character and absolving them and did the film have to give up moral judgment entirely in order to love them this much?

For sure. I wouldn’t say I absolve, endorse, or forgive their actions per se (I mean–be gay, do crime, obviously), but I definitely see these characters in a different way than I see everyday people, so my willingness to open my mind to their darkness is different. But to answer your question more specifically, I would say that I did indeed have to sacrifice my moral judgment to open my mind in the first place.

Through writing these characters over several drafts, I came to adore their sense of self, be it cruel and unusual, because I found it so uncommon in real life. Take away the murder aspect, and these are people with a strong sense of self and great confidence. That’s something I feel like I don’t see in many people across my generation because people are too afraid of being disliked or canceled. So, I guess you could say my love for them comes not only from a mind forcibly opened, but from a deep-rooted desire to see people with an unflinching sense of self.

Empathy is usually manufactured through access, confession, backstory, a character explaining themselves. You’ve stripped most of that out; this is a film that barely speaks. So, how does the empathy get made when the usual tools are gone?

That very question is why I wanted to make the pilot relentless and without explanation, because I couldn’t imagine something like that. What I had to do to accomplish that was to be fully aware of the circumstances that brought us to where we are. There is a world of backstory to these people that I only hint at in the pilot.

None of these actions is met with cartoonish evil satisfaction; it’s met with silence and loneliness.

I think if you’re looking at this film as a standalone piece rather than the first chapter of a larger story, the key to finding empathy for these characters lies in their dissatisfaction with the decisions we deem unempathetic. Whether you’re looking at Dove’s cat exploration, Larry’s satyriasis, or Janet’s psychopathic tendencies. None of these actions is met with cartoonish evil satisfaction; it’s met with silence and loneliness. We’re all capable of empathizing with that.

You describe Dove’s relationship to death as maternal, an instinct to nurture, aimed at roadkill and decay. That’s a striking inversion: care directed at the one thing that can’t receive it.

Exactly! I believe Dove sees herself in roadkill. Intelligent creatures now discarded and empty, left to die. She desires to hold and connect with them because she herself craves that love and attention.

You’ve got two women with relationships to death across a generation — Dove tending what’s already dead and Janet, who by the end we understand makes the dead. One nurtures, the other controls. Is Dove an early, innocent version of what Janet has become? Is maternal feeling toward death the thread that secretly binds them and does the season read that as a warning or a kinship?

Dove serves as a mirror reflection of Janet at that age. The bond they share concerning death, whether maternal or linked to a desire for control, runs deep. I want to explore this throughout the season, depicting Janet’s awareness of Dove’s violence and her wish to shape Dove into the person Janet has become, sparing her years of fighting the monster she’s meant to be.

Most Popular

You’ve said faith functions as a character in its own right. Mechanically, what does that mean on screen – is faith a presence that acts on these people, a structuring pressure, a temptation, an antagonist? And how is it embodied: through the Reverend, the architecture, the music, the moral weather of the town?

Initially, I wrote the religious aspect into the script through a darkly comedic lens. I wanted to juxtapose the kinds of people you see in churches in a small town like that. But over time, I came to despise the notion it promoted: “these are the bad people. Isn’t it funny how they are pretending to be good?” Humans are far too complex and nuanced to be simply one or the other, and I wanted to reflect that not only in my depiction of the church but also in my characters.

The church then became a point of community in the story. Something all the characters adhere to, whether it’s the siblings, most likely forcibly there due to their foster mother’s wishes, or Janet, who attends in an attempt to blend in, or even to accept the intimacy she craves in a less outwardly open way. Like all places, it is not entirely safe or run by idolized individuals, but I feel that its place in the story can represent the idea that the church, or religion as a whole, doesn’t necessarily exist for the ‘good’ people to maintain their goodness, but rather, it exists to host a community for everyone around us.

Puke Bitch collides faith with desire and even with transaction – Larry’s church arrangement, the donations, the puritanical setting. Is faith the thing you’re critiquing for its hypocrisy, or the pressure that generates the darkness in the first place, repression breeding transgression?

Repression always breeds transgression. Being told to conserve ourselves in any way makes us rebel, whether we’re entirely conscious of it or not. We can critique the hypocrisy of organized religion all day, but I think what I was trying to do more so was to show not how religion can breed transgression in the traditional sense, because we’ve seen that over and over, but rather, to show how conservative communities like this can feed transgression underneath the surface.

It’s as if merely seeing someone closed off to life entirely flips a switch within me.

When I’m interacting with people my age who are conservative, I intuitively almost level up my ‘inner evil monologue’ as I describe my life to them. Suddenly, the one extremely lame party I went to a few months ago turns into a wild rager in which I, and everyone there, I describe not as actual people, but stylized, punk rockers who like to drink, fuck, and do drugs. These are always exaggerations of the truth. It’s as if merely seeing someone closed off to life entirely flips a switch within me. One that doesn’t make me want to understand their psyche, but rather, want to fundamentally juxtapose their being entirely.

You describe the turn the project took as moving away from something lighter and quirkier toward something darker, more grounded, more realistic, and less stylized. But what landed reads as more stylized, not less: gothic, macabre, a heightened look, a designed soundscape. It’s almost as if the darkness pulled its own aesthetic toward it.

I agree – my original vision of how we would execute it was a bit more openly ridiculous and less patient than the final version we see. The first script was about 20 pages, in which we only followed Larry and Dove and saw Janet from afar. The kids were more active members of society, caring about relationships beyond their own, and participating more in school and extracurricular events. While still adhering to a small-town mentality, the show adopted a darker, more openly comedic tone.

After sitting with this version of the script for a few months, I felt like taking on a larger challenge, which was really writing people who I felt made little to no effort to adhere to the rules we do, and let that disobedience live in a non-comedic lens, which is how we came to the final version. So I guess it was always going to be stylized. The version we landed on is just done differently.

Were you navigating a distinction between tonal realism and visual stylisation and did going dark, paradoxically, give you permission to go bigger?

Oh yeah! I think I wanted it to be digestible, and given the darkness, it became exactly that. Originally, I planned for no music besides the ambient score, which would come in sparingly. But through the edit, I wanted it to be a bit easier to swallow, so it grew.

Tied to that: reviewers have clocked a naturalism in the performances and rhythm sitting underneath a very designed surface. The film holds both at once. How do you stop the heightened, macabre style from flattening the realism of the people inside it—what keeps the gothic from swallowing the human?

I’m so glad we get to talk about this. From the very beginning, I looked for actors who not only saw these characters through a non-villainous lens, but who I thought juxtaposed them as people entirely and challenged them as actors. If it’s okay, I want to take a moment to speak about how I worked together with the three leads in the show.

On the page, the character of Larry is even crueler than we might notice on screen. His body language, his dialogue, he’s a real manipulator. Brandon Engel, who plays him, and I had many conversations leading up to production about keeping his mean nature lived-in rather than performative. We found his relationship with his sister, Dove, the most fascinating. When isolated, he’s loving towards her, yet when they’re around others, he becomes more of a bully. There’s a lot of insecurity and jealousy there, which Brandon and I often discussed as we worked on ways to incorporate it into his performance.

It’s a layered, very human performance that I feel often gets underappreciated.

Working with Kimberly Cruchon Brooks on Janet was a dream come true. I’m lucky to call her a long-time friend and collaborator. In real life, Kim is theatrical, hilarious, loud, polite, lovable, and more. She couldn’t be further from Janet, which is exactly why I needed her to play her. We had many conversations about her character, who she was at different ages, why she does what she does, and how she sees the world. All of them melted into a single topic: intimacy. I myself am quite closed off and threatened by the kind of exposure that comes with it. I guess you could say Janet is my self-insert in a way. Where we differ, however, is that once I’ve been exposed in that way, I don’t then feel the need to take back my power in the way she does, but both Kim and I found Janet’s choices (questionable, as they are) to be delicious, relatable, and deeply tragic.

And finally, there’s Jaclyn Iskow, who plays Dove. Jac and I went to school together in Detroit, and have also collaborated a few times beforehand. Like both Janet and Larry, Dove is quite the monster on the page. With even less dialogue than the others, she feels even less morally grey, so in casting her, I knew I needed to find someone special who could balance her darkness and innocence with ease. Unlike Kim and Brandon, Jac is not classically trained as an actor. While some may see this as a disadvantage, I thought it gave Jac an upper hand as she brought herself into Dove and allowed her performance to be very subtle; it gives Dove a very secretive nature that I find so perfect on screen. When we watch her panic, her smile, her freak-out, each one feels like there’s a world beneath her skin that we’re not privy to, and I adore that. It’s a layered, very human performance that I feel often gets underappreciated next to the other, more outward performances in the show.

You’ve talked about wanting the sound and score and the soundtrack to live in the body—tension, butterflies in the stomach—rather than just signalling mood. That’s composing for the gut, not the ear, and it’s doing it under a film that barely speaks. What were the actual techniques you and your team used to manufacture that physical unease, and how does the score manage anticipation across the episode, given how much of the dread here is about waiting rather than the event?

The score was composed by the brilliant Ben Fox Smith. This is actually his first film score, funny enough. He and I worked closely on the music, trying multiple things before we landed on this guttural anticipatory one. For a while, we were scoring the outside—the events, the movement—rather than scoring from the interior of the characters, which I felt was crucial due to the lack of explanation for their actions, as you had mentioned before. If we don’t know why, we can at least understand how these characters feel, which can suggest a history within them. The eagerness, the familiarity, the fear, I wanted us to feel right there with them. I think the best example of this is Ben’s piece when Dove examines the cat. We wanted to hear the butterflies in her stomach, which I think he executed beautifully.

There’s music by other amazing artists throughout, including Skin (Hailey Howe & Henri Jones), as well as from Peachhole and Tareneh, two amazing bands. Their songs weren’t composed for the sake of the pilot, but they were kind enough to allow me to use them in the finished piece.

The pilot is quietly doing three jobs at once: it works as a self-contained short, it’s episode one of a series and it’s effectively a proof of concept that could scale to a feature. Those pull in different directions but work! Where does the series go from here and are you working on anything else?

Thank you for asking!! My goal for the show was to create a one-season limited series. I have everything planned out. The main storyline revolves around Janet and Dove, with Janet attempting to groom Dove into the killer she is destined to become. Alongside this journey, we also follow Larry as he seeks attention from both the Reverend and her son in an attempt to make himself whole. You might find it surprising, but I actually intended for the show to explore humanity rather than focus solely on darkness.

What’s the short film you keep coming back to — the one that showed you what the form is actually capable of, and why did it catch your attention?

Oh, there are so many. I spend an unhealthy amount of time watching short films daily on platforms like Directors Notes, No Budge, and Vimeo Staff Picks. Antonio Marziale’s Starfuckers is an all-time favorite. I feel like I haven’t been able to escape since I’ve seen it. So romantic, yet also threatening. Brilliantly written, directed, performed, edited, you name it. It inspires me endlessly, and I love rewatching it.

item.title: Five Shoots, One Year and Zero Fundraising Shape Bertil Nilsson’s Intimate Identity-Shifting Feature Debut ‘Masc’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Ahead of its LFF 2026 European premiere, Bertil Nilsson returns to discuss the instinct-led process which enabled the creation of his debut feature, 'Masc'.
item.content:encoded:
With Directors Notes celebrating its 20th anniversary in 2026, we’ve had the privilege of watching countless filmmakers make the leap from short film to features. Yet, it’s never any less exciting when we hear news of one of our previously featured filmmakers taking that next step, particularly when their debut feature retains so much of what first drew us to their work. That’s certainly the case with DN alum writer/director Bertil Nilsson’s Masc, which screens tomorrow (Thursday 8 October) as part of the London Film Festival.

Knowing relatively little about the film, beyond my familiarity with Nilsson’s earlier work, watching Masc felt like a welcome reminder of why we remain so committed to independent filmmaking here at Directors Notes. Shot with a skeleton crew over the course of around a year, the freedom afforded by that approach has resulted in one of the most singular pieces of filmmaking I’ve seen this year. At times, it’s difficult to pin down exactly what we’re watching, as the boundaries between performance and reality, fiction and lived experience, gradually begin to blur. However, rather than making the film feel elusive, that uncertainty is precisely what makes Masc so captivating.

Fresh from watching the film, I sat down with Nilsson to discuss his first foray into feature filmmaking, his collaborative partnership with Masc lead Joshua Griffin and the challenges and freedoms that come with taking a slower, more contemplative approach to making a film.

You’ve been making films for quite a few years now and we’ve watched you move between portrait work, dance films and narrative shorts. So, I’m interested…What made now feel like the right time to take on your first feature?

I always wanted to make feature films. I guess that was my original exposure to filmmaking when I was young and I was excited by the worlds that you have a chance to create in a feature. But I never really thought that was for me. I didn’t come from a background in art or film or anything like that, so it seemed like a completely different universe. Over time, working in the industry, doing photography and making movement, portrait and narrative films, I guess I was building my confidence. I was moving closer to where I originally wanted to go in some ways and obviously learning along the way. It wasn’t really an intentional journey. I think it was just a development of my confidence in even thinking that I could do it.

With shorts, especially narrative shorts, it takes a lot of creative energy and time to put together a short film that doesn’t necessarily get seen by a lot of people. I’ve been lucky with some films getting great distribution, but it’s still quite hard to get a narrative short film seen. So I was thinking that I wanted to make something bigger that could have a bigger audience, but I was also thinking about how to do that without the support or money that people normally spend on feature films. That’s kind of how we came to this process. It was about asking: can we do something with what we have access to right now in terms of equipment, knowledge, collaborators and connections? Can we find a way that we can make a feature film?

That leads nicely onto the practical side of making the film. I think a lot of our audience will be filmmakers themselves, so they’ll be interested in that transition from short film to feature. How did you go about finding the money and support to get Masc made?

It was mainly self-produced, so it was more about us finding a way to not have the money [Laughs]. It was about finding a way to do it without needing to raise money, because that didn’t seem possible. We wanted to find a way to do it that was less stressful and gave more room for exploration. That ended up fitting together with this idea of making the film in five blocks. Each one was almost like a short film in its own production. We had separate locations and, to a certain extent, separate casts. We were casting in between the blocks and prepping each block separately.

It was about finding a way to do it without needing to raise money.

That broke the feature production down into something more manageable, but it also allowed us to be a little bit bigger in our scope. Instead of thinking, “We have very small resources, so we can only make a film in one room for one week,” we could use a few different locations that we had easy access to. It meant we didn’t have to build this house of cards of favours and opportunities that all had to fit into a really tight space.

That sounds like a very liberating way to make a film, with a real independent spirit running through the production. Were there times when you wished you had more resources or more money?

Yeah, of course. There are a lot of problems that you can pay to not have. One of the biggest struggles with spreading out the filming was the logistics of scheduling it and making sure that cast and crew were available for the various blocks. So that’s definitely the downside of it. But I’m very happy with what we set out to do, which was to enjoy the process of making a film like this. When you make a small film, it’s very unlikely that it will go anywhere. If you’re over-focused on trying to get into a festival or whatever goal you have, then that process can be horrible – a sort of nightmare of stress and overextending yourself. I didn’t want to do that. I’ve been part of those productions.
