What we were hoping was that if we could have a more enjoyable process and give more space to the actors, the whole energy on set could be more relaxed and we would get more out of it in terms of the final product than if we tried to rush it. There’s this weird paradox where, when you’re starting out, you have the least amount of resources and you also have the least amount of experience, so you kind of need the most amount of time. Whereas a very experienced crew and director can probably do it very quickly because they have all that experience to fall back on.

Whatever you did, it really worked. I’m fresh from watching Masc and I’m still unpacking the layers of the film, but I found it incredibly moving and totally refreshing. There are a lot of relatable themes in the film – from masculinity to identity and the performative nature that surrounds both of them – but you seem to be exploring them from a fresh perspective. To focus on the subject matter for a minute, why were these the themes you wanted to explore and how did you want to approach them?

I’m really interested in performance and in how that works. It’s something that has never come naturally to me, so I’m really interested in how it works. A lot of it is more intellectual than instinctive for me. Both Joshua and I are interested in where the line between performance and reality ends. We’re making a film, we’re putting on a performance, we’re creating a character, we’re telling a story, but that’s also what you do in your own life.

We go to all these different environments where there are very different codes of conduct. I was really interested in how you can be a different person, or at least be expected to be a different person, in those different places. And how that kind of performance is maybe not necessarily visible to other people, especially in spaces where women or trans people might not be welcome. How is that negotiated? I feel like it’s a negotiation of what the rules are, what’s allowed and what’s right in a particular space.

I wanted the story of Masc to show that we’re not just one thing. You’re not just a gay person; you might have different identities and there’s an intersectionality there in terms of everyone being unique in where they’re coming from and their experiences. That changes how you have to negotiate all of those different environments.

Most Popular

You’ve mentioned Joshua Griffin a few times already and you developed the original idea with him as well as having him play Robin. He’s obviously an integral part of the production. How did that first idea form between the two of you, and how did you develop it into what we see on screen?

I first met Joshua when we were casting for my short film Repair and our relationship started there. I’d written a script, but then he came in with some ideas and was very open and collaborative about developing the story and the character. The idea actually came from a conversation about process – about whether films could be made in a different way. We came up with the idea of doing a story that made sense in chapters. That meant we could play with appearance, change the hair and the costume and Joshua was very open to everything. So it was very fluid.

At some point I wrote a sort of outline and then we would develop that. We would take from our own experiences and come up with scenarios. They would start more literally and then develop as the story developed, becoming more fictional. It was a fluid process. I would be the secretary and write the script and keep an eye on the structure, while Joshua was key in the emotional journey of the character and figuring out what was driving him in different moments.

The idea actually came from a conversation about process – about whether films could be made in a different way.

He was also very involved with the casting and finding the right people. As we brought more people in, we would open it up to them and discuss their experiences. Sometimes things would come from them, or we’d shape the character and adapt it to something that felt right for them. Some of the people we actually cast were slightly different from what I had originally written. You make something up, and then you find a real actor and think, “Oh, this person is really interesting. Let’s adapt it so it fits them.”

It sounds like you and Joshua had a lot of trust in each other throughout that process. When you were building Robin together, did the character evolve during the development? Is that character on screen how you imagined them at the start of the production?

I guess Robin is this expression of something joint from us – Joshua and I. In that sense, I feel like we just came closer to something more truthful in an emotional sense, rather than a literal sense. We moved away from the literal towards something more fictional and that helped us create more truth. It’s definitely different from where we started, but it also feels like it’s just where it’s supposed to be.

I think the whole process for us was very instinctual – going with what makes sense and not trying to force things. Within a scene, if the dialogue we’d written, whether that was before filming, on set or in the edit, wasn’t really working or didn’t feel like it was coming from the characters, we would get rid of it or find other ways of putting it together.

One of the things I loved about the film was how intimate it feels when you’re spending this time with Robin. How did you think about that intimacy when you were making the film? Was there a conscious effort to make the audience feel close to him without ever feeling like we’re intruding on his experience?

I definitely love that type of intimacy – that feeling of really being with the character. Even though we’re playing with layers of performance in Masc, I wanted it to feel like you’re actually getting something that Robin doesn’t want to reveal. A lot of the words are where he’s hiding, where his masks or his personas are. But his actual physicality and his presence are where we can see the real Robin come through.

I think, in all aspects of the filmmaking, because a lot of those things were just shot with me and Joshua—maybe with one other person—it was very intimate in the way we captured it. Sometimes, someone was helping with sound, but it wasn’t like there were 20 people on set. That’s one of the things I’ve learnt from my photography and making my other films. If you can create that intimacy on set, then it can carry over into the actual filmmaking, because it’s not something you’re trying to force. It’s actually what happened. It was very intimate.

I like to operate the camera because I prefer to direct while watching through the viewfinder.

You just mentioned that you shot the film yourself. What made you want to take on the cinematography, alongside directing?

I think it’s a combination of things. On the one hand, I knew that having a cinematographer would create one of the biggest logistical issues, because I wanted to work across the year and the cinematographers I want to work with are busy and off doing great things. But then it was also about the intimacy and directness of it. Even when I work with cinematographers, I like to operate the camera because I prefer to direct while watching through the viewfinder. It feels more like I’m literally in the audience’s seat and I can respond to what I’m seeing. If I’m watching it on a monitor, it feels like I’m starting to become detached from the actual scene and more focused on the presentation of it.

I really value that closeness of being part of the performance in a way. That’s what I enjoy about photography and filmmaking. There are definitely challenges to doing both things at the same time. There are certainly more things to think about, but with Masc we solved that by just giving ourselves more time.

Do you think the film would have been different if you hadn’t been handling the cinematography and directing at the same time? Were there moments where you wished you could step away, or was that intimacy vital to the way the film turned out?

There was definitely no moment where I wanted to step away. Again, I think it’s just about the balance. I like to keep things smaller and be more nimble, but obviously sometimes it’s useful to have a few more people who can help you. At times it was physically hard to hold the camera. You get tired and you wish you weren’t the person shaking and could just sit in the chair. We did bring in additional hands when we needed them, especially when we literally couldn’t do everything at the same time. If the camera was moving on a rickshaw, for example, then I needed someone else to do that. But I loved the process and wouldn’t have changed it.

One of the things I loved about the film is the way it moves through time. I know you shot it in these different chapters, but when you put the film together, there’s a real fluidity to it. We’re often left questioning exactly what we’re watching or where we are in the story. What was the editing process like, and what drew you to that structure?

The film is actually quite linear. It just has the appearance of being less so, with a few non-linear moments and some layers being revealed that make you question what’s going on. I was interested, on a more self-indulgent film-nerd level, in this idea of the film representing the process that we were going through – learning about these things and figuring them out together. I wanted the film to reflect that process in some way. For the metafictional layers, I didn’t want to do it in a way that I’d seen before, in terms of it being about a film shoot and going to that particular place.

It definitely created some challenges, but we had an amazing editor, Anna Miller, who’s a good friend and who I’ve worked with on most of my films. We had to find the right balance, giving the audience things to hang on to, so they can follow it, without trying to be too explanatory. We went with the emotional truth, the emotional continuity or flow of it, rather than trying to be too informative and saying, “Okay, now we’re going to orient people, now we’re in Wales.” Anna was super valuable in creating that audience perspective and challenging us on distilling things. I think what she did really well was help shape things and maintain the unique way we wanted to approach the film, while also keeping that idea of how we wanted to reveal Robin. She didn’t try to apply a conventional narrative structure and say, “Here’s how it has to be, and this is exactly how it should flow.”

Without giving too much away for people who haven’t seen the film, I do want to touch on the ending. You conclude Masc with this mesmerising piece of choreography and having followed your work for a while, I know movement has always been a recurring element in your filmmaking. What keeps drawing you back to movement and choreography and did you always know that was going to be the end of the film?

Yeah, I did actually. That was one of the very first scenes I wrote. I knew I wanted to do that. I think I’m fascinated by movement because I can’t do it myself. It’s such a powerful form of communication; it’s beyond words. You can get something from it emotionally, but for me it’s also very mystical. I don’t really understand it, so I guess there’s a fascination there. It’s amazing, but it’s also quite mysterious to me.

Joshua also has a background in physical theatre, so he loves working with the body. It became a way of showing something true of Robin, while also having a more lyrical element to the physicality he’s revealing. It was an early idea that made sense because I’d worked with movement before. It wasn’t like, “This film has to have that element,” but it managed to sneak in quite early on and then develop.

I’m keen to protect that process. I don’t want to immediately abandon it and do something in a very traditional way.

It’s such a fitting end to your debut feature. Has the experience of making Masc changed the way you think about your filmmaking? Has it cemented any beliefs you have, or is there anything you’ll take into your next project?

I think what I’m most happy about is that we were able to make the film in this way. Instead of being told, “This is how you have to make a film,” I just made the film in the way that made sense to me and it seems to have worked. So I’m keen to protect that process. I don’t want to immediately abandon it and do something in a very traditional way. I think there are ways to adapt it.

For me, it’s always about who you’re working with and figuring out what works for everyone together, rather than going in with a prescribed idea of how something has to be done to be a proper film, or a proper way to do it. I think it’s important to treat everyone respectfully and not take advantage of people. But beyond that, it’s about finding ways that make sense for you and for every person involved

Have you already started thinking about what’s next?

I’ve got two projects that I’m developing. One is a queer thriller, which is a little bit more of a genre-driven film, but obviously it will have some of my elements and some of my approach. And then there’s another film that’s a sort of love triangle around seeing and hearing. That one maybe follows on more directly from some of the aesthetics and ideas in Masc.

And finally, is there a short film that has really stuck with you which you’d like to recommend to the DN community?

This is of course totally biased because it’s my partner, but Lustlings by Nico Carmandaye is quite a unique exploration of relationship anxiety from a neurodivergent perspective through horror tropes. And you’ll recognise the brilliant Cayvan Coates from my short Alfie’s Island. It’s just starting its festival journey, playing next at Chéries-Chéris in Paris.

item.title: Subverting Stereotypes and Capturing the Authentic Drunken Perspective in Daniel Chisholm’s Dizzying ‘Don’t Puke’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Daniel Chisholm distils the disorientating, woozy sensation of being smashed into a comic odyssey that lets audiences experience the drunkest night ever.
item.content:encoded:
Buzzed, merry, legless, smashed – there are countless ways to describe being drunk, but capturing any one of those states convincingly on screen is no easy task. Conventional depictions of inebriation tend to rely on slurred speech, uncontrollable hiccups and characters stumbling into furniture, but do these familiar tropes ever really convey the alcohol-fuelled perspective, or have they simply become lazy cinematic shorthand? With his perfectly titled short Don’t Puke, director Daniel Chisholm sets out to offer something more authentic, following a wasted woman on her increasingly disorientating journey home to her trusty sofa.

Opening with an epilepsy warning that also contains a tongue-in-cheek disclaimer about the film’s potential to induce vomiting, Don’t Puke makes its intentions clear from the outset and delivers on them over the following seven minutes. Disorientating, hilarious and at times painfully accurate, Chisholm elevates a relatively simple premise through an inventive and immersive production that puts us firmly inside his protagonist’s drunken perspective. Naturally, it left us with plenty of questions. Eager to dive into those, the writer/director/editor/producer joins us to discuss the challenges of recreating a drunken night out — spinning rooms, cold chips and all.

Hey Daniel, thanks for joining us on Directors Notes. We’re excited to talk about your wonderfully titled short film, Don’t Puke. The film seems intent on capturing an unusually hyper-accurate depiction of what it feels like to be drunk. What inspired you to explore that experience on screen and what did you find interesting about trying to recreate it for an audience?

I’ve often watched depictions of inebriation on screen and been a bit disappointed. They often did a token attempt at depicting what it feels like to be drunk (usually with a Snorricam), but never quite went far enough for my personal taste. I wanted to go the extra mile and take the concept to its logical conclusion – how close could I possibly get on screen to what it feels like to be drunk? What are the symptoms, and how can I best translate those into something that is filmable? The goal was to make the audience feel like they’ve had the most drunk night of their lives, but hopefully without the hangover.

Authenticity seems to have been a key aim throughout the production. What did your pre-production process look like and how did you work out the details that would make the experience feel genuinely drunk rather than simply like a cinematic depiction of drunkenness?

My first step was to think back to my own (way too many) experiences with alcohol and how it made me feel. The plan was to really figure out what was happening in detail and to be as faithful to that as possible in the film. Two feelings seemed essential to me: The dizziness that makes it hard to walk or focus on things, and the feeling of the world spinning around when lying down and closing one’s eyes.

If that’s what my eyes are doing, why not just do the same with the image on screen?

Thinking back to the dizziness I felt, I realised that my eyes constantly seemed to be flicking from right to left, again, and again, and again. Apparently, this is called “nystagmus” and people can experience it horizontally or vertically. I personally am of the horizontal persuasion. So, I figured, if that’s what my eyes are doing, why not just do the same with the image on screen? I tried moving the camera in that manner (repeatedly panning it from right to left) and cutting out the pan back (from left to right) to make the movement seem like it was always going in the same direction. Unfortunately, that led to big continuity issues when filming dialogue, because it required me to cut so much out. Instead, I ended up doing it in post, by slightly cropping the image and then keyframing it repeatedly from one direction to the other.

The world turning effect took a bit more work, though I knew that I wanted to transport the idea by having the camera spin around Charlie (the protagonist), because that is what I myself visualised when I was lying on my bed, trying desperately to distract myself from the need to puke: I visualised the room spinning around me, then the house, then the whole world, and then the galaxy. I did lots of tests to see how I could achieve something like this, and after lots of trial and error, I broke that sequence into multiple stages, each of which has its own technical solution, including techniques like photogrammetry, gaussian splatting and 3D modelling, using mostly Blender and After Effects. More about those later.

Janka would ceremoniously have a single shot of vodka, just to get in the headspace.

A lot of the film’s authenticity comes through Janka Horakova’s performance. How did you work with her to get into that inebriated headspace and were there particular aspects of the character’s physicality or behaviour that you wanted her to focus on?

Janka Horakova was an absolute godsend! When I auditioned her, I immediately knew that she would play the part. She is a consummate professional, so she had prepared thoroughly, and it showed in her performance. Her energy was incredible! It really looked like she was trying hard to stay upright, trying hard to enunciate her words, but instead, she was staggering and slurring like someone who’s downed the better part of a vodka bottle. To be completely honest, there was very little ‘directing’ I needed to do at all – she just turned up and nailed it. I’m incredibly lucky she decided that she wanted to play the part, because without her, I’m not sure it would have worked at all – she totally carries it.

Most Popular

We were a fairly dry set (until wrap-time anyway). The temptation would of course have been to go full method, but Janka heroically resisted. At the beginning of each shooting day however, Janka would ceremoniously have a single shot of vodka, just to get in the headspace, while of course still staying totally in control. I think it also helped that the atmosphere on set was really good – people were having fun and that allowed the party-vibe to take hold, which was particularly important for the first scene, where Charlie (played by Horakova) begins her journey after escaping from her pushy friend Alex (played by Claire Uicker) and the crazy birthday party they’re at.

The film constantly shifts our perspective between first-person shots and the close-up camera that follows Janka. How did you decide which moments should be experienced from her subjective perspective and which should place us outside of her?

My initial instinct was to go full subjective perspective throughout the whole film, meaning I wanted the audience to experience each scene as Charlie, the protagonist, through her view of the world. Of course, that doesn’t mean literally seeing everything through her eyes in a point-of-view shot, but rather we shot almost the entire film using a mix of POVs and close-ups on Janka, to put us in her headspace and still show us her emotions.

The close-ups were shot on an old, adapted projector lens that Dillon Ritchie, our DoP, got from our mutual friend Shane Kang, who graciously lent it to us. This lens is ultra-soft and has some beautiful distortions around the edges. Together with the chaotic hand-held action and the constant focus shifting, I think this gets close to the blurry, fuzzy, dizzy feeling that can kick in when properly sozzled.

It almost feels like security camera footage and gives us a good look at what Janka looks like from the outside.

We didn’t stick with the subjective perspective through the whole film however – there are two scenes where we break out into an objective, observational perspective, meaning we see Charlie from the outside, as an onlooker, a spectator: The first is at the kebab shop, the second is when she arrives home. Dillon came up with the idea for the perspective break during our early conversations about the film, and I think juxtaposing what Charlie looks like from the outside with what she feels on the inside adds some lovely humour.

To really emphasise the perspective shift, the objective, observational shots are the only ones in the entire film that are wide shots, and they are shot with a locked-off camera, and a clean lens and a deep depth of field. It almost feels like security camera footage and gives us a good look at what Janka looks like from the outside. She’s pretty funny to look at as she staggers around completely legless.

With that in mind, were you more interested in showing the audience what drunkenness looks like from the outside, or trying to make them experience what it feels like from the inside?

Definitely the latter. I wanted to avoid making a film about drunk people as some kind of social statement. When making a film about something that has as many downsides as alcohol, I think it’s easy to end up with a simplistic message, like “alcohol is bad”. I was hoping to avoid that by focusing purely on the experience itself rather than the consequences. After all, I think the feeling of being completely smashed is something that many of us can identify with. I wanted to connect with that experience and make people go: “Ah yeah, I recognise that. That’s pretty accurate. And a bit funny when I can experience it at arm’s length and without the fear of waking up to realise I did something really stupid last night” (that’s how I usually felt after getting plastered, at least).

So yeah, entertainment was definitely a lot higher on my list of priorities than education. I suppose that for anyone who has never had the doubtful pleasure of being totally shitfaced, after watching this film, I hope you might have a better idea of what it feels like to be hammered. Maybe that’ll help some kids make a more informed choice.

There’s a particularly striking sequence where your protagonist slumps onto the sofa and we experience that familiar spinning-room sensation as the camera orbits around her, before pulling back beyond the building. How did you conceive and execute that sequence?

This moment in Charlie’s journey was inspired by (too) many sloshed nights lying in bed, feeling the world spin around me. On occasions when it was bearable, I would visualise the world spinning around me. My addled mind found it entertaining to depict myself in the room, the whole house spinning, then taking it further out to the whole world spinning, with me perched atop it, and then the whole galaxy. That was fun, until I desperately needed to puke. Which I did. And this is, of course, exactly what I tried to replicate in the film.

At first, I thought about ways to achieve this practically (at least the first step of showing the movement around Charlie on the sofa), but I quickly realised that this would be pretty much impossible to do on the budget I had available. I’d never even heard of a rig that would spin around a fixed point, so I gave up trying to come up with one myself. Instead, I looked into ways to do this digitally.

I’d only dabbled in Blender up until this point, and I knew there was no way in hell I would be able to sculpt a photorealistic Janka myself, but just around this time, I’d seen something online about relatively new techniques to capture photorealism for 3D, called photogrammetry and gaussian splatting. I did some more research and started experimenting with some free solutions that I found online. After lots of trial and error, I decided that a mix of both would probably work best.

The thing that gave it away initially was the hair, which came out looking flat and unrealistic. So, I learned how to create a hair system in Blender and replaced her hair.

For the shot on the sofa, I took lots of footage of Janka sitting there, then fed those into Polycam, which at the time was still new and had a lot of free options. This gave me a 3D model of Janka and the room. When trying to capture the entire room, the quality was really low, so I used that mostly as a reference to rebuild the room in Blender using assets I downloaded online from various sources, like Sketchfab – where there are tons and tons of community-created assets, many of which are on a Creative Commons license and free to use. For those bits of furniture that I couldn’t find a good match, I modelled them myself in Blender.

For the model of Janka, a detailed photogrammetry scan gave me enough quality to feel like I might get away with it. The thing that gave it away initially was the hair, which came out looking flat and unrealistic. So, I learned how to create a hair system in Blender and replaced her hair. Once I had the room and Janka assembled, it was just a question of animating a camera around her.

For the house shot, I decided to go for a gaussian splat, which is a 3D point cloud that can create stunningly photorealistic environments. I was lucky enough that my friend Marvin Borchers, who is a drone operator, agreed to help me out. We did a flight around my parents’ house, taking footage of it from all angles. I then fed this into PostShot, which is software that creates a gaussian splat out of pictures or video. Once that was done, I could animate a virtual camera around the point-cloud house, and the result is what you see in the film. It’s not perfect, because PostShot was still in Beta at the time, and my graphics card isn’t exactly top-end, but the shot moves fast, so I hope I got away with that bit of jankiness.

The shots of the Earth and the Galaxy spinning, I both animated in After Effects, which is more my comfort zone. The legendary Video Copilot has a great free plugin called Orb, and a brilliant tutorial to go along with it, that makes creating a semi-realistic Earth in After Effects a breeze – I’d recommend that to anyone doing something similar.

For me personally, I found some visual parallels with music videos such as The Prodigy’s Smack My Bitch Up and Pulp’s Do You Remember the First Time? when watching Don’t Puke. What were the visual influences that shaped the way you approached your film?

Funny you should mention music videos – I absolutely love music videos, and I approach projects where I know the music is going to play a large role, like in Don’t Puke, a bit like editing a music video at times. Paul Child, the composer, is a longtime friend and collaborator of mine, and he was on board well before the shoot began. We tossed ideas back and forth for what the music would need, and once the film was ready, I primarily let the music dictate the rhythm of the edit rather than vice versa.

Wow, I just checked out the video to Do You Remember the First Time? by Pulp, and they really did the same spinning effect, but they did it practically! I’d not seen this one before – that’s amazing! Now I really want to know how they did it! Smack my Bitch Up is of course a legendary video and I’m honoured that you would be reminded of it while watching Don’t Puke!

To be honest, I didn’t really have any direct references in mind while coming up with the visuals for Don’t Puke (apart from what I could remember of my personal experiences). I thought about Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas as a film that goes to similar lengths to depict substance abuse, but it was more of a spiritual reference than a direct one. Of course, I’m not creating my work in a vacuum – there are definitely influences from other filmmakers that have found their way into my work, but I think they’re mostly on a subconscious level a lot of the time. Some of the filmmakers whose visual style has impressed me in the past are Luc Besson, Chris Cunningham, Gaspar Noé and Hayao Miyazaki. Charlie Kaufman’s unique approach to subjective perspectives has also deeply impressed me and got me thinking about how to reflect some of those concepts in my own work.

The film also has a wonderfully repetitive quality to its editing, which seems to mirror the cyclical nature of being drunk. Was that repetition something you planned from the script, or was it something you discovered during the edit?

Yeah, the repetition was definitely baked in from the start, but the detailed execution was then often found in the edit. I knew from the get-go that I wanted the process of getting from A to B, the ‘shoe leather’, which is usually the first thing to be left out in films because it’s usually repetitive and boring, to feature prominently here. In my experience, getting anywhere when your legs aren’t working properly is a lot more interesting than it normally would be. So, I tried to use the recurring walking scenes to pull us into Charlie’s state of being, to make us walk in her shoes for a little while, so to speak.

Charlie needed to almost puke a few times, so that the climax would really land.

I also knew I was going to use a lot of repetitive jump-cuts, both to add to the chaos and the lack of orientation, but also to give myself the freedom to mash loads of different takes together, finding the moments with the right kinetic energy and the best performance. The drinking of beverages and the nauseating result thereof was something I didn’t want to leave at just a one-off either. After all, the pay-off at the end needed a set-up: Charlie needed to almost puke a few times, so that the climax would really land. And what better way to make someone want to puke than by forcing them to drink something they’d rather not?

More generally, how did you approach finding the rhythm of the film in post-production? Was there a point where you felt you’d finally found the right pace for the audience to experience the night alongside your protagonist?

It took a few re-edits to get the right pacing and length, that’s for sure. Though I frequently freelance as an editor, I usually try to avoid editing my own films. I feel that it is usually easier to get a good result if the editor has a healthy distance from the material, which I, as a director, almost never do. But this time, I decided to do it myself anyway, because of the highly specific nature of the visual language. If I had saddled someone else with the edit of this film, I probably would have ended up micro-managing the poor sod, which wouldn’t have been fun for either of us.

At some point I guess perfect becomes the enemy of good.

As a result, however, I did indeed find it difficult to get the necessary distance from the material, and I needed lots of detailed feedback from my friends and family to find the right length for the piece. I even killed a whole scene because it felt unnecessary and like one repetition too many. In hindsight, I think the chips eating scene still could probably be a little shorter, but I guess one can keep tweaking forever. At some point, I guess perfect becomes the enemy of good.

What’s next in your filmmaking journey? Are there any upcoming projects you’re working on that you’re excited to share with our audience?

Heh, yeah, I’m always working on something. My biggest project is an arthouse, contained, near-future sci-fi feature that I’m writing, and which I am very excited about. In parallel I’m also developing a short film with Dillon Ritchie (the DoP on Don’t Puke) which he’s written. It’s a dark, off-kilter comedy about a son-in-law connecting with his wife’s dad while on a hunting trip. It’s a really fun story, and we’re hoping to shoot in spring next year.

I’m also developing another short film I’ve written, which is a fictionalised engagement with my own post-colonial guilt. Both my parents grew up in Africa (Zimbabwe and Mozambique), and I have lived in South Africa and Kenya. The inequality I experienced while growing up there was staggering, and it left a deep impression on me. I’m trying to work that experience into a story about a character who has to deal with a similar past, while being thrust into a situation in which he must decide between paying a hefty price in order to atone for his guilt, or ignoring it and pretending it doesn’t matter.

And then I’m also developing a fun vertical drama together with Janka Horakova called Das Revier (German for Hunting Territory and Police station – we love double-meanings, us Germans). It’s a bit of a piss-take on German procedural police shows (of which there are about a billion – it’s the most popular format over here). We’re just having a bit of fun with that, and hopefully the first episodes will be dropping in the not-too-distant future.

And finally, this is a question we ask all our featured filmmakers: what’s one short film by another filmmaker that you’d recommend to the Directors Notes audience, and why?

One of my favourite short films of all time is Soft by Simon Ellis. I watched this back in 2008 or 2009, and it still is one of my favourites. The film hits like a truck. I really admire the emotional punch that it delivers. For me, the sign of a really good film is when I feel properly shaken about after watching it. When it really makes me feel something. It could be any emotion really. As long as I feel my insides twisting and turning, that means the film is connecting with me. And Soft most definitely did that.

item.title: A Houseguest Too Many Tips Everything Into Chaos in Kiyan Ahmadi’s Tense & Tender Short ‘PIERRE THE GREAT’
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: How much can a relationship withstand when an outsider disrupts its delicate balance? Kiyan Ahmadi explores that tension in his cramped, darkly comic short.
item.content:encoded:
In LA-based filmmaker Kiyan Ahmadi’s second short film, Pierre the Great, we follow Omar as he takes in his injured uncle Pierre in an attempt to help quickly disrupt the dynamic between him and his girlfriend Lindsey, turning an already cramped living situation into a chaotic night where small tensions begin to spiral. What more could go wrong? Where does the line between being a good host and trying to protect one’s mental sanity start blurring?

The self-taught director drew on his own experiences and anxieties when developing Pierre the Great’s characters, shot in just three days. Very much taken with how the film explores masculinity, communication, and the strange ways people behave when pushed beyond their comfort zones, we speak to Ahmadi about finding humour in discomfort, allowing the film to take shape through the filmmaking process, and learning when to let go in the edit.

Hi Kiyan! Welcome to the Directors Notes community. Your film began as a much simpler story about a woman realising that her boyfriend was an opportunist, before becoming something much more personal and rooted in family dynamics. Do you think films are inevitably telling something about the people who make them?

I have a superstitious belief that, depending on the film, the characters you write are a version of you. Not you exactly, but pulled from you — and I think there’s a risk that writing them out means you’re manifesting that, running the risk of sharing a similar fate to the people you’ve written. As I steered away from the boyfriend being an opportunist toward someone lacking backbone, I was pulling from myself. At the time, I had difficulty speaking up for myself, and I was worried how that would manifest in my relationships with people. I was afraid of becoming a pushover, and I was working that out while writing this, which made it more personal. Looking back at the character afterwards, I realized I didn’t resemble him as much as I thought—which was liberating. I still hold onto this belief that you can unlock a path for yourself to become your characters, or share their fate, almost like speaking it into existence. I’m not a superstitious person at all, but it’s something I do believe, however ridiculous it sounds.

Pierre the Great seems to sit in an interesting space between discomfort, humour and tenderness. How did you find the right tonal balance between those elements? Was humour something you used to make the uncomfortable moments more bearable, or do you see comedy and discomfort as naturally existing alongside one another?

I never really approached it as consciously balancing three tones. I reckon when you’re writing characters that are clashing, the humour naturally emerges from the conflict and the way these people communicate, or attempt to communicate with each other. Rather than trying to manufacture a balance, I trusted that if the characters were honest and well written, and the actors had a sense of timing, a funny moment was bound to surface on its own — the funniest films, to me, are rarely ones that set out to be comedies, but ones that stumble upon humour through character. Discomfort is naturally tied into that. It’s funny that something is only funny once we’re removed from it — rarely is anything actually funny when you’re experiencing the discomfort firsthand, in real time.

The two weren’t something I balanced against each other so much as something that came from the same place. Tenderness was the one I had to work for. That was something I was striving for towards the end of the script, and it was genuinely difficult to find where it lived in the story and place it correctly, which was something I was hoping shone through the chaos.

I still hold onto this belief that you can unlock a path for yourself to become your characters, or share their fate, almost like speaking it into existence. I’m not a superstitious person at all, but it’s something I do believe, however ridiculous it sounds.

You say you’re interested in films that feel ‘discovered’ rather than completely structured from the beginning. It reminds me of Michelangelo’s idea that sculpting was, in a sense, about revealing the figure that was already hidden within the stone. Do you then think filmmaking can work in a similar way—where the story or characters already contain something that you’re trying to uncover through the process?

Yeah, one hundred per cent. I don’t think, for me at least, a film is really worth making if you know the answers. Art in general is exciting to me because of discovery. Otherwise, you’re simply executing a blueprint, which, in a way, you are. A script is a blueprint in a way. But I find the process of writing to be in itself a discovery. You start with a blank page. If you really wanted to reach, you could say it’s like a giant rectangular piece of blank marble. You have to sit, listen to yourself, and trust that you’ll find your way to something hopefully interesting. I don’t think I would be interested in making films if I had all the answers.

During production, I would say it’s the same process, if you allow it to be, where the idea you had of a scene—how it’ll play out, how it will feel, what beat you’re gonna hit, what moment someone will cry, what moment someone will scream and shout—all those things have the potential to be subverted. And I think more often than not, when it is subverted, you’re left with something you didn’t anticipate, which can be more interesting and revealing about the characters or the story, etc. For me, a film that feels discovered is a film that remains curious.

During the shoot, you were very open to letting scenes become something different from what you had originally imagined. What does that openness look like practically on set? How do you know when an unexpected interpretation from an actor or someone from the crew is something actually worth following?

Openness on a set walks a fine line. If you’re too much of an open valve, you end up wasting time or losing the plot a bit. It’s also directly tied to the crew and cast you’ve chosen. The people you choose to be a part of your project are directly tied to your level of openness: knowing whether an actor or crew member’s suggestions or ideas are worth following is instinctual. It has to serve the story and/or the characters. If you know your script well enough, it gives you the freedom and ability to make those judgment calls.

For me, a film that feels discovered is a film that remains curious.

I believe a good example of this is the bus stop scene. The two actors, Kate Adams and Adam Hagenbuch, who play the couple being very cloying with each other, decided to start sharing a piece of gum. That wasn’t in the script, and I think it was my job to create the environment for them to be comfortable enough to bring that to the scene. I felt that it added a lot to their characters.

Most Popular

The film was shot in just three days and you ultimately cut almost everything you shot on the third day. What did that experience teach you about the importance of editing when it comes to the final result?

It taught me to exercise restraint in the editing room. I found myself often really attached to certain moments, and wanting to include them in the cut because I thought they were funny or interesting, but that’s actually what kills a film. You never want your own satisfaction to get in the way of a good film. Restraint in editing proves a level of maturity. I think you can usually tell when a filmmaker is really impressed by themselves and includes everything they thought was brilliant in their final cut. As a filmmaker myself, we’re all guilty of that.

As a self-taught filmmaker making only your second short, there’s something interesting about the very instinctive way you describe your process—writing from experience, allowing actors to play, and discovering the film through editing. Has being self-taught given you a particular freedom in the way you approach filmmaking?

I believe it did. I don’t want to bash on film school graduates to say that they are more limited: lots of very talented, interesting, and inventive people come out of film school. I can say for myself: I don’t do well in classrooms. I tend to thrive when I’m told to go figure things out myself, or I stumble on things independently.

I think you can usually tell when a filmmaker is really impressed by themselves and includes everything they thought was brilliant in their final cut. As a filmmaker myself, we’re all guilty of that.

The cramped environment seems particularly important because it allows small interactions and personality clashes to become heightened. How did the physical space you were in influence the blocking, performances, and visual language of the film? Did the house itself dictate any of your visual decisions?

This was the camera our cinematographer, editor and colorist Robby Piantanida already owned, so we had a choice of some different lenses he had and I thought the Lomo anamorphics had a really strange quality to them. Lomo lenses are old soviet lenses, and they tend to be pretty soft on the skin. I had seen some test footage Robby had shot with them, and I instantly fell in love. We did have some second thoughts as it’s hard to go wide on Anamorphics, especially older ones such as the Lomos. The widest in the set was 35mm, so it was either going to be a strength or a weakness, and I decided that being tighter on the subjects was going to make it more interesting visually. In my opinion, the anamorphics contribute to the claustrophobia by being widescreen enough for a sense of scope, but tight enough to feel like you’re trapped.

We often had to work around the space, which informed the blocking. Since the space was small and the lenses were shooting long, we were limited in how much we could include in the frame, so there was a lot of compromise and pivoting involved in how characters were blocked.

What is currently on your table that we can look forward to?

I have a couple of things I’m working on right now. I have two other short films written and am currently trying to build funding for, and a feature I’m working on as well at the moment.

And finally, what’s your favourite short film of all time? What does it mean to you and why is it so important?

That’s hard. I don’t think I have a favorite. I will mention one that I saw recently from a friend, Play Gun by Noah Kentis—who actually shot the polaroids that are featured in the beginning of the film. It is a fantastic short. I’m pretty sure it’s on YouTube for anyone interested in watching. Very funny, short and simple.

item.title: Animator Kate Renshaw-Lewis Peels Back the Repetition, Rhythm and Absurdity of Mass Production in ‘Busy Bodies’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Kate Renshaw-Lewis explores the hidden complexities of consumerism driven mass production in a surreal, tactile world of Rube Goldberg systems of production.
item.content:encoded:
When you think about films exploring consumerism and mass production, you might expect observational documentaries or investigative journalism pieces filled with familiar images of huge factories and automated production lines. For experimental animator Kate Renshaw-Lewis, though, their exploration of the everyday objects we consume was always going to take a much more tactile and surreal route. Inspired by the mechanical, repetitive process of printed animation itself, Busy Bodies takes us inside a strange domestic factory where tiny workers operate an elaborate production line, manufacturing the mundane objects and ingredients that fill our everyday lives.

Winner of Best Animation Short at Slamdance 2026, Busy Bodies is a charming and surreal film packed with inventive craft and plenty to think about. Beneath its warm colours and absurdist humour is a meditation on the hidden labour and questionable ethics behind those everyday products we rarely stop to question. In this interview with DN, Renshaw-Lewis joins us to discuss how the film’s process shaped its narrative, the meditative quality of repetition and the joys of creating a soundtrack from lemons, vacuums and vintage synthesizers.

Hi Kate, thanks for joining us on Directors Notes to discuss your animated short Busy Bodies. I wanted to begin with the ideas behind the film. In your synopsis, you describe it as exploring the “journey of disposable objects” and the “destructive nature of the factory method supply chain”. What were you hoping to say about these ideas and why did you choose this particular story as a way of exploring them?

Hi Rob, thank you so much for including Busy Bodies. I’m very honored to join Directors Notes. Busy Bodies began with the choice of medium, which is printed animation. I wanted to tell a story that was deeply connected to the mechanical, intensive, step-by-step process of printed animation. The idea for the film came to me while I was grabbing lunch during my lunch break, and I noticed a small sticker on my pre-packaged tuna wrap that said, “made by hand”. I started wondering: Whose hand? How did they make it? Will I ever know what goes on behind the fluorescently illuminated presentation of the grocery store? I was also struck by the repetition of grocery stores, rows and rows of produce that seem to live outside the rules of seasonal availability.

Consumption has evolved at a monstrous rate, while production has grown more opaque.

I wanted to comment on the disconnect I feel between the convenience of very familiar, mundane, and disposable objects and the mysterious journey of creation and distribution they go through. We live in a time when convenience is expected at every scale. Consumption has evolved at a monstrous rate, while production has grown more opaque. I was also deeply inspired by Rube Goldberg Machines and The Natural History of the Chicken by Mark Lewis (particularly a scene where little baby chicks are carried up a metal conveyor belt and sorted through various machines).

The film imagines this bizarre domestic factory, where tiny workers operate an elaborate production line to create something as mundane as a rubber glove. How did this central concept develop and what appealed to you about using something so absurd to explore the realities of mass production and consumption?

I really think our systems of production are absurd when you break them down – very efficient, and very absurd. There’s so much engineering and process behind delivering something as simple as rubber gloves, or even something as natural as a lemon. I’m particularly interested in the production of these mundane, organic objects because their factory journeys contrast so sharply. When I think of a lemon or a fish, I don’t immediately think about all the machinery and tools used to prep and deliver them to the store.

I am a huge fan of rubber gloves as an object, they also add a layer of bureaucratic protocol to the film. There is a main character that is never fully seen, just their large hands. They can’t use the sink because there are fish instead of water, so they wash their hands with lemon juice and then plop on a pair of gloves made in the cabinet under the sink. The film follows a rigid set of rules and logic that point to the accepted absurdities of modern convenience. I also set the film in a domestic space (a kitchen and backyard) because mass production feels so huge and unknown. I wanted the domesticity to make the subject more familiar and comfortable, while highlighting the mysterious element of our factory systems.

There’s a wonderful Rube Goldberg quality to the machinery, with each action triggering another in an increasingly elaborate chain of events. How did the logic of the Rube Goldberg machine connect with the themes you were exploring?

I love love love Rube Goldberg Machines, both as a visual and a concept. The logic of Rube Goldberg machines felt so important to the film because of its redundancy and delicacy. Rube Goldberg machines are intentionally overly complicated; they emphasize the process rather than the final result and they differ greatly from the mechanisms of mass production in that sense. But mass-production systems are surprisingly delicate, that delicacy has recently become apparent with supply chain issues. The visual inspiration of Rube Goldberg machines also brought levity and humor to the subject, which feels natural to animation, and highlighted the absurdity of factory production methods.

Most Popular

Your choice of animation technique – 2D hand-drawn printed animation – feels particularly well suited to the themes of your story. How did the narrative and the animation technique influence one another during development?

This was my first film where the medium came first. I was teaching printed animation classes at the time and had free access to a print studio. Many choices for the film’s visuals and narrative came from the printing process’s restrictions. The film uses a combination of inkjet printing (using individual color passes) and silk screenprinting. Screenprinting requires separate screens to be burned for individual colors, resulting in a limited color palette for the film.

The film was initially intended to be entirely screenprinted, but inkjet printing came into play because of budget and time limitations, creating a major plot point. The film switches from inkjet to screen printing just as one of the characters steps away from their role in the machine and looks out at other parts of the factory. The switch to screen printing visualizes the machine’s deterioration through investigation and identification of the factory process.

Can you take us through the production process? What does an individual frame of Busy Bodies go through before it becomes part of the finished film and how long did the animation take from those first drawings to the final edit?

Busy Bodies was animated digitally in Photoshop, then sent to Arius Ziaee, who digitally colored the film frame by frame. I then composited the digital animation and exported image sequences separated by color. I made contact sheets from the image sequences, with multiple frames scaled down so about 20 frames could fit on the paper I printed on. Scenes that were going to be screen printed were then sent to a printing house for printed transparent sheets. I printed the inkjet scenes on my Canon printer one color at a time, replicating the beautiful color misregistration that is natural to screen printing.

I’ve now got a pretty sizeable filing cabinet drawer filled with the prints from the film, they’re wonderful objects to have

For screenprinted scenes, I prepped and exposed the silk screens, then printed one scene and one color at a time. I scanned the printed sheets at 1200 dpi and hand-aligned them in After Effects. There was very little editing after the alignment because almost every frame of the film was printed, most of the loops had digital pans and zooms that were physically printed. I’ve now got a pretty sizeable filing cabinet drawer filled with the prints from the film, they’re wonderful objects to have. The entire film took about one year, the animation and printing went by pretty quickly. The hand alignment was very tedious, and I’m very grateful for audiobooks.

There’s an incredible amount of repetition in the film, both in the movements of the workers and in the machinery they operate. Was that something you were consciously building into the animation and did the repetitive nature of the process affect the way you approached making the film itself?

Yes definitely. I was very intrigued by weaving loops and knew I wanted them to be a large part of the film because they visualized the repetitive nature of factory production methods. Initially, it was also an idea I hoped would save time during printing. I had planned to print the loops and then pan and zoom around them digitally post-printing, but the digital movements looked much better as a pre-printing decision.

It’s a moment that feels large to me, even if it goes unnoticed.

I am a big fan of slowness and meditative qualities in animated films, which the repetition and looping heightened. I also wanted the workers to feel harmonious with the mechanisms within the film, their identities are very connected to the production and products. I tried to do this with their colors, design, and movements. There is one small moment, an idea from my wonderful friend Josh Cloud, where one of the workers falls into the sink, and the film does not stop or acknowledge it. It’s a moment that feels large to me, even if it goes unnoticed, because it nods to the loss of workers’ individuality and rights for convenience within these large systems.

I really love the colour palette of Busy Bodies. How did you arrive at those colours and were there particular ideas or emotions you wanted the palette to evoke? Did the physical process of creating the animation influence the choices you made?

The limited color palette resulted from the printing limitations; I decided to stick to three colors due to printing them separately, which also translated into three objects and mechanisms for the film. I chose yellow for the lemons, green for the fish because trout is my favorite fish, and red for the gloves because it enhanced the bureaucratic feeling of the film’s systems, in my opinion.

I wanted the colors of the film to create a warmth that invites the viewers in, maybe even a bit of nostalgia or familiarity to pair with the strangeness of the world of the film.

The paper was a large and fun decision to make. I loved this paper because it added a really beautiful texture to the entire film, a texture that can’t really be seen on the printed pages in person, but is highlighted because the scans are so scaled up. I love the paper’s tone because it felt like an old document left in a filing cabinet, found decades later with an aged hue.

The color tones are personal favorites of mine, my apartment is filled with earthy greens, reds, and yellows. The film’s topics are very heavy, but the humor in the animation style lightens them. I wanted the colors of the film to create a warmth that invites the viewers in, maybe even a bit of nostalgia or familiarity to pair with the strangeness of the world of the film.

Sound plays an important role in giving the factory its sense of life. How did you approach the sound design and score and what did you want the audio to contribute that the visuals couldn’t?

I’m very particular about sound in my films, I have yet to make a film with spoken dialogue. Some huge sonic inspirations for this film were Raymond Scott and Joe Meek. I worked alongside two wonderful musicians, Arius Ziaee and Alex Edgeworth, who joined me in recording synthesizers for the film at the Vintage Synthesizer Museum in Los Angeles.

I love adding sound that gently nods towards the darker subjects and layers of the film.

Alex introduced me to the musician Ursula Bogner, who became a major reference point for the film’s sound design. I didn’t initially plan to do the sound design myself, but I had a very particular idea for the film’s sound, and my producer, Eric Ackerman, suggested I do it myself because I could see it so clearly in my head. I’m very shy about my musical skills, and I felt incredibly vulnerable making the final score and sound, but it was also very exciting, and I used a lot of strange tools, including vintage synthesizers, clarinet, harmonium, keyboard, water, pillows, lemons, hay, metal sheets, and vacuums.

For me, it feels incredibly important that sound adds a subtle, ominous, and dark tone to my films. My animation style, and animation in general, can be seen as quite cute and as a medium intended for children. I love adding sound that gently nods towards the darker subjects and layers of the film.

Towards the end of Busy Bodies, the complexity of the production seems to collapse, with the film reducing this production process down to its constituent parts. Was that shift something you always had in mind? What did you want that change in aesthetic to leave us thinking about?

The film’s ending was an unexpected result of the printing process. As I said before, the shift in printing styles resulted from budget and timing restraints, but it became a pivotal narrative point. The final ending, where the cycles repeat as the different color layers are peeled away, was also a discovery that came from the printing process. It feels so obvious now, but I didn’t initially think to include the screen-printing element of separate color passes.

Originally, the film kept looping with all the colors, but it was incredibly boring. For me, peeling the layers away is a metaphor for the importance of hidden elements within mass production. There’s a lot of questionable ethics and darkness in our mass-production systems, and I believe (and hope) that the more we uncover, the more our systems are questioned and begin to break down and evolve.

Busy Bodies is quite a surreal story and your previous work also seems to embrace abstract narratives, so I’m interested in what draws you towards this kind of storytelling. What can you communicate through this approach that you feel would be harder to achieve through a more conventional narrative?

I’m a personal fan of abstract narratives, and I’m a huge fan of magical realism. Some of my favorite books are The Third Policeman, The Hearing Trumpet, and The Master and Margarita. I’m deeply interested in abstract subjects and surreal narratives, and I think animation lends itself so perfectly because it is a completely unlimited medium, truly, anything can be created.

Even if I tried to create a film that would be seen as a very conventional narrative, it would still be just as abstract as my other films.

I also think it’s much more fun to leave room for interpretation and add layers of abstraction that let my films be viewed on different levels. To me, my films are pretty conventional narratives. When I start a film, I have a clear, simple plotline that grounds my process. I think even if I tried to create a film that would be seen as a very conventional narrative, it would still be just as abstract as my other films.

Thanks so much for joining us and sharing Busy Bodies with us, Kate. Before we wrap up, do you have any other projects you’re currently working on that you can tell us about?

Yes! I’m currently working on a new short film, deeply inspired by my grandparents’ stories of growing up with 10-12 siblings and my experience of growing up in a very small family and pretty self-secluded in my bedroom. The film loosely follows someone desperately trying to sleep, unsure whether the interruptions come from reality or the world of their dreams. I’m planning to return to hand-painted cel animation and multiplane animation. I’m very excited to work on the film during my fellowship at MacDowell this winter.

And finally, this is a question we ask all our featured filmmakers: what’s one short film by another filmmaker that you’d recommend to the Directors Notes audience and why?

Ah, this last question is so hard. However, the film I want to recommend—although it’s not released yet—because it’s wonderful, and because I worked on it while working on Busy Bodies (and vice versa). The film is Lil Gibbos by Arius Ziaee. While Arius animated Lil Gibbos, they also colored Busy Bodies. While I edited Busy Bodies, I also animated the background characters in Lil Gibbos. Arius is a huge inspiration to me, and I’m very grateful we get to keep working on each other’s films.

item.title: Creating Space to Breathe in the Film Industry: Inside the No Man’s Land Creative Retreat
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: An antidote to constant hustle, the team behind the No Man's Land Creative Retreat in Italy discuss why spaces like this are so important to creativity.
item.content:encoded:
What happens when filmmakers are given five days to step away from the pressures of the industry to simply pause and reconnect? That’s the premise behind No Man’s Land, a new creative retreat bringing ten filmmakers to Calabria, Italy, for a week of workshops, reflection and what its organisers describe as “serious play” and “fresh perspectives”. Set among the Apennine Mountains and overlooking the Tyrrhenian Sea, the retreat is designed to offer something increasingly difficult to find within the film industry: time and space to “step away from the noise and slow down”.

The first in Curation Hour’s Creative Retreat Programme, No Man’s Land takes place at the artist residency created by DN alum filmmaker Daria Geller and Yuval Orr as hosts and Rachel Leah Jones as mentor, the retreat promises a temporary escape from “deadlines, devices and the stress of the day-to-day”. In an industry defined by financial pressures, tight schedules and the constant expectation to be producing, the idea of stepping away from it all raises an obvious question: what can five days of disconnection actually achieve?

On paper, it sounds appealing – for the cynical among us, perhaps even a little too good to be true. With that in mind, we spoke to Niccolò, Daria, Yuval and Rachel to look beyond the idyllic setting and get a better understanding of what No Man’s Land is really trying to achieve. We discuss the thinking behind the retreat, what they hope filmmakers will take from the experience, and why creating space for genuine creative exchange might be more important to the future of filmmaking than ever.

Hi Daria, Nico, Rachel and Yuval, thanks for joining us to talk about No Man’s Land, your new creative retreat taking place in Calabria this spring. I wanted to begin with the thinking behind the retreat itself. What was missing from your own experiences of working in film that made you want to create a space like this? And what do you feel is missing from the industry, in general, that a retreat like No Man’s Land can provide?

Yuval Orr & Daria Geller: Our industry can often feel like a hamster wheel, but in our experience, the best creative work is done through contemplation and stepping away from the busyness of our day-to-day. No Man’s Land began as a production company and then became the name of our art residency in the south of Italy, where the retreat will be held and where we have made our home for the last two years. We want to bring the same principles to the retreat that we began our residency with: a place out of space and time. We want the retreat to be friendly, safe and trigger insights.

Niccolò Montanari: I’ve been working in the film and advertising industries for over a decade. My role includes attending and participating in events, including film festivals and commercial awards. As an introverted publicist, which apparently is a thing, I realised my strength wasn’t talking to a whole room of people, but forming meaningful connections one-on-one, which got me thinking that I’m probably not the only one who feels this way. People are tired of having to fight for attention, we already do that online, so what if we created a space for people to connect intimately, without the pressure of having to talk to everyone and land a pitch?

That’s how I thought setting up a series of creative retreats through Curation Hour would make sense: places for people to disconnect and reconnect, with themselves and with one another. A curated room of filmmakers and creative professionals who know they’re all there for the same reason, and who, over several days, get to truly know each other.

A filmmaker’s work doesn’t need to be rushed. It needs time to breathe, grow and develop.

You describe the retreat as being built around “serious play” and “fresh perspectives”. These are intriguing ideas, particularly when filmmaking is so often associated with stress, deadlines and productivity. What do those terms mean to you in practice and why do you think filmmakers need permission to play?

YO & DG: Filmmaking, but documentary filmmaking in particular, is far too often a very serious affair. The topics we touch are serious, the way we speak about the work itself is serious, and the end result is often, well, very serious. But it’s very important to find joy in our work, and to protect our joy, too. The most incredible moments in filmmaking are when you enter a flow state, and a sense of play and lightness is necessary to reach that state. The retreat is a chance for all of us to get back there.

NM: Our society is built around productivity, having to deliver more, and more quickly. And we can see where that’s led us. It doesn’t look like things are slowing down either (hello AI!), and a filmmaker’s work (or any creative work, for that matter) doesn’t need to be rushed. It needs time to breathe, grow and develop, without the guilt of taking time off. We’ve selected our locations specifically because the pace there is slower, so you’re almost forced to slow down and be reminded that you don’t need to be on 24/7, and that your health, relationships and work will all benefit from taking a few days off.

There’s also a strong emphasis on stepping away from devices and the day-to-day noise of the industry. Why was creating genuine distance from the normal filmmaking environment so important to you? Do you think filmmakers need to physically remove themselves from their usual surroundings in order to think differently? And what role does the retreat’s location play in this?

YO & DG: The noise of the industry and our screens can put tremendous pressure on artists, and the result is too often that we lose connection with ourselves. We cannot create meaningful work from such a place. A seaside village in the south of Italy is almost like an antidote to this state. The sound of the waves, the slow pace of life, the incredible food, the warmth of the people – these things can bring us back to ourselves, to our bodies and our motivations for doing this work.

NM: Any change of location gives you a change of perspective. Think about going on holiday: it takes you two or three days just to get into holiday mode, to actually slow down. So being placed in a gorgeous environment, with people specifically selected for their skills and portfolio, led by a mentor who can carefully look at your work, get to know you, and give you the time and confidence you need to develop it, is exactly what’s needed.

People aren’t coming to the retreat for a packed schedule. They’re coming for key moments, and to let the environment do most of the work.

Let’s talk about the people you’re bringing together. Who is No Man’s Land intended for and what are you looking for when selecting the filmmakers who attend?

NM: The focus is documentary, as the mentor for this edition is Emmy Award-winning director Rachel Leah Jones. We’ve tapped into the Curation Hour network of filmmakers, as well as our own contacts from festivals and awards we’ve participated in. The No Man’s Land creative retreat is designed specifically for filmmakers who want their work reviewed by someone with extensive experience, but who also want to come away with a fresh perspective and new ideas. Or simply any creative who wants to disconnect, as it’s important to move away from the idea of necessarily “having to deliver” something.

How much thought have you given to creating a balance – different experiences, disciplines and perspectives – within the group?

NM: A lot. I have plenty of experience running film festivals, awards and retreats, and one thing is certain: less is more. People aren’t coming to the retreat for a packed schedule. They’re coming for key moments, and to let the environment do most of the work. Somewhere like Calabria, one of Italy’s hidden gems, is a gorgeous setting between mountain and sea, with great food and great people. I could try to describe it, but you really have to experience it. I spent some time there myself and fell in love with it, to the point that I’ve thought about moving there.

Most Popular

Rachel Leah Jones is an important part of the retreat as a mentor. How did that collaboration come about and what was it about Rachel’s approach and experience that made her the right person to help shape this experience?

YO: I worked with Rachel on Advocate, the Emmy-award-winning documentary she co-directed with Philippe Bellaiche, over a decade ago. Since then, we have stayed close friends and both Rachel and Philippe have become mentors and role models for my own documentary practice. Besides being an incredible director, Rachel is first and foremost an incredible writer and storyteller, and she has the ability to read a filmmaker’s work-in-progress writing about their own work and put her finger on the beating pulse of the story that they hadn’t seen before. It’s a truly unique skill set that she can bring to her work as a mentor. Rachel also knows the importance of creating space for silliness and play and exploration, which are such crucial but overlooked skills to have when you’re trying to find your voice and your story.

For filmmakers considering applying, what can they actually expect once they arrive? What might a typical day at No Man’s Land look like and how structured is the experience?

Rachel Leah Jones: The short answer is: we are not going to wake you up at 8:30 for a how-to workshop. There will be structure, but not an insane amount of it. Or at least it ought not feel like it. We want people to have a reason to be together, but also permission to reflect, experiment, get lost a bit.

There might be a convening in the morning, then a few hours when you work on your own or in duos. We might watch somebody’s material in a group in the afternoon, or have a one-on-one conversation about a problem they’re struggling with. We’ll eat together. We’ll watch films. People will talk, listen, suggest, share. Hopefully people will wander off and stare at the sea or a tree or a supermarket parking lot (we are, after all, documentarians). We’ll do some hands-on “ways of seeing/representing” exercises.

What we don’t want is for people to arrive and immediately start performing their professional selves for each other – pitching, networking, asking who your sales agent is before they’ve asked what your film is about.

YO & DG: At most industry events, time is neatly structured so that you are running from one workshop to another, one meeting to another, from early morning until late at night. We wanted to design an experience that is the exact opposite, that encourages deeper connections among participants but also with our mentor.

Days will start with coffee and pastries at the cafe, followed by workshops held in the No Man’s Land residency, an 18th century renovated house at the top of the old city, where we will focus on a specific element of craft. From there, we’ll keep the conversations that arise in the workshop going as we spend time sharing a home-cooked meal prepared by a local chef with fresh ingredients, and then have free time for writing or reflection, followed by a long sunset stroll on the wild, untouched beaches of the Tyrrhenian Sea where our group will be the only ones for miles in any direction.

Sometimes you leave with a better problem. A clearer question.

You’ve described No Man’s Land as a space for filmmakers to focus on “the important work you never have time for”. What kinds of creative problems or questions do you imagine filmmakers bringing with them? Are you expecting people to arrive with a specific project, or can they come with something much less defined?

RLJ: I think non-fiction filmmakers are very good at being busy. There is always something that absolutely has to happen: an application, a cut, a shoot, a finance plan, a pitch deck, a trailer. And meanwhile, there are these much bigger questions sitting there quietly, waiting for you to have time for them. Sometimes the question is very specific: Why is this film not working? Why do I suddenly hate my protagonist and/or subject? Why have I been editing the same twenty minutes for six months? Sometimes it’s more fundamental: What kind of film am I trying to make vs. want to make? What is my relationship to the story I’m telling? Do I still want to make films this way?

You can come with a film. You can come with footage. You can come with an idea that is nascent. You can come with an archive, a character, a formal problem, a political problem, a crisis of confidence, or something you’ve been circling around for years without knowing what to do with it. But it should be rooted in a project. Something tangible enough that we can sink our teeth into together. The idea is not that everybody arrives with a problem and leaves a few days later with a solution tied up in a bow. Sometimes you leave with a better problem. A clearer question.

YO & DG: A sad truth about filmmaking is that it’s often a very lonely affair, despite the fact that it is ultimately a collective process. Often, a director is working alone in the long slog of development for quite some time before the first real collaborators join a project. And so time for work sharing is important, no matter what stage a project or an idea is at, but so is time for sharing our struggles in creating art, which is a very real thing that too often gets brushed aside.

I personally attended a similar-sounding retreat earlier this year – the Ouray Film Sabbatical – and one of the questions I was asked most often afterwards was what the organisers themselves got from bringing a group of filmmakers together. So I’d like to turn that question back on you: As facilitators, what do you get from hosting No Man’s Land?

NM: Personally, the chance to change a system that doesn’t feel healthy or sustainable. I’ve run similar retreats before, and I’ve seen how genuinely shocked people are that you can have such a nice experience and meet such nice people working in this industry. Filmmaking is an art, but the way we’ve structured its industry feels like we have to step on top of each other to succeed. I think a little kindness can go a long way, and this is our contribution to doing something different.

YO & DG: The motivation for us has always been to provide a space for others that we as artists would want to be in. There’s a great joy and reward in creating community and in giving back.

The ideas themselves are the pride and property of the filmmakers.

There’s an interesting question around what happens to ideas that emerge during a retreat like this. If someone develops a new project while at No Man’s Land, how do you think about ownership and attribution? Do you have any expectations around crediting the retreat or its facilitators on work that originates there?

YO & DG: Our goal is to create a place and space that people will feel at home in, that they will want to come back to. And nobody can feel at home in a place where a question of ownership is hovering over them. To us it is very clear: we own nothing of what other artists create while they are here. We ask for a credit mostly as a way of widening awareness of our existence, and so widening the circle of community. We see our role in offering a playground where new ideas can take root. The ideas themselves are the pride and property of the filmmakers themselves.

NM: We’ve talked about this, whether we should expect people to create something. Ultimately, we wanted to move away from that expectation. We want the experience to feel bound-free, and to have faith that if a project does arise from it, people will naturally talk about how it comes about, through the experience they’ve had. It’s about having a bit of faith, rather than constantly guarding our resources out of fear that people will take from us. I genuinely believe people with a similar ethos find themselves and support one another.

Finally, this is the first iteration of No Man’s Land, so how are you thinking about its future? Do you already have future plans or do you want to allow the experience of this first gathering to determine what comes next?
