YO & DG: Our artist residency is already open biannually, once in the fall and once in the spring, and our hope is to do the same with these retreats.

NM: This is the first edition of the No Man’s Land creative retreat, but also the first in the Curation Hour Creative Retreat programme. As Curation Hour, we’re simply facilitators of the experience, opening up our network to the retreats we feel are most aligned with us. We build each retreat together with the host, and that’s the beauty of it: each one is personalised and built in a very holistic way.

item.title: From Cosmic Head Explosions to Awkward Third Wheels: 11 Short Films to Discover at Encounters Film Festival 2026
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: From experimental documentaries to animated dance, DN selects 11 short films to discover at Encounters 2026.
item.content:encoded:
While much of the film industry’s attention will soon turn towards the BFI London Film Festival, for those of us more deeply embedded in the short film world, it’s festivals like Encounters that hold the strongest appeal. This year’s programme brings together 142 films from 39 countries in competition, spanning live action, animation and documentary, once again offering plenty to get excited about—especially the Sirāt Live soundsystem set, which we’re looking on with particular longing—at the Bristol-based festival. As has become something of an annual ritual for us, we’ve scoured the programme, watched the shorts and picked out eleven films we think are worth seeking out if you’re heading to Bristol or keeping an eye on if, like us, you’re not lucky enough to be there in person this year.

There are, of course, a number of films in the programme that will already be familiar to regular DN readers. Sacha Beeley’s Babyface, Laurence Thérien’s Ball Face, Amrou Al-Kadhi’s Original Sin, Fanny Capu’s Pickled and Chris Lavis & Maciek Szczerbowski’s The Girl Who Cried Pearls have all been discussed in depth in interviews on Directors Notes. Meanwhile, Jenny Jokela’s Dollhouse Elephant, Ariel Zengotita’s Imago, Aneil Karia’s Vote Gavin Lyle, Rory Waudby-Tolley’s i have a, Zsuzsanna Kreif’s Adgwa-Ata and AJ Jefferies’ Ducks have already featured in our festival best-of selections elsewhere this year.

While we’re delighted to see all of these films represented in the Encounters programme, we’ll be focusing here on eleven shorts that are, hopefully, new discoveries for our audience.

A Pint of Bitter – Conor Kehelly

A misunderstanding in a pub, a fatal mistake by a father and a surreal journey into the unknown – Conor Kehelly’s animated short A Pint of Bitter thrusts you into a situation that feels strangely relatable, even as it becomes increasingly difficult to understand. It’s a visual and thematic headfuck of a watch – in the best possible way – using a skewed perspective to immerse us in the grounded confines of a quiet bar before catapulting us into much more cosmic and existential territory, via an exploded head.

A Shot at Art – Ilke Paddenburg

A short I regretted not including in my SXSW article earlier this year, Ilke Paddenburg’s A Shot at Art initially makes an impact through the ‘controversial’ art exhibition at the centre of its story, but ultimately lingers because of its exploration of gender and power. Driven by the commanding presence of its two leads, Juul Vrijdag and Bo Bojoh, as the tension of Paddenburg’s film intensifies, it’s a strong reminder that compelling storytelling and performance can be just as powerful as any elaborate visual approach. I also don’t think you’re going to see a better end scene all year!

Hag – Anna Ginsburg

A celebration of self-love told through a purposefully off-kilter aesthetic, Anna Ginsburg’s Hag takes a hugely relatable subject and transforms it into something distinctly individual through the introduction of a touch of magical realism. Brimming with both humour and emotion, Ginsburg’s story captures the tension between societal expectations and the desire to remain true to oneself, finding a unique expression of this conflict through both its narrative approach and visual language. It’s the balance between the surreal and the everyday that makes Hag such an affecting and memorable exploration of self-acceptance.

Most Popular

Hyena – Altay Ulan Yang

Combining stark black-and-white photography with a strict art school setting, Altay Ulan Yang’s Hyena occupies an unusual space between experimental filmmaking and narrative drama. While this combination could easily have become a pretentious mess, Yang instead uses a heightened aesthetic to reinforce the film’s unusual premise, resulting in a work that feels both ambitious and assured. Apparently marking Yang’s directorial debut, Hyena showcases a remarkably confident approach to visual storytelling, suggesting a filmmaker with a distinctive voice that will be worth following as his career develops.

Klonter – Levi Stoops

No one makes films quite like Levi Stoops. While his previous film, Drijf, stranded a couple at sea to explore relationship problems from an utterly unique perspective, his latest, Klonter, is another fine example of the unpredictable filmmaking that has become a trademark of the Belgian animator. Beginning as the story of a man struggling to see the point of life after believing he’s about to die from kidney stones, Klonter soon takes an unexpected turn. Inadvertently transforming into a planet and spawning an entirely new race of beings, the film expands its narrative from one man’s health crisis to something far grander, exploring broader questions of existence and the meaning of life.

Life on the Line – Vadim Vandenven

Taking its audience on an extraordinary journey from the waters of Alaska to a plate in front of hungry diners, Life on the Line employs animation, photography and GoPro footage to immerse us in the world of industrial fishing. An experimental documentary piece driven by an evolving soundtrack, Vadim Vandenven’s short can feel overwhelming at times—but in an exhilarating way, as its constantly shifting visual and sonic language mirrors the scale and intensity of the industry it explores. It’s also an important watch for anyone who has ever taken the food on their plate for granted, offering a visceral reminder of the vast amount of effort that goes into putting food on the table.

Once in a Body (Una vez en un cuerpo) – María Cristina Pérez

Animation features heavily in these recommendations, but the more I watched from the Encounters programme, the more films I found myself wanting to include. María Cristina Pérez’s incredible Once in a Body is one that proved impossible to ignore. Its breathtaking aesthetic is a testament to the possibilities of hand-drawn animation, while González pairs this visual beauty with a poetically haunting exploration of the human body and the ways it shapes our experiences. The result is achingly beautiful, thematically rich and utterly unforgettable—a singular short from a singular voice.

Please – Anna Mantzaris

Returning to the vignette style of her earlier film, Enough, which actualised the catharsis of explosive impulses, Anna Mantzaris’ latest short, Please, follows an ensemble of characters searching for human connection in an increasingly isolating world. Sporting her unmistakable felt-animation style, the film’s dark humour gradually builds to a crescendo as these individual stories converge to form a harmonious ode to longing and acceptance. Already making an impression on the festival circuit, Please feels like another standout addition to Mantzaris’ distinctive body of work and one that could well find itself in the conversation when awards season rolls around again.

The Death of the Fish – Eva Lusbaronian

An animated dance film exploring grief and depression—excuse the hyperbole, but Eva Lusbaronian’s The Death of the Fish might be the most beautiful piece of filmmaking I’ve seen in some time. From its intricately rendered backgrounds and hypnotic animated choreography to its pulsating score, every element feels carefully composed, making it somewhat surprising that, among the thousands of short films I’ve watched over the years, animated dance films remain such a rarity. Lusbaronian has spent much of her career animating the work of other filmmakers since graduating from Gobelins in 2015, but with The Death of the Fish, she more than proves herself ready to step into the role of director.

Trio – Morten Borgestad & Fridtjof Stensæth Josefsen

A film for anyone who has ever experienced being the third wheel, Trio, by Morten Borgestad and Fridtjof Stensæth Josefsen, takes a distinctly physical approach to exploring the difficulties of finding your place within a friendship. As we follow the short’s titular threesome as they walk and talk, the restrictions of their environment repeatedly conspire to leave one person—always the same person—out, behind, or even in the road. At under four minutes, Trio makes a strong case for the ‘short short’, using its brief runtime to deliver a simple but remarkably effective idea without ever overstaying its welcome. In fact, it might just end up being your favourite film in the block.

Uncle Filmi – Nazgol Kashani

If you’re expecting a short centred on the Iranian Revolution and the censorship that followed to be a dour and sobering watch, Nazgol Kashani’s mixed-media film Uncle Filmi sets out to subvert those expectations. Presented as a light-hearted anecdote shared between friends, Kashani combines conversational voiceover with a playful, kinetic visual aesthetic, creating a film that is immediately welcoming while retaining considerable emotional and political weight. Featuring Islamic Revolutionary Guards, body-hair removal parties and bootleg VHS tapes, it’s an extraordinary story brought to the screen with an infectious sense of love, warmth and humour.

item.title: Lola-Rose Maxwell Turns a Vintage Coat Into a Voyeuristic Menace in Her Debut Horror Comedy ‘Attack of the Coat’
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: Lola-Rose Maxwell outlines how she stepped behind the camera, engineered a creepy puppet antagonist & blended comedy with atmospheric horror for her debut.
item.content:encoded:
As children, many of us harboured the fear that the objects in our homes were actually alive and that during the night they would suddenly wake up and attack us, fulfilling our worst nightmares. I personally would point the finger at the popular series of children’s horror books Goosebumps, which certainly didn’t help us feel any better when our parents sent us to bed and turned off the light. Well, Lola-Rose Maxwell’s debut short Attack of the Coat reminds us of those irrational feelings of terror, and does so while fully embracing the comic absurdity of battling possessed clothing. In this instance, a voyeuristic garment with designs on its wearer. Why, out of all objects, a coat? Perhaps there is also a literary reference here to Gogol’s masterpiece, The Overcoat, though this telling is a good deal less solemn but just as haunting.

In fact, Attack of the Coat is a perfect example of how to balance two genres that naturally seem antithetical, holding its comedy and its horror in genuine tension, never letting either undercut the other. The result is a short with a thoroughly malevolent sense of humour, anchored around a fabulous performance from comedian Amy Gledhill. As Attack of the Coat premieres on DN today, we speak to Maxwell about developing an entire physical language for the antagonistic coat with puppeteer Phil Yarrow, how much she enjoyed the control which directing afforded her, and rewriting the lore of her curse when the rules of consecrated ground refused to bend.

The whole film began with a very simple but incredibly relatable experience: seeing a coat in the dark and mistaking it for a person. How did that particular image shape the actual coat in the film?

It definitely informed the character of The Coat/Montgommery Schnatchell as voyeuristic and insidious. Catching an inanimate object just as it seems to have stopped moving is ominous AF. It’s like the feeling of being watched. And in the film, before ‘we’ see The Coat, ‘the coat’ sees Amy. It’s watching her in the vintage shop and calls to her. So the whole character really grew from there.

You originally wrote the lead role for yourself, before being encouraged to direct the film. Did Attack of the Coat make you realise you could — and perhaps should — direct your own material? And having initially planned to play Alice yourself, what did Amy Gledhill bring to the role that made you realise she was the right person to take it on?

Definitely. It was a very ambitious directorial debut but I knew I could do it. I didn’t know how much I’d enjoy it though, and making all those decisions and having control was surprisingly fun. Casting Amy was one of the best decisions I made, not only is she a very talented actor and a hilarious comedian but she’s very generous on set. I mean, she crouched in a sunken grave in the middle of January and never complained once! After I cast her she also told me she used to ballroom dance professionally, so I added that ‘dance into the graveyard’ scene. She gave the character and the film so much, I don’t think anyone could have done a better job, even me.

Casting Amy was one of the best decisions I made, not only is she a very talented actor and a hilarious comedian but she’s very generous on set. I mean, she crouched in a sunken grave in the middle of January and never complained once!

The coat is obviously one of the biggest creative challenges in the film. You worked with puppeteer Phil Yarrow to develop a whole language for how it moved. How did you decide what the coat should physically be capable of?

Yes, Phil was incredibly helpful, as I had no idea about puppets really. Weirdly, I’ve actually always had a phobia of Kermit the Frog. But I did have a vision of how the coat should move and he knew the right questions to ask to make that a reality. We decided it should be that Montgommery Schnatchell is ‘wearing’ the coat rather than making the coat move. I was quite inspired by The Invisible Man 2020 which I loved.

 I wanted a theme that we could then distort as the coat gained more power over Alice.

Music seems to have been another key part of defining the identity of the coat. Did you want the score to guide the audience’s emotional response, or were you more interested in creating something stranger and more distinctive that could give the coat a sense of its own mythology?

I love what John Carpenter does with music, so heavily influenced by him, I wanted a theme that we could then distort as the coat gained more power over Alice. I also knew I wanted to use piano rag music as the base, as that’s Montgommery’s era. After that Bear Bites Horse did an amazing job of bringing those ideas together, once the music was on, it was like a completely different film.

Most Popular

Let’s talk about my favourite moment in the film: the outstanding grave scene. You found out that you weren’t actually allowed to dig on consecrated ground. How did you navigate the practical limitations of graveyard rules?

Let me start by saying that graveyards are my favourite places in the world. I know how emo that sounds but it’s true. I would go and learn my lines for school plays in West Norwood Cemetery when I was like 13 years old. I walk in a graveyard about three times a week, I would live in one if I could. However, filming in graveyards comes with a lot of limitations! I originally wrote that the coat would be burned and that would break the possession but that was literally impossible. So I changed the lore of the curse and burying it seemed the next best thing. My location manager Jacob Dowdle was amazing and luckily found sunken graves we could cheat to look as though Alice had dug. I have to say, when the haze drifted through the graveyard as we were about to shoot, that felt very cool.

You’ve talked about having to “kill your darlings” and cut a whole scene despite loving Tracy Rakira’s performance. Were there moments where editor Zach Pridding suggested a cut or a different structure that completely changed how you understood a scene?

Tracy was so great. She has such a strong look and amazing presence on screen, but on watching back, I just knew we had to get through the story quicker. Being an actor myself I felt incredibly guilty but Tracy was very gracious. It’s sort of a rite of passage in a way. It happened to me in a film by Daniel Kaluuya – that one hurt! Zach was instrumental across the whole thing, adding so much pace but he was particularly helpful in the graveyard scene where Alice is remembering all the men who’ve called her spineless, weak, etc. He landed that flashback slow-mo joke from ‘Dr Mac’ in a way I never would have thought of.

Filming in graveyards comes with a lot of limitations!

Could we discuss the hilarious TV scenes, which add a lot to the comedic side of the film? How did they end up in the film? What sparked the idea?

This idea of having TV scenes within the story, like a lot of this film, was inspired by The Mask. Jim Carrey’s character sees a professor on TV talking about his new book The Masks We Wear or something. It just always struck me as hilarious that that happened to be on TV (especially as practically the next scene he’s talking to the author in his office). I also watch a lot of daytime TV, that’s how I turn my brain off. I love it and some distorted version of it seems to seep into anything I write. I also think there’s a Late Night with the Devil influence in there too. But it’s really down to the comic genius of Jonathan Broke, who I’ve been friends with for years from the London improv comedy scene.

You were making your directing debut, without having gone to film school, working with Morgan Sinclair as your DoP. How technical were you in your approach to the camera? Did you arrive on set with very specific ideas about shots, lenses and movement, or did you rely on Morgan to help translate the look you had imagined?

I very much relied on Morgan, who was exceptional and I continue to work with now and hopefully forever. I have zero technical expertise but I did have very specific ideas and I’m very good at explaining exactly what I want. I gave Morgan a bunch of comps, I storyboarded and blocked the scenes using a floor plan and some horror Lego (…don’t ask), but mainly I let him do what he wanted. He brought a very talented crew and made everything work, despite some tricky limitations. What’s great about Morgan is, not only is he very kind and easy to discuss things with, but he also gets comedy.

What’s on your desk at the moment that we can look forward to watching in the future?

Well, I just made a proof of concept for a series with Hat Trick about two exorcists in couples therapy, which we’ll be developing more and whoring about town. And I’d love to make my horror feature Salt Pig, about a cannibal chef with daddy issues… if anyone’s interested?

item.title: When Friendship Becomes a Nightmare: Hugo De Sousa on His SXSW Short ‘Best Friends with the Devil’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Hugo De Sousa digs into the guilt of letting old friends go and takes that to the absolute extreme in the tonal tightrope of his SXSW comedy thriller short.
item.content:encoded:
Relationships have long been fertile ground for storytellers, but while romantic entanglements dominate so many narratives, stories centred on friendship are comparatively rare. In his latest film, Best Friends with the Devil—a short I highlighted earlier in the year in our SXSW Best of Fest picks—filmmaker Hugo De Sousa looks to redress that imbalance by focusing his narrative on a woman who sets out in desperate search of her missing friend, enlisting the help of a mysterious stranger along the way. Straddling the line between horror/thriller and dark comedy, De Sousa’s film has a remarkable ability to shift gears, gripping you with tension one moment before provoking an unexpected burst of laughter the next. It’s the kind of film whose impact is difficult to discuss without giving too much away, so we’d recommend watching Best Friends with the Devil before diving into our conversation with the filmmaker. With spoilers kept to a minimum, we welcomed De Sousa back to DN for his third interview on our site to discuss the importance of keeping things simple, challenging yourself creatively as a filmmaker and remaining faithful to the characters at the heart of your story.

Hey Hugo, welcome back to Directors Notes. The last time we spoke to you – in November 2023, about your film Je Ne Suis Pas Une Star De Cinéma – you said that every short film you make is “an exercise in simplicity”. How does Best Friends with the Devil fit into that ethos?

I used way more tools with this one so I guess I betrayed that a little bit. The camera work is more dynamic and the filmmaking is overall much more muscular than anything I’ve done, but at the core it’s still a very simple story. Can I make two people on a hike feel big and exciting? That was the challenge I set for myself.

And has your understanding of what simplicity means – in filmmaking terms – changed since we last spoke and did making Best Friends with the Devil challenge that perspective in any way?

To me, simplicity means less is more. What’s the absolute minimum you need to tell the story? It’s a great approach, but I do think it can turn into a crutch like anything else and it can 100% stop you from trying new things. I’ve just become really conscious of that in the past few years. Maybe the story you’re writing does need more, you know? Are you cutting things down because that’s the right decision or are you scared to step out of your comfort zone? Less is more is a great starting point but I feel like you should be a little fluid and let the story go where it needs to go. Maybe you do need a canary to fly across the room for no logical reason. Maybe you absolutely don’t. It just depends.

Simplicity is a great tool but you shouldn’t always be 100% positive it’s making your film better. It can stifle your creativity too if you let it.

I originally wrote more locations into the story, only to quickly realize that I couldn’t afford any of them. So I cut it down to just the hike and I think it works but it also weakens characterization. So I guess simplicity is a great tool but you shouldn’t always be 100% positive it’s making your film better. It can stifle your creativity too if you let it.

That previous short was a little more experimental than this latest piece, which feels much more like a genre film. What motivated you to switch things up and make something ‘different’?

It was a direct reaction to Je Ne Suis Pas Une Star De Cinéma. It’s still possibly the film I’m the most proud of, but it was definitely challenging for some people. I wanted to push myself, try a different approach. I’m still finding my voice, you know, so I want to try as many styles as possible. Short films are a great way to do that. Now that I’ve made a genre short, I feel like writing something a little more raw and where performance is at the absolute center of the film, with room for the actors to move and breathe and discover new things. I want to work with a big cast too. That feels exciting to me at the moment.

Most Popular

Despite those genre elements, Best Friends with the Devil is ultimately a film centred on friendship. What motivated you to make this relationship the core of the story? And what do you think this film says about friendship that you couldn’t have explored through a more conventional drama?

The honest answer is that I’m married and I’ve been in a very stable relationship for a really long time and I tend to find way more hardship in friendships. I feel like in a more conventional drama a lot of the neurosis and anxiety around a failing friendship and the guilt and trauma that comes with letting go of old friends would have to be communicated through dialogue and in a more literal way and I feel like this film allowed me to express those feelings in a more creative way. The guilt Lola is feeling is very self-destructive, and this film really allowed me to take that feeling to the absolute extreme where she basically self-combusts. That was really fun.

One of the things I really love about Best Friends with the Devil is the way it balances and plays with tone. At times, it feels like a straight thriller, while at others it descends into comedy. How did you work to find the right balance between those two sides of the film?

If you don’t betray your characters and you think very logically from their POV, you will strike a good balance. I think you only get in trouble when you’re forcing characters in directions they wouldn’t go. You need to really know who you’re writing.

I feel like the title is also guilty of playing with our expectations, as it immediately leads us to make assumptions about what we’re going to see. How did you land on the title and what was the thinking behind it?

It just came to me and I didn’t question it. It felt like a good continuation of the movie. Who’s the devil? Is Lola being led on by Amy? Or is Lola a total psycho?

The guilt Lola is feeling is very self-destructive, and this film really allowed me to take that feeling to the absolute extreme where she basically self-combusts. That was really fun.

Ellyn Jameson’s performance is crucial to the unpredictable nature of the film, with her portrayal of Lola bringing both tension and humour to the story. How did you work with Ellyn to develop the character and give her this particular edginess and energy?

Ellyn is just a really committed and gifted actor. She’s able to play really high stakes very honestly which is really, really hard. We didn’t have a ton of conversations. She just got the story immediately and knew what the character was going through on a very personal level. I told her to play everything at a 10 and she did and it was so fun to watch.

You also star in the film as David. How do you balance the roles of director and actor and what have you found works best for making sure you’re able to give both roles the attention they need?

Not very well. I think they get in the way of each other. Directing tenses you up, it’s a struggle. The only benefit is that you end up spending zero time in front of the monitor, and ultimately I think that’s a great gift. Keeps you in the moment.

I want the writing to dictate what we’re filming, and I like to think very practically, and trust that we’ll find great shots just by following the story.

Sarah Whelden’s cinematography does an excellent job of placing us in Lola’s headspace, as she feels increasingly isolated and on edge while searching for her ‘missing’ friend. How did you work with Sarah to develop the visual language of the short?

Location scouts were very helpful. Even though I made that rookie mistake of not bringing stand-ins, they were incredibly productive. Sarah has great instincts and thinks very efficiently about coverage so we had a really great time coming up with shots. I’m not big on mood boards, I really hate making them. I want the writing to dictate what we’re filming, and I like to think very practically, and trust that we’ll find great shots just by following the story.

Last time we spoke, you mentioned that you were working on the screenplay for your first feature film. Is that something you’re still developing and do you have any other exciting projects you’d like to share with our audience?

I’m currently casting my debut feature Drug Test Cowboy. It’s a character based story about a lone traveler who lands in Los Angeles for a lucrative clinical trial that completely shatters the foundation of his life. It’s very, very different from Best Friends with the Devil, which has been tricky to navigate.

Finally, this is a question we’re asking all the filmmakers we talk to for Directors Notes: what’s one short film by another filmmaker that you’d recommend to our audience and what makes it so special?

I saw a short film from the Netherlands at SXSW that I really loved called A Shot at Art by Ilke Paddenburg, about two women who volunteer at an art museum. Super provocative and funny, and masterfully cast. The two leads are just perfect. You rarely see 60-something-year-old women humanized this way. It’s so funny and endearing.

item.title: Political, Powerful and Playful: 10 Captivating Shorts from Bolton International Film Festival 2026
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: From bold animation to hilarious comedy-horror, DN picks out 10 favourites from Bolton Film Festival's 2026 vibrant and surprising shorts showcases.
item.content:encoded:
A perennial highlight of the film festival calendar for us, Directors Notes has the pleasure once again to bring you our personal favourite selection of films screening at the mighty Bolton International Film Festival 2026. Picked from the varied offerings of the 300 shorts strong programme, we have purposely chosen films which span the festival’s various strands. Nonetheless, with a programme this rich and limiting ourselves to a strict list of only 10 films, it’s inevitable that we had to leave out some really great titles – including beloved DN alum films such as K-9INE!, MEAT, Pickled and Nostalgie.

Taking place from Wednesday 30th September to Sunday 4th October 2026 (with the online programme running from Wednesday 7th to Sunday 18th October), this year’s festival once again brings together an exciting showcase of short filmmaking as well as insightful industry talks and the return of the Slick Films Pitch, of which Directors Notes is proud to be a partner. As always, team DN will be attending in person to celebrate this gathering that continues to grow year on year, while never failing to surprise and delight.

Cegsex – Alun Rhys Morgan

What could possibly go wrong when a guy decides to explore his sexuality on his own in the comfort of his bedroom? All adult websites are banned, and the only option seems to be this mysterious thing called “Ceg Sex”… Well, in this incredible horror-comedy, we get an answer we never thought we would need: a mouth suddenly appears on our unfortunate protagonist’s forearm, and the only way to get rid of this misfortune is… You’ll have to watch the short to find out!

What definitely makes the situation even worse (funnier) is that, meanwhile, his mother has organised a prayer meeting, and the rather annoying noises coming from upstairs certainly disturb the peace and quiet expected during the spiritual retreat. Alun Rhys Morgan admitted that he was inspired by the fact that adult content has been locked behind age verification gates in the United Kingdom, and that the film is therefore a kind of social commentary on the need to allow young people to discover their sexuality, including through the Internet. Regardless of the interesting discussions the short may provoke about the rights and wrongs of the Online Safety Act, there is a lot to laugh about here. This kind of embarrassment is something we have all experienced (to a degree) when we’ve found ourselves in similar situations with our parents, and Cegsex is absolutely fantastic at portraying a surreal version of that cringe-inducing experience.

Vote Gavin Lyle – Aneil Karia

A long time favourite DN director and a project we recently dug into from the commissioning perspective, in Aneil Karia’s worryingly pertinent Vote Gavin Lyle, we’re faced with an impressive combination of political commentary and comedy. Irony and sarcasm are used brilliantly to send up the performative politics of the film’s titular middle-England family man and aspiring right-wing parliamentary candidate. Some scenes are pure poetry, such as the moment when Gavin and his daughter go to hang a Union Jack flag on a motorway bridge. The technical qualities and use of framing are delightful icing on the cake of a short film that, despite or perhaps because of its real life counterparts, is an absolute delight to watch. Also, Jack Lowden’s performance is a key factor in the perfection of Vote Gavin Lyle.

A Little Death – Leto Meade & Jonathan Rockefeller

Without a doubt, the fact that I have a soft spot for animation plays a part in this pick, but here we are in front of a short that I defy you not to love. Leto Meade and Jonathan Rockefeller’s gem sees Death’s patience tested when his sweet and gentle apprentice appears incapable of carrying out his task, forcing him to seek professional help from the most unlikely of places. What could easily have been a dark and disturbing story about death instead becomes something surprisingly tender and even cathartic. The spectacular use of colour is one of the film’s greatest strengths: the electric black-and-white imagery occasionally disrupted by touches of pink and red, creating a striking visual contrast that reflects the story’s themes.

The ingenious way the narrative draws from the graphic novel on which it is based (Nicholas Gurewitch’s book Notes on a Case of Melancholia, Or: A Little Death) also makes these twelve minutes feel incredibly rich and complete. The decision to tell what is essentially a nightmare through animation is particularly effective. The protagonists are, of course, closely connected to death, yet the small assistant is so incredibly cute and gentle that he completely transforms the way we experience the story. There is a beautiful tension between the fear and inevitability associated with death and the sense of warmth and catharsis created by these adorable characters. It is precisely this contrast that makes A Little Death such a joy to watch.

Most Popular

Moderation – Benedict Cohen

This deeply sardonic and slightly disturbing short explores the importance of the images we watch every day online, and, above all, the crucial role of content moderators — the people whose job is to monitor what we are allowed, or not allowed, to see on the internet by subjecting themselves to the worst that humanity can point its collective lenses at. Benedict Cohen—whose on set motion capture artist exes comedy Rushes premiered on DN a few years back—tells the story of two content moderators who find solace in one another in order to cope with the stress that their job enforces on them. Give it a few days, and they’ll find themselves developing an addiction to trauma bonding that threatens to consume them both. Moderation combines strong technical qualities with a fascinating central idea: a reflection on the images that shape and transform us, and the impact they have on our fantasies and even on our sexual desires.

Rainy Day – Jack Hartley

Here we have another highly inventive British short film, featuring an unexpected plot twist. Jack Hartley’s brainchild Rainy Day offers a decidedly innovative take on the familiar story of elderly people being scammed by scummy individuals who manage to get into their homes under some kind of pretext. Without revealing too much and spoiling the surprise, I can simply say that the typical setting of Northern England and the cinematography—which is particularly impressive considering the production’s low budget—make this an absolutely delightful watch, further elevated by the performances of its two leads, Neil Ashton and Susan Hilton.

A Crime Across Four Landscapes – Aidan Weaver

The striking element of Aidan Weaver’s short film is its originality. The idea of creating a sort of visual test for the viewer, in which the audience is directly invited to almost physically enter the scenes themselves, is already remarkable in its own right. It almost seems to be challenging the shorter attention spans that have resulted from the constant bombardment of visual information that we are subject to on a day-to-day basis. What makes A Crime Across Four Landscapes particularly impressive, however is from an aesthetic point of view, the fresh way it captures these typically American landscapes that we’re already so accustomed to seeing in cinema, while simultaneously creating a sense of uneasiness. The fact that Weaver manages to achieve all of this in just over six minutes makes it truly worthy of being considered one of the most original entries selected for the festival this year.

Dance of the Spirits – Andreea-Lorena Florea

This extraordinary animated short immediately captivates the viewer through the beauty of its imagery, its colours, and the way the visuals continuously transform throughout. Matei, a young shepherd boy living on the outskirts of Romania, finds more comfort among his sheep than with his abusive, alcoholic father. However, as Matei begins to mimic his father’s violence, he is confronted with a fundamental question: “Who am I?”

Despite the powerful and often difficult nature of the story, which may primarily resonate with an adult audience, Andreea-Lorena Florea’s use of animation creates a much more universal and symbolic language. The transformation of the images allows the film to communicate emotions and ideas that go beyond the specific narrative, making its themes of violence, identity, and inherited behaviour accessible to a much wider audience. In this sense, the animation is not simply an aesthetic choice, but an essential part of the storytelling, enabling Dance of the Spirits to speak to everyone through its striking visual language.

Pale Sun (Soleil Pâle)- Adrian Moyse Dullin

Adrian Moyse Dullin’s deeply dramatic story hits you right in the heart with disarming simplicity. There is a purity and innocence in the eyes of a child who feels uncomfortable when his father, who is suffering from cancer, gets into the water to take a swim while he is there with his new friends. At its core, the film is an exploration of childhood perspectives. The children who are with him and make fun of his father’s appearance simply do not understand the implications of what they are seeing: the appearance of a man whose body has been ravaged by cancer. At the same time, however, their words inevitably hurt the young protagonist, who feels embarrassed by his father and wishes that he would hide, making the feelings of a man who is already going through something extremely delicate and difficult even worse.

The way Pale Sun is filmed also makes it an exceptional exercise in cinematic synthesis. The film manages to contain all of these complex dynamics within a summer seaside milieu, pairing a sumptuous visual atmosphere with an emotive narrative which culminates in a final scene I’ll be thinking about for quite some time.

Ningú Borda (Nobody Barks) – Júlia Coldwell Serra

What makes this short film stand out is the fact that it was made in a student setting – during filmmaker Júlia Coldwell Serra’s Directing Master’s at ESCAC (Escola Superior de Cinema i Audiovisuals de Catalunya). The level of maturity in its narrative construction, but especially in the attention to the cinematography and framing, would suggest that it was the work of someone with far more experience than a student. Candela has a monotonous life in an inland town, but during the town festival, she accidentally runs over her nephew’s dog and decides not to confess. Instead, she invents a legend about a dog pilgrimage to a sacred tree and invites him to join her in the search. This simple premise allows the film to explore the lies we tell children, particularly the so-called ‘white’ lies that, as adults, we often believe are the right solution to prevent children from suffering. In Candela’s case, however, the lie gradually begins to eat away at her, raising the question of whether hiding the truth about death is really the best way to protect a child.

Although the story itself is fairly straightforward, what really stands out are the performances and the casting, which are absolutely spot-on, especially in the role of the protagonist. Ningú Borda’s real strength lies in the way it turns this apparently simple story into a thoughtful reflection on the consequences of protecting children through lies, suggesting that what we consider harmless or soothing falsities are not necessarily the right solution.

TAXI MOTO – Gaël Kamilindi

In Gaël Kamilindi’s TAXI MOTO, we find a wonderful representation of Black queerness, while at the same time engaging with a discourse around cinema that is entirely refreshing. This is because of the effect created by the question of whether what we are watching is fiction or real life: I am watching a fictitious representation, but is the reality depicted in that film the real reality? Or, within the film, is another one being shot? This kind of matryoshka effect is what makes TAXI MOTO truly incredible. It manages to intersect questions of social discourse and representation within cinema—particularly within short films—with this extremely intelligent narrative device.

You can find more DN film festival favourites in our Best of Fest collections.

item.title: ‘Fjallferð’ Finds Song, Storm and Community Strength in the Mountains of Iceland’s Annual Sheep Round-Up
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: Three Self shooting directors, $6.5k and six days of unpredictable Icelandic weather. Caution Media on why scale is a question of ambition rather than budget.
item.content:encoded:
If you love enchanting landscapes and the beauty of nature, as well as the risks that come with it, from sudden snowstorms and heavy downpours to extreme heat, you’ll definitely love Fjallferð. These dramatic elements may be beautiful to capture and view on screen, but they’re not quite as enjoyable to experience firsthand. That’s the power of cinema. In this case, a short that lets you immerse yourself in Iceland’s breathtaking landscapes from the cosy comfort of your own home or the cinema screen. Working under the collective banner of Caution Media, directors Jesse Smolan, Ollie Maine Smith and Josh Mitchell Jimayu Fairmont’s documentary pulls off the incredible job of placing us within the shifting mountain elements while also highlighting a side of Iceland that is often overlooked: the warmth of its people. All too often, the coldness of Iceland’s climate is mistaken for a lack of community and shared rituals. Premiering on DN today, Fjallferð is here to prove otherwise. Ultimately, the film’s extraordinary visual beauty may well inspire you—as it has us here at DN—to experience Iceland’s landscapes for yourself. In our interview, Smolan reveals why they chose to resist the cinematographic pull of a beautiful landscape, the logistics of covering concurrent action with three people, and why losing their most famous collaborator turned out to be a gift.

You went into the Icelandic highlands with essentially no budget, a three-person crew, and a set of coordinates, only to discover that photographer Ragnar Axelsson wouldn’t actually be able to accompany you. That sounds like the kind of production problem that could completely derail a film. What was going through your mind when you realised you could turn this unexpected problem into a strength?

I think the challenge of not having Ragnar on the trip ultimately benefited us as filmmakers and shaped the way we interacted with the farmers. First and foremost, it set the tone for the trip and became the first of many unpredictable roadblocks that ended up turning into something positive. Because we had interviewed Ragnar beforehand and he was somewhat removed from the trip itself, we were able to focus exclusively on the farmers. If he had been there, it may have diverted some of our attention and shifted the immediacy and present feeling of the film. Having Ragnar, as the only non-farmer character, remain outside of the main narrative helped keep the film grounded in the farmers’ experience, while still allowing us to use his incredible photography and voiceover when it made sense.

A week-long odyssey with a distinct goal, all contained within a very specific timeline. It felt ambitious, but just doable enough with the time and resources we had.

Speaking of Ragnar, he essentially became the person who made the film possible, and the whole relationship began with a cold Instagram DM. What did you write to him in that first message, and how does this prove that, apart from having a strong idea for a film, it’s all about the people who commit to it?

When I first reached out to Ragnar, I had no idea that the project we would eventually embark on would be about Icelandic sheep farmers. Ragnar’s body of work spans the Arctic and beyond, and while we knew we wanted to make a film about an isolated, self-sufficient community, we hadn’t narrowed down where or what that story would be. I really didn’t know if he would respond, so when he did, I was pretty amazed. After scheduling a call, Josh, Ollie, and I spoke with Ragnar for about two hours and went through several potential ideas before eventually landing on the sheep farmers. It immediately felt like the perfect project. Ragnar had been photographing them for more than 35 years, so he was able to refer us and provide access because he was so deeply trusted within the community. We also loved the natural structure of the trek itself: a week-long odyssey with a distinct goal, all contained within a very specific timeline. It felt ambitious, but just doable enough with the time and resources we had.

Looking back, it really was the best topic we could have chosen. Ragnar was incredibly generous with his time from the very beginning, and we’re eternally grateful for how supportive he was of the project. It was amazing to have him so fully on board. In the end, it took the generosity and commitment of so many people for the film to come together. That became one of the most meaningful parts of the experience for us. There are so many people in the world who are willing to help, share their knowledge, and open doors for others without expecting anything in return.

The original note I sent Ragnar was actually pretty formal. This is an excerpt: “I’m a film major at Colorado College planning to shoot a documentary this coming summer in some of the most remote spots on the planet. I’ve been following your work and career and am incredibly impressed by the communities, individuals, and stories you showcase through your photography. I have a background in outdoor cinematography and storytelling and would love to have the opportunity to create a short film about the communities you work with.”

The réttir is an extraordinary visual event — thousands of sheep, huge landscapes, unpredictable weather — but the film seems deliberately resistant to treating Iceland simply as a spectacular backdrop. You’re much more interested in the people who inhabit that landscape and the relationships between them. How did you work on reaching this goal while filming and editing? Why was it so important to you?

The edit was a pretty laborious process. There were so many different versions of the narrative that were possible, which, as any documentarian knows, is often the most difficult part of the process: figuring out what the film actually is. From the beginning, we knew the réttir and the landscape were incredibly visual, but we didn’t want the film to become a collection of beautiful images of Iceland. The landscape and weather were important because of how they shaped the farmers’ lives and the relationships between them. While filming, that meant trying to stay close to the farmers even when there were obviously spectacular images happening around us.

Most Popular

That same idea became really important in the edit. After the trip, when we had two days left in Reykjavík, we conducted an additional interview with an environmental professor in an attempt to build out a conflict the farmers had mentioned. There had been growing criticism, particularly from some urban Icelanders, that the farmers’ longstanding methods of sheep farming were damaging the land. When we started editing, though, we realized that while the subject was interesting, it was pulling the focus away from the heart of the film, which was in Landmannalaugar with the farmers we had been following. Jumping out of the round-up and into Reykjavík slowed the momentum and suddenly made the film feel more like it was explaining an issue from the outside rather than experiencing this world alongside the farmers. Ultimately, we scrapped the entire segment.

That decision became representative of a lot of choices we made in the edit. Whenever we had to choose between expanding the film outward or staying with the people and relationships we had experienced firsthand, we generally chose the latter. The scale of the landscape is obviously a huge part of the film, but we wanted the spectacle to serve the farmers’ story rather than become the story itself.

From the beginning, we knew the réttir and the landscape were incredibly visual, but we didn’t want the film to become a collection of beautiful images of Iceland.

You really managed to ‘live’ in your story: sleeping in the same cabins, travelling alongside the farmers, and navigating the highlands with very little idea of what you were doing. Did being so embedded in the experience change the way the farmers interacted with you, or the kind of footage you were able to capture?

Being so embedded within the farmers’ community was crucial to how we interacted with them and ultimately how we were able to film. The first day felt pretty isolating. We struggled to get close to many of the farmers and were mostly on our own. It wasn’t until one night, when we put down the cameras and just got to know everyone as friends, drinking, singing, and dancing, that things really shifted. The farmers began to open up, and we were able to connect with everyone and become much more integrated into the community. From that point on, the relationships we built completely changed the way we were able to experience and capture the story.

Fjallferð takes place in an environment where the weather can change incredibly quickly. How much of the film’s visual language was shaped by unpredictable conditions you simply couldn’t control? Were there moments when snow, sleet, fog, or changing light forced you to change your vision or was it something that enhanced it?

The rapid weather changes and unpredictable conditions definitely shifted our vision for the film. Weather is such an important part of the landscape up there, and we wanted to capture how quickly it can change. The farmers go out regardless of the conditions, and we wanted to embrace that same mentality and make sure we were out there with them. Although the constantly changing conditions were definitely difficult for us amateur sheep herders, the extra challenges were worth it because they gave us the opportunity to show the environment in pretty much every state it could exist in: rain, snow, sleet, dust, flooding, and beautiful sunny weather.

Viewers often tell us they can’t believe the entire short was shot over just six days because there is so much visual variation, but it was. The title of the film, Fjallferð, translates to “mountain trek.” We heard the word used many times throughout the trip, and it ultimately felt like the most fitting way to describe the essence of the experience and the film itself.

You were working with a very small crew and a minimal budget, but you still had three different cameras — the Sony FX3, FX6, and A7S III. How did you divide them between different situations?

Splitting up was pretty intuitive. Each day, the farmers would divide into smaller groups and head to different locations, so we did the same. Sometimes all three of us would follow one group, and other times we would each head off with different farmers. This allowed us to get much broader coverage and capture crucial moments of the round-up as they unfolded.

For example, during the windstorm sequence, I (Jesse) was with one of the lead farmers, Ingvar, which was important because I was able to hear directly from him about the logistics of guiding everyone through the storm and get the context for what was happening. I was also with Ingvar when the horses ran off. At the same time, Ollie and Josh were out with the groups Ingvar was guiding, battling the wind and blowing sand and capturing footage of what everyone else was experiencing on the ground. Splitting up was critical to capturing the different important moments of the round-up as they were happening concurrently.

In the editing process, what was your approach to archive materials? At what stage did you decide to blend it in? How long did it take to choose which were going to be the chosen parts of all the material you had access to?

The archival footage process was actually pretty tricky at first, and it took us a while to get everything licensed. We went through Ísland á filmu, an Icelandic archival library, to find the footage we needed. Once we had access to it, finding the right moments and places to use it became a challenge of its own. We didn’t want to include archival just for the sake of it, so we were pretty selective about where it fit into the film. In the end, the footage really speaks for itself and felt especially natural alongside the characters’ monologues about the history of sheep farming and life in the Icelandic Highlands. A lot of the selection process came down to finding moments that added context without interrupting the flow of the story.

Iceland changes so dramatically from one area to the next, so we wanted the aerial footage to help communicate that sense of scale and movement throughout the journey.

Thinking about all the aerial shots you captured throughout the film, how did you manage to get those with such a small crew and limited budget? What was your setup for filming from above?

In total our production budget was $6.5k USD. That included our rentals, transportation, hotel, food expenses, etc. We rented a DJI Mini 3 Pro from Charthouse Productions, and they were great about working with us and our tight budget. That drone allowed us to capture all of the aerial footage in the film. Having only three people might sound limiting, but I actually think it helped make us more efficient. If the light was good and something big or visually interesting was happening, we would get the drone in the air and capture as much as we could. Everyone had to be ready to switch roles quickly and take advantage of whatever was happening around us. The hardest part was making sure we captured enough variety to show the different landscapes we travelled through over those five days. Iceland changes so dramatically from one area to the next, so we wanted the aerial footage to help communicate that sense of scale and movement throughout the journey.

Could you all share your favourite short of all time with us?

Ollie: One of my favorite shorts is Yikes, directed by Michael FoderaI. I picked Yikes because it felt really confident in what it was trying to do and had an unusual sense of humor. I loved the pacing, visuals, and tone, and how it never felt like it was trying too hard or over-explaining itself. More than anything, it just stuck with me after watching it, which is probably why I always recommend it!

Josh: Mine is Slomo, directed by Josh Izenberg because it offers a unique and positive perspective on life and what it means to live meaningfully. I love how it explores finding fulfillment in a simple, unconventional way. I also really appreciate the raw simplicity of how it was filmed. There’s nothing overly complicated about it, it’s simply telling Slomo’s story, and that’s what makes it so compelling.

Jesse: I’d like to pick Gatorville, directed by Freddie Gluck and shot by Matteo Moretti because of the intentionality of its pacing and storytelling. In a somewhat similar way to Fjallferð, rather than focusing on the spectacle of an alligator farm in the middle of Colorado and all the dramatic elements that come with it, the film is a quiet, intimate portrait of the family that runs the farm, centered on two children with the gator farm as a backdrop. The filmmakers’ restraint and willingness to sit with shots really struck me.

What are you working on next?

Since finishing Fjallferð, we’ve all been working on separate projects. Jesse recently released a short documentary, The Knights of NYC, while Josh and Ollie are starting on a documentary project within the world of freeskiing. We’re also all hoping to work together again on another project with Ragnar Axelsson, potentially exploring Arctic life and some of the communities and environments he has documented throughout his career.

Finally, we must say we are very grateful for the incredible festival run Fjallferð has had this year and for all the doors it has opened for us. Having our undergraduate thesis film screen at Oscar-qualifying festivals and some of the biggest international film festivals, and now being a part of DN is genuinely a dream come true.

item.title: Theo Matza Zooms in on Digital Deception and Tourist Naivety in His Paris-Set Catfishing Comedy ‘Faux Amis’
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: Theo Matza flips the fantasy of Paris and rewrites the rules of catfishing through an unexpected story of digital deception and toxic friendship.
item.content:encoded:
Forget the Paris of dreams, stereotypes, joy, and happiness that you usually see in films. This one doesn’t give anyone a free pass. In a nice twist on Emily in Paris’s naïve look at Americans in Paris, Faux Amis (False Friends) from writer/director Theo Matza blends a critique of the use of artificial intelligence in online catfishing with a reversal of gender roles, smartly turning the usual ‘woman scams man’ dynamic on its head. When Adele and May travel to the Ville Lumière in search of Jacques, the handsome man who has been courting Adele on Instagram, the two young American women are in for a shock. Who can hide behind a polished and catchy profile? In slightly less than fifteen minutes, we are left with very little certainty about what we thought we knew about the French capital and digital scams, and the frustration is real. Eager to find out more about this darkly comic mystery, we sat down with Matza ahead of today’s premiere to discuss the challenges of shooting a short film across two intercontinental locations, as well as his fortuitous and serendipitous encounter with French star Vincent Macaigne.

You describe this as your most ambitious project to date, shooting across Paris and New York with two different crews. International shoots can be challenging. What was the experience like for you? How long did you spend working across both sets?

The most rigorous part of the production was quite literally filming the bulk of this independent short on location in Paris (6 production days there, 1 day in New York). Because of our script, the initial stages of pre-production revolved around the logistics of getting us overseas. While we were still in NYC, we focused on travel preparation, budgeting, and fundraising. My producers (including Farmhands Productions, led by our two leads, Michelle Moriarty and Clarice Reiner), my DP, my co-writer, and I were in frequent communication. We strategized about how to bring our key American crew (our operator, gaffer, sound artist, and costume designer) to Paris for prep, how to effectively utilize the resources we had to navigate a foreign city with a small footprint, and how to incorporate our essential local Parisian crew members. Angelo Chammah, who joined us early on, produced the project with great dedication. As a Parisian local, he was invaluable in facilitating our indie shoot, mostly in public spaces, especially since most of us were not fluent in French.

Once I was actually on the plane to Europe, the more fun part of the pre-production process could begin. It was, of course, not without its challenges, but it could be guided by the sense of discovery we’d intended. From the exterior locations I found while wandering the city with my DoP Max Fly-Goldstein for two weeks leading up to prep, to meeting Vincent Macaigne (which I know we’ll discuss), there was a feeling that the movie would start to reveal itself to us more organically now that we were on-site. The floodgates of fun coincidences opened after that.

I wanted the geography itself to become part of the comedy and the story.

Paris’ charm has been used endlessly, but your film finds ways of showing the city that feel fresh and unexpected and also manages to remove the dreamy approach towards the city that a lot of films, especially American ones, tend to have.

I really appreciate that. I challenged myself on this project to be very specific about the location choices. You watch these clueless tourists arrive in the heart of Paris (when you see them atop the Eiffel Tower two minutes in) and then gradually make their way to a more local area. I wanted the geography itself to become part of the comedy and the story.

The production feels full of fortunate accidents. One of the most remarkable is meeting Vincent Macaigne and casting him on the spot. What was it about that encounter—or about him—that convinced you he was Jacques? How did that meeting impact your script?

One of the luckiest moments of my life was that day Vincent invited us over to his table to have coffee with him. It helped that I had no idea who he was at the time. I got to be surprised and arrested by his confidence as a performer, and experience working with all sorts of directors. He agreed that day to play Jacques after I discussed the role with him and the team. In the months since, we’ve become close friends, and I am looking forward to working with him again. It was a true gift meeting him, but what made it even more special was that Vincent didn’t just become a collaborator. He became a friend to all of us. I’m looking forward to seeing all of the upcoming work he has on his slate, most notably Radu Jude’s Diary of a Chambermaid.

Most Popular

The film features these striking, sustained zooms across Paris, made possible by a combination of Fujinon zoom lenses and also on an ultra-zoom box lens. Those shots give the city a very distinctive feeling, almost as though the audience is spying on the story from afar. What drew you and your cinematographer toward that visual language, and how did those lenses allow you to achieve this feeling of voyeurism in the images?

For the first half of the story, when Adele and May arrive abroad as tourists, we used the camera to make it feel like they were small in the eyes of the city. Then they arrive at that cramped apartment above a bakery. So we were aiming to invert the typical romantic vistas of Paris depicted in American films, instead portraying the city as a sinister force watching its non-citizens’ every move, and dishing them tough love.

The glass we ended up using fit just what Max and I had been looking for. We shot on the Alexa 35 camera with Fujinon zoom lenses, and also this incredible box lens made for sports broadcasting. That’s what those long, sustained zooms at the Eiffel Tower and from the Sacré-Cœur looking down over Montmartre were shot on. Albrecht Gerlach at PhotoCineRent in Paris collaborated with Max to identify the best tool for sustaining a zoom shot at both extremes. Upon hearing our goals, he suggested using a broadcast zoom. We then enhanced this approach by stacking multiple focal extenders on the lens. This setup effectively created a telescope that could zoom out to capture wide landscapes of Paris, all without compromising light or image quality. We paired this zoom with a matching set of those Fujinon lenses, which were used for the rest of the film.

We were aiming to invert the typical romantic vistas of Paris depicted in American films, instead portraying the city as a sinister force watching its noncitizens’ every move, and dishing them tough love.

You were living in your producer’s home for nearly a month, surrounded by people who believed in the project. Did being so embedded in Angelo’s world change your sense of what the film was becoming, or give you access to local experiences that might otherwise not have informed the final piece?

Angelo was a tremendous asset to all of this happening as producer, communicating with our rental houses, food vendors, and location reps in French. Without him, we never could have gotten through our guerrilla shooting, which was not without a public confrontation or two, so efficiently. And he did it all effortlessly. I consider myself very lucky. I stayed for weeks, along with all the rented gear, at his family home. Endless thanks are owed to the generosity, encouragement, and hospitality of his parents, titans of cinema Ronald Chammah and Isabelle Huppert, who housed large volumes of gear (and American human bodies) in their home. They basically allowed Angelo to run production out of that apartment. Their support means the world.

You’ve said that one of your priorities as a director is keeping your team close-knit and personal. Film sets can often be transient spaces, with people coming together briefly before moving on. What kind of creative environment are you trying to cultivate? What are your strategies to ensure that the human factor on your set is always right and how did this affect Faux Amis?

When we got back home to New York, we pulled our friends together and the scraps of resources we had left to shoot our opening scene. I finished the edit within the next five months with the support and undivided attention of all my key collaborators. My DP and colorist has been my roommate and is my business partner. Jefferson Randall-my co-writer-was at my side, making waves every step of the way. I spent months with Tim Perdoch, working on the sound at his home studio. Tim is amazing and one of my closest pals. He’ll be married by the time this interview runs. We all lived this project alongside each other. So yes, that is definitely true.

Let’s discuss the frantic moments when Adele and May meet Jacques in his apartment. The editing captures the scary, fast-paced realisation that follows absolutely perfectly. What was the process like? What did you use for the editing, and how did being both the director and the editor affect the way you were cutting the film in your mind even before shooting it?

Those were cracked off like fireworks while working with Michelle and Clarice and Vincent in that crammed apartment hallway. I wanted the shots to feel handheld, with kinetic zooms, to keep contained all of the tension and miscommunication that takes place. Getting into the technical approach to those scenes you’re talking about, we had multiple camera operators rolling on opposite sides of the hallway at any given time. This was a key factor in those claustrophobic and emotionally erratic sequences. It also proved a strong strategy for visually balancing the written dialogue and improvisation. It proved an exciting mode of trying to get the audience to sense the buckets of sweat dripping off the actors’ faces. I sort of ripped this approach watching that eruptive dinner table confrontation scene in Between the Temples. So thanks, Nathan Silver. As for the actual editing, as I said, the only person who was there in the room with me at every critical stage was Jefferson. The edit fell into place quickly because camera positions and blocking were planned (at least roughly) before we shot.

I wanted the shots to feel handheld, with kinetic zooms, to keep contained all of the tension and miscommunication that takes place.

What are you working on right now?

I’m going to direct a script for a feature written by Jefferson Randall. It’s in development. I’m jazzed about it, and I’m feeling lucky he and I already have longstanding collaborators (including prod. Bruto Films) in on the ground, at such an early stage. That’s the big fish right now. Then I’m doing music videos, cultivating seedlings for other passion work, promoting the pilot I produced/edited (Fellas, directed by Matthew Danger-Lippman), and editing freelance.

What lessons from making this short do you feel you’ll carry directly into your first feature? Looking back on the process, is there anything you encountered along the way that you know you’d approach completely differently now?

It’s not completely different, per se, but one thing I’d like to do on the next gig is to focus on one single element of the craft to master that is appropriate for the film I’m making. For instance, sharp, controlled camera moves and extreme high-angle wide shots—those are two techniques I’m looking to really begin experimenting with on that next project. I am lucky to continue to direct material by talented storytellers who I care about deeply, which I hope to keep doing forever.

item.title: The Seven Year Intergalactic Journey of Shahaf Ram and His Independent Animated Space Opera ‘Orange Story’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Shahaf Ram reflects on the seven years in the making solo journey of his animated DIY space opera — an intimate story of heartbreak told on a cosmic scale.
item.content:encoded:
When we talk about independent filmmaking, we usually mean a filmmaker working outside the structures and expectations of the studio system. For Shahaf Ram, however, independence has taken on a more literal meaning. His latest short, Orange Story, is a remarkably personal production that he created almost single-handedly, without funding or institutional support, over the course of seven years. An ambitious space opera about a heartbroken astronaut forced to abandon his mission to save humanity after crash-landing on an alien planet, Orange Story initially appears to operate on an epic scale. Yet beneath its cosmic setting, Ram has created an intimate exploration of loneliness and heartbreak. Conceived originally as the first episode of a 12-part series, the film offers only a glimpse into a much larger world that Ram has been developing since 2019.

The remarkable circumstances of its production would be reason enough to speak with the filmmaker, but it is the combination of ambition and vulnerability that makes Orange Story particularly compelling. Following the film’s recent online release, we invited Ram back to Directors Notes—having last featured his work on our site in 2018—to discuss the seven-year journey of bringing his astronaut to life, the challenges of working solo and the importance of feedback when working on an independent production.

Hi Shahaf, we’re really excited to have you return to DN to talk about your epic new short film, Orange Story. Your film follows an astronaut on an extraordinary journey, but I wanted to begin by talking about your own journey in bringing the film to life. I know you started working on it back in 2019, so can you take us through the process of making Orange Story and what it has been like to finally release the film to an audience?

Hi! It’s great to be back! Honestly, my obsessive thoughts about the astronaut started back in 2019. After a long period in Tel Aviv of work and routine, I found myself between apartments and between projects, and I felt like it was a good opportunity to do something strange. So instead of looking for a new apartment in Tel Aviv and jumping into the next project, I sublet a room in Paris without any clear reason, and without a clear date for when I would come back. I didn’t know anyone there, and there was nothing waiting for me. I just wanted to experience something completely different for a while — to shake off some of the dust of routine and fantasise about new possibilities. And honestly, it was quite lonely and sad there. I never really felt connected to the place. But I would sit in cafés and parks, and somehow the astronaut started appearing on the pages of my sketchbook everywhere I went. I think that feeling of being a stranger, disconnected from the world around me, somehow connected with the character.

I wanted to make one film where, when people watched it, I would really feel that they were seeing something very clean and authentic from me.

I especially remember one day when I went to this huge park and, almost like a stream of consciousness, started writing more and more ideas about the astronaut’s world. What came out of that day was actually a rough storyline for an entire season of the astronaut — twelve episodes. Looking back, it wasn’t really a structured story yet. It was more a chain of associations — themes I wanted to explore, moments, characters, and ideas about the logic of this world. It probably helped that it was my first time getting high in Paris, after not smoking anything for several months. Of course, in that moment I felt like I had completely figured it all out. Then you go back to the studio, sit with it again, think, erase, change things, and realise that what you have is really just the foundation you’re starting from.

As for what it feels like to finally release it to an audience — mostly, it feels like a relief. I felt that I was trying to make something that would distil my artistic beliefs. After years of making commissioned work and collaborating with other people, I wanted to make one film where, when people watched it, I would really feel that they were seeing something very clean and authentic from me — without mannerisms, without trying to pretend to be something I’m not. So that I wouldn’t have to explain who I am every time.

Seven years is a long time to live with a single project and a lot has happened with the world in that time. Did the film, or your relationship to it, change significantly during that period?

Yes, it’s been a very long period. Most of the animation for the film was made during the COVID pandemic. Before COVID, I was working in theatre, and when the pandemic hit and the theatre closed, I felt like it was exactly the right moment to pull the astronaut ideas I had developed in Paris back out and finally start producing the first episode. I already had ideas for a whole 12-episode season, but I decided to focus on the first episode and start from there. It was a very intense period. At some point I realised that I needed someone to bounce ideas off — someone who could help me make sense of the endless amount of ideas I had for the world of Orange Story. That’s when I approached the screenwriter Tom Madar, who became almost like my complementary half. If I’m chaotic and full of ideas and thoughts running in parallel, Tom has an incredible ability to take all those thoughts, arrange them into something linear, understand what is important and what is not, and bring some order to the chaos.

I ended up cutting four minutes of animation from it. Some of it was really beautiful, so that was quite painful, but I believe it was the right thing for the film

After that intense period during the pandemic, the film was about 90% finished. But those damn final ten per cent… COVID was over, I went back to work and to everyday life, and new projects came along. The astronaut, however, stayed somewhere in the back of my mind. I kept returning to the film — changing little things, adding things, editing, recording again, deleting things, having new insights about particular moments. At one point the film was 21 minutes long, and I ended up cutting four minutes of animation from it. Some of it was really beautiful, so that was quite painful, but I believe it was the right thing for the film. I still hadn’t reached the point where I loved the film and felt that it represented me in the way I had imagined.

Most Popular

One interesting thing that happened was that I changed the voice of the main character four times. Eventually I realised that I was never going to be satisfied with an actor doing it, because somehow I needed to do it myself. That was the last major change I made to the film, and it happened quite recently. Only after that did I finally feel that the film was ready.

There seems to be a recurring theme of heartbreak and relationship grief running through your work. We saw it in Separation, and it returns in Orange Story. What is it about this particular kind of emotional experience that continues to draw you towards telling these stories?

That’s a good question. I think on the most immediate level, it’s because it’s something I haven’t figured out for myself yet. But honestly, Orange Story isn’t really about one specific relationship or one specific woman. In a way, I think it’s trying to distill ten years of being single in Tel Aviv. Actually, the name of the astronaut’s ex-girlfriend and commander, which you hear through the radio, is K.T. It’s an inside joke: if you type the Hebrew word “לא” (“no”) on an English keyboard, you get “kt”. So K.T. represents the big “no” – the general disappointment with the fantasy of romantic relationships, and at the same time the desire to be alone.

Do you choose a relationship, or do you completely devote yourself to your work and bring whatever gift you have into the world? I think that’s something I’m still trying to figure out.

There’s this familiar idea of “save the world, lose the girl” – like Spider-Man. I think people who don’t really know how to do anything other than create can struggle with something similar: do you choose a relationship, or do you completely devote yourself to your work and bring whatever gift you have into the world? I think that’s something I’m still trying to figure out. I still don’t know how to fully give myself to a woman and build something that makes her want to stay, while at the same time remaining true to the part of me that, as an artist, feels almost compelled to question everything and keep asking endless questions about life, myself, and the world around me. I really hope it’s possible to have both. What about Spider-Man? Did he figure it out eventually?

There’s an interesting contrast between the scale of Orange Story – an astronaut travelling through space – and what ultimately feels like a very intimate emotional story. What appealed to you about using such an epic setting to explore something so personal?

I think this is a contradiction that we all feel all the time. We are inside this insane cosmic system – the moon, the sun, space, life itself – and nobody has any answers. Nobody really knows what the hell this stupid game is. And yet, we can’t help but take things personally, as if our individual problems are the most important thing in the universe.

In a strange way, I feel that it works the other way around too. In the moments when I’ve managed to connect with another person completely, to somehow make that person more important than everything else in the universe – which I guess is what we call love – it actually became easier for me to see how cosmic the universe is. How this strange, chaotic, one-of-a-kind thing we’re part of can also feel incredibly precise and meaningful. When that connection isn’t there, everything can start to feel quite arbitrary, grey and meaningless, and you almost don’t understand why we’re trying so hard.

I also think that life in Israel, whether you want it or not, forces you to be political, even when all you really want is to live your private life. It’s almost impossible to separate your life from politics, war, survival and the everyday struggle. Three of my ex-girlfriends have left Israel, and another only had Russian citizenship, so she could only stay in Israel for a limited amount of time and ended up moving between countries and between wars.
