Even our private lives are constantly being pushed around by the reality of living between one war and the next.

Alongside your astronaut protagonist, the film features two animal characters, a crocodile and a dog. What do these characters represent to you and why did you feel they needed to be part of this story?

It’s not a coincidence that I do the voices for both the astronaut and the crocodile. In a way, they represent two different ideals of masculinity. The astronaut is sensitive and searching — looking for meaning and believing in true love. The crocodile, on the other hand, is strong, aggressive, intimidating, grounded, realistic, stable and supportive. From the beginning, this was part of their relationship. In the 12-episode story, the crocodile is actually the ‘villain’ the astronaut is fighting against. But as their story unfolds, they gradually come full circle and start to understand each other. Like the classic hero and his sworn enemy, they discover that they have opposite but complementary qualities, and that each of them has something to learn from the other. I wanted to bring these two characters together and let them have a dialogue – not just literally, but also between these two different ways of being. I felt they could contribute something to each other.

And then there’s the dog. She is, of course, based on my beloved dog, Gush. She’s a sweet Boxer, and you could say she’s the love of my life – the ultimate refuge of a single man. She has taught me a lot about unconditional love, about myself, and in her own way, helped me open up to the world. So I guess the dog actually represents… dog.

Visually, Orange Story has a very distinctive aesthetic. What were your initial visual ambitions for the film, and how did you go about developing its visual language over such a long production period?

I wanted to create something very naive, but where the naivety would almost be a cover for talking about deeper emotions. I’ve always loved the illustrations of Winnie-the-Pooh, and the way that, beyond any particular drawing, you get the feeling that there is a whole world existing somewhere outside the frame. You’re just seeing one specific moment from it, but the world is much bigger and continues beyond what you’re shown. That’s actually how I feel about the world of Orange Story. The first episode mostly focuses on the astronaut, the crocodile, K.T. and the dog, and takes place mainly in the desert, but between my sketchbooks and the scripts for the future episodes, the world has grown much bigger, with many characters I know and love and lots of places that could still be explored.

I had to keep everything very simple. Otherwise I could easily fall into a hole of incredibly detailed animation that I wouldn’t be able to climb out of on my own.

I don’t think I consciously spent that much time trying to ‘develop’ the visual language. I was mostly trying to draw in the way that felt most natural to me, without forcing it, and just surrendered to that. I already had so many sketches and ideas for this world before I even approached the first frame that I didn’t feel the need to design a whole new visual system for the film. I just went back to my sketchbooks and to the simplest, most naive things that came naturally to me. I also realised pretty early on, from a production point of view, that I had to keep everything very simple. Otherwise I could easily fall into a hole of incredibly detailed animation that I wouldn’t be able to climb out of on my own, especially without a budget.

Looking at the credits, Orange Story is a remarkably independent production, with you taking on so many different roles yourself. Is that a way of working you actively enjoy, or was it primarily a necessity dictated by the resources available to you?

Hmm, I think it’s probably a combination of both. I’m naturally like this – I’m an obsessive person who tends to want to do everything myself, and I enjoy working on lots of different things at the same time. But I also think it was very much a necessity dictated by the circumstances. From my experience with the Israeli film industry, Orange Story was a difficult film to imagine getting funded. It didn’t fit very neatly into the kinds of subjects that are often easier to fund in Israel – it wasn’t directly political, it wasn’t a Holocaust story or about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, it wasn’t a children’s film, and it certainly wasn’t religious.

I wanted this strange, universal world to still carry something from where I come from.

In fact, in some ways it’s almost a film without a nationality. It takes place in space, it has an astronaut at its centre, and there isn’t much in the story that immediately says ‘Israel’. But to me, it’s still very much an Israeli film. Maybe that’s why it was important for me to bring Hebrew into it, and to use my very distinctly Israeli accent. I wanted this strange, universal world to still carry something from where I come from. I felt that if I had to wait for someone to understand my vision and agree to put money into it, it might never happen. And I really believed in the world of Orange Story, and wanted to make other people believe in it too. So instead of waiting for a ‘proper’ budget, I simply made it. I hoped that maybe someone would see it and think, “Hey, this is cool. This is also an Israeli film. Let’s make more things like this.”

When you’re so deeply involved in every stage of a project, how do you create enough distance from the film to judge whether something is working? Did you have people you could turn to for an outside perspective during the seven-year process?

It’s honestly difficult, and I don’t have a very clear answer to that. I try to show the film during the process only to people whose opinion and artistic taste I genuinely value, rather than just showing it to everyone. Otherwise, I think it can become confusing. I do believe in testing things throughout the process — seeing what works, what doesn’t, what comes across to the viewer and what doesn’t, drawing conclusions from that, and being willing to make the necessary changes, even if it means throwing a lot of work away.

I showed many different versions of the film to many people over the years, and that was an important part of the process. But when I reached the point where I had to finally finish it, it became just as important to stop asking what everyone else thought, close the door, sit alone with the material, and trust my own judgment.

Music is one of the major creative contributions from outside yourself and the score feels incredibly tailored to the film. How did that collaboration come about and at what stage did the music enter the process?

The main and most substantial part of the sound was created by the incredibly talented Yuval Goren. Most of the sound design happened after the animation was finished. I would go to his studio and we would obsessively go through the film, part by part, recording sounds and playing around with all the strange instruments and equipment he had there.

The film was actually very musical from the beginning, even though at that stage I hadn’t realised it was going to have actual songs. A lot of the songs came later, after we already had the sound design. By that point, Yuval was no longer living in Israel, so I ended up developing the songs myself in my studio. Because the film was so musical to begin with, it felt quite natural to take that extra step – from background music into an actual song with lyrics whenever I suddenly felt that a particular moment wanted to become one.

With Orange Story finally out in the world, do you have any other projects on the slow burner that you’re able to tell us about?

I’ve been working for quite a long time on a feature film in collaboration with the director Gur Bentovitz, who also wrote the screenplay. It’s very different from the world of Orange Story – a much more realistic film, set in Tel Aviv, with characters who feel very real, almost as if they’re based on people we know. Definitely no astronauts or science fiction this time. And yet, I think it could be just as beautiful, if not more so. The main mission right now is simply to get it across the finish line.

Finally, this is a question we ask all our featured filmmakers: what’s one short film by another filmmaker that you’d recommend to the Directors Notes audience and why?

I’d recommend Pillowz by Moshe Ben Avraham, who I think is the best Israeli animator working today. It’s a beautifully animated film, with incredible backgrounds by Dafi Ben Ami. On the surface, it’s presented almost like a children’s film, but I think there’s something darker and much deeper underneath it – ideas about right and wrong, intention versus outcome, and especially expectations.

item.title: Jasper Martin Finds Comedy in the Sisyphean Horror of AI Customer Service in ‘Listen Then Repeat’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Jasper Martin maps out using live off-stage cueing and intentional dialogue mistakes to build tension in his satirical AI customer service nightmare.
item.content:encoded:
Having recently encountered the frustration of AI customer service, it’s easy to understand why satisfaction with this form of ‘support’ is reportedly at its lowest level in a decade. Yet, while the subject might be both topical and immediately relatable, that doesn’t necessarily make it compelling screen material. Particularly when the central dramatic situation involves a person sitting on the phone, waiting for a machine to solve their problem. None of these challenges deterred writer/director Jasper Martin when it came to making his latest short film, Listen Then Repeat. Following a woman who finds herself locked out of her email account and turns to an AI-powered customer service hotline for help, the film transforms an increasingly familiar technological frustration into a tightly contained piece of comedy that gradually takes a more unsettling turn.

With the film relying largely on a single location, a single on-screen performer and the disembodied voice of an AI, Martin and his team faced some interesting creative constraints in bringing the story to life. Keen to explore how they overcame those limitations, as well as what Martin ultimately wanted to say about our increasingly complicated relationship with technology, he joins us to provide a behind-the-scenes look at the making of Listen Then Repeat.

Hey Jasper, welcome to Directors Notes. I’m really excited to dive into Listen Then Repeat with you today. I wanted to start with the film’s relatability. There’s something immediately recognisable about the experience of being trapped in an automated customer-service system. How much were you thinking about capturing something that felt real when writing the story?

Thank you for having me. I really appreciate the opportunity and I’m so excited to share the film with your audience. Short films are so important for the eco-system of our industry and art form, so long live Directors Notes!

Well, reality and authenticity were definitely at the top of my mind when writing the screenplay and approaching how it should be directed. But looking back, I think it was from a place of trying to avoid unreality more than anything else. Technology, when used on screen, can very quickly skew into completely ridiculous territory, used as a cheap exposition device by hackers and law enforcement personnel running impossible commands that bear no relationship to the reality of what these devices can actually do.

If you turn on any show or film set in a contemporary setting, you’re undoubtedly going to see an obviously comped phone screen with a completely fabricated operating system and a poor actor’s rotoscoped finger, thumbing between imaginary buttons. But these devices are so ubiquitous in our lives now, and we spend so much time looking at them, that we’re able to spot when a text bubble is even a millimeter too small to design specifications. It’s one of my biggest cinematic pet peeves. When it happens during something I’m watching, my suspension of disbelief immediately bursts. I was trying my best to avoid any moments like this and treat the audience as an expert on the subject.

The AI-powered customer service hotline feels like a particularly fertile setting for exploring some very contemporary frustrations. What was it about this specific scenario that made you want to build a story around it?

I had the idea and wrote the first draft in 2022 when ChatGPT had just been released. I had heard how revolutionary and useful the tool was, so I began to test it. Quickly, I became struck by how good the illusion of its intelligence was, but also how unbelievably useless and frustrating it could be. I tend to have a cynical streak, and my mind rushed to speculate on all the ways LLMs could be used to make the world a paradise for company owners and a living hell for consumers trapped in their subscription services. What followed was the instinct that customer service was about to become outsourced and ‘enshittified’ to a level I didn’t think was possible. And in that world, one in which it would be next to impossible to talk to another human being, it would be both horrifying but at the same time so absurd that you’d almost have to laugh about it.

Stammering and struggling to find the right word and string a sentence together is what ultimately makes us human.

I had the realization that when I tried to poke and prod the LLM to make something “less refined and perfect”, it was incapable of imitating roughness and making a mistake. But our stammering and struggling to find the right word and string a sentence together is what ultimately makes us human. Like an actor in a play imitating an accidental trip down the stairs, the question is, can you fake an accident? In the future, when trying to discern whether the voice on the other end of the line is a real person or a chat-bot, I think that will be the test. Can it make a realistic error?

It took me about three years until we were able to produce it and get the film shot, but by that time what read as prophetic a couple of years earlier was almost trite compared to the reality of what’s now happening.

Frustration is arguably the film’s dominant emotion and you gradually push that feeling throughout the film. What interested you about exploring this idea of irritation in such a way?

I don’t know if you can have a customer service interaction now without getting completely frustrated and pissed off. I can’t tell you how many afternoons I’ve waited on hold and how much cortisol I’ve overdosed on, trying to fix a problem with a service that I pay a lot of money for and deserve help with. I could be enraged, seething and clenching my teeth, but I still always feel a trepidation to be assertive when you finally get on the line with a representative. I think that’s common with my generation. Maybe it’s a little bit of the purging of catharsis, writing a script where I can swear at the top of my lungs at the other end of the line.

This film is a cautionary tale about placing your trust in amorphous infrastructure.

Alongside that frustration, questions around trust gradually emerge. How did you approach the relationship between your protagonist and the AI and what did you want the film to say about our willingness (or reluctance) to trust technology?

If I sit back for just a moment and think about all of the ways in which my life could be disrupted, the simple breach of my primary email could end up as an apocalyptic event. If something like that were to happen, I would quickly be locked out of every service that every company has ever sold me; services that have become so ingrained in my day-to-day life that not having access to them would mean a complete inability to function.

Most Popular

I think that this film is a cautionary tale about placing your trust in amorphous infrastructure. It’s really easy to be complacent and trust that over a decade of emails and a terabyte of cloud storage full of sentimental data is safe and sound. But the reality is, it’s so fragile. I don’t think we realise how much we are all innately dependent on companies like Google. We are stuck, lock-step with a company who doesn’t even have a customer service number you can ring if something were to go wrong.

Your lead actor Ruby Blinkhorn does an outstanding job of capturing the exasperation and confusion at the heart of the story. What were you looking for when casting her and how did you work together to develop such an authentic performance?

Ruby’s a childhood friend of my partner, and early in our relationship we would go and watch revues and sketch comedy shows that Ruby would perform live around Sydney. I thought she was unbelievably funny as a base-line, but when she got angry, it was electric. So, I wanted to work with her on a film, and I particularly wanted to write something where she got enraged. I probably wouldn’t have even come up with the idea had I not been banging my head against the wall and pleading with the universe to give me something suitable to write for her. I encouraged Ruby to use her years of stagecraft chops, improvise and really dirty up the dialogue I had written. We needed stammering and self-consciousness and so I wanted her to feel free that she could do whatever she felt like in the moment and that mistakes and accidents were actually what we were looking for.

It was really a two-hander, a push and pull between Ruby and the actual disembodied voice.

The strategy for directing that I’ve arrived at is to do whatever you possibly can to make the experience realistic for the actor. One of the things we did to try and make it as immersive as possible was to put our trusty production assistant Cameron Greenlees in another room with a laptop and a piece of cueing software loaded up with all of the various audio cues. So when Ruby called the line from her phone, he would answer as the AI. If you were in the room, it really just looked like a frustrated customer desperately trying to get a problem fixed. The timing could be modulated, I could go and ask Cameron, “This time, cut her off, really try to frustrate her”. The slight change of cue timing, whether too soon or too late, could dramatically affect how Ruby responded to the line. So it was really a two-hander, a push and pull between Ruby and the actual disembodied voice. I think it would have been a very different film had it just been me off-screen reading out the other lines of dialogue.

The film takes place entirely within a single location, which could easily have become visually restrictive. How did you work with cinematographer Julian Pertout to create a visual language that keeps the space interesting while reflecting the protagonist’s increasingly claustrophobic experience?

This is definitely something we were concerned about. Julian and I discussed various solutions we could implement. Could she be pacing down a hallway? Is there more dynamic blocking that we could implement here? But at the end of the day, I was confident in Ruby’s ability of owning the stage and keeping an audience engaged as I’d seen her do countless times. Our job was to simply capture the scene in the least frilly way and let her do the work of keeping the audience engaged.

The film is really two scenes set in the same room, one during the day and one during the night, bifurcated in the middle. In order to split it up and try to ensure it all didn’t feel the exact same way the whole runtime, we set ourselves some rules. We had a strong feeling that the start should be frenetic and handheld and quite close-up and claustrophobic to match the character’s stressed-out state. We stayed really close most of the first scene, so that when cutting to a wide you had the ability to really disrupt and shift the energy and hit home a punchline. Then, with the second scene, we decided to plant it all on sticks and shoot through a mirror. It has a different energy, and so we wanted the camera to be less of an active participant matching the character’s frame of mind, to more of a disembodied, omniscient view of the proceedings, as if from the perspective of the AI.

James Tate’s score is also crucial to the film, particularly in transforming the protagonist’s irritation into something increasingly unsettling. What conversations did you have with James about the sound and musical language of the film?

It’s amazing, isn’t it? James is a childhood friend of mine and a prodigal musician. He’s scored a few films and other projects I’ve directed. I sent him the script well before production and said I was thinking it could be something like a blend between Jon Brion’s score for Punch Drunk Love and Cristobal Tapia de Veer’s work on Utopia. It had to be rhythmic, percussive, possibly distorted electronica, all around anxiety-inducing. He sent me a few sketches of what he thought the score might sound like. One of those pieces is in the film, practically unchanged from the final; it’s the song you hear at the start. It was amazing because I could play it on set and get the cast and crew into the tempo of what I thought the film should feel like.

It’s a drastically different short with the music layer turned off, I think a lot of the tone comes from the music.

It was a long process to transform those original sketches and conform and arrange them to the film. I’m very particular about music and we worked for a few months just making sure that the peaks and valleys were falling at the right spots, that crescendos’ we’re landing on jokes, that the music wasn’t just an afterthought applied in post but really embedded and snugly fit into the film. It’s a drastically different short with the music layer turned off, I think a lot of the tone comes from the music.

As both writer/director and editor, you had a lot of control over the film’s rhythm. The edit does a great job of continually shifting our expectations and building an unpredictable sense of momentum. What was your approach to finding that rhythm?

I was cognisant of the rhythm in the writing process and tried where possible to embed these rises and falls of momentum into the screenplay. However, once the post process began, my first port of call, after I’d laid down all of my selects of the takes, was to try and cut them as infrequently as I could. I set myself the challenge that, where possible, I would stay on the current shot and only cut if there was a shift in energy or the stakes were raised or there was a reveal of some information.

After I’d finished that process, I arrived at an assembly still without music, and I became horrified, thinking that I had made something unbelievably dull and akin to the torture of actually calling a customer service hotline. It was only when I started laying in James’ tracks and conforming the takes to his music that I realised that it added a whole new dimension to the energy. The score became a kind of momentum engine for the film and it informed the areas where I should refine and squeeze down and the areas where I should open up and allow for breath.

And having been so involved in the film from the writing through to the edit, how do you create enough distance to judge whether something is actually working for an audience rather than simply working for you?

I think the director’s job is to be the audience, that’s our role. We have to constantly put ourselves in the headspace of an uninitiated observer. Of course, this is easier said than done. Sometimes it’s nearly impossible to see the forest from the trees. But I have picked up a few editorial tricks along the way to try and switch and freshen it up. My mum (who lends her voice as Eve’s mother in the film) is a painter and I remember she always told my siblings and I to occasionally flip the canvas upside down to get another perspective on the work. One strategy which is quite common in the editing room is to watch the film in black and white. You have to use constant strategies to trick your brain into seeing something you can no longer see after repetitive viewing.

I’m detail-oriented and my process is constantly trying to eliminate distractions and things that make me cringe, and whittling those unwanted elements away until I’m no longer distracted by a mistake I made on the day or a cut that just doesn’t feel right in my stomach, until the moment when I watch it back I’m not pausing every few frames to fix something. Once I got it to a place where I was no longer fiddling and tinkering, I have a great community of filmmaker friends in Sydney who I trust will tell me the unadulterated truth, and so I sent around a copy and got some feedback; some that dramatically shifted the film.

Originally, I had something entirely different as the prologue and epilogue. I thought it worked on the page, but something in the translation to screen made it obtuse and confusing, and it wasn’t achieving its potential of being a guttural punch. Based on some feedback I received from some director friends (Peter Skinner and Orla Harper Doyle), I actually rewrote these two parts and went and reshot them over a year later. It can be nerve-wracking showing your work, but I really believe in feedback screenings, particularly with comedies. Often, the crowd can help you make it better. Let people in!

Listen Then Repeat occupies an interesting tonal space, existing largely in comedy before gradually flirting with something closer to horror. How did you approach that tonal balance and what does moving between comedy and horror allow you to explore?

For whatever reason, I’m drawn to stories that typically fit the mold of what you might call existential or cosmic horror. But it’s not necessarily because they scare me, it’s more because they make me laugh. The inverse occurs when watching standup. The jokes I respond to tend to be the ones that end up in such an unpredictable and horrifying place you have to nervously laugh through a slack jaw.

Often, the crowd can help you make it better. Let people in!

The path is well trodden in press interviews with wonderful filmmakers like Jordan Peele and Zach Cregger who walk the line between the genres, and many salient things have been said on the topic of the symbiosis of comedy and horror. Anything I could say is probably a regurgitation of what has been better said before me. But, yeah, I don’t know if you can have one without the other. A scare and a laugh are very similar and they probably work on the same psychological underpinning. I think of them as being a very similar energetic force. I like my laughs horrifying and I like my scares funny. It’s my sense of humour, I can’t really help toeing the line between the two. It sort of just came out that way.

Before we wrap up, what does your filmmaking future look like? Are there any new projects you’re working on that you can tell us about?

I recently moved to London from Australia, but before I left, I made a short film called No River Runs Here which has just been finalised. It’s treading in similar tonal territory to this one. It’s all about a consultant working for a water company who has a run-in with a disgruntled farmer she’s pitching new infrastructure to. I’m hoping to get that out soon. Other than that, I’ve got a couple of feature film scripts I’m developing. One of them is Curiosity Killed the Cat, and there’s a little bit of thematic overlap with Listen Then Repeat – it’s another techno-satire, black comedy meets cosmic horror. I’m very excited to make it happen.

And finally, this is a question we’re asking all the filmmakers we speak to: if you could recommend one short film by another filmmaker to the Directors Notes audience, what would it be and why?

I love short films that feel like a timeless bar-stool story you might overhear at the pub, now or a hundred years ago. The first thing that came to mind – there’s an Argentinian anthology of short films called Wild Tales by director Damián Szifron. It’s amazing, but particularly the first entry Pasternak, has been a big inspiration for me. You have to watch it. It’s amazing, a masterclass in how to structure a comedic short film.

item.title: Andy Reid Calibrates the Cost of Making Something Honest in His Meta SXSW Short ‘Brief Somebodies’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Andy Reid confronts his own experience of sexual assault by staging a film rehearsal where two actors negotiate the ethical boundaries of depicting trauma.
item.content:encoded:
Filmmaking has long provided artists with a means of processing difficult experiences. When the subject is deeply personal, however, the process of transforming these lived experiences into a fictional narrative can also become an act of vulnerability, requiring the filmmaker to negotiate the boundaries between reality and performance. For writer/director Andy Reid, this tension sits at the heart of Brief Somebodies, a short film that explores his relationship with his own experience of sexual assault through the story of two actors rehearsing a complicated scene depicting sexual violence.

Rather than approaching the subject directly, Reid situates the film within the environment of a film production, creating an intriguing distance between the filmmaker’s experience and its onscreen representation. With Brief Somebodies having recently reached a new audience through its online premiere as a Vimeo Staff Pick, as well as being a film we’ve kept an eye on since highlighting it in our SXSW 2025 Best of Fest selection, this release offers Directors Notes the perfect opportunity to explore the filmmaker’s approach to such intensely personal material. In our conversation, Reid reflects on whether making the film proved cathartic, why he chose to explore his experience through the context of a film set and the complexities of casting the actor portraying his assaulter.

I’m never a big fan of interviews with filmmakers that begin by exploring the inspiration behind a film, but with Brief Somebodies it feels impossible to ignore, as I know this is a very personal short. Can you explain a little about why you decided to tell this story and the impact it’s had on you since sharing it?

At the time, I was writing a feature that similarly drew from my own experiences with sexual assault. I thought it would be cathartic, but I was growing anxious that it might actually be traumatizing in its own way. I found myself in this constant state of negotiating how much of my own comfort I was willing to compromise for the work. Initially, I wrote Brief Somebodies as an exercise. This was my way of saying, “okay, here’s what following through on this might look like,” and I ended up with all these questions about the process, the personal toll, and the professional ethics of making my colleagues go ‘there’. I made the short to see if the work itself offered any answers.

In sharing the film, I’ve actually been surprised by how my relationship to my own assault has changed. It’s a little less ‘mine’ now. It’s become its own thing. That’s been a relief. I took an Ativan before pitching it to my producer, and now I’m typing my responses for this interview with a bowl of ice cream beside me.

It also feels like there were numerous ways you could have explored these themes, so I’m intrigued to know why you chose to set this particular story within a film production.

I love films with meta elements, so this was the perfect opportunity for me to add to the tradition of films about their own creation. I’m definitely speaking through Joel when he worries his work is self-absorbed, so maybe I’m trying to offload that burden a bit here too. It’s not just me, even the film is interested in itself!!

This film was very process driven, and I knew that someone as engaged as him was what it needed.

You’re an actor yourself and, from researching the film, I know you considered casting yourself in the lead role of Joel. Why did you ultimately decide against doing that and what drew you to Aldrin Bundoc for the role instead?

Well, thank God I didn’t, because Aldrin absolutely crushes it, doesn’t he? That was a tough decision to come to. Like I said, so much of the film is about calibrating how much of my own comfort I’m willing to spend to make something that feels honest, and as we started pre-production, it just became increasingly clear that my emotional wallet couldn’t afford that particular ticket price. I think it was assumed by everyone involved that – since this is a personal story and I’m also an actor – I would be playing Joel, and it wasn’t until I gave myself permission ‘not’ to play him that I was able to really show up and be as present as the filmmaker must be.

Most Popular

My day job is in casting, and so I have a lot of exposure to actors in Toronto. I had actually seen Aldrin in a play a couple weeks earlier and had my casting director request a tape from him. He’s great, and talented, and has this innate vulnerability to him which makes you lean in, but above all else, he was the most collaborative actor I worked with in callbacks. This film was very process driven, and I knew that someone as engaged as him was what it needed.

Sticking with casting, I’m also interested in the process of casting Matt O’Connor as Calvin. Given how personal this story is, was that role particularly difficult to cast and how did you approach finding the right actor?

I wouldn’t say it was difficult, per se, but rather odd to watch these men and assess both whether I believed their performance and if they had the capacity to hurt the version of me that’s in this story. In the film, we’re exploring ideas of ‘what’ makes a sexual encounter an assault. We all understand images of sexual violence when we see them in the form of an attack, but it was important for me to show the kind of sexual assault that happens because someone is made to believe that what they want doesn’t matter.

Whether or not it’s comfortable to believe this, the man who assaulted me is probably a good person (beyond my experience with him).

Most of the men who auditioned played him with a roughness, as if Calvin would have gotten the role because he seems like the kind of man who would assault someone. That’s never really the case though, is it? Whether or not it’s comfortable to believe this, the man who assaulted me is probably a good person (beyond my experience with him). What really struck me about Matt’s audition was that his approach was quite soft. His instinct was to play Calvin as someone who’s wholly present and curious, and when we got to the assault scene, his character has lost that interest.

One last question on casting and performance and then I promise I’ll move on. One of the key elements that makes Brief Somebodies so compelling is the burgeoning connection between Joel and Calvin. How did you work with Aldrin and Matt to develop that relationship and portray that chemistry on screen?

What was really exciting to me about this production was that, by design, much of what happens on screen directly reflects the experience of making it. Aldrin and Matt really trusted me with bringing the meta format of the film into our process, so our only rehearsal was to choreograph the assault scene with our intimacy coordinator, Krystle Ferdinand. I used that rehearsal to watch how Aldrin and Matt – who, like in the film, went from meeting with a handshake to dry humping minutes later – calibrated their physical and emotional boundaries and revised the scripted rehearsal to match.

I cast them because I could tell they wanted to do the work.

We also shot chronologically, so Aldrin and Matt would only have had time to get to know each other for as long as their characters had at any point in time. When we shot the rehearsal scene, they were still relative strangers to each other; at the lunch scene, they’d had enough downtime on set to start to get to know each other as people; and their hug was the last thing we shot, after they’d just spent days going through this intimate and intense thing together. Like I said before, I cast them because I could tell they wanted to do the work. Building the chemistry in this way could really only succeed because Aldrin and Matt were invested in the process.

Visually, the film seems to move between distance – through locked-off, wide compositions – and intimacy, with close-up handheld camerawork. Can you talk a little about how you worked with cinematographer Colin Cameron to develop the film’s visual language and what you wanted the aesthetic to communicate?

Colin is someone I’ve worked with since film school – he’s shot everything I’ve made for nearly a decade. This film is fiction, but in many ways it’s not, and so we tried to harness that contradiction visually. Our visual language became defined by saying “it is, but it isn’t.”

We shot on sticks, but didn’t lock off the head so it could feel handheld. The film looks like celluloid, but we shot digitally. Our ‘real world’ feels cold, yet our film within the film is lit all warm and full of life. And yes, even composition-wise, we bring the audience in to feel like they’re a character observing the scene, then pull them away from it to remind them they’re not quite there.

We knew we wanted a slight change in visual language for the film within the film, but not large enough to let the audience know this is no longer Joel and Calvin. I believe it was Colin’s idea to introduce a constant, subtle zoom – a sense of force on the image that just ‘is’.

Narratively, the film ends on an intriguing note. Joel and Calvin share another moment of connection before Joel retreats into an isolated space to watch the playback. There’s no clear resolution, but that ambiguity gives the film an even greater emotional impact, allowing it to linger long after it ends. Can you offer some insight into why you chose to conclude the story in this way? Did you ever consider ending it differently?

It was always the intention for things to be a bit ambiguous. I fulfilled my duty to resolve the central narrative conflict, but I knew that, by bringing the audience into Joel’s headspace in the way that this film does, it would be sort of insulting to then tell them how to feel. As an audience member, I want to be trusted and I want to participate.

Thanks so much for your time, Andy. I’m a huge fan of Brief Somebodies and really grateful we’ve had the opportunity to discuss the film. To finish, can you tell us a little about any upcoming projects you’re excited about and where our readers can follow your work?

Thanks, Rob! I’m now deep in development on the feature that inspired Brief Somebodies! It’s called Pickups and it follows a tap dance teacher who develops a fixation on the father of his favourite student. Crucially, it’s full of my favourite things: tap dancing, cringe humour, and self-loathing. We’re still trying to close our financing gap, so reach out if this sounds like your jam!

I’m @ndyreid on Instagram if any of you want to see what else I’m up to.

Before you go, this is a question we’re asking all the filmmakers we speak to: What’s one short film – by another filmmaker – that you’d recommend to our audience and why?

I was really lucky to have Brief Somebodies screen alongside Alexander Farah’s One Day This Kid a number of times. It’s beautiful, and affirming, and epic in scale yet intimate in execution. He’s got such a strong sense of his craft… I’m just in awe of it. I’ve seen the film five or six times and it always moves me.

item.title: Anna Hopkins Cooks Up Connection After Closing Time in Restaurant Set Two-Hander ‘Dish Pit’
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: Eschewing restaurant chaos for stillness, Anna Hopkins’ short film finds drama in small gestures, shared meals and intimate conversations after closing.
item.content:encoded:
A restaurant is usually portrayed on screen as a place of chaos: shouted orders, sizzling dishes, hurried footsteps and plates moving from kitchen to table in a seemingly endless rush. In her TIFF-premiering short Dish Pit, Anna Hopkins offers a different take on the familiar setting, bringing us into the quiet moments after the shift has ended, when the restaurant becomes a space for connection and unexpected vulnerability. At the centre of the story are two men, each searching for something they feel they have lost — or perhaps have yet to find. One dreams of building a career in cinema, while the other has found himself washing dishes, despite his true calling lying in being a chef.

Working with the simplicity of a single location, Hopkins transforms the restaurant into an intimate stage for their after hours encounter. Away from the noise and pressure of service, the two characters are given the space to talk, reflect and reveal themselves, allowing the film to explore ambition, disappointment and the desire to find one’s place in the world. What may initially seem like a simple conversation between two restaurant workers gradually becomes something more profound: a meeting between two people at very different points in their lives, yet united by the same uncertainty about what comes next. Joining us on DN, the actor/writer/director talks through her decision to build a film around stillness rather than service, the rehearsal process that put a real chef’s movements into an actor’s body, and why the simple act of cooking someone a meal after hours felt like the truest thing she could point a camera at.

You worked in restaurants when you were younger, and it’s fascinating to think that, after leaving hospitality to pursue filmmaking, life brought you back into owning a restaurant yourself. How did returning to that environment as both owner and filmmaker change the way you saw the story you wanted to tell? How has your perspective shifted after all the years spent away from that industry?

I think what being part of ownership of our restaurant gave me was a very holistic understanding of its ecosystem, because at various times I was deeply embedded in front of house, back of house, construction, food, design and everything in between. And what this allowed me was to connect with so many different people and observe human behavior within so many different contexts. It’s such a privilege as a writer to be able to immerse yourself in another world and get to observe. It was from all those observations that this story emerged.

You’ve said you wanted to capture a side of restaurant life that isn’t often seen — finding drama in the quietness of a job usually portrayed as very lively. It’s a beautiful inversion of how restaurants tend to appear on screen, where filmmakers usually focus on the adrenaline and chaos of service. Did you ever worry that building a film on this stillness was a creative risk, and that audiences might expect a more hectic environment?

No, I never worried, because while it may not be everyone’s cup of tea, I know what films I love to watch, and what I’m drawn to, and I know there’s an audience for that as well. When I was writing Dish Pit, I had just seen Trần Anh Hùng’s The Taste of Things, and just loved it so much. It gave me that feeling of wanting to live inside a film. And while some people who I love and respect did not like that film, it made my soul vibrate, and that’s what you’re looking for when you’re making something of your own.

It’s such a privilege as a writer to be able to immerse yourself in another world and get to observe. It was from all those observations that this story emerged.

I also thought a lot about the scene in Tampopo where one of the characters breaks into a kitchen in the middle of the night and makes a fried rice omelet for a little boy. For me, I could’ve watched an entire film that was just that scene and those two characters. It’s intimate and quiet and wondrous and delicious. There is absolute chaos in the restaurant world for sure, but I guess it’s what you as the writer observe as the most pertinent parts of that world that mean something to you. And for me it’s connection and quiet after that chaos that is special and worth paying attention to.

The restaurant also becomes a very different space from the one we’re used to experiencing as customers. How did you and cinematographer Mat Barkley approach photographing that transformation?

We wanted the space to feel completely intimate, cozy and safe from the wild outside world, in a sense. A space that was conducive to slowly opening up. So the biggest thing for me was to create a sense of warmth throughout, which Mat achieved so beautifully. The fire from the pizza oven in the center of the space gave us so much, as did practical lamps throughout.

Most Popular

Working within a real, functioning restaurant must have shaped how you could move actors through the space. How did you approach blocking within those tight, practical constraints — the pass, the kitchen line, the floor?

Having access to the space prior to shooting was really what shaped the film. I worked with the actors in the space, workshopping the scenes and building specific blocking from their instincts and insights. I didn’t change the environment much, but encouraged them to use the space and the tools already there as much as possible, so that we could incorporate as much behavior into the scenes as possible. While I made sure this was first explored in a fluid way, once a certain physical behavior worked well, I would incorporate it into the blocking and we would rehearse a lot. The key to this was tons of rehearsal, to get the movements into the actors’ bodies so that on the day it felt genuine and seamless.

Going further into the technical side of the film: you shot on the RED Komodo X with Zeiss Super Speed lenses to give it a very intimate feel. It seems like the right choice: a camera small enough to stay close to the characters, paired with lenses that bring warmth and character to the image. Was the compactness of the RED Komodo X important in preserving that sense of closeness and spontaneity during the shoot, even before getting into the edit to shape the film’s look?

Yes, absolutely. The genesis of this shoot was an experience I had a few months earlier, where I was the second unit director on a large-scale commercial. I worked with a tiny skeleton crew with awesome talent, and the freedom that I felt doing that was something I wanted to emulate on my own shoot. While, of course, certain size shoots require specific things, I felt like I wanted to challenge myself to work really minimally and wear a ton more hats to achieve that. When I described the kind of freedom and flexibility I was looking for to Mat, he immediately understood and built out his gear appropriately. While there was a tremendous amount of prep prior to the shoot, we were small enough on the day as a crew to move around seamlessly and really capture as much spontaneity as possible. This approach also allowed us to shoot during actual restaurant service for a few hours each night without creating much disruption at all.

Both Max and Joe are, in different ways, people who have stepped sideways from the futures they once imagined for themselves. One is still chasing a dream, the other has deliberately retreated from the pressure of one. Did writing them change the way you think about what success or fulfilment looks like?

I think what writing these two did was allow me to focus on the sort of simple moments of connection in the present — that may seem mundane — but that ultimately create a sense of fulfillment in themselves. We don’t know what will happen to Max or Joe, or where their lives will take them, but I do know their shared meal meant a little something to both of them. As I get older, it just becomes clearer and clearer that there will always be a certain degree of uncertainty plaguing you at all times, and so appreciating unexpected human connection, and a simple pleasure like eating something delicious, can give us a few fleeting moments of relief.

Let’s focus on the film’s only outdoor scene — a brief moment that interrupts the intimacy of the restaurant. It gives tangible form to something that had previously only existed in conversation: Max’s longing to break into the film industry, and, in the same breath, the sting of rejection. How early did you know you wanted to externalise that part of his journey, rather than leaving it as something only talked about?

I wanted to create a tiny bit of a ticking clock in the story, to have a touch of momentum in this otherwise relatively still story. As I explored what it would look like for Max to really go after the thing he wanted, it just instinctively felt right to have him be rejected quite swiftly. I think that just came from my unconscious, because rejection is such a huge part of going after any artistic or creative life, and I wanted him to experience that, but still be okay by the end. Maybe even have a bit of hope and a laugh too. It just made sense to head outside into the world for that moment, and to come back into the safety of the restaurant afterwards, to do a bit of healing.

As I get older, it just becomes clearer and clearer that there will always be a certain degree of uncertainty plaguing you at all times, and so appreciating unexpected human connection, and a simple pleasure like eating something delicious, can give us a few fleeting moments of relief.

One of the things Dish Pit captures beautifully is expertise that’s almost invisible. You made the most of your restaurant, not just as a location but as a source of authenticity, ensuring the believability of the acting by having Chef Jon Pde choreograph the kitchen movements and serve as a hand double for actor Matthew Gouveia. Why was this important to you? Do you think physical truth is something audiences register instinctively?

As I come from an acting background and studied with many incredible acting teachers over the past 20 years, what’s been nailed into my mind is the paramount importance of behavior. “Acting is behaving truthfully under imaginary circumstances”, as Sandy Meisner famously said. I knew if we didn’t have the truthful physical behavior for Joe (the chef) in particular, the whole thing wouldn’t work. To achieve that, first I had the privilege of working with the immensely talented actor Matthew Gouveia, who is the perfect mix of not taking himself too seriously, but taking the work incredibly seriously. Then I brought our real chef, Jon Pde, into the fold, particularly during rehearsals, so we could break down every single physical moment with Matthew and allow him to practice until it felt right. For anything like chopping or searing, I used Jon Pde’s hands as a double for Matthew, which added a really important element of authenticity.

I also filmed Jon Pde actually cooking the meal in rehearsals, and adjusted the script while doing so, adding some moments in the story that weren’t there before. Austin Hutchings, who so beautifully played Max, was also a bartender at our restaurant prior to filming Dish Pit, so he knew the space so well, which added in that layer of ease that I needed to sell this late-night conversation. I do think audiences absolutely register anything inauthentic behaviorally, and when that happens you get taken out of the story, which is the worst-case scenario.

As I come from an acting background, and studied with many incredible acting teachers over the past 20 years, what’s been nailed into my mind is the paramount importance of behavior.

Food on screen usually gets the glossy, sensuous ‘food porn’ treatment — glistening close-ups designed to make an audience salivate. Dish Pit feels more interested in the labour behind the plate than the plate itself. Did you consciously resist that seductive way of shooting food, or did you want moments of that beauty to sit alongside the grind?

I think I just love watching a meal come together, and the life that happens at the same time while that’s going on. This is something I witness all the time at the restaurant, like for instance watching someone engage in the complex process of making dough while chatting to their colleague about the date they went on the other night. It’s those two activities in tandem that I find beautiful. As for the dish itself, I wanted to show the deliciousness of the food in its most simple form. Because I wanted to show that Joe can cook for real, without any frills. What he ends up making says a lot about him.

Could you share your favourite short film and tell us why you chose it?

That’s a hard question! There are so many! But I’d say a short film that has always stuck with me is An Extraordinary Person (Quelqu’un d’extraordinaire) by Monia Chokri. It’s such a brilliant mix of depth and humor and sophisticated character studies all packed into a wild ride. It’s a must-see.

Finally, what are you cooking up next (pun intended)?

I’ve just finished a new short, titled Full Circle, which captures an intimate conversation between a mother and son throughout the entirety of a total solar eclipse. Mat Barkley worked his magic on this one as well. We had so much fun practically emulating the eclipse light shifts from beginning to end, building out that strange experience of witnessing such a cosmic phenomena. I’m also writing a few feature screenplays at the moment, continuing to act, and of course helping out at the restaurant when I can.

I think I framed the restaurant as a safe haven in Dish Pit, because in a sense that’s what it is for me. As I’ve navigated the world of freelance work in creative fields my entire life, there’s something comforting about going back to the restaurant and working with your hands, with people who you admire and respect, who have absolutely nothing to do with the film industry. If there’s any advice I’d give to writers, directors, and actors, it’s finding a world you can engage with sometimes that is far removed from your day-to-day in filmmaking. It’ll give your writer/director/actor brain a rest, which in turn primes it for more creation.

item.title: Natural Selection Comes to Homeroom as Kyle Sims Pits Teacher Against Student in His Wordless Thriller ‘Galapagos’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: A snake that wouldn't strike, a craigslist rabbit and a wordless script — Kyle Sims takes us inside his unnerving tale of shifting classroom power dynamics.
item.content:encoded:
Dialogue is often seen as one of cinema’s most fundamental tools for developing character, establishing relationships and guiding an audience through a story. To remove it from the process will undoubtedly place an unusual amount of focus on physical performance to convey the emotions and tensions of a story. In Kyle Sims’ captivating short film Galapagos – the story of a lonely teacher whose classroom rabbit suddenly disappears and the increasingly unsettling encounter with one of her students that follows – this challenge becomes central to the film’s exploration of power, vulnerability and evolution.

A Tisch School of the Arts alum and commercials director, Sims joins us on Directors Notes to discuss the decision to make a dialogue-free film, the process of working with actors Catherine Curtin and Trace Talbot to develop such a complex relationship and his long-held desire to return to his childhood school as a filmmaking location. He also takes us inside the challenges of working with the film’s animal performers, the visual language developed with cinematographer Alex Hass and the idea of evolution that sits at the heart of Galapagos.

Hi Kyle, welcome to Directors Notes. Let’s dive straight in and talk about your striking film, Galapagos. You’ve chosen to tell this story without dialogue, instead relying on your actors’ physical performances. Can you talk a little about that decision and why you felt it was the right approach for this particular story?

First off, thanks for having the film on Directors Notes. As for dialogue, it just never featured in my initial conception of the film. I was always open to whatever those two characters might say, but I could never come up with something that didn’t feel anti-climactic. This particular teacher and student – theirs is a silent relationship. It happens in glances and gestures. It’s never something they would verbally acknowledge to each other, or anyone else. Or it could be that I just write terrible dialogue… who knows.

There’s something liberating about abandoning the dialogue convention and focusing entirely on the physicality of the performances.

But with this particular story, I always felt that words would not only puncture the tonal atmosphere I wanted to explore, but would also spoil this strange connection these two characters discover. Plus, there’s something liberating about abandoning the dialogue convention and focusing entirely on the physicality of the performances.

With that dialogue-free approach in mind, I imagine finding the right performers was crucial to the success of the film. How did you go about casting Catherine Curtin and Trace Talbot and what did you feel each of them brought to the story?

I still remember discovering Trace Talbot in this short called Two Little Boys. It’s an incredible piece of work. And with Trace in particular, seeing how far he could go in that one scene – I just knew I wanted to do a project with him. So I worked backwards and reverse engineered the ‘student’ character for him specifically. And he was an absolute treasure to work with. He was willing to go through all sorts of oddities on behalf of the film, and the way he readily adopted the character was just so frictionless. I certainly plan on working with him again.

For the teacher character, we had a wish list of our ideal actors. Cathy was right at the top of that list, and I was shocked when she agreed to come on board, especially since the script was still somewhat embryonic at that stage. But she’s an incredible talent, and as someone who simply loves the work, she was willing to try something stranger than usual. We’re still great friends, and Galapagos just wouldn’t have any kind of punch if it weren’t for her. I’ve certainly got other roles planned for her as well.

There was no need to yell action and cut and constantly interrupt the chemistry.

It feels as though the power dynamic between these two characters is at the heart of what makes the film so captivating. How did you work with Catherine and Trace to develop that relationship and make it feel so intense, yet strangely authentic?

They met on the first day of shooting. So there was a certain distance at first, and because we shot chronologically it worked in our favor. They only got to know each other more between takes, and there was a kind of camaraderie that developed. A sort of “we’re in this weird thing together, aren’t we” mentality. And so when it came time to shoot the bathroom scene, where she’s actually touching his hair and feeding him lettuce, there was really no friction in terms of finding the exact blocking and figuring out how they were going to interact with each other physically.

Most Popular

It’s an oddly intimate scene. I remember thinking, “this is almost a sex scene.” It certainly has some of those trappings. But really it all came back to the fact that no matter how strange an interaction this was, it didn’t require any speech. I think that gave Cathy and Trace a certain relief, in that it wasn’t about delivering lines, it was a matter of finding the right posture and the right gesture. And even the way we shot that scene, because there was no dialogue, there was no need to yell action and cut and constantly interrupt the chemistry. Instead, we ended up with a whole series of takes strung together. And so even that ability to just let them go for minutes at a time, it allowed them to find those expressions and gestures that couldn’t really be rehearsed in advance.

Staying with that power dynamic, it continually shifts throughout the film, keeping the audience on edge before culminating in that unforgettable ending. Can you explain why you chose to conclude the story in this way, particularly why you decided to tip the balance of power in that direction?

I try to think of writing as discovering a series of images more than dictating a set of conditions. So I was always open to the ending that was waiting for us, so to speak. And after meditating on the characters for a long time, I realized that there was no way this teacher was going to lose this conflict. She starts out as this vulnerable, isolated creature, unable to register the threat sitting in her classroom. And it was always obvious to me that the student was not going to kill the rabbit. He never needed to. After what happens in the bathroom, it’s over. He’s gotten his thrill. But I knew from the beginning that this teacher had the potential to evolve. What she does at the end – it was really the only logical conclusion given how badly she’d been humiliated in that bathroom.

It’s a testament to Cathy and Trace and their talent as actors that they were able to visualize that through expression alone.

I sensed that there was almost a benevolent motivation on the part of the teenage boy – almost as if he were trying to show her where she was vulnerable and maladapted to the harsh law of the jungle – and it’s only after realizing that for herself that she’s able to reclaim the personal authority she’d been lacking all along. One of my favorite aspects of the last scene is how it instantly gets all of the other kids’ attention. They’re blabbering all through homeroom. They don’t see her. They don’t respect her. And then, in that one decisive gesture, she’s able to silence all of them and force them to drop what they’re doing and pay attention. She reclaims her authority and earns his respect in a way even he couldn’t have predicted, which is what leads to that thinnest of grins he gives her as a parting gift. There’s been an irreversible evolution in their dynamic, and it’s a testament to Cathy and Trace and their talent as actors that they were able to visualize that through expression alone.

The cinematography also plays an important role in shaping the relationship between your two main characters. How did you work with Alex Hass to develop the visual language of Galapagos?

Alex is a dear friend from film school. And he was willing to go into this unsettling film world without hesitation. Luckily we were able to access the high school the week before shooting. So he and I got to go in together and figure out how to exploit the specific architecture of each room we were in. And so the cinematography was really dictated by the design of each space – the classroom, the courtyard, auditorium, etc.

The bathroom was a very late discovery. We were almost panicking trying to figure out which of the bathrooms on hand would be the least bad option, in terms of the blocking of that interaction. And then by chance we drifted into what was once my locker room. And we turned the corner and there was that windowless, symmetrical set of toilets and urinals. One of those liminal spaces. And so we always leaned into the architecture of that school, which was built back in the 1950s, whenever we were stumped as to where to put the camera.

We turned the corner and there was that windowless, symmetrical set of toilets and urinals.

Talking of the school, the setting is integral to both the tone and narrative of the film. Was it always your intention to set the story in an educational environment, and how did you go about finding the right locations?

The same way I knew I wanted to make a film with Catherine Curtin, I always knew I wanted to make a short film at my high school. I can remember sitting in classes as a teenager picturing all sorts of ‘scenes’ that might take place in the halls, in the courtyard. That school has an incredible character and texture to it that you just can’t find in modern schools. And so the whole film emerged only after I decided on the school as the definitive location, since I knew it was a location I could secure for free (thank you Principal Pigeon).

I like to write for particular settings the way you might write for a particular actor. And if anything, we only scratched the surface of that particular high school. The nooks and crannies are endless. I mean, the scene where the student sits in front of a mirror in a basement dressing room – that’s a real room. We didn’t dress that at all. It’s certainly a location that seems to suggest other stories.

Alongside the two excellent central performances, the other ‘characters’ that steal the spotlight are the film’s animal co-stars. What was it like working with such a menagerie of creatures and did they present any unexpected challenges during production?

It was definitely a challenge. Animals and children usually are. And with this film we needed a whole zoo of creatures to really round out the cast. We ‘rented’ a rabbit from a craigslist vendor that was trying to sell it, and we then had a local rabbit breeder come on set as our rabbit wrangler. We named the rabbit Sallie. Then returned her to the owner the day after shooting.

The snake was a bigger challenge, because snakes aren’t nearly as active as you’d expect. They’re largely inert creatures, happy to sit there for hours at a time in one position. We achieved the snake’s movement by placing the snake into the enclosure and waiting for it to curl itself back up – then reversing the shot in post so it seems to be rearing to strike.

The way that one dog barks incessantly, that does so much more than a mere sound effect.

We did actually put the rabbit and the snake in the same glass terrarium, with a thick piece of plexiglass between them. The snake wrangler told us that because this snake has never seen a rabbit, it isn’t going to react aggressively. And she was absolutely right, that snake didn’t care less. Neither did Sallie. But because the snake was actually relatively small compared to Sallie, showing them in the same frame felt wrong. That last punch had to rely on the sound design to suggest what was beginning to happen offscreen.

One of my favorite moments in the film is this interaction Cathy has with the offscreen animal dealer. This scruffy conman selling baby rabbits, chickens, dogs and a rare blue macaw out of the back of his truck. This kind of traveling menagerie. I felt that just getting a bunch of different potential pets into one shot would have its own unsettling effect. Sinister, but shootable. And in that moment, just the way that one dog barks incessantly, that does so much more than a mere sound effect. It’s this pitiful howling that really echoes how despondent that character – the teacher mourning her missing rabbit – is feeling by the end of that awful day.

Before we wrap up, I just wanted to ask about the title – Galapagos – what does it mean and why did you choose it?

The title was meant to suggest the film’s core theme: evolution. The Galapagos Islands are where Darwin developed his theory of natural selection, and between the evolution of the teacher character and the biodiversity of the film, Galapagos felt like a subtle but evocative nod. An early edit even included an insert of a Darwin poster on the wall (which we ended up cutting for time), but other references are sprinkled in throughout – from the design of the end credits to those specimens in the jars in the biology classroom – giving that sense of ‘evolution no more’. In other words, look what happens to these creatures who don’t evolve fast enough to avoid getting caught… it’s ultimately the unspoken question the student asks the teacher: will you be prey? Or will you evolve fast enough to become the predator?

With Galapagos now available online, what are you focusing on next? Are there any upcoming projects you’re particularly excited about? And where can our audience go to follow your work?

I’m currently in pre-production on my next short film, which will feature one of my favorite living actors. We’ll be shooting that in Buffalo later this year. Beyond that, I’ve written a feature film called Kathleen’s which was recently selected as a semifinalist in the Pipeline Screenplay Competition. I’m still in publicity training, but you can follow my Instagram @kylemsims and check out my website at kylemsims.com

Finally, this is a question we’re asking all the filmmakers we interview: if you could recommend one short film by another filmmaker, what would it be and why?

World of Glory (1991) by Roy Andersson. My experimental film professor Darrell Wilson showed it to us in school, and I was absolutely floored. The first scene alone is a masterpiece – visually, aurally, narratively. It just stabs you and lets you do the most horrible math as to what’s happening. Roy Andersson is definitely a master of the short-form. What he’s able to do in terms of stringing micro vignettes together into a wider tapestry – it’s just incredible. I was definitely aping World of Glory when I made my college thesis film, which was just 10 unbroken shots, 10 little vignettes. And I remember being flattered when a real Hollywood director saw it and said, “Roy Andersson – I love him!”

item.title: Jacque Rabie Sets Aside Judgement to Find the Man Inside Japan’s Museum of Sex Dolls in ‘Hyodo’s Paradise’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: Jacque Rabie discusses trust, intimacy and confronting his own relationship with sexuality while making a doc about the man behind Japan's museum of sex dolls.
item.content:encoded:
There’s an obvious visual appeal and heightened intrigue to a documentary about a man who lives in a museum of sex dolls. But in Hyodo’s Paradise, director Jacque Rabie is less interested in the novelty of the situation than in the person living it. Over 22 minutes, Rabie observes Hyodo in the everyday rhythms of his home – vacuuming, washing his dolls, talking about his life and revealing increasingly personal aspects of himself – while resisting the easy temptation to turn his unusual circumstances into spectacle. Instead, Hyodo’s Paradise becomes an unexpectedly complex examination of judgement, sexuality and more.

That complexity was not necessarily something Rabie understood from the outset. Having previously worked exclusively in narrative filmmaking, he initially approached Hyodo’s home wondering how he could turn its unique and visually compelling environment into a short film. It was only through spending time with the man that he realised the more meaningful story was already there. For Directors Notes, Rabie joins us to discuss the transition from narrative to documentary, building intimacy across a language barrier and how making Hyodo’s Paradise unexpectedly encouraged him to confront his own relationship with sexuality.

You’d only made narrative films before this. Narrative lets you author a character; documentary hands that authorship over to your subject. Was there a moment this stopped being a film you were making and became one you were receiving?

I remember thinking when I came out of the first visit with Hyodo: how can I turn this into a short? How can I use his house in some interesting way for a film? Would he be willing to act in whatever I made? Eventually it clicked that I wasn’t going to be able to make anything more interesting than what was presented to me. The most interesting, and frankly meaningful, story was already there. So I pitched the idea to Tegan Slattery and decided to try something that felt very unfamiliar, but also felt like the most natural way to channel the inspiration I found at Hyodo’s place.

You reached Hyodo through several layers – your limited Japanese, his limited English, a translator, and, later, Tina Imahara catching things in the edit that you’d missed. Did all that mediation flatten the intimacy, or do something else to it?

On my new doc project, a feature entitled Kur, I just filmed another segment that was translated. In all honestly, this go around it felt totally stilted compared to my dialogue with Hyodo. I attribute this to a couple of things. The first simply being the speed of translating and nuances caught by our translator Stephan May (where he would frequently qualify responses by saying there was no perfect English translation and giving poetic alternatives). The second was that I really felt a connection with Hyodo, especially by the end. I didn’t need to know exactly what he was saying to really be there with the meaning of it. Even when the Japanese was way beyond my level, I almost knew what was coming just by his expression.

The edit was a totally different story. I struggled big time, and it’s only through Tina Imahara’s fantastic editing and fluency that the intimacy found on set could be brought out in the edit.

At what level was he open with you? Were there things he offered easily that felt polished, and quieter things that seemed to slip out unguarded?

Hyodo was quite guarded the first day. His responses were very matter of fact. When I tried to go a little more emotional, there was some clear resistance. I think that faded right at the end of day 1 when he realized what the film was. Hyodo had been filmed a few times before in the past, but those films always portrayed him as a novelty. Local TV programs would come to his house just to gawk at how ‘strange’ it all was. When he realized we were trying to do something a little different, he sort of started to play into it – seeing, hopefully this doesn’t sound too pretentious haha, the attempted artistry – and really allow himself to be vulnerable.

I really felt trusted by him and didn’t want to betray that trust in the edit.

Actually, now that I’m thinking about it, it was after I saw a poster of Tarkovsky’s Stalker in his room somewhere and we started speaking about it. Hyodo loves films, especially the same slow-burn ones I do, so I think that was a turning point where he started to trust me as an artist and trust my intentions with his portrayal. By the last day, he was very willing to let out some really deeply personal things I wouldn’t put on the film for the sake of his privacy. I really felt trusted by him and didn’t want to betray that trust in the edit. It also didn’t hurt that he had a few beers at a few points…

Most Popular

What did you actually feel, hour to hour, inside that house? And did it shift as you got to know him?

I felt like I was on a rollercoaster. I don’t remember exactly how I left feeling, but I know it oscillated between judgmental, excited, confused, tired, even a bit scared at points!

You’ve said your first cut read as judgmental because you were projecting your own judgments onto him. What did the film end up showing you about your own discomfort?

I tried to put aside my own worldview or perspective so the viewer of the film can just view Hyodo as rawly as possible, but speaking only for myself, I personally don’t think it’s healthy or particularly internally productive to put all that on display for the world. There is something potentially beneficial to society in having a sense of decency and mindfulness of how our behaviors impact others (and I’m not just speaking in terms of sexuality but all of the things we tuck away), but far worse than the exhibitionism of our shadows is their repression. Hyodo’s complete openness, in that way, is inspiring. I feel that it is a first step to genuine healing and integration that most of us don’t take. I don’t think I would have taken that for a long time without meeting Hyodo.

This film really let me open up about my own sexuality.

This wasn’t something I noticed until we started showing the film to others, but this film really let me open up about my own sexuality. While I don’t share the same fantasies or worldview as Hyodo, I certainly can recognize elements of him and his house in myself. I think all of us can to some degree. And as I stopped judging Hyodo, I think I honestly did stop judging myself for feeling certain things and having certain lenses through which my mind views the world of its own accord. And only from that place of welcoming could I start to really make peace with sides of myself I had so long shunned.

Critics singled the film out for refusing to mock Hyodo where it easily could have. Where do you land on judgment in documentary – is the compassionate eye an ethical choice, a craft one, or the same thing?

Honestly – I think it’s fine to judge. We all judge everything every second of the day. It’s more important to me what place are you coming from when you’re judging. Are you judging because it’s entertaining? Or are you judging against the viewpoint of peace and compassion? Most of my favorite doc directors do the latter. But at the same time, I think a truly powerful film, like The Act of Killing, for instance, is saying the most clear thing without needing to say anything overtly judgemental at all.

Can a filmmaker ever give a subject like Hyodo a truly fair portrait, or is every edit a verdict? How did you make peace with that much power over how he’d be seen?

I think it’s always casting some kind of eye that isn’t wholly true. I mean, there’s no such thing as true objectivity. You can’t ever truly see someone, truly. So I do feel some degree of remorse that some aspect of this comes from a position of power over Hyodo (in the context of this film). I think that realization has made filmmaking harder for me, as I’ve come to see that you’re playing God a bit with your subjects (even actors in narrative). I simply hope that the film does more good in opening the hearts of others than it does harm towards Hyodo and those who see him.

You’ve said it was the women on the project who brought the compassionate, unjudgmental eye. What do you make of that pattern, and why do you think it fell that way?

I’m not sure if it was due to gender or societal influence based on gender norms, but I think that myself and the men I’d shown it to all almost immediately tacked on some level of condemnation and subtle belittling to Hyodo. In stark contrast, all the women approached it with a deeply compassionate, understanding eye. Part of me wants to joke and say it’s why women should be world leaders, but I think it more importantly points to the way the patriarchy affects men. To me, it points to how deeply ingrained ideals of masculinity, propriety, and an unhealthy relationship to sexuality affect men.

There’s no such thing as true objectivity. You can’t ever truly see someone, truly.

Was there a cut you loved that you had to kill because it served your judgment of him rather than the film?

Yes, but sadly sharing it would be breaching the internal sense of confidentiality I have for Hyodo! Let’s say there was a long CG sequence in the middle over a VO of a story he told me. Would’ve been pretty cool, but unfair…

The crude and the heartbreaking sit right up against each other, rather than in tidy tonal blocks. Was that deliberate, or just the texture of the man?

It really was just putting on display the mind of Hyodo, which sits in a myriad of contradictions.

You stayed late shooting B-roll while Hyodo got ready for bed. What were you chasing in those hours?

Shots of his house! It was more practical since we spent all day interviewing that I wanted to get tons and tons of footage of every corner of his place. I unfortunately found in the edit that I got a lot, and I mean a lot, of cool shots of the same things rather than diversifying as much as I should have! Lots more cat stuff to be found in his place!
