The festival run’s been strong. What reaction has surprised you most – and you mentioned a feature in there you’d have loved to capture. Is that still alive, and what’s next?

I remember at our screening at Big Sky, a woman asked a question to Tegan and I with a startling amount of intensity: “Why did you make this? I felt incredibly uncomfortable watching this.” I think I just said something like, “I just felt like I had to, it felt like I was just expressing myself”. After the screening she came up to me and revealed how hard the film was to watch, but that my answer made her realize it was all coming from her. I think the process for the film did that for me too.

It’s a globe-spanning production where we will team up with directors across the world.

At that same fest, I met a wonderful producer – Chloe Campion. Chloe, Tegan, and I have teamed up to work on a new project entitled Kur. Kur is a feature-length doc about death, and how the way we relate to it shapes the way we live. It’s a globe-spanning production where we will team up with directors across the world (as of now, one in South Africa and one in Morocco) to film the deeply intimate aspects of death we so oft overlook.

And the one we always end on: if you could send our readers to a single short film you love, what is it, and why?

Lance Oppenheim’s The Happiest Guy in the World. While I don’t like that the portrayal felt a bit unfair to the subject, I must admit this little short is the one that most deeply changed my life and opened me up to shooting docs.

item.title: 10 Unforgettable Short Films DN Spotted at Sarajevo Film Festival 2026
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: A bold, strange and unforgettable selection lights up this year’s Sarajevo Film Festival, bringing fresh voices and unexpected stories to the screen.
item.content:encoded:
Like every August, the Sarajevo Film Festival returns as the largest and most important film festival in the Balkans. It brings powerful stories to the screen, often political and rooted in memory, exploring the recent history of the region where the festival takes place. At the same time, it offers a compelling and above all diverse selection of short films from all over the world. The competition programme is divided into three sections: Short Films, Student Films and Short Documentary Films. We also peeked at non-competitive sections such as Dealing with the Past. The selection includes films making their world premieres, as well as films coming from major festivals that take place earlier in the season. Several of the films selected here have already screened at festivals such as Annecy and Cannes, among others. In fact, Asparagus Bear, in the Documentary Competition, was part of our SXSW London Best of Fest selection and we also highlighted Cosmonauts in our Annecy Best of Fest.

Here is a selection of ten of the most interesting and groundbreaking shorts in this year’s Sarajevo Film Festival selection. The themes are as diverse as the genres, with animation given significant space in the festival’s programme. Overall, what stands out is that quality is not only about technique but, above all, about the stories and themes explored. These films offer fresh perspectives and confident voices. Most interestingly, some come from the student film selection, making the maturity of their direction all the more striking.

Holy Defiance – Karla Jelić

After its premiere at Sheffield DocFest, Karla Jelić’s short is one of a kind. On the first Saturday of every month, on the main squares of Croatian cities, hundreds of men kneel and pray together. Calling themselves The Knights of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, they prevent women from entering and, in their prayers, they advocate for re-traditionalization, patriarchy, and the restriction of women’s freedoms. Multimedia artist Arijana Lekić-Fridrih travels to a different city each time and performs her feminist piece ‘Silent Mass’ as the men pray. As you might predict, the group has tried in various ways to prevent her performances. In disclosing this absolutely anachronistic and almost unbelievable tradition, Holy Defiance focuses on an alternation of scenes between those dedicated to the protagonist and those focusing on hundreds of men who take part in this kind of performance. The film’s remarkable and brilliant direction allows us to discover this story—one that would otherwise remain confined to its own region—and encourages us to reflect on what it still means today, in Europe, to risk not having women’s rights on an equal footing with men’s.

Over the Threshold (Preko Praga) – Tara Gajović

Presented at Cannes as part of the La Cinef competition, this is undoubtedly one of the films with the most striking cinematography in the programme. Serbian filmmaker Tara Gajović, only 26 years old, made Over the Threshold as her graduation short at the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Belgrade, hence it screening in the Student Films section. The 15-minute short is impeccably flawless, also in terms of its set design. The story is relatively simple: it follows a newlywed couple who feel the need to escape the formal context of their wedding and spend the evening together discussing their future. It’s a situation many people will recognise, but the film places it firmly within the specific geographical and social context of Serbia. This creates a very interesting discussion around traditions and what they represent, whether they are religious traditions or simply traditions shaped by the history of a country.

Unwellness – Réka Pinczés

World-premiering in the Student Films competition, Réka Pinczés’ Unwellness follows an ordinary woman in the midst of menopause, attending an accountancy course at a spa hotel. When a hearing-impaired woman unexpectedly awakens her long-suppressed desire for physical intimacy, Ildikó is forced to confront a new phase of her life and come to terms with changes she can no longer ignore. The transition into a new stage of life, in this case menopause, which brings with it a different relationship to sexuality and one’s own body, is rarely explored in cinema. Too often, it is treated comedically, or at least without the sensitivity and nuance that characterise this film. Here, we have an incredible performance by lead actress Réka Pelsőczy, as well as an excellent screenplay that manages, within the short running time, to convey all the emotions this woman experiences, which are ultimately released toward the film’s climax through a spectacular editing sequence.

Most Popular

Paradaïz – Matea Radić

Chosen as part of the festival’s Dealing with the Past section, Paradaïz is a masterclass in short animation filmmaking. In less than ten minutes, and without any dialogue, Sarajevo-born artist Matea Radić explores a return to Sarajevo after the Bosnian War, where childhood memories of Yugoslavia collide with the trauma and violence of the past. Through haunting animation, nostalgia, and surreal imagery, the film reflects on displacement and the impossibility of returning to a lost paradise. Lost in a place where the houses have holes, tomatoes are ticking time bombs and snails wander the streets in search of a safe space, we find a haunting human reality: memory matters more than we realise.

Motherhood – Anca Damian

Anca Damian’s Annecy title Motherhood, here part of the Short Film Competition, tells a beautiful story of motherhood, seen through the eyes of a woman who, before being a mother, is obviously a daughter, and who, before being a mother, is also a partner. The animation spectacularly conveys this inner torment, mixed with the joy of motherhood. Without a doubt, Damian’s ability to tell an intimate, personal story that is, of course, also so universal, and to do so in such an original manner, is remarkable. As we know, motherhood is often explored within the cinematic medium, but here we are faced with a story that makes use of its necessity and urgency to tell a story that becomes unforgettable thanks to the way it’s told.

Porkatal – Sis Gürdal

World premiering in Sarajevo, Sis Gürdal’s film tells a heartbreaking story, but at the same time, it is striking for its hopeful style, which never allows itself to be overwhelmed by the darkness of the story. The fact that the short is centred on a child who knows no life outside the prison where he was confined with his mother is fundamentally an original idea, because it creates the impression that the child is, in a sense, being born again when he leaves the hospital, as if he were discovering life anew, emerging from the hospital as one emerges from a womb. Moreover, the concept is somewhat similar to Rousseau’s Émile, which tells the story of a child who is raised in a rural setting, in an environment where he grows up somewhat without constraints, restrictions, or preconceived ideas. Despite the enormous conceptual differences, in some respects, the context here can remind us of Émile. Furthermore, the interpretation of the child protagonist is extraordinary, as is the simplicity of the scenes and their composure. All in all, the different aspects of the Porkatal form an incisive, perfectly complete, and solid film.

The Future Is in Your Hands, But Why Not Lend It to the Specialists? – Alexandra Schinteie

With The Future Is in Your Hands, But Why Not Lend It to the Specialists?, Alexandra Schinteie has built a film with an atmosphere that very easily recalls Radu Jude’s films, also thanks to the casting of Ilinca Manolache, one of the muses of the famous Romanian director. This unmissable satire gets to the heart of the issues surrounding plastic surgery, Botox, and cosmetic enhancements. The transformation of a woman pushed to alter her appearance by a man also plays cleverly with the perception of the female body through the male gaze. The film handles this transformation particularly well, both in terms of its production and performances. It maintains a distinctive atmosphere that may not appeal to everyone, but is instantly recognisable and feels promising within contemporary Romanian cinema. Rather than simply copying Radu Jude, it feels more like an homage, while offering a promising glimpse of a director with a distinctive voice in the making.

Adgwa-ata – Zsuzsanna Kreif

This striking piece of animation is unpredictable, richly colourful, and distinguished by a strong sense of originality, even if its visual language and heightened use of colour are not entirely unfamiliar. Following its screening in Cannes, Adgwa-ata feels like a film with a long future ahead of it. Zsuzsanna Kreif uses its colourful, almost hypnotic surface to tell a story of emancipation, female solidarity, and the discovery of one’s own body. The film is not always easy to decipher, but perhaps that is precisely what makes it so compelling. We are invited to lose ourselves in a succession of increasingly intense images that gradually become more immersive. Dominated by shades of green and pink, Adgwa-ata is a visually arresting short that lingers in the mind.

Of Light Ghosts – Isabella Fellinger

Of Light Ghosts, a 27-minute Austrian short, is a film that focuses entirely on atmosphere rather than chronological development or conventional narrative logic. Here, colour, cinematography, and, more broadly, the sensations the film evokes are its greatest strengths. Its extended runtime, which can often work against a short film, instead allows the viewer to become fully immersed in this world of light and, above all, darkness, with one existing in constant contrast to the other. Isabella Fellinger handles the film’s underlying narrative with restraint, allowing the images to carry much of its meaning. These evocative visions gradually take on greater weight, ultimately serving the film’s broader themes and leaving a lasting impression.

Fahrudin – Alen Drljević

Animation gives the story a rawness that might have been difficult to achieve in live action. Told almost entirely through shades of brown and dark charcoal, Fahrudin creates a visual language of sadness, despair, and alienation. This approach allows the story to unfold without the limitations of a live-action production, even though animation itself is an incredibly time-consuming and costly process. Alen Drljević hits hard with a film that tells the survival story of Fahrudin Muminović, who miraculously escaped a mass execution during the Srebrenica genocide when he was only seven years old. Given the subject’s profound local significance, it is perhaps unsurprising that the Sarajevo Film Festival selected the film for its Documentary Competition. What makes that choice particularly interesting is that the film is animated, and yet, despite its form, it remains firmly rooted in documentary, using its form to reconstruct and convey a real-life story that might otherwise be difficult to represent.

You can find more unmissable films like these in our Best of Fest collections.

item.title: Two Sisters Fracture Under a Collapsing World in Leandros Braounos & Daniel Howells’ Afrikaans Short ‘Winter Slaap’
item.dc:creator: Mark Brennan
item.description: Guilt, grief and inherited expectation press down on two sisters in Leandros Braounos & Daniel Howells' wintry portrait of family disintegration.
item.content:encoded:
True world-building can be such a tricky thing to master in a short film. By definition, the budgets are not always there to physically create it, nor is the available runtime sufficient to fully explore it. That said, when done well, it can be a genuinely absorbing and transportive experience. Winter Slaap (Hibernation), from co-directors Leandros Braounos and Daniel Howells, is exactly that—and, even more impressively, it’s also a student film. Inspired in part by the collective global trauma of the pandemic lockdowns and the world we encountered as we emerged back into society, the film explores how two sisters respond when the events unfolding around them outpace their understanding. Joining us today, Braounos talks to Directors Notes about the challenges of shooting in South Africa’s stunning natural landscapes, the production considerations required when filming in black and white, the meticulous crafting of the soundscape to make it as immersive as possible, and the lessons they took away from a difficult shoot that, at one point, felt as though it would never be finished.

Winter Slaap transports audiences to a time and place in South Africa not often seen on screen. What was the inspiration for this story, both thematically and narratively?

Daniel and I had established years prior that if we ever collaborated again, it would be on an Afrikaans period film. We wanted to craft a type of film that hadn’t really been seen in South Africa before. Our country has a fascinating, complex history deeply shaped by conflict — not just along racial lines, but across deeply fractured cultural ones as well.

Narratively, the film is about a family disintegrating under pressure, exploring how two sisters navigate the unique guilt, scars, and expectations placed upon each of them.

When we sat down to write the script, the world was emerging from the Covid-19 lockdowns, and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine had just begun. The global landscape felt like it was shifting at a terrifying pace; we were collectively stepping into the unknown. We found ourselves asking: How would society change after being isolated indoors for so long? How do people react when confronted with monumental events entirely outside of their control? Do they wither inward, passively accepting their reality, or do they grow outward, driven by a conviction to act — no matter how misdirected or dangerous that belief might be? We wanted to place all of these ideas within a slightly fantastical world full of metaphor and allegory, but anchor them with a very intimate story at its heart. Narratively, the film is about a family disintegrating under pressure, exploring how two sisters navigate the unique guilt, scars, and expectations placed upon each of them.

The striking black and white cinematography against wintery landscapes is at odds with most depictions of South Africa. How did you go about defining the visual style and tone you wanted to capture?

Deciding to shoot in black and white was one of our very first creative choices. Stylistically, it served as a stark, almost supernatural window into that specific era. As you mentioned, it subverts the typical, vibrant depiction of South Africa, which was exactly the fresh perspective we wanted to explore.

Working with a very limited budget, we knew that stripping away colour and leaning into high-contrast, atmospheric lighting, would help us transform a region that is typically quite lush into a cold, dying world.

We desperately wanted the film to possess the texture of a 16mm film stock, but sourcing, shooting, and processing physical film in South Africa is incredibly difficult and cost-prohibitive. To overcome this, we worked closely with our Art Director and colourist, Chloe Iacovou. Together, we dove into deep research surrounding digital film emulation techniques and the specific ‘colour’ theory of monochromatic grading, meticulously crafting that organic grain and tonal depth in post-production. However, the choice was also born out of practical necessity. Working with a very limited budget, we knew that stripping away colour and leaning into high-contrast, atmospheric lighting would help us transform a region that is typically quite lush into a cold, dying world.

The tone of the film is matched and complemented on screen by both the main and supporting cast. What was the casting process for both the leads and the many background artists featured?

The casting process was an intentional mix of industry experience and raw texture. For our supporting cast and background artists, we balanced established South African actors with non-professionals. We were hunting for faces that carried a distinct weight — faces that held a presence on screen almost like the landscape itself.

Most Popular

For our leads, the journey was a bit different. We knew very early on that we wanted Sam Faure for Magda; she was a fellow acting student at our film school, and we had long been admirers of her screen presence. For Elna, we needed an actor who possessed a very soft physical and vocal quality to capture the character’s inherent insecurity. Yet, she also needed to be entirely unreadable, never fully letting the audience into her internal world. We put out an open casting call on social media, and Zonya Swart was one of the first to respond. The moment we saw her, we knew we had found Elna.

With much of Winter Slaap shot outdoors in natural landscapes, what were some of the challenges you faced filming outdoors?

We shot the entire film in the Drakensberg region of KwaZulu-Natal — an incredibly beautiful, rugged, and largely untouched landscape far from any city. We intentionally scheduled the shoot for September, which is historically one of the driest months in the region. Instead, we were hit with a week of torrential downpours, the highest rainfall the area had experienced in years. This completely derailed our logistics; the dirt roads leading to our main homestead location became a thick sludge. At one point, our generator slid completely off the road, and we had to track down a local tractor to pull it out.

We had to surrender to the environment, and leaning into that unscripted chaos of the elements is exactly what gave us our most striking and unexpected moments on screen.

It made for an incredibly high-stress shoot. We were constantly fighting a disappearing timeline, and chasing the rapidly shifting natural light in those deep valleys was a massive challenge. Ultimately, we realised we couldn’t fight nature. We had to surrender to the environment, and leaning into that unscripted chaos of the elements is exactly what gave us our most striking and unexpected moments on screen.

As well as the exterior locations, there are some impressive interiors such as the farmstead and the church. How did you go about sourcing and securing these locations?

We knew from the start that our locations had to carry the same raw texture and atmospheric weight as other aesthetic elements of the film. We deliberately avoided shooting in a studio; there is an artificiality to built sets that audiences subconsciously pick up on, which would have shattered the immersion. Instead, we spent a significant portion of pre-production researching and scouting across the province to find spaces that naturally exuded a sense of historical aura and profound isolation.

We initially chose the Lotheni Nature Reserve for our exterior landscapes. While scouting there, we stumbled upon their museum — a preserved homestead built in the exact historical period our film is set in. It contained beautifully preserved furniture and period artefacts, which we were able to use either directly on screen or as precise references for our production design.

The church was brought to our attention by a friend from the Underberg community. The moment we stepped inside, we were in awe of its striking architecture and rich history. It was built in the late 1800s by Trappist monks who had journeyed into the interior to establish a mission to support the local community. Remarkably, it still functions as a school today. Securing it was a testament to the local community, who were incredibly hospitable and enthusiastic about supporting the project. In fact, that was true for our entire experience in the region — it was the warmth and excitement of the local people that truly made the film possible.

The period is captured beautifully through the production and costume design of the film. How much research/work was needed to achieve that authenticity?

We wanted every single frame to feel historically grounded, but we were also chasing a sense of haunting, melancholic beauty that directly mirrored the inner world and hopelessness of our characters. To achieve that, we did extensive historical research into the brutal realities of daily life during that period, delving into everything from scarce food sources to the living conditions. It was an era defined by conflict and famine, so pristine clothing and cleanliness simply wouldn’t have existed. Because of that, a massive amount of the work went into distressing and aging the costumes and set pieces. We wanted a heavily weathered, lived-in texture where absolutely nothing felt like a prop pulled new out of a packet.

Designing for a monochromatic film also introduced a fascinating technical challenge. Because we were shooting in black and white, our primary focus had to be on tonal separation and maximising contrast rather than colour harmony. Amusingly, if you were to see the costumes in colour, they looked like a chaotic mishmash of clashing tones. But when translated through the black-and-white monitor, those specific colour values allowed the characters to pop perfectly against each other and the stark, wintery background.

Because we were shooting in black and white, our primary focus had to be on tonal separation and maximising contrast rather than colour harmony.

There is a thick atmosphere that helped in no small part to create an absorbing soundscape, with natural sounds echoing throughout. How did you approach the sound design?

Mood and atmosphere are always at the forefront in our minds as filmmakers; we constantly strive to create immersive worlds that completely transport the viewer and evoke a visceral, subconscious response. For Winter Slaap, we felt the sonic landscape was perhaps the most integral component in achieving that sensation. We knew we wanted the sound design to rely primarily on minimalist, diegetic elements, but we chose to subtly distort and hyper-texturise those natural sounds. The goal was to create an environment that felt recognisable but fundamentally off-kilter — mirroring the psychological state of the characters and the dying world they inhabit.

At the same time, we wanted the film to possess a distinct musical motif that could act as both an overture and an epilogue, anchoring the narrative arc. Collaborating with our composer, Braam du Toit, was an incredible experience because he deeply understood the visual and thematic textures we were exploring. Instead of leaning into a standard, modern minimalist score, Braam researched and utilised period-accurate instruments and traditional cultural tones. Through that approach, he crafted music that feels less like a traditional accompaniment and more like the voice of the landscape itself.

You mentioned to us that you’re fans of slow cinema. What does that mean to you and what makes you feel so strongly about it?

We both deeply appreciate the artistry on display when a filmmaker is able to subdue time, placing the viewer entirely at its mercy. There is something incredibly bold about a director who isn’t afraid to hold on a shot far longer than what modern pacing dictates, forcing the audience to actively stretch their attention span – especially in a world as fast-paced and hyper-stimulated as ours today.

For us, this cinematic patience returns us to a more ancestral way of experiencing life, where the mundane was given room to breathe and allowed to find its own meaning. As filmmakers, that is exactly the boundary we wanted to explore with Winter Slaap: to see if we could successfully command that silence and invite the audience to truly inhabit the space with us.

As a student film, what were some of the biggest lessons you learned both in making the film and screening it to audiences?

Making Winter Slaap was a massive learning curve that deeply humbled our entire team. We completely underestimated how brutal and unpredictable shooting in a remote location could be; at certain points, the logistical pressures were so intense that we genuinely felt we had failed and wouldn’t be able to finish. We had to make dramatic script changes on the fly, but that forced adaptability taught us our most valuable lesson: you have to keep pushing forward, because you’ll always be surprised by how resourceful you can become when your back is against the wall. We can look at the film now and clearly see its narrative and technical faults, but that has only made us hungrier to rectify them on the next project. That is the nature of filmmaking — nothing will ever be a flawless replica of what you imagined before the shoot.

We completely underestimated how brutal and unpredictable shooting in a remote location could be; at certain points, the logistical pressures were so intense that we genuinely felt we had failed and wouldn’t be able to finish.

Screening the film to audiences has been equally eye-opening, revealing a fascinating divide in how people react to this style of cinema. While we’ve been incredibly fortunate to receive praise and win awards, we’ve also had viewers tell us it was simply too slow or boring. Ultimately, it taught us that you cannot please everyone. A film that tries to cater to every taste is a compromise of vision, and we’d rather make something that polarises than something that leaves people indifferent.

What’s next for you?

I am still based in Cape Town and currently developing a few new projects. I am hoping to head into production on a new short film either at the end of this year or early next year. It’s another historical piece with elements of fantasy, following a group of Dutch sailors searching for their missing captain on Table Mountain. Beyond that, I am in the early writing stages of my first feature film. Daniel is now based in Ireland, but we stay in close contact and are actively talking about these upcoming scripts, with the intention of hopefully working together again in the future.

What’s a short film by another filmmaker that you would recommend to the Directors Notes community and why?

We would highly recommend Sycorax by Lois Patiño and Matías Piñeiro. It might seem like an unconventional pick, but it served as a constant creative reference for us throughout every stage of making Winter Slaap. The film possesses an incredible, deeply immersive atmosphere and a remarkably rich sound design. Watching it for the first time gave us the creative courage to trust our instincts and pursue a piece of cinema that is slow, atmospheric, and unapologetically experimental — one that respects the audience enough not to spell out every narrative beat.

item.title: Filmmakers of the Future: 10 Essential Shorts from the Locarno Film Festival
item.dc:creator: Veronica Orciari
item.description: From war and political unrest to grief, tech and climate crisis, these 10 Locarno shorts showcase the radical, inventive voices shaping cinema's future.
item.content:encoded:
As every year, in the very middle of August, the Locarno Film Festival comes back, bringing one of the most revolutionary selections of films and allowing audiences to discover some of the most radical and out-there voices in contemporary filmmaking. In fact, the Swiss festival manages to strike a really difficult balance by blending strong authorial voices with a selection that also winks at a more mainstream audience through Piazza Grande, ensuring its position as one of the most awaited film festivals of the year.

Continuing to prove that it is always able to connect with contemporary trends in cinema, this year’s selection of short films shows a really strong predominance of political themes. It may seem obvious, with the current ongoing wars and all the political turmoil we are facing, but we’re not talking about just a trend—we’re talking about the vast majority of the selection. It may seem inevitable that a festival like Locarno would be looking at these themes with special attention, but the sheer amount is striking. Goes without saying that a really high number of the shorts available at the festival (in this list, we count all sections, including those outside of competition) have very peculiar narrative and visual styles, so don’t look if you’re not ready to be taken into unforgettable rabbit holes of radical filmmaking.

Typhoon Mambo – Domenico Singha Pedroli

The age of AI is here, and everyone is aware of it. We are seeing all sorts of audiovisual works that either take sides for or against it, use it to tell a story, or simply turn it into part of the plot. What Typhoon Mambo does is approach AI through the experience of coping with grief and mourning after someone’s death. It also shows an elderly woman becoming dependent on a technological device for comfort following her husband’s death. The concept is nothing that Spike Jonze’s visionary (and cautionary) tale Her had not already predicted, but the film’s interesting approach to the intersection of old age, death and artificial ‘humanity’ makes it well worth watching. Is this the future waiting for us? After all, the protagonist admits that she cannot understand how people dealt with loss before technology. Domenico Singha Pedroli’s brainchild was selected for the Concorso Nazionale.

Elegy for the Forgotten, on an Endless War – Bani Khoshnoudi

Bani Khoshnoudi’s short focuses on the return of war and destruction in Iran, after the revolt of January 2026, almost 40 years after the Iran-Iraq War. The images of Israeli and American bombs falling have been tightly controlled by the regime within the country, and, stemming from this concept, the film focuses on the interesting question: “Who produces and controls the images that we see, and how do those images impact the reality that we imagine?” Made as a patchwork of videos that speak for themselves, Elegy for the Forgotten, on an Endless War reflects the importance of an open discussion without forcing a narrative, simply letting the frames tell a story that perhaps would be better left untold. The short screened in the Concorso Corti d’Autore section.

Goat – Judy Kibinge

This 28-minute short film, directed by Kenya’s Judy Kibinge, encompasses multiple themes within its running time. First is the relationship between humans and nature, already hinted at in the title, which unfolds through the interconnectedness of plants, animals and people. The story itself develops in fact within a natural environment, when Suki’s fiancé takes her to an isolated farm to buy a goat. She is a vegetarian, she doesn’t feel comfortable there and immediately wishes to leave. However, when she realises that the ancient Mugumo tree is demanding that she repay a debt she didn’t even realise she was carrying, the young woman rethinks her whole view of the world, including her future marriage with her partner. This is where the other element of Goat kicks in, showing the impact of personal beliefs within love stories. A really interesting supernatural folk thriller presented in the Open Doors screenings.

Most Popular

Maids of Petroleum – Hans Baumann

The only American short across the entire selection—and can you get more American than this? Even though it’s competing in the national competition of Pardi di Domani, director Hans Baumann is Swiss-American, Maids of Petroleum is as star-spangled as it gets. Every five years, for nearly a century, a California oil town has crowned its ‘Maids of Petroleum’. Teenage girls rehearse, parade and perform, asked to carry an inherited civic mythology into a future that can no longer be promised to them. A satire of overly performative American society, the film also focuses on the importance of the symbolism behind oil. Is a society built around it ready for its collapse? Are these Americana traditions simply laughable attempts to hold on to a world that no longer exists? A must-watch to spark these reflections.

The Architect Who Built His Own Collapse – Chun-Tien Chen

The first animated short in this list (the festival was quite abundant in this sense), and one that blends beautifully crafted visuals with a strong yet simple idea. The 20-minute The Architect Who Built His Own Collapse follows a former activist-turned-architect who joins an urban redevelopment project led by an old friend who is now the city mayor. Chun-Tien Chen’s story focuses on the loss of shared memories and ideals that disintegrate and change as things get demolished. A reflection on translation and on legacy, that boasts a masterful visual look. A true gem of animation, we hope to see more coming from the Taiwanese director in the future.

Gherking – Claudius Gentinetta

Screening in the Pardi di Domani’s Concorso Nazionale, this seven-minute, dialogue-free animated short is directed by Swiss filmmaker Claudius Gentinetta. Gherking’s story is simple, but it works thanks to beautiful visuals that are unsettling and yet comforting, as if the gestures of the old woman on screen were those of our own grandmother. In this politically charged and visionary tale, the voice of the hegemon growls from an old radio as propaganda plays the march of war and the people applaud. Meanwhile, a granny carries out her familiar autumn ritual: heating the stove, preparing herbs and spices, and arranging her preserving jars. Could these simple rituals be a form of resistance to dictatorship? Heart-wrenching and heart-warming at the same time.

The God that Destroys – Jyoti Mistry

In the Concorso Corti d’Autore, we find this experimental co-production between Austria and Sweden, directed by Jyoti Mistry. Black and white images from the first half of the 20th century are woven together with newly shot 16mm footage that mimics the archive and animation to create a tapestry that intertwines Sámi cosmology with commentary on capitalist destruction. The Siren of the Future, performed by Sara Ajnnak through traditional Sámi yoik and voiceover tells the story, aided by original songs performed by the Gothenburg Opera’s Children’s Choir. This beautiful chanting as a soundtrack is by far the most enjoyable element of The God that Destroys, which might otherwise feel too cold or distant in its narration. Its focus on the legacy of Swedish colonialisation of the Sámi people offers a perspective on an ever-perpetuating cycle of forced assimilation and cultural oppression that is, unfortunately, not exclusive to the region.

Ãsheghetam – Filmsaaz

With a title derived from the Persian Ãsheghetam, meaning “I am in love with you”, Filmsaaz’s work screened in the Concorso Corti d’Autore. Stunning, original, absolutely unhinged in the best way possible. An unforgettable testament to the power of love and freedom in a world that is burning all around them (as they speed inside a car). The visuals of this film are very powerful and also extremely original: in some moments, it really feels like a blend between a funky videogame and a nightmare or lucid dream. The interesting point is that none of this is made just to be visually pleasing; instead, its main core lies in its protest and political engagement. Ultimately the power of the bond between the two young girls is the key to unlocking true freedom. Clearly, we are in front of one of the most visionary experiments of contemporary Iranian cinema.

Las damas – Camille Zéhenne

Visual, sensorial, sexual and experimental, Las damas does not rely on a clear plot, as is often the case with many of the other Locarno films, but much more on the sensations and atmosphere it builds. Alba, an artist-in-residence at the Casa de Velázquez, struggles to find her place in the world and in her own body. During her research, she discovers the Dama de Elche, a statue of mysterious origins that becomes an obsession for her. Most of its scenes are striking in their breathtaking simplicity and composition. None of them are particularly original in themselves, and the film is indeed part of a longer cinematic tradition. Nevertheless, there’s nothing better than getting lost in the images of a well-directed and edited short. Well done to French director Camille Zéhenne for telling a story made of women through the lenses and the sensibility of a woman.

Dans les rêves, quand on dort pas la nuit – Rachel Gutgarts

“15 years ago, I completed my military service in the Israeli army’s spokesperson unit. Today, based on real texts I found during my time there, I open up a dialogue with a young Israeli sniper.” This is the premise of Rachel Gutgarts’s brilliant short film. Using a heat map effect with false colours thanks to thermal imaging, it creates a sense of artificial distance, also allowing the director to mask the true facial features of the protagonist in dialogue with her. The distance in the way he talks about killing is chilling, and the visual style enhances the feeling that what we are watching is not real, but some sort of dystopia. Yet, that is the world we live in, and not just a story on a screen. Together with all the other selections of this 2026 Locarno edition, Dans les rêves, quand on dort pas la nuit reminds us of the atrocious conditions of the current world beyond the safe haven of cinema.

You can find more unmissable films like these in our Best of Fest collections.

item.title: Li Anne Liew’s Gentle Ghost Drifts Through Strangers’ Secret Selves in ‘glide (all the people i’ll never be)’
item.dc:creator: Sarah Smith
item.description: In Li Anne Liew's tender ghost story reverie, a young woman wanders Los Angeles unseen as she mourns the life she's leaving and the ones she'll never live.
item.content:encoded:
Ghost stories usually run on threat — the cold spot, the thing that shouldn’t be there, the dread of being watched. Li Anne Liew’s glide (all the people i’ll never be) runs on something far quieter and more unnerving: the ache of being the one who watches, unseen. Her ghost, Ophelia, drifts through a sun-softened Los Angeles that has no history of hauntings and no need of her, slipping into the private lives of strangers — a phone call at a jetty that looks like the end of the world, two sisters walking a river toward nothing, a girl reading a poem in a bookshop — and mistaking their curated closeness for company. She is sentimental not for the life she lived, but for all the lives she never will.

It’s a beautiful film, and that beauty is precisely what unsettles. Shot on 500T in available light, glide holds the wind in every exterior and lets post-rain blues and greens bleed across grey concrete until Southern California turns melancholy and strange. Eyes that should meet don’t. A voice arrives distorted, too late. Funeral oranges and white chrysanthemums punctuate the drift. Nothing lunges; everything simply fails to see her — and the film leaves you, gently, haunted.

A film which I described as, “A work of profound atmospheric sensitivity, haunting and ethereal, and quietly impossible to shake.” in our NFFTY 2026 Best of Fest selection back in March, glide premieres on Directors Notes today with Liew joining us to discuss chasing a dreamlike reverie on a single roll of film a day, letting composer Yoki Ng’s score become the voice her ghost cannot use, and calibrating when to give the audience a foothold on Ophelia’s otherworldliness.

glide grew out of a very particular emotional weather — losing a job you loved, preparing to leave the US, drifting through sentimental corners of LA and feeling, quite literally, like a ghost yourself. How did that internal state begin to find a shape on the page? What was the bridge between the feeling and the script — the first images, fragments, or scenes that told you this was a film?

For a while, I knew I wanted to make a film about a ghost reacting to a world that cannot see her. I drew out scenes of a very turbulent character surrounded by a world filled with noise, unnoticed and reckless wherever she goes. When I decided to leave the US, the story pivoted to something quieter and focused. I wanted to capture what it meant to feel temporary in a place: all the possibilities I would leave behind, the different ways we leave people, and a growing longing for a place in the world. It naturally built off the bones of the ghost story I had in my head. The life I was living felt so close to its end of existence, and I was ready to mourn it even though I was still there, so I rendered it in the form of a ghost trapped between worlds. Much of what I had written was filled with the ghost intentionally inserting herself into situations. I filtered out all the noise from earlier versions and decided to follow the ghost’s aimlessness instead.

I wrote most of it on plane rides and road trips, showing my thesis film at festivals while trying to see as much of the country as I could before I left. Everything felt fleeting; every trip was like a sad goodbye. This feeling slowly bled into the script on my walks around LA. I kept getting distracted by distant strangers whose faces I couldn’t see, but it felt like they were looking at me. I would catch brief glimpses of conversations that would somehow make me emotional. It was also at the time when I saw the photo En su propia cárcel (1950) by Lola Álvarez Bravo. It shows us a lone woman sitting in a window, and a lattice-work shadow casts over her. The woman’s face had this quality of omniscience, and she looked so deeply lost in her own world. I built an ensemble of characters observed by an outsider looking into their secret internal lives, trying to find connection and meaning from a distance.

For a character who can’t interact with the world, I wondered what it would be like for her to make sense of who she is through fragments of conversations she’d find herself in. These strangers feel like they have been perfectly curated for her life, as if they are haunting her. Instead of walking through her old memories, she becomes sentimental about a life she hasn’t lived. Though she wants to transcend the past, she still holds on to it.

I built an ensemble of characters observed by an outsider looking into their secret internal lives, trying to find connection and meaning from a distance.

You describe Malaysian ghosts as threatening, and Southern California as ‘ghost-less’, and you were drawn to writing a gentle ghost trying to find her place in the world. What made gentleness the right register for this character, and how did your idea of what a ghost could be shift across the writing?

I only saw it as ‘ghost-less’ because I had moved to a place where I had no history. I grew up around Malaysian ghost stories that all felt very visceral and frightening. So when I moved to California, where the only ghost stories I knew about were fictitious monsters in Western movies, it kind of felt like a cleansing. Naturally, I started writing ghost stories of my own. I was interested in what people are like when they can’t be seen. Instead of exploring it through a violent, trapped rage, I wanted to write a story about a young girl navigating through a slow-moving grief. We live our lives surrounded by ghosts, so I wondered about a ghost observing the life around her.

The ghost’s gentleness stems from who she was when she was alive. She wouldn’t change just because of death. She is still as reserved as she was when she was alive. She has every reason to behave recklessly, but she still keeps to herself even though she cannot be seen or heard. At first, I thought it felt antithetical to what a stereotypical ghost would be like that she finds a silver lining in it. She’s hardly lived her life and has now been given the freedom to meander. She finds a new sense of openness being in a place where nobody knows her. It all feels limitless at first. But though she is now ‘immortal’, a certain fear of mortality strikes her. She treats this new state of being as fleeting, so the thought of it ending bites at her. She doesn’t think she can face the people she knows; she can’t even face herself.

In Malaysia, the scent of jasmine means the presence of something supernatural nearby. Strangely, I smelled jasmine constantly in the month we shot the film and I left LA.

Most Popular

Your ghost drifts into the lives of strangers and the ‘secret selves’ they reveal when they think no one is watching — a beach, a river walk, a playground, a phone call. How did you choose the situations she observes, and what made each one earn its place in her night?

Ophelia finds connection and eventually her own disconnection through these strangers. I chose the jetty because it looked like the end of the world. And I chose a phone call because I wanted Ophelia to feel as if she were the one on the other side of the phone call. Just like Ophelia, the man on the phone represses his feelings for a loved one so that they may move on without them. The sisters’ river walk represents Ophelia’s uncertainty. This scene is a long-drawn conversation filled with quiet pauses and looking back to the past, yet it wanders and goes nowhere. A young woman struggles to say goodbye to a place she loves, while her sister grapples with accepting a life she is no longer a part of. All of this resonates with Ophelia. The sisters also do their own bit of people-watching while Ophelia watches them.

The house is where Ophelia begins to feel detached. She doesn’t hear her mother’s voice there, unlike the others. There is a bit of sadness when she sees her mother still holding onto her, and there is nothing she can do about it. When the window shuts and the light goes off, she can’t quite reach into the warmth of her old bedroom. The bookstore is where Ophelia finds someone who reminds her of herself — someone who keeps to herself — and thinks they are sharing a private moment. Though she doesn’t fully grasp the meaning of the poem, she understands all of its emotions. The playground at night, where no one should be, is rooted in nostalgia. Ophelia seeks childlike comfort there until she is confronted by an unexpected presence. She recognises the man from the beach. Very briefly, she hopes that another lonely soul sees her, but it only makes her feel further hidden.

Strangely, a year after we shot the film, I was walking in London just ahead of someone on a phone call. He was reassuring his friend, who had just moved to LA, to stay and try it out — that everything would be okay. It was so vividly reminiscent of the phone call at the beginning of the film. I felt affirmed, and so comforted by it, even though I wasn’t the one on the other end of the line. Life imitates art; art imitates life; life imitates art.

You’ve spoken about wanting to embrace “natural observation with a supernatural funk”, a phrase that captures something really specific about the film’s register. Could you unpack what that means to you?

Daj and I were both drawn to the street photography of Nguan and Vivian Maier — that way of catching people completely inside their own worlds. The idea was to embrace that same natural observation, but with a supernatural funk. I wanted to maintain a naturalistic approach in capturing these vignettes of everyday life, like we’ve been dropped right into these spaces the way Ophelia has. Since the approach was so rooted in naturalism, I tried to dig into Ophelia’s funk in a slightly abstract way rather than leaning into special effects. I say ‘supernatural funk’ because I wanted her perspective to feel omniscient, like a bird gliding over a scene. I also wanted to convey her lingering presence. Ophelia is always roaming, watching a little too long. There’s a degree of pretence with the strangers. While I wanted them playing out realistically, I also wanted a bit of it to look staged for Ophelia because all she can do is watch. Ophelia is portrayed as quite ordinary, but her presence feels transcendent. It needed to be very clear that she is completely separated from the people around her, even when they inhabit the same frame.

Since the approach was so rooted in naturalism, I tried to dig into Ophelia’s funk in a slightly abstract way rather than leaning into special effects.

There are several interlude shots in the film. Each act is separated by a series of insert shots that depict a funeral altar. White chrysanthemums, oranges, the burning of joss paper. Ophelia’s mother (and Ophelia herself) mourns for her. There are also several shots of the sea. I used the ocean as a symbol for the vast unknown to represent Ophelia’s temptation and fear of the unknown. I also inserted little nods to the classic sheet-ghost image with students clad in all-white uniforms and a picnic cloth thrown over Ophelia. We shot in available light on location. I really loved seeing the wind in each exterior scene. I thought it gave such a magical quality. Along with that, the colour palette is filled with vivid blue and greens of post-rain LA permeating grey concrete structures to portray a melancholic view of Southern California.

It’s never thrown in the audience’s face that this is a ghost story; it surfaces through small tells, and eventually through hearing Ophelia’s distorted voice. How did you calibrate when to give the audience a foothold and when to leave them gliding?

I wanted to open scenes from the ghost’s point of view, and then give the audience a foothold on her otherworldliness when Ophelia begins to feel unsettled. There is a slow build-up that reveals an unsettling quality about her. We see eyes that should meet and connect, but they don’t. When she desires closeness, we see her suddenly teleported, but still unacknowledged. Then, when enough desperation creeps at her, we hear her voice. Though Ophelia feels that she may be a part of their worlds for a moment, they are still separated. I also wanted to shift perspective from hers to the audience’s. She is no longer just observing, but finds herself empathising.

The film tracks an arc from aimless drift toward something like acceptance, without ever announcing itself. How did you plot that emotional shape on the page, and were there beats whose meaning shifted between script and edit?

I approached the film by asking the question, “How do you say goodbye?” For Ophelia, she says goodbye by avoiding it, so I plotted the story around where she goes when she tries to evade her old life. She has nowhere to be, but everywhere to go. Her reality blurs to protect herself from the anxieties of moving on. At the first sign of nostalgia, she returns home, where she sees her old bedroom completely unchanged and still taken care of. It renders her motionless. She even misses her mother’s nagging. She knows her mother can’t hear her, and she doesn’t feel ready to give up her newfound independence, but the longer she stays away, the harder it is to go back.

Ophelia begins to feel burdened and finds more fragments that remind her of her old life. She attempts to start reaching out, but it only makes her feel more disconnected. These encounters weigh on her more and more, and eventually culminate in a sense of loneliness and stagnancy, particularly when she sees the reunion between two loved ones at the playground. It seems as if all of these people have come to haunt her. She finally comes to the realisation that her vices carry on with her no matter where she goes. Before Ophelia goes back to her mother, there is a roaming shot of an empty street. This is where she lets go. All she needed was a very long, still moment to relinquish everything she was holding on to. Her mother finds some lightness too.

The edit stayed close to the script, just tighter. We dropped some shots that leaned conceptual and very stylistic. These successfully emphasised Ophelia’s loneliness, but felt out of place in the big picture of the film. We did lose one character: a very cute cat. In the scene of the bedroom window, we cut a moment where her cat doesn’t see her. It disrupted the emotional beat of the scene, so Aleia Jacobs (my editor) and I chose to embrace the connection purely between her and her mother instead. But we thank Poof the cat for her stellar acting abilities.

You and Dajiana Huang shot on an ARRI SR3 with 1600 feet of Kodak 500T, one roll a day across four days, ten minutes of footage at a time. How did that constraint shape the way you went after the dreamlike reverie the film holds, and how much of it was waiting for the light versus chasing it?

Shooting on film, I knew I wanted to be quite minimal with the diversity of shots and instead emphasise the blocking, camera movement, and composition. I wanted to convey the emotional distance within a relationship in a single shot. We’d focus on one or two key shots per scene, where we would see these characters completely in the open from Ophelia’s perspective before shifting to a more subjective shot. In tighter frames, we composed layered shots of Ophelia and the strangers as she attempts to fit her life into theirs. We cut sparingly, so that each cut shows us that some sort of change has happened, whether it is a change in the strangers or in Ophelia. I knew I wanted minimal traditional coverage of scenes, and that, in turn, worked well with the limited rolls we had.

I wanted to convey the emotional distance within a relationship in a single shot.

I’d written most of the film to be set in the day (partly for thematic reasons; partly for convenience; partly because most of my California experiences always looked sunny). We shot in the summertime and had such a long window of high-angle sunlight. I wanted Ophelia’s world to feel like one very bright and endless landscape. When we see her out of the afternoon sun, it conveys a deeper yearning and melancholia within her. Those were the scenes where we only had brief windows of that beautiful golden and twilight hour. Because of these brief windows and the limited rolls of film, we rehearsed heavily, so it never felt like we were waiting for the light. Lots of props to scheduling (thank you to Claire Loudis, our AD, and Jess Stossel, our producer). The only shot where we were simultaneously waiting and chasing the light is the shot of shadows running past Ophelia while she sits against a wall. The clouds kept covering the sun!

I love your deception of the music becoming the ghost voice. What were those sessions like in developing this crucial side of it?

Ophelia hums a very simple, repeating five-note melody that Kallie Pong (who plays Ophelia) and I played with together. It feels like something a teenage girl would have stuck in her head, singing it as a way to fill time. Something like a bird song. It is also something that pulls her back to her old life. Yoki Ng, our composer, builds off of this hum so hauntingly. I wanted the music to echo Ophelia, like an extension of her voice attempting to reach out, but no one can hear it.

Yoki and I dived deeply into what Ophelia is feeling and how we might express those thoughts sonically. Longer notes would represent doubt; swelling layers of harmonisation to express conflicting thoughts or a mournful cry; heavier synth sounds that bring about alienation; pauses that feel like we are coming up for air. We’d share songs, poems, and essays that would explore Ophelia’s headspace. Some pivotal songs were Change by Big Thief, Class of 2013 by Mitski, and On the Sea by Beach House.

There is one specific moment when the piano comes in while the student reads her poem. Before the piano enters, there are empty spaces and pauses in the music, where we hear the movement of the characters and their environment: her footsteps, the touch of paper, a pencil tapping. The first section of the piece feels hesitant and like stumbled whispers, while Ophelia and the student keep themselves hidden. When the piano enters, the music creates an emotional push (almost filling in for their voices), and that contrast makes the silence feel more intimate. It almost feels as if they’ve started revealing themselves to each other.

What shorts have been catching you lately — ones you’d press into a friend’s hands?

Bi Gan’s A Short Story explores a vignette of different characters, seen through the eyes of a black cat. It is the much better expression of this short

glide is your first film after your thesis, made in the strange between-space of leaving the US and finding your way back to Malaysia, with your producer, DP and sound designer all scattering to different cities and countries after the wrap. Where does it sit in the bigger picture of what you’re building, and what’s the next thing pulling at you?

I feel very close to home now, and as I age into it, I find that the art I want to make is to preserve my home, and like glide, my memories of it. I want to make so many films here in Malaysia. These days, I’ve mainly been experimenting with animation. Everything lives in a very playful, childlike realm.

item.title: Defiant Black Trans Sisterhood Crashes Upscale Gentrification in Nana Duffuor’s Heist Short ‘Rainbow Girls’
item.dc:creator: Dianora Hollmann
item.description: As tech money prices them out of their own city, Nana Duffuor's trio of friends turn brazen luxury theft into an act of belonging, defiance and love.
item.content:encoded:
Inspired by the real-life Rainbow Girls—the name the media gave a loosely connected group of young women who staged a string of brazen thefts across San Francisco’s Union Square in the early 2010s—Nana Duffuor’s Rainbow Girls transforms a charged moment in Bay Area history into a vibrant heist story about sisterhood, identity, and belonging. Taking that as her catalyst and drawing on the traditions of the heist genre, Duffuor crafts a fictional narrative centred on three young Black trans women whose friendship and resilience play out against a backdrop of gentrification, displacement, and inequality. Rooted in her own experience living in the Bay Area during a period of rapid transformation, Duffuor explores the tensions between wealth, belonging, and the changing relationship communities have with the places they call home. Rainbow Girls already turned our heads when it landed among DN’s picks for our Best of Fest coverage of BFI Flare 2026. Now Duffuor joins us to discuss reimagining a half-remembered media legend as fiction, casting three Black trans women as her leads and building the fierce sisterhood at the film’s heart, and pulling off a window-smashing heist on the very first day of a student-budget shoot.

With such rich inspiration, how much did you want to ground the story in facts versus treating them as a catalyst for your own creative vision?

I wanted the real-life events to serve as the jumping-off point for a wholly imagined story. The name Rainbow Girls was coined by the media around 2013, and the truth is, there’s very little known about those who participated in the many thefts that took place across Union Square spanning several years. I’m careful to make the distinction that this is a story ‘inspired by true events’ rather than ‘based on a true story,’ as the characters and plot of my film are entirely fictional.

That said, when I learned of the real-life Rainbow Girls, I was immediately inspired by these groups of young women brazenly taking items associated with the type of wealth, privilege, and prestige that they are so often denied. That, plus the backdrop of the hypergentrification and displacement in the Bay Area, felt like an inevitable kind of underdog heist story that served as the catalyst for the film.

Audiences needed to see these women in their full humanity, understanding their motivations by stepping into the intimate spaces of their world.

At the core of the film is a powerful sense of sisterhood among this crew of young Black trans women pulling off these retail heists. How did you approach mixing these different cinematic temperatures, finding the right balance between their intimate and nuanced, identity-driven narratives and the humour and adrenaline of a heist movie?

Before writing, I knew I wanted the film to touch on the very real issues of displacement and fighting for survival in the place you call home. At the same time, I wanted audiences to be entertained and have fun while watching this film. I love telling stories that use levity as a way of getting to the heart of something substantive.

I took a lot of inspiration from the 1996 feature film, Set It Off, which is actually much more heart-wrenching. But a large part of what makes that film so spectacular is the bond we witness between its lead characters. As viewers, we are wholly invested in that friendship, and we are rooting for them the entire way. This was what I wanted for Tati, Angel, and Gemini—which meant that, similar to Set It Off, audiences needed to see these women in their full humanity, understanding their motivations by stepping into the intimate spaces of their world before going on the wild ride of the heist.

How did you approach building the three leads on the page, their individual energies, and the way they balance one another?

Tati, Angel, and Gemini are meant to fit together like pieces of a puzzle, balancing each other out. As the lead, I knew I wanted Tati to be a character unaware of her own power and agency, and for Gemini and Angel to be much more emboldened and unafraid to take up space in the world. I had a strong sense of Tati and Angel and their shared history from the beginning, but Gemini was the last character to come to fruition for me. I took inspiration from a friend of mine, someone who is incredibly endearing, has absolutely no filter, and who I see as fearless. In many ways, Tati and Gemini have opposite polarities, with Angel being the bridge between them.

Once we cast, the actors contributed significantly to bringing their dynamics to life. We sat together in rehearsal and revised the script to make the characters’ behaviour and dialogue feel as truthful and lived-in as we could.

Most Popular

You’ve mentioned experiencing some struggles to find Black trans women for the lead roles through initial casting calls, with Tati proving to be a major challenge. How did you envision the energy for that specific role, and what made Jai Stephenson the right fit for the character?

Jai had written, directed, and acted in a short called All My Niggas Surround Me and I’m Surrounded by All My Niggas, which had won the Jury Prize at Comfrey Film Festival in Durham, NC. My collaborator, Sowj Kudva, was wowed by their short and shared it with me. I was equally impressed, and I saw a quality in Jai’s performance that captured the kind of earnest yet rebellious quality needed for Tati. I immediately asked Jai if they’d audition for the role. When we did a chemistry test with Jai, Sis, and Céline as the leads, it was clear we’d found our Rainbow Girls.

The heist scene was shot on your very first day of production, navigating a tight budget and an untested stunt for this challenging sequence. How did you approach the shoot to translate your vision onto the screen under those constraints?

I initially wrote the scene as a kind of brawl between the Rainbow Girls and the security guard. Nava Mau read an early draft and was like, “What if they break the store window?” I loved the idea, but I was also like, “Girl. This is a student film. What do we look like?”

Nevertheless, I brought the idea to our production designer, Olivia Kanz, and our cinematographer, Evan Weidenkeller, to see if it was something we could pull off. They figured out how to do it using C-stands to prop up a smaller pane of glass, which we filmed from a side angle to give the appearance of the door breaking. We could only afford two panes of glass, so we just had to go for it on the day. It was the first shot up, and we were all holding our breath on set once cameras started rolling. I felt everyone on set breathe a collective sigh of relief when the stunt went exactly as we’d hoped. I wouldn’t advise anyone to put their most challenging scenes up front, but sometimes that’s the way the cookie crumbles.

We discussed how we could use the score and sound design to build moments of internality.

The music and sound design bring a distinct sense of drama and energy to Rainbow Girls, peaking during the heist. Can you guide us through the overall process of finalising the sound mix with Saman Khoujinian and Sowj Kudva, and how you tailored it for that specific sequence?

We finalized this sound mix in a recording studio in Durham, North Carolina (where Sowj and Saman are based). It was my first time in a sound studio, and we just had fun experimenting and trying things. Once we knew we’d use the track Fashion Killa for the heist scene, Sowj cut the scene to the music. We discussed how we could use the score and sound design to build moments of internality while Tati is searching for shoes for her mom by increasing the sound of her fumbling through the shoes and adding an effect that washes out the background noise.

Saman brilliantly took inspiration from that same Fashion Killa track to compose the score once the heist starts going awry, building suspense as Tati contemplates their escape, coalescing towards Tati throwing the mannequin arm through the window. The scene feels much different without that score and sound design.

Since you filmed in the Bay Area, how did you approach the location scouting process, both in terms of shops and streets, and what did it take in terms of set design to adapt the consignment store you found into the perfect backdrop for the heist scene?

My producer, Raman Nimmala, and I were both still in film school in New York while preparing to film Rainbow Girls in the Bay Area. We relied heavily on our co-producers, Nurie Mohamed and Jackson Gravagno, who are both filmmakers based in the Bay, as the boots on the ground. Given our tight budget, we tried to use as many practical locations as possible, while filming exteriors in public spaces across San Francisco’s Union Square, the Tenderloin, and West Oakland. This allowed us to save on cost while focusing on more intensive set design locations like the interior of the apartment where Angel and Gemini live.

We put together a list of potential retailers that could serve as the boutique where Tati works, and the backdrop for the heist scene. Finding Labels consignment store in Walnut Creek was like an answered prayer. First, the space already had an amazing layout for filming. Second, because it was a luxury consignment store, it already included the type of merchandise we needed as props. We held a blocking rehearsal the night before filming while the art department reorganized the space and brought in additional props to get everything production-ready. The store’s owner, Lynn Nice, was incredibly generous to our production, and her son ended up being a beloved PA on the shoot!

You are now officially developing Rainbow Girls into a feature film. Where are you currently at in that development process and what else is next for you?

I’m working with a trusted team of collaborators—folks I’ve collaborated with on Rainbow Girls and other past shorts—towards filming the feature in the Bay Area. Given the overwhelmingly positive response to the short, we know there is an audience that wants to see more, and we feel very passionate about delivering on the promise of the short. Right now we’re in the script development process and are looking to attach a producer. I’ve been fortunate to receive early support from SFFilm’s Rainin Screenwriting Grant to focus on feature screenplay development. The short was very much designed to leave audiences wanting more of the story and its characters. Now, I’m enjoying getting to expand on the lives of the Rainbow Girls, what happens after that first heist, and the dynamics between Tati and her mother.

There’s really no set path to how to build a career as a filmmaker, and as someone new to this industry, I’m learning as I go. Right now, my main focus is writing and developing the feature, and building a team that can bring this project to fruition. I also want to continue developing other stories, including a period piece that takes place in my family’s home of Ghana. It’s a coming-of-age story about a boy in Ghana in love with American soul music, inspired by the soul music concert that brought artists like Wilson Pickett, Carlos Santana, and Tina Turner to Ghana in 1971. All that to say, more stories to come!

Is there a short film that has stayed with you over time that you would recommend to the DN community?

Truthfully, I didn’t really watch short films until attending film school. Shorts represent such a unique and exciting format for filmmaking. Lonely Blue Night by Johnson Cheng was one of the first short films I was introduced to while at Columbia, and it was like a masterclass in what a short film can accomplish. It’s rich with family dynamics, interiority, and has a sense of humor and emotional weight that feels culturally specific. It’s clear the director trusts the intelligence and curiosity of the audience. I felt inspired about the possibilities of a short after watching that film.

item.title: Nathan Xia Interrogates Hollywood Representation and Personal Ego in Satirical Short ‘Flavor of the Month’
item.dc:creator: Rob Munday
item.description: What do you do when your values are at odds with your own ambitions? Nathan Xia turns that question into a squirming, darkly comic piece of self-scrutiny.
item.content:encoded:
Conducting interviews for Directors Notes, it’s easy to fall into the rhythm of asking the same questions over and over again. Anyone who’s attended a few filmmaker Q&As at festivals will probably know exactly what I mean. While a certain degree of laziness can undoubtedly creep in, it’s also true that there are simply some questions you instinctively want to ask. In the case of Nathan Xia’s Flavor of the Month – a sharp, darkly comic satire of representation politics in the film industry – it was immediately apparent that the story was rooted in lived experience and that was something I was eager to explore.

It was therefore difficult not to make one of my opening questions about the inspiration behind the film. When the answer begins with Xia revealing that he had “screen-tested to be the lead in a major Hollywood blockbuster film”, I think that instinct is more than justified. Yet Flavor of the Month is far more than the product of an extraordinary backstory. As our conversation unfolded, Xia spoke candidly about the challenge of simultaneously directing and starring in the film, developing its “hyperspecific visual vocabulary”, and why creating an atmosphere with the “freedom to play” was essential to both the performances and the filmmaking process.

Hi Nathan, welcome to Directors Notes. We’re really excited to talk to you about Flavor of the Month today. Before we dive into the specifics of the film, though, I wanted to talk a little about your filmmaking career. You’ve been incredibly prolific over the past eight years, directing 13 films in that time. What first made you want to become a filmmaker, and where does that drive to keep creating come from?

My ‘filmmaking career’ began in 6th grade when I discovered a passion for creating highly unserious YouTube videos to entertain my friends and make my peers laugh. Growing up, I had always felt like a bit of an outsider, but these videos helped me cultivate a sense of community and find my voice as a human being. With every project, my love for creating snowballed, and I quickly discovered a strong sense of purpose.

There is no lonelier feeling than feeling misunderstood, and to me, filmmaking was the antidote. Every film I have ever made was born out of a deeply impactful experience that required a vessel to help me process. Their creations have not only relinquished a part of my burdens, but also miraculously transformed the loneliest parts of myself into a way to connect with others.

For Asian American cinema to truly progress, we must set aside our egos.

Sticking with the idea of inspiration, I know Flavor of the Month has a pretty unusual real-world starting point. Can you take us back to that experience and explain how it evolved into the narrative of your film?

Flavor of the Month was loosely inspired by an experience I had screen-testing to be the lead in a major Hollywood blockbuster film. While the short pokes fun at the way modern-day Hollywood navigates Asian American representation, the core of the story ultimately stems from my own insecurities.

Most Popular

For years, I have spoken on panels, done Q&As at film festivals, and preached the importance of representation in the film industry. However, when I found myself competing against other Asian American actors for a life-changing opportunity, I noticed my attitude subtly shift to “fuck these other guys, I’m the best Asian.” Reflecting upon my own hypocrisy inspired a question – what do you do when your values are at odds with your own ambitions? I believe that for Asian American cinema to truly progress, we must set aside our egos and have the maturity to come together, even and especially when we have nothing to gain.

One of the things I love about the film is the balance it strikes between humour and topicality. It’s hugely entertaining, but it also leaves you with something important to think about once it ends. How did you work to get that balance right and what do you hope audiences take away from Flavor of the Month?

I never deliberately try to be funny when writing a film, but somehow, the brain-rotted, Gen-Z, child-of-the-internet always finds a way to trickle in during the production process. Inspired by the works of Joachim Trier, Abbas Kiarostami, and Richard Linklater, I spend the majority of my time in development, crafting a strong philosophical understanding of my themes.

My favorite kind of humor isn’t forced, but rather birthed organically from conflict.

Once I believe I have found a unique and nuanced perspective, I reward myself with the freedom to play, improvise, and fuck around on set — discovering the humanity in the absurd. My favorite kind of humor isn’t forced, but rather birthed organically from conflict. In my films, the drama inspires the comedy, and the comedy inspires the drama — forging a complex yet unique tone that leaves you unsure how exactly to feel, but feel a lot nonetheless.

Staying with that idea of balance, we see two very different sides of Harrison Huang throughout the film: the private moments in his car or staring into the restroom mirror, and the more performative version of himself on set or in interviews. Why was it important for you to present that duality?

I think it’s ironic that the best acting Harrison does in the film isn’t when he’s performing at the screen test, but rather when he’s virtue signaling during the press interview. Emphasizing the contrast between who Harrison is and who he feels he has to be helps the audience empathize with such a flawed character and creates accessibility for the themes I explore. It is the duality of Harrison Huang that forces us to look within and confront our own hypocrisies.

Speaking of Harrison, alongside directing the film, you also play the lead role. What made you decide to cast yourself and how did you balance the demands of directing while also performing?

Directing a film while simultaneously acting is no easy feat, but with the right team around you, it can actually be an advantage. On Flavor of the Month, most of my department heads were artists I have worked with for years on short films, music videos, and commercials, which established an innate shorthand and trust going into the project. That chemistry, paired with meticulous pre-production, allowed me to shift focus to my performance on set.

In the prep, my collaborators and I spent most of our time discussing the intent (rather than content) behind every creative decision. This opened up the floor for more inventive ideas and a smoother workflow in the production. I often joke to my department heads that if I were to die in a car accident on the way to set, they would be able to direct the film themselves. They don’t like that joke very much.

Sharing the stage with brilliant actors like Kevin Changaris, Jade Kaiser, Jack Wang, Dustin Hahn, and Iunia Dinu made life infinitely easier. I had been a fan of their individual work for a while now, so collaborating with this ensemble felt like a dream come true. With this group, it was very difficult not to break mid-take in any given scene, and I found myself laughing more than I have on any other set. Their natural ability and openness to improvisation led to many beautiful discoveries and lightning-in-a-bottle moments that made this film a stronger one.

Sometimes I’ll watch playback, but generally, you can tell when you’re “in it” or not.

When it comes to tracking my own performance, I often lean on my department heads – people who have a strong understanding of who I am as an artist and a human and, because of that, can call me out when I’m ‘bullshitting’. In this case, I had Nishanth Ramasubramanian, our script supervisor, and Jacob Staudenmaier, one of the assistant directors, to help me with this. Sometimes I’ll watch playback, but generally, you can tell when you’re “in it” or not.

To simultaneously act and direct requires setting aside your own ego and having relentless faith in your team. You don’t have to be the most brilliant person in the room, nor should you ever be. You just have to recognize who has the most brilliant idea. I believe that is how you make a truly exciting film that not only surprises your audience, but yourself as well.

Visually, the cinematography does a wonderful job of reinforcing that duality, shifting between Harrison’s private and public worlds. How did you work with cinematographer Ayinde Anderson to develop the film’s visual language?
